'Fernandes back to his best in training'

Sky Sports News' Danyal Khan at Carrington:

"Bruno Fernandes is absolutely back in contention. From what I understand and what I've been told from sources around Manchester United, Bruno Fernandes has been back to his best in the last 48 hours.

"Now, what does that mean, and how has that come around?

"It was quite out of character, you have to say, for him to come out last week, airing a lot of frustrations after the Como defeat.

"I would also assume that the reaction or lack of by the fans towards him on Sunday, when he's warming up, no shouts of Bruno from around Old Trafford, and then the boos, not just Fernandes, but also the players faced after Michael Carrick had gone down the tunnel.

"What I've been told, Bruno Fernandes has come back to Carrington since Monday. He was here on Monday to receive treatment to maintain his fitness, but since then all has seemingly been back to normal, and that is the message we have received at Manchester United, it is business as usual for everyone involved.

"I imagine he'll have a much bigger part than he did on Sunday against Bournemouth, and he is absolutely back in contention to play for Michael Carrick's side on Saturday."

Neville: Fernandes let himself down - read the room Bruno!

Following the defeat to Bournemouth, Sky Sports' Gary Neville said Fernandes had let himself down.

"Eric Cantona was very unorthodox as a captain," he said. "Roy Keane could sometimes be explosive in his interviews after matches, but they weren't whingers about the tactics, about pressing, or excuse merchants.

"Bruno can't press. To come out and whinge after the game about the manager's tactics, when you've just lost 4-1, and a few thousand fans have paid thousands of pounds to travel over in that far corner and get wet through. I'm sorry, read the room, Bruno.

"This is not a time for whinging, throwing your arms up in the air. This is a time for you to stand up and say, that's not good enough. Be positive. Do something with a positive influence as a captain. But he's not.

"He's gone and basically thrown his manager under the bus the week after [Lisandro] Martinez did the same."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Gary Neville believes Fernandes 'let himself down' with his comments following Manchester United's 4-1 Champions League loss at Como

Neville added: "They weren't singing for Bruno Fernandes to come on today, they're backing Michael Carrick. So get in your box. You know where you stand.

"Michael Carrick's won things for the football club on a constant basis, and proven that he can have the humility, the resilience. And Bruno has got that. Bruno has delivered for Manchester United in more ways than any other player in the last 13 years.

"And he's the one player I think you could take back in time, and I think he could play in a Manchester United team in the 90s, in the 2000s because he's massively talented. But he let himself down this week.

"He didn't need to do that, because he's basically stuck the knife into his manager."

What did Fernandes say after Como defeat?

"It's a decision from the staff to not press man to man and sometimes leave a little space in behind and try to get the ball in the first moment, to wait for them, to give them the ball," said Fernandes.

"But sometimes when you give too much the ball to these teams they get confident, they have so many bodies behind the ball that make you run a lot, make people get frustrated, and then obviously when you recover the ball the legs are, and the brain, much more difficult to make it work."

Asked if the tactics were to blame for the defeat, Fernandes replied: "That's on the manager and on the staff to see it, it's not on me.

"I just said, I think sometimes we have to be more brave on the pressure, trying to take a risk of getting that press very high and making them uncomfortable - as they did to us."

Sky Sports News reported on October 22 that Fernandes would not be stripped of the captaincy for his comments, but at his pre-Bournemouth press conference the following day, Carrick refused to rule out disciplinary measures against Fernandes.

"The most important thing for me is the team and the dynamics in the squad. It is about the football club. Whatever the situation is, I will always do what is best for the football club," he said.

"If I've spoken to him or haven't... this isn't the time to go into details."

Fernandes was the second United player to publicly criticise the club in October after Lisandro Martinez's comments following the Champions League defeat at Atletico Madrid.

Martinez said: "I expect more from our technical director [director of football, Jason Wilcox]. We expect more from the top, from upstairs, to bring in more players to compete."

Martinez was not dropped for United's following game, playing 45 minutes of the 1-1 draw at Leeds - but was also benched for the visit of Bournemouth.

Sports.title: Serrano to have final fight against Falzon with three-minute rounds
Sports.content:
Amanda Serrano will fight one last time when she takes on Skye Falzon in Puerto Rico on January 9.

Serrano will defend her unified WBO and WBA featherweight world titles at the Coliseo de Puerto Rico in San Juan against Australian contender Falzon, 12-2 (7), over 12 three-minute rounds, under equal championship rules to men.

Not only that, she will be seeking to break the all-time women's knockout record.

Serrano is a Guinness World Record holder for winning world titles across seven weight divisions and the first and only Puerto Rican boxer, male or female, to become undisputed world champion.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Highlights of the fight between Serrano and Lucrecia Manzur (Credit: MVP)

Serrano made history alongside Katie Taylor in the first women's boxing match to headline Madison Square Garden in 2022 and then their historic rivalry continued with a rematch in 2024 followed by a trilogy fight that headlined an all-women's card at Madison Square Garden in 2025.

She also made history in 2023 by competing in the first women's unified world championship bout over 12 three-minute rounds, later voluntarily vacating her WBC title rather than abandon her commitment to competing under equal rules to male champions.

Serrano said: "Boxing has been my life and I never could have imagined the journey it would take me and my family on.

"From the early days when women's boxing was fighting for recognition in small theatre shows, to headlining Madison Square Garden in New York, reaching millions of fans around the world on the biggest shows, and helping open doors for the next generation of female fighters, Jordan [Maldonado, Serrano's manager and trainer] and I always believed and I'm proud of everything we've accomplished. But none of it happened alone.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Serrano showed she had too much power and aggression for Cheyenne Hanson as she forced a stoppage in the second round and equalled the most knockouts in women's boxing history

"Nakisa [Bidarian], Jake [Paul] and MVP believed in me and in women's boxing, and together we've helped change what's possible for women in this sport.

"We've fought for respect, equal opportunities, fair pay, and the choice to compete under the same rules as men. There's still more work to do, and I'll continue fighting for the next generation long after I hang up my gloves.

"To close my career at home in Puerto Rico, in front of the people who have supported me from the beginning, means everything."

Nakisa Bidarian and Jake Paul, founders of Most Valuable Promotions, added: "Amanda Serrano is the MOAT. The Most Of All Time. The most accomplished female boxer of all time, the most watched, the most paid, and one of the most influential athletes this sport has ever seen.

"When Amanda became MVP's first signee, we made a commitment to build a platform where the greatest female fighters in the world could receive the recognition, compensation and opportunities they deserve.

"Amanda has been the foundation of that vision, and her success has helped change the entire landscape of women's boxing."

Sports.title: Vickery's bodybuilding transformation amid life-changing diagnosis
Sports.content:
Phil Vickery, a World Cup winner with the England rugby union team, has unexpectedly reinvented himself as a bodybuilder; the 50-year-old discusses that transformation and his diagnosis of probable chronic traumatic encephalopathy

From World Cup winner with England to bodybuilder, Phil Vickery is embracing his new career and opens up on how it has helped with his diagnosis of probable chronic traumatic encephalopathy

In an interview with Sky Sports News' Gail Davis, former England international Phil Vickery discusses his bodybuilding transformation and living with his diagnosis of probable chronic traumatic encephalopathy (CTE), a brain condition associated with repeated head impacts...

The picture was nothing short of astonishing. At first glance I joked it must be AI, but behind that moment on stage in Hull and beyond the bodybuilding poses and two tons of fake tan is something far more eye catching.

Phil Vickery has rebuilt his body, but he has rebuilt his mind too. Along the way he has found something to help fill a little of the void left behind after retirement from rugby in friendship, community, a sense of belonging and - perhaps most importantly - the feeling of being valued.

All of which matter immensely as he faces an uncertain future.

The hour or so I spend with the 50-year-old former England captain is one of extreme emotions, from laughing about his chosen shade of mahogany and his inability to get the most out of his glutes on camera, to the sadness and frustration when he talks about struggling to remember simple things.

He is searingly honest. There's no bravado, no hiding the difficult moments, just a determination to show up and live his best life.

Which right now looks very different to a few years ago. "I'm not really a bodybuilder. You know, I'm the wrong size," jokes Vickery.

Image: Former England rugby union international Vickery is now a competitive bodybuilder

"I've got long levers. I've got a massive rib cage. It began six or seven years ago when I was struggling. I was in just a really bad spot. I just looked at myself, and I thought, well, look at the state of you. Do something about it."

Vickery's life changed when he stepped into the Wolfpack gym in Gloucester and the hard work began.

He goes on: "I just loved just being in that environment again."

His coach Chris Bradley guided him through the good and bad days of training. After Vickery's initial and dramatic transformation he suggested he should enter a bodybuilding competition.

Vickery's first response was emphatic. "Mate, no way. There's no way I am getting on a stage."

Deep down, though, the competitive streak is still there. After Bradley accused him of lacking courage his response was: "Right, let's do this."

As a player Vickery never shied away from a challenge. 'The Raging Bull' - as he was affectionately known - wasn't going to start now. The idea of being on stage and performing excited him and then the reality hit.

"You are backstage, the nerves are so bad. It reminded me so much of the changing room. Am I going to be sick? Am I good enough?

"Then there's the posing, left shoulder down, right arm across. Keep that tight. I've lost my glutes, my hamstring's not engaged..."

Image: Vickery has undergone a physical transformation

At this point I had to do a reality check. This was, after all, a man who spent years being battered at the highest level of Test rugby and he was now worrying about the appearance of his backside. It was an unlikely new challenge.

He adds: "The thing is, you want to show off all that work and my glutes are the worst, and they were so much better than it showed on pictures."

Maybe the glutes will come but what Vickery has gained is far more precious. "You cannot replace that feeling of being in that changing room and wearing that jersey." But maybe the gym is that place where he can be... "appreciated?" I ask. "Yeah, and just valued."

It is also a way of taking some control, I suggest. Vickery has spoken about his cognitive difficulties and his diagnosis of probable chronic traumatic encephalopathy (CTE), a brain condition associated with repeated head impacts.

For him, the effects can be felt in everyday moments that other people might take for granted. He admits he used to become angry when he could not remember something simple. Now he is trying to respond differently.

He makes himself laugh as a way of coping, rather than allowing the frustration to take over. It does not mean the worry has disappeared.

"Of course, it worries me," he admits. His response has been to concentrate on what he can do. He believes in the body's ability to heal and is exploring ways to support his health. He was off for baseline brain testing that afternoon and is using oxygen treatment.

"I take comfort from knowing that I'm doing everything I can to be the best I can and to go as long as possible, and to try and be that positive aspect of it."

Image: Vickery and Sky Sports News reporter Gail Davis

There's a similar determination in Vickery's commitment to the legal action involving former players and rugby's governing bodies which has a new legal team behind it.

Former players have claimed long-term consequences of repeated concussive impacts has lead to conditions like early onset dementia and CTE and that the governing bodies failed in their duty of care to protect players from the risks of brain injury.

The governing bodies, which include World Rugby and the RFU, have consistently denied any breach of duty of care and have argued that the risks were part of the sport.

"Things are moving along," he says. "It is not at the forefront of my life. I'm there to support everybody who's on it. I am 100 per cent committed to it."

Vickery makes it clear he still loves the game and there is no real bitterness.

"We did what we did. If we knew then what we know now, we wouldn't have done it because we know the risks. But that was just what happened, and that's what you did," he added.

Image: Vickery had a stellar rugby career at international level

"People ask me, would you do it all again? Yeah, 100 per cent I would. My only gripe is: look after me when I get too poorly. I don't think that's unreasonable."

For him it's not simply about winning or losing. "People talk about money. It doesn't change my diagnosis. What it does do if we were to win, it allows you then to be able to plan for people to be able to look after me," he said.

"It gives comfort in that sense. I want it to go to trial and for people's voices to be heard. There are some just dreadful stories of people suffering, which need to be aired.

"Staying silent and not saying anything is not a defence against brain injury because I'm telling you, there's a lot of suffering out there and we need to take some responsibility."

For all the physical changes it is Vickery's warmth and humanity that leaves the strongest impression. Alongside his determination to make every day count.

Sports.title: Anderson set to continue playing career in Italy
Sports.content:
James Anderson is set to continue his playing career in Italy.

He will captain and co-own the Napoli ‌Knights, one of six teams in the Italia T10 league as the 44-year-old extends his career after being released by Lancashire, his club of 25 years.

Anderson, who played more than 400 times for England across all formats and took nearly 1,000 wickets, is a big name to join the format.

The Italia T10 league is a 10-over-a-side ​competition, which takes place over 12 days at the Roma Cricket Ground from November 18.

It was created by Nadeem Shahid, a former professional cricketer, and Aamir Akhtar, who helped set up the Everest ​Premier League in his native Nepal.

High-profile players such as Chris Gayle, Shaun Marsh and Dawid Malan ‌will also feature, joined by members of the Italian national side who impressed earlier this year when they narrowly lost to England at the T20 World Cup.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player We take a look back at some of Anderson's best moments for England including the moment he reached the landmark of taking 700 wickets for his country

"The potential for cricket in ⁠Italy made it a big draw," Shahid told Reuters. "One of the things ‌that made it attractive is the Italian Olympic Committee beginning to take it seriously after it became an Olympic sport."

He noted: "Tickets will be free for all the matches, and there will be coaching clinics on the sidelines."

Anderson's company, Activate Sport & Leisure, will be involved in ‌some of those clinics, as Italy looks to develop homegrown talent capable of competing at Olympic level by the time of the 2032 Games in Brisbane.

"Of course, we want Napoli Knights to be competitive and challenge for the title, but we also want to contribute to something that continues to grow well beyond the tournament itself," Anderson said.

Sports.title: Fernandes tells Carrick he is committed to turning season around in clear-the-air talks
Sports.content:
Michael Carrick and Bruno Fernandes held clear-the-air talks on Tuesday after the Manchester United captain criticised the manager’s tactics last week, with him now expected to start at Chelsea on Saturday.

Carrick and Fernandes met before training on Tuesday morning at United’s Carrington training base. The 32-year-old, it is understood, offered the manager assurances that he is fully committed and intent on trying to turn the team’s season around. There was also a squad meeting with Carrick at which the rest of the players made the same vow.

Dismal results have left Carrick’s job in the balance. Later on Tuesday it emerged that the 45-year-old will remain in charge for the trip to Chelsea after Jason Wilcox, the director of football, decided he should be given more time.

But to remain as the head coach for the long-term, Carrick has to start winning games. So having dropped Fernandes, who is considered United’s best player, for Sunday’s 3-0 home defeat by Bournemouth due to the criticism, him now being available for Chelsea is a considerable boost.

After last Wednesday’s 4-1 loss at Como, Fernandes questioned the team’s strategy. “It’s a decision from the staff to not press man-to-man,” he said. As Carrick decides tactics this was seen as a direct attack on the manager.

On Wednesday morning Kobbie Mainoo was back in training after missing the last four games due to injury.

Carrick’s side have won twice in 12 games and were eliminated from the Carabao Cup by Brighton. United are 16th in the Premier League, a point above the relegation zone.

United host Roma in the Champions League three days after playing Chelsea, then Aston Villa in the league the following Sunday before a two-week international window, which would offer a longer period for the board to assess the situation.

Carrick’s reprieve may be a move to allow time for Wilcox to secure a replacement should the decision be taken to sack him. The director of football’s prime candidate is Eddie Howe, the former Newcastle manager, while Christopher Vivell, the head of recruitment, favours the former Germany head coach Julian Nagelsmann.

Sports.title: Max Dowman’s Fleetwood fracas leaves him, Arsenal and Arteta red-faced
Sports.content:
Mikel Arteta’s reaction said it all. As Max Dowman trudged towards the touchline after becoming the youngest player sent off in a League Cup match at 16 years and 300 days, the Arsenal manager could not help himself.

Arms folded across his chest like an angry father who has caught his teenage son sneaking in after midnight, Arteta leaned over and aimed a few choice words in Dowman’s direction before the forward headed sheepishly down the tunnel. What he said remains unknown, although that hasn’t stopped the amateur lip-readers speculating on social media. “Get in the changing room. Now,” appears the most likely guess.

There is no doubt Arteta had made up his mind about the incident that ended with Dowman seeing red for reacting to an overly aggressive sliding tackle from Fleetwood’s Harrison Neal. Although Arsenal intend to appeal and Arteta told Sky after the shock penalty shootout defeat by the League Two side 84 places below them in the pyramid that he wanted to watch it again before “assessing the situation”, the Spaniard made no excuses for Dowman in his post-match press conference.

“It was something that we discussed before the game,” he said when asked about their touchline exchange. “We knew when we prepared the context of the match, we were very clear on the things to expect, the things that emotionally we have to dominate.”

Whether Dowman’s reaction warranted a straight red card remains open to debate given there was minimal force when he lifted his right knee towards Neal. The referee, Michael Salisbury, could easily have decided to give both players a yellow and defused the situation, especially given Cole Palmer was booked for barging into Tottenham’s Matheus Fernandes off the ball on Saturday in what seemed a far more aggressive act. But, as Wayne Rooney and David Beckham infamously found to their cost while playing for England at the World Cup, acts of petulance are not usually tolerated by officials. Dowman was deemed to have overstepped the line.

It is a pressure Arteta has warned the record-breaking teenager would have to deal with as Dowman’s reputation has grown. Only last month Dowman was sent off playing for England’s under-19s against the USA after a poorly timed tackle that most present at the behind-closed-doors match deemed a harsh decision. He is said to have been on the receiving end of a host of strong challenges in that match. Last year, Arteta urged Dowman to follow the example of Bukayo Saka after revealing Dowman was fouled nine times in a the first half of an England under-19s game against Spain.

View image in fullscreen Max Dowman is the centre of attention for Fleetwood’s players after the teenager’s reaction to a tackle from Harrison Neal. Photograph: Ryan Browne/Shutterstock

“It’s going to happen, he’s going to have to learn when to release the ball and when to attract his starting position,” Arteta said. “Very similar to Bukayo in the beginning as well. Those players are going to attract players, contact, attention and they have to be very smart about when you want that contact and when you don’t want it, and what you have to do to avoid it.”

Asked how Dowman tends to react, he said: “He just gets up … very rare! Sometimes I get surprised emotionally how cool he can be. I think it’s about repetition. He’s so used to it that now he knows to let the referee deal with it and my teammates probably to defend me, and I will carry on playing.”

When the dust settles after a seismic defeat that ranks alongside Arsenal’s League Cup upsets against Swindon, Birmingham and Bradford, Arteta may come to regret such a public admonishment of a 16-year-old. His actions were criticised by Paul Merson, who questioned whether Areta would “do it differently” given another chance. But part of Arteta’s frustration will be that Dowman took the bait. He also knows opponents will now target Dowman even more to see whether they can provoke a reaction.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

If Arsenal’s appeal fails, Dowman’s immediate punishment will be a three-match domestic suspension, causing him to miss Sunday’s trip to Liverpool and games against Hull and Newcastle. The timing is far from helpful: Saka’s thigh injury, expected to keep him out for several weeks, had opened up the possibility of more game time in the Premier League, and Noni Madueke did not travel to Fleetwood owing to an ankle issue.

Dowman burst on to the scene last year by becoming the first 15-year-old to play in the Champions League, then broke the Premier League’s youngest goalscorer record against Everton in March, and this is the first major setback in his fledgling career.

He has been training with the first team since he was 14 and Arsenal have been extremely careful not to overexpose one of the most talked-about players to emerge from their Hale End academy. Arteta resisted the temptation to give him many more minutes in the Premier League after Dowman scored twice against Ipswich in the previous round of the Carabao Cup last month. The challenge will be how Dowman responds to the extra scrutiny – on and off the pitch – that is bound to come his way.

Sports.title: Lise Klaveness: ‘Certainly there are people that can challenge Infantino’
Sports.content:
As the rain whips around Oslo’s government quarter, Lise Klaveness is shielding herself from the wind, trying to work out tactics. “Of course we cannot probably do everything alone, but we have a voice, we have the right to speak, we have the right to suggest, so let’s see,” she says. “We will at least try to be a spearhead.”

The president of the Norwegian Football Federation wants to re-engage Fifa, and other governing bodies, on the topic of remedy. A slightly arcane aspect of human rights policy in normal times, the importance of remedy became very clear in the aftermath of the World Cup in Qatar, when the families of those injured or killed in the work that led up to the tournament were left without financial compensation after Fifa chose to direct a legacy fund elsewhere.

At Klaveness’s prompting, Fifa conducted a review into the process. The report ultimately found the organisation did have a responsibility to provide remedy, but Fifa chose not to redirect the money. Klaveness wants to focus minds on the topic once again and make sure new practices are in place for Euro 2028, co-hosted by England, Scotland, Wales and the Republic of Ireland, as well as the World Cup of 2034 in Saudi Arabia where labour movement sources suggest there is currently little to no external scrutiny on worker’s conditions.

She is doing so at a delicate juncture. While Gianni Infantino has assured those listening that the “vast, vast majority” of Fifa’s electorate will back his re-election as president next year, many within the game regard this as an opportunity for change. Klaveness is one of them, having been a thorn in Infantino’s side since she first raised the topic of remedy on the floor of the Fifa congress in 2022 and having called for him to resign this summer after the scandals of the Balogun red card and the Fifa Forward Enterprise fiasco.

The 45-year-old Klaveness has been touted as a possible candidate in the Fifa presidential election, earning a perhaps less than desirable endorsement from Sepp Blatter. The disgraced former president said Klaveness “deserved the utmost respect” and that “the time has come for a woman to take over the leadership”. Klaveness responded by recalling that Blatter “wanted us to play with shorter shorts”. Her position on a run for president today is to almost, if not entirely, rule it out.

View image in fullscreen Lise Klaveness prefers a collaborative approach to achieving solutions, rather than deals struck behind closed doors. Photograph: Stian Lysberg Solum/NTB/Alamy

“My name has come up a few times and I take it as a sign that [people are concerned] about governance because we have been very outspoken about governance,” she says. “We’ve had a role internationally that is not the most efficient way to get votes. I think we’ve been very outspoken so this time around I don’t think that would be a possibility for me and it’s not been a real subject for me either.”

Not quite a no, then, but whether she runs or not Klaveness is a consistent champion for reform. She believes there are other candidates out there who could challenge Infantino and deliver change. She says it is crucial that any such individual is persuaded to stand before the deadline for nominations on 18 November. “It’s really important to have a candidate and one who can win,” she says. “We will welcome any candidate, but just putting up somebody who will lose is …” She shrugs. “I think it’s important to now discuss who can have a platform to win.

View image in fullscreen Klaveness has been a thorn in Gianni Infantino’s side since she first raised the topic of remedy on the floor of the Fifa congress in 2022. Photograph: MB Media/Getty Images

“There has been distrust, and not just in Europe, many other places than Europe,” she says of the challenge to Infantino. “Of course, it’s become very political, that’s why I refer to it as the Game of Thrones. Candidates need to have a base in different confederations. We don’t know how challenged Infantino can be until there’s a counter-candidate like that. But certainly there are people that can challenge him.”

On this day at least Klaveness is reluctant to make too many pugnacious remarks about Infantino or Fifa. “People ask me all the time about Infantino, but it’s not about him,” she says. “For me it’s about the governance going forward. He was elected on a platform of reform, which we really believed in, but it was not really implemented and that disappointed us.”

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

Klaveness says she wants any reforms around remedy to apply to all organisers and competitions. She talks about building alliances to back proposals that would ensure funds are set aside for remedy before a tournament takes place and that mechanisms are established for how any money should be distributed. She wants to submit such proposals at the next Fifa congress. “It should also be in Uefa and other places but let’s start with Fifa, let’s start at the top, and now that governance is on everybody’s lips let’s make this part of the suggestions we will make to the congress, together or alone.”

View image in fullscreen Klaveness (fourth row, second left) joined Norway men’s football team in a viking row on their homecoming in Oslo after their successful 2026 World Cup. Photograph: Trond R Teigen/EPA

A collaborative approach to achieving solutions, rather than deals struck behind closed doors, is Klaveness’s preferred way and on Tuesday the former midfielder, with 73 Norway caps, made her case on remedy to a gathering of politicians commemorating the 50th anniversary of the OECD’s guidelines for ‘responsible business conduct’. No longer the lone voice speaking out on the conference floor, Klaveness has allies and a growing number of people who – at least in private – would claim to share her values. That she also presides over two successful national sides doesn’t hurt.

Norway’s women’ face a playoff against Wales to qualify for next year’s World Cup. The men, meanwhile, won hearts and matches in the US this year. Klaveness recalls with some bemusement the World Cup experience. “I was on the road for seven weeks with 65 men,” she says. “I also saw Erling Haaland with a dead raccoon. Football is a lot of things, a sport, a competition, a cultural phenomenon. It’s also a social tool, but if we want the game to be for everyone there is going to be conflict.” It won’t be too long before that conflict resumes.

Sports.title: West Ham’s Viviane Asseyi: ‘When I was four I said I wanted to be like Zidane’
Sports.content:
On Saturday, once West Ham’s Viviane Asseyi was home from the match, she picked up her phone and called her mum. It has become almost ritualistic for them to speak after a game.

On the other end came a familiar sound. “She was just laughing,” says Asseyi. “She was like: ‘Oh, you were so bad!’ She was laughing but that helped me. She knows that she can tell me anything and everything, I’m good, I’m not good. I will just keep going and working to be better.”

When Asseyi had called, she was annoyed. West Ham had lost 3-0 at Brighton and, despite the home team dominating possession, the Hammers were far closer to their opponents in terms of shots, shots on target and touches in the opposition box than the score suggested. “I’m someone who really lives the game,” the forward says.

The collective laughter of her family has been a constant. Asseyi was born in France to Gabonese parents and spent her childhood with Gabonese culture around her. Her parents were so determined she have a relationship with her African heritage that everyone ate together on Sundays and the food, music and things happening in the country were always around.

She was four when she asked her mum to buy her a football. “It all started with the World Cup in 1998,” she says. “I watched the French winning against Brazil and after the game I said to my mum: ‘Buy me a football. I want to play football. I want to be like [Zinedine] Zidane.’

“We are a family who laugh at each other a lot. In the beginning there was a lot of laughing because I was really skinny and they were like: ‘How will you play? People are so much stronger than you!’ They were just laughing because that is the mood of the family, but they were really directly behind me.”

View image in fullscreen Asseyi scores during West Ham’s 2-1 win over London City Lionesses last month. Photograph: Action Foto Sport/Alamy Stock Photo/Alamy Live News.

Asseyi embraced the laughter then, as she does now, but the tiny, skinny child was deadly serious. “First my mum bought me one of the fake balls, the cheap light plastic ones,” she says. “She saw it and thought I wouldn’t know the difference but I was like: ‘No no no, I want the same ball as Zidane.’”

Her family embraced it, but her teachers didn’t.

“You know when you are at school and you have to say what you want to be when you grow up? I always said I wanted to be a professional footballer, that I wanted to be like Zidane. The teacher was like: ‘Is she OK?’ Women’s football wasn’t visible then, so all the teachers thought that I was crazy, but my friends understood, because they all played football. Every day I would just go to school and play with them.”

Her mum put her in clubs in Normandy, where she grew up. Eventually, the journey took her to the home of French football, when she earned a place at the national football centre in Clairefontaine. When the letter arrived confirming she had a place, it was “a dream”.

“I wanted to do the same as Zidane and, for me, Clairefontaine was the national team. It’s the best place you can be when you are young. [Kylian] Mbappé went there, so many players come through there.

“You go through some tests beforehand and from across the whole of France you are one of, like, 13 to 15 who get in. So, it’s a really big opportunity. I read the letter and my mum, all my family, were just crying around me. I was the only one who wasn’t, because I was so focused on the football and my dream and having the opportunity to live my dream every day.”

View image in fullscreen A young Asseyi tries an acrobatic shot while training with France at Clairefontaine in 2015. Photograph: Franck Fife/AFP/Getty Images

At Clairefontaine, boys and girls are treated the same. They are in school together and eat together. Asseyi became friends there with the goalkeeper Alphonse Areola, who is now also at West Ham. “We were in the same class,” she says. “Outside of that, we were friends, all the time together, chilling.” Raphaël Guerreiro, who has gone on to play for Portugal, was also a friend and part of her cohort. “At school his favourite player was Cristiano Ronaldo and he went on to win the Euros with him, which was crazy.”

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Weekly Sign up to Moving the Goalposts No topic is too small or too big for us to cover as we deliver a twice-weekly roundup of the wonderful world of women’s football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

Life away from her family, seeing them only at weekends, helped prepare her for the nomadic life of a footballer. Asseyi spent time with Rouen, Montpellier, Marseille and Bordeaux before having two years in Germany with Bayern Munich. She swapped Bavaria for London in 2022 and is in her fifth season with West Ham.

She has played 117 times for the club and will probably break Kate Longhurst’s WSL era record of 130 West Ham appearances. Asseyi instantly sensed she had found a second family there.

“When you feel valued by everyone, when there is mutual respect everywhere, you will always feel good and want to give everything,” she says.

View image in fullscreen Viviane Asseyi’s mum, Sidonie, is her biggest fan, and also one of her biggest critics! Photograph: Catherine Steenkeste/Getty Images

As one of the more experienced players and vice-captain, 32-year-old Asseyi is part of setting the culture and standards. “It’s an easy job when you have a team like this because everyone comes here with a smile,” she says. “We lose games sometimes, but everyone just comes back here ready to give everyone everything”

West Ham have two wins from their opening seven games. Asseyi says consistency is missing and is sure results will improve. “It’s sometimes mental and it’s sometimes about the small details,” she says.

Asseyi relishes her role as a visible Black female footballer. When she was growing up, the tennis champion Serena Williams was her idol. “I didn’t previously understand or recognise how much we can inspire people,” Asseyi says. “But the more and more I see, and the more people reach out on social media and in other ways, telling me that I inspired them and thanking me for everything, the more I see what we can do.

“We just go on the pitch and enjoy playing with our teammates and we don’t necessarily realise the impact it has on small girls watching, that maybe want to be you or are just inspired by your football. I’m happy if I can inspire anyone and will do my best to do it more. It’s good for my family too. My mum always told me to never forget that a lot of people are looking at me and to be a good role model, to give everything and never give up because I can help that next generation do the same.”

Sports.title: Kylian Mbappé’s China crisis shows how sensitive Mao’s legacy remains
Sports.content:
It’s been a bad start to the week for the France forward Kylian Mbappé. He missed out on joining the elite roster of Ballon d’Or winners, and instead became the latest high-profile addition to a far less illustrious list – that of foreign brands and individuals charged with “hurting the feelings of the Chinese people”.

The saga began when a video of the Real Madrid player making light of a meme involving him and China’s former leader Mao Zedong began spreading.

Within hours Mbappé found himself condemned online, before being unceremoniously dropped by brands, then held responsible for state television suspending the entire top Spanish league from its schedule. On Tuesday Mbappé apologised – “My comment was ill-judged, and I now understand that it hurt many people in China – as did La Liga, which released a statement saying it “deeply regrets the offence that Kylian Mbappé’s recent comments have caused among Chinese fans”.

Foreign brands from Mercedes to Versace and celebrities from John Cena to Katy Perry have previously been sent to the sin bin for crossing China’s political lines on Tibet, Hong Kong and Taiwan.

Mbappé’s case shows how sensitive Mao’s legacy remains in China 50 years after his death – to the extent that most Chinese coverage of the affair does not even mention what the footballer said.

In the video, Mbappé references a meme of himself and “a guy … I think he was a Chinese dictator”, after which a composite image of Mbappé’s face on Mao’s body pops up. (Mbappé has been nicknamed “the dictator” since his time at Paris Saint-Germain, a joke referring to his perceived influence at the club.)

The football app Dongqiudi was among the first to release a statement condemning his “inappropriate remarks”, but said: “Because his comments were offensive to China and the Chinese people, we cannot translate them.”

Chinese media have reported on reactions such as the brand desertions, and the China Football Association’s lodging of a “stern protest” with Real Madrid – who on Wednesday apologised “to the Chinese people for any offence caused” – but have generally steered clear of outlining Mbappé’s precise offence.

The topic was still trending on Chinese social media on Wednesday morning, with one hashtag relating to the superstar’s apology boasting more than 600m views.

Some posts asked variations on a simple question: “What did he actually say?”

View image in fullscreen An  for a drink brand, featuring Kylian Mbappé, in Shanghai. Photograph: Ying Tang/NurPhoto/Shutterstock

“Many netizens without a VPN are still left in the dark about why all the talk about boycotting Mbappé is actually happening,” said Manya Koetse, editor of the Eye on Digital China newsletter, on X.

Still, many expressed anger at what was characterised as disrespect for, as well as a misunderstanding of, China’s history.

“For the majority of the [Chinese] people, Mao was and is still not seen as negatively as it is believed in the west,” said Mobo Gao, professor of Chinese studies at Adelaide University.

Mao was the founding leader of modern China, but his legacy includes radical policies such as the Great Leap Forward, an industrialisation policy blamed for a famine that killed as many as 30 million people by some estimates.

The ruling Communist party (CCP) maintains Mao was a revolutionary hero, though after his death it acknowledged another extreme policy, the violent Cultural Revolution, was a “grave mistake”.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

“There has been intense tension between Mao hatred and Mao support among the Chinese themselves,” said Gao. “This tension is even more keenly felt since the economy has slowed.”

Some scholars have pointed to a resurgence of interest in Mao among younger Chinese, with a yearning for a time they regard as more idealistic and egalitarian – something the CCP is keen to keep in check.

Jennifer Pan, professor of communication at Stanford University, said the difficulty of doing independent social science surveys over the past decade meant “our understanding of what Chinese people actually think is weak”.

“Social media doesn’t fill that gap,” she said. “It’s noisy, unrepresentative, and censored … What we see is that companies, platforms, broadcasters and the foreign ministry moved together quickly. Did this follow public anger, or did this produce public anger? Either is possible, and we can’t tell which came first.”

Whichever way round, the financial cost for Mbappé is the same. His face is a common sight on Chinese buses, in subways and in online ads, and his commercial deals could be worth “as much as $30m (£22.6m) per year”, estimated Mark Dreyer, author of Sporting Superpower, a book about China’s ambitions in the sector.

However, “as soon as someone else has decided you’ve crossed the line, it’s a race to who can cut ties quickest, who can be the most patriotic”, he said. “Then you have to kiss the ring – there really is no other way if you want to stay in the market.”

Mbappé’s and La Liga’s swift apologies suggest they are trying to avoid a fate like the NBA, whose lucrative pre-season matches were shut out of China for six years after the Houston Rockets’ then general manager, Daryl Morey, voiced support for Hong Kong pro-democracy protests in 2019.

La Liga may have better luck, with the state broadcaster CCTV saying it would listen to what Mbappé had to say, and “more importantly” watch what he does.

On Wednesday a foreign ministry spokesperson, Guo Jiakun, said: “We take seriously the apology the individual concerned has made.”

Dreyer said: “It doesn’t sound like it’s an instant: ‘All is forgiven.’ But it sounds like they’re going to be a little bit more, for want of a better word, reasonable.”

Sports.title: Which footballers have scored in the same minute as their surname? | The Knowledge
Sports.content:
“Justin Seven-Seven came on in the 75th minute and then scored in the 77th minute for West Brom Under-21s against Sutton United in the National League Cup. You have probably already guessed my question, but has anyone else ever scored in the same minute as their name?” wonders Peter Skilton.

Readers of a certain age may recall Didier Six, the mercurial French winger who had a brief spell at Aston Villa in 1984-85. A number of you mentioned some or all of the following sixth-minute goals, which includes two in consecutive seasons against Bordeaux:

Valenciennes 2-1 Nancy (agg: 2-3) Coupe de France quarter-final, 1975-76

Valenciennes 3-2 Bordeaux Ligue 1, 1976-77

Lens 2-0 Bordeaux Ligue 1, 1977-78

VfB Stuttgart 5-1 Karlsruher Bundesliga, 1981-82

We’d imagine Alphonse Six, who won nine caps for Belgium and scored goals galore at club level before he died at 24 years old during the first world war, managed at least one in the sixth minute, but goal times for club football in the 1910s are not easy to come by. Pete Tomlin also offers “Austrian striker Martin Six, who also scored a goal in the sixth minute of a match. He was playing for SV Allerheiligen against DSV Leoben in the Regional League Central on the 1 April 2011.”

“Scottish lower league mainstay Armand Oné scored for Stranraer in the first minute of a League Two game against East Stirlingshire in 2010-11,” writes Richard Wilson, and yes we do believe it. “At the time of writing, son Ryan – at Sheffield United – hasn’t managed the feat, but he has plenty of time.”

This isn’t just an English-language question, as Filippo Varanini points out. “Some Italian football nerd (not me, unfortunately) dug up a Serie C game from 1998, when Raffaele Quaranta (whose surname means 40) scored for Casarano in the 40th minute.” Pete checks back in to mention that “Swiss midfielder Claude Sixt does not strictly have the same name as the number, but he did score a 60th-minute goal in the Swiss League for Sion v Urania Genève on 28 May 1966. Also, Marculino Ninte scored a 90th-minute goal for CD Mafra v SU 1° Dezembro in the third tier of Portuguese football on 5 October 2025.”

We will leave the final, not entirely serious, word to Mark Johnson. “On 2 August 2003, in a match between Banik Ostrava against Slovan Liberec, Marek Heinz (57 varieties) scored in the 57th minute.”

Clarets and blues

“Burnley have gone a calendar year without a home league win. What is the longest home drought, in the league or in all competitions?” asks our own Niall McVeigh.

Burnley beat Millwall in the FA Cup in January, but it’s 376 days since their last league win at Turf Moor, a 2-0 victory over Leeds on 18 October 2025. Still, could be worse …

View image in fullscreen Lesley Ugochukwu celebrates scoring in Burnley’s October 2025 win at home against Leeds. Photograph: Craig Brough/Action Images/Reuters

“In the NWSL, Sky Blue FC (now Gotham FC) went without a home win between 26 August 2017 and 8 September 2018, a stretch of 378 days,” writes Dave Mellinger. “The victory came over Orlando Pride in their last game of the 2018 season and was their only win, home or away. Had they failed to win, the streak would have rolled on to the start of the next season in April 2019. Unfortunately for us stats nerds, they shocked the world and won that final match.”

Reggiana made no such mistake in Serie A 30 years ago. “Apologies for going all Football Italia on you again,” writes Daz Pearce, labouring under the misapprehension that stimulating the Proustian rush of Football Italia is an act worthy of apology, “but I was quite amused by Reggiana’s magnificent winless home at run in 1996-97, especially as they managed to nick two victories on the road.” Reggiana won their last home game of 1995-96 and the first of 1997-98, both in Serie B. But they did not win a single match at Stadio Giglio in 1996-97, not even in the cups. Their winlessness lasted from 23 May 1996 to 30 August 1997 – a whopping 465 days.

Pre-Christmas goal centuries

“By my reckoning, Ross County have already scored 81 goals this season: 38 in 10 league games (including beating poor Queen of the South 8-0 and 7-1), 30 in six Challenge Cup group games, 13 in six League Cup games. They may well have scored a century of goals by the end of October! Surely that cannot be bettered. What is the earliest a team has hit a century of goals in a season?” asks Stephen James.

Before we get to a pre-Christmas century from the distant past, we need a modern reference point. Last season, Vincent Kompany’s Bayern Munich reached 100 goals during a 5-1 win at Leipzig on 17 January. This was the breakdown:

Bundesliga 71 goals in 18 games

Champions League 18 goals in 6 games

DFB-Pokal 10 goals in 3 games

Franz Beckenbauer Supercup 2 goals in 1 game

View image in fullscreen Harry Kane celebrates after scoring for Bayern Munich against Hoffenheim early in the 2025-26 Bundesliga season. Photograph: Heiko Becker/Reuters

But the Turnbull Tornadoes – as the Hibernian side of the early-1970s, managed by Eddie Turnbull, were known – can beat that by a month. “In 1972-73, Hibernian reached their century of goals on 16 December after beating Ayr United 8-1,” notes Mark Shipway. “They had 41 league goals by then, in 14 games, and had also scored 12 in the Drybrough Cup (three games), 32 in the League Cup (12 games) and 15 in the European Cup Winners Cup (four games).”

Hibs played more games than Bayern, 33 to 28, but that wasn’t the question so pipe down. Their answer to Harry Kane, Michael Olise and Luis Díaz was Alan Gordon, Jimmy O’Rourke and Arthur Duncan, who scored 98 goals between them across the whole season.

That included six of the goals in a legendary 7-0 win at Hearts on 1 January. Weirdly, Hibs’ season ended in a binary fug. In the last eight games, starting with a Cup Winners’ Cup quarter-final defeat to Hajduk Split, the team scored only twice.

Knowledge archive

“Who were the first football club to have an official website?” wondered Chris White in 2016. “And how about an unofficial website? I noticed that TWTD, Ipswich Town’s unofficial fan site, has been going since 1995, so surely must be one of the first. Also, who were the first clubs to start using social media platforms?”

“I can help,” yelled Martyn Amos, thrusting his arm in the air. “Ipswich Town were, indeed, the first club to have a website (unofficial or otherwise). In fact, I used to help maintain it. It was set up in 1990 by Phil Clarke, who worked at BT in Martlesham (near Ipswich) when the web was still very much experimental. He then passed it on (1993-1995) to Paul Felton, who was a student at UEA in Norwich (boo, hiss).

“After Paul graduated, he passed it on to me as I was, at the time, a PhD student at Warwick (1995-96). Paul then took it back in 1996 and ran it until 2001, when the club finally woke up to the potential of the web, and got a local company called AWS to run it … There used to be some discussion with Sheffield United fans about our claim to primacy, but I believe that it was decided in our favour.”

As for unofficial websites … “Very likely to be Reading’s Hob Nob Anyone which has been knocking around since November 1994,” reckons Peter Sorrill. “Although the distinction between official and unofficial was moot in the early 90s as most clubs weren’t that tech savvy. Here’s the Evening Post’s report on its 20th anniversary from 2014.” In it, the founder Graham Loader explains that “I did computing and then I found out about the internet and realised you could do email and all that stuff. I didn’t think it would get big but it got quite big quite quickly. People would contact me and say how exciting it was that they could read about Reading in places like Canada and Australia.”

But Alex Lopez-Ortiz thought he could go earlier. “The ‘What’s New, September 1993’ NCSA webpage lists: ‘Information on the Sheffield Wednesday Football Club at Nottingham University [website] is online.’ This is very early in the life of the web. NCSA mosaic, which was what popularised the web, was introduced in January of that year.”

Can you help?

“In their 3-0 win over Milan, Bournemouth scored two penalties in the first half taken by different players against two different goalkeepers. Has this ever happened before? And, excluding shootouts, what is the record for the number of penalties scored by one team in a game by different players?” wonders Matthew Wilkie.

“What is the soonest a manager has been sacked after signing a contract extension?” asks Dave Smythe.

“Who was the first manager to wear a tracksuit while watching his team play?” muses Gordon Smith. “I remember that Sir Alf Ramsey used to wear one for England games so did he wear a tracksuit when he managed Ipswich?”

“Newcastle played Hull at 3pm on Saturday 19 September and will play Fulham at 3pm on 7 November at 3pm. All the previous fixtures haven’t been the traditional time,” begins Mark Reilly. “None of our planned fixtures to 7 January against Manchester United are Saturday 3pm kick-offs. What is the fewest number of Saturday 3pm kick-offs in a Premier League season by a club?”

Sports.title: João Pedro out for ‘a few weeks’, reveals Alonso; Donnarumma gets Maresca’s backing
Sports.content:
1. Alonso’s Liverpool return hit by João Pedro injury layoff

Xabi Alonso will celebrate if Chelsea score at Liverpool tonight, but the manager’s attacking plan will have to change with João Pedro likely to be out until after the international break with a thigh injury.

João Pedro picked up the problem during training and faces an extended layoff after missing last Saturday’s 2-0 defeat at home by Tottenham. It is a major blow for Alonso, whose side struggled without the Brazil striker.

Chelsea will have to adjust when they visit Liverpool in the fourth round of the Carabao Cup and Alonso revealed that João Pedro would probably not be back until the end of November at the earliest.

“He has an injury on his thigh and he is going to be out for a few weeks,” Alonso said. “Let’s see how many. We don’t want to predict on that, but he’s not ready for the next games.”

Alonso clarified that João Pedro would “probably” be out until after next month’s international break, meaning he will not be available for Brazil after missing the last camp with a knee issue. For Chelsea, the question is how to play without the former Brighton forward. There was surprise at Alonso’s decision to play without a recognised striker and overlook Danny Welbeck against Spurs. Welbeck is pushing to start against Liverpool.

It will be an emotional evening for Alonso, who won the Champions League with Liverpool as a player in 2005. This will be his third game back at Anfield as an opposition manager – he lost with Bayer Leverkusen in 2024 and Real Madrid last season – and he will not hold back if Chelsea score.

“Of course I will celebrate,” the Spaniard said. “With full respect because my warmth with Liverpool was there as a player. But now, I am in a different role, I need to support my team, I need to support my club, I fight for my club and if we score, I will celebrate with whole respect.

Alonso, who travels to Anfield without the suspended Cole Palmer, was considered by Liverpool when Jürgen Klopp stepped down in 2024. “At that time I was at Leverkusen and I was aware of the situation, but I decided to stay,” he said. “That was my decision at the time.” Alonso said he never held talks with Liverpool, who instead appointed Arne Slot.

Liverpool sacked Slot last summer and replaced him with Andoni Iraola. Alonso, available after losing his job at Real Madrid last January, had already agreed to join Chelsea. He has made a promising start at Stamford Bridge, but doubts over his approach flared against Spurs, who had 68.5% possession.

Alonso was a passing midfielder who played for Pep Guardiola. He was asked whether he valued possession or saw the game in a different way. “You evolve, you adapt,” Alonso said. “You want to have possession. Knowing the context, knowing what we are building, I think that we have room for improvement in that part. I think we need to play more confidently with the ball.”

Sports.title: Pierre Sage given more time by Crystal Palace but remains under pressure
Sports.content:
Pierre Sage has been given more time to turn around Crystal Palace’s fortunes but he remains under huge pressure and could be dismissed if they lose against Tottenham on Saturday.

The Frenchman’s position was in serious doubt after another poor performance in the 2-0 defeat against Newcastle at the weekend. That followed a 5-0 thrashing against Brighton when Sage was warned that he could be dismissed if results did not improve quickly.

However the club’s chair, Steve Parish, has decided not to act given the tight turnaround in Palace’s schedule: the side face Fulham at Craven Cottage in the Carabao Cup on Wednesday, before their trip to Tottenham in the Premier League. But Sage, who attended the Ballon d’Or ceremony in London on Monday evening, is understood to have been left in no doubt that the meeting with Spurs on Saturday is crucial to his future.

Palace are 17th and have conceded 19 goals in eight Premier League matchesthis season – the highest in the division. But, it is understood, Sage retains the support of his squad, with two leading players having sent him messages saying that they still have faith he can turn things around.

Palace’s hierarchy are said to be split over whether to fire the former Lens manager after only 12 games in charge, with some in favour of bringing in Thomas Frank or Sean Dyche to steady the ship. The former Wolves manager Rob Edwards has also been mentioned as a potential contender.

There is sympathy for Sage at boardroom level given that Axel Disasi – who was signed on loan from Chelsea to replace the key defender Maxence Lacroix – has only just returned from a three-match suspension. There were also signs of improvement in the 2-2 Europa League draw at Besiktas in midweek, with Sage believed to have been delighted with Jean-Philippe Mateta’s response since returning from injury. The France striker is in the final year of his contract but failed in an attempt to have it ruled invalid by an independent Premier League tribunal and Fifa.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

There are concerns about Ismaïla Sarr, however, who missed the defeat against Newcastle after a recurrence of the groin injury that ruled him out earlier in the season. The Senegal forward has made no secret of his disappointment after Palace rejected a bid from Liverpool in the summer and Sage needs the club’s player of the year last season back on the pitch if they are to recover from a poor start to life after Oliver Glasner.

Sports.title: Spanish FA takes significant action after devastating fatal train crash
Sports.content:
All 24 Copa del Rey matches that were scheduled for Wednesday have been postponed by the Spanish FA.

It comes after two trains were involved in a high-speed crash south of Madrid.

1 More than 500 passengers were travelling across the two trains and at least 170 are injured Credit: Getty

At least 64 people are confirmed to have died in the country's worst rail disaster since 2013.

Beyond the human impact, the collision has caused widespread rail disruption across the country.

The Spanish FA said: "Today’s Copa del Rey matches have been suspended.

“As a sign of respect and solidarity with all the victims of the tragic train accident that occurred early Wednesday morning in the province of Toledo, the RFEF (Royal Spanish Football Federation) has suspended all 24 matches of the first round of the Spanish Championship-Copa del Rey (King’s Cup) originally scheduled for this afternoon and evening.

“The RFEF will announce the revised tournament schedule and the final times for the postponed matches in the coming days.

“The great Spanish football family remains united in grief over this tragedy, offering its support to the authorities to help the victims of this devastating accident.”

The first round of the Copa del Rey saw 18 matches played on Tuesday, while 24 were scheduled for Wednesday and a further 14 on Thursday.

It remains to be seen whether Thursday's fixtures will go ahead.

Among the postponed fixtures on Wednesday are: Navalcarnero vs Real Betis, Salamanca vs Celta Vigo, Tavernes vs Valencia and Xerez vs Cadiz.
