World.title: Espionage threats blur lines between security and dissent in Iran
World.content:
Iran is using the threat of spy networks to detain and execute political opponents, analysts say.

While two wars on Iran by the United States and Israel have exposed serious vulnerabilities in Iran’s intelligence and security institutions, Iran is using the threat to crack down on dissent, analysts have said.

Saeid Golkar, an associate professor in political science at the University of Tennessee at Chattanooga, said the genuine espionage threats faced by Iran were illustrated by the killing of high-level figures, including former Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, on the first day of the latest assault by Israel and the US on February 28.

“At the same time, the regime has historically used real or, most of the time, perceived security threats to justify political repression and expand its coercive apparatus,” Golkar told Al Jazeera.

“The current crackdown appears to reflect both legitimate counterintelligence concerns and the regime’s broader efforts to suppress dissent and intimidate society.”

Spy threat

Former Israeli spy chief David Barnea recently said that in the weeks before Israel launched its 12-day war on Iran in June 2025, he had approved the entry into the country of dozens of agents with clear intelligence or sabotage assignments.

“I can’t say that they are here with us. But they are there in Tehran, living their lives,” he told a conference in Israel on October 22.

According to Barnea, who was the director of Mossad for five years until June 2026, Israeli intelligence tried to maximise the number of Iranian citizens arrested by local authorities in order to shield its genuine agents inside Iran.



Just hours after launching the war and killing senior commanders and nuclear scientists, they deliberately released footage of agents inside Iran with a Mossad logo, leading to the arrests of thousands of people with no links to the Israeli intelligence service.

Barnea claimed the strategy worked, and almost all of their assets remained unidentified. Eight months into a second war launched by Israel and the US against Iran, with the stated aim of overthrowing the Islamic republic, Iran’s paranoia remains.

Iranian authorities have significantly accelerated judicial punishments for cases linked to national security since the 2025 war. That has entailed mass arrests, expedited prosecutions, lengthy imprisonment, asset confiscations and executions.

The people targeted include alleged spies but also protesters, journalists, lawyers and minorities. Amnesty International and Human Rights Watch have documented cases involving coerced confessions, the denial of effective defence and national security charges applied to dissenters.

“The espionage threat facing Iran is very real. The two US-Israeli wars exposed serious vulnerabilities in Iran’s intelligence and security apparatus… Tehran has legitimate concerns about foreign infiltration, sabotage, and intelligence operations inside the country, especially as the threat of another military escalation remains high,” Negar Mortazavi, a senior fellow with the Center for International Policy, said.

“But there is a fundamental distinction between espionage and dissent,” she added. “Espionage involves covertly gathering sensitive intelligence or assisting foreign intelligence operations. Criticising the government, reporting on its failures, engaging with foreign media, or challenging official narratives does not, in itself, constitute espionage. The Iranian authorities have increasingly blurred this distinction, treating political opposition and independent reporting as extensions of foreign intelligence activity.”

‘Hybrid war’

Iranian authorities argue that foreign intelligence operations are aimed not only at overthrowing the government but also fragmenting the country.

Iran’s Ministry of Intelligence said in May that “enemies” were combining espionage, sabotage, hostile media, exploitation of economic crises and fuelling ethnic and sectarian tensions as part of a “hybrid war”.

Judiciary chief Gholam-Hossein Mohseni-Ejei has repeatedly invoked wartime conditions and domestic laws to argue for urgent security measures, and accelerated the punishment of alleged collaborators as a means of protecting the country.



Judiciary spokesman Ali Kazemi said earlier in October that there were active cases involving at least 1,895 people, including 94 media workers, accused of cooperation with Israel or other hostile states. Police had announced at least 21,000 arrests following the June 2025 war, while at least 50,000 people were detained in connection with the nationwide protests in January 2026. Thousands of civilians were killed in the crackdown against antigovernment protests across Iran, according to US-based rights organisation HRANA.

The authorities have referred to the nationwide protests as a “coup” orchestrated entirely by Israeli and US intelligence agencies. The Iranian government also claims that Mossad and other intelligence agents killed protesters. But an independent United Nations fact-finding mission said the authorities committed crimes against humanity during their most violent crackdown since the revolution.

Executions linked with security charges have also increased following the wars and protests. At least 19 people were hanged in espionage-related cases between June and December 2025, according to the UN.

Iran Human Rights, an Oslo-based nonprofit group, said it recorded 16 espionage defendants executed between January and September 2026, alongside 33 protesters and 13 prisoners affiliated with banned groups. The group had tracked at least 604 executions by early October.

Amnesty International reported at least 34 executions this year linked to the January nationwide protests by October 13, including five between September 30 and October 5.

‘Securitising every aspect of life’

Iranian authorities have warned the public about Mossad and other intelligence agencies running cyber-operations to expand their influence in Iran, accusing them of recruiting people through social media and online offers.

Sending images or information to networks deemed to be hostile to the Iranian government – including BBC Persian – could result in sentences of 10 to 15 years in prison and heavy fines. Combined with other offences, it could lead to potential charges of “corruption on Earth”, which carry the death penalty.

The authorities also regard the Starlink satellite internet service as a “tool of war” used for espionage, information gathering and even operating drones by “enemy” agents inside Iran. Tens of thousands of Starlink terminals have been smuggled into the country despite severe punishments for distributing and using the service. Iranian authorities have tried to confiscate or jam them.

For several days during the 12-day war, 20 days during the January protests and 88 days at the start of the current war, Iran imposed a near-total internet shutdown on 90 million Iranians. The official reasons ranged from protecting national assets against cyberattacks to disrupting hostile drones. The global internet remains severely filtered in Iran, and authorities have warned it could be disrupted again in case of military escalation.

University of Tennessee at Chattanooga’s Golkar said that by blurring the line between espionage and political opposition, authorities increasingly treat protesters, journalists and ordinary citizens as potential threats to national security.



“Ultimately, the Islamic republic increasingly treats regime security and national security as interchangeable concepts. While counterespionage is a legitimate state function, it has also become a tool to protect the ruling establishment and expand the influence of security institutions,” he said.

“In brief, and over time, the Islamic republic has transformed into a security-dominated regime that increasingly securitises nearly every aspect of political and social life, including peaceful civic activism, treating even nonviolent expressions of dissent as potential threats to regime survival”.

World.title: Why are three of the UK’s four nuclear deterrent submarines at sea?
World.content:
The deployment marks the first time in years that three Vanguard-class vessels have been at sea at the same time.

Share Why are three of the UK’s four nuclear deterrent submarines at sea? on social media

The United Kingdom has simultaneously deployed three of its four nuclear deterrent submarines at sea for the first time in five years, The Times reported on Wednesday.

At least one of the vessels – known as Vanguard-class submarines – was said to be armed with ballistic missiles which carry nuclear warheads.

The report named the three submarines at sea as HMS Vanguard, HMS Vigilant and HMS Vengeance, with the fourth, HMS Victorious, currently undergoing maintenance.

A navy source quoted by The Times described the deployment as “unusual”, without elaborating.

The UK continuously deploys at least one of the four submarines as a security guarantee.

The deployment has raised questions over whether the UK has changed its defence posture after Defence Secretary Wes Streeting warned last week that Britain should be prepared for war.

Here’s what we know:

Has this happened before?

The last time three submarines were at sea was more than five years ago, according to The Times.

Navy Lookout, the UK’s leading independent publication on the Royal Navy, says one submarine carrying ballistic missiles has been at sea without interruption since 1969.

It said the second vessel was believed to be preparing to relieve a patrol boat, while the third was likely conducting sea trials or work-up activity.

Last year HMS Vanguard patrolled the seas for 200 days, just a week shy of the longest known submarine deployment of 207 days, carried out by HMS Victorious in 2021.

What has the UK government said?

According to Sky News, a spokesperson for the defence ministry said the country’s nuclear deterrent is the “cornerstone of our national security, protecting the UK and our NATO allies every moment of every day”.



“We remain the only European ally to commit its nuclear deterrent to the defence of NATO. This means that all NATO allies already benefit from the protection of our nuclear deterrent,” the spokesperson added.

Last week, British and French fighter jets flew together in their first joint exercise involving France’s airborne nuclear capability.

The French armed forces ministry said British RAF Typhoon fighters escorted the French jets, simulating a nuclear strike.

France’s Armed Forces Minister Catherine Vautrin said that having “independent nuclear forces does not preclude coordination”.

“Our nuclear cooperation with the United Kingdom continues to deepen,” she added.

The UK’s Streeting said that in an “increasingly dangerous world, our adversaries should be in no doubt”.

“The United Kingdom and France stand together in their commitment to European security and to maintaining the deterrence that has helped preserve peace for generations,” he added.

What are the UK’s ‘war readiness’ plans?

On Saturday, Streeting wrote in the Telegraph newspaper that Britain must be ready for war within 1,000 days.

“Our adversaries’ willingness to harm us is not new. What has changed is their capacity. By 2030, their force strength and war economy could put them in a position to attack,” Streeting wrote.

“That gives us a little over 1,000 days to complete our mission: to be ready with our allies to fight and win. This Government will make sure it is mission accomplished,” he said.

His message followed last week’s launch of the government’s “Be Ready” campaign, which called on households to store three days’ supply of tinned food and water bottles, cash and a wind-up radio in case of a cyberattack or a weather event which disrupts infrastructure.

The warning also followed reports that Russia has been using fishing trawlers to track and spy on the UK’s undersea cables.

World.title: Spanish football postpones 24 Copa del Rey games after train crash
World.content:
Real Madrid and Barcelona offer messages of support following train crash as Spanish football orders Copa postponement.

Spain’s national football federation has postponed all 24 Copa del Rey games scheduled for Wednesday because of a train accident that killed at least 30 people in the country’s central region.

About 80 people were injured after a high-speed service slammed into the rear of another train that had stopped on the track. Authorities said the death toll could rise.

“Shocked by the tragic train accident,” the Royal Spanish Football Federation (RFEF) said in a statement, adding that it had postponed the games “in solidarity with the victims.”

“The entire Spanish football community stands united in grief over this tragedy and has made itself available to the authorities to assist the victims of this devastating accident,” the RFEF said.

It said it would later provide a revised tournament schedule. First-round games on Thursday have not been postponed. The Spanish league has not announced any postponements for the weekend’s games.

Among Wednesday’s games to be postponed were Navalcarnero against Real Betis, Salamanca against Celta Vigo and Tavernes against Valencia.

Several Spanish football clubs expressed their condolences and solidarity following the incident.

“The club wishes to convey its support and solidarity to the families and friends of the victims and to wish all those injured a speedy recovery,” FC Barcelona said on social media.

Real Madrid also offered condolences and in a statement said the club shared “in the grief of everyone impacted during these moments of profound sadness.”



Sevilla FC observed a moment of silence ahead of their training on Wednesday and cancelled manager Luis Garcia Plaza’s news conference, which was scheduled for Wednesday ahead of their match against Sporting de Hortaleza.

World.title: Iraqi PM Ali al-Zaidi meets Ahmed al-Sharaa in historic Syria visit
World.content:
Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi has arrived in Damascus to meet with Syrian President Ahmed al-Sharaa on the first visit of an Iraqi prime minister to Syria since the fall of Bashar al-Assad.

The visit comes as the two neighbours seek to strengthen bilateral ties and boost economic and oil cooperation.

According to the official Iraqi News Agency (INA), the two leaders discussed the export of Iraqi oil through the Baniyas line, increasing the volume of trade exchange and joint work to develop the agricultural sector to achieve food and economic integration.

Iraq has recently begun exporting limited quantities of oil through Syria following the outbreak of the US-led war on Iran.

Last July, the two countries signed agreements to revive the Haditha Baniyas pipeline to transport Iraqi oil in addition to signing a memorandum of understanding with a consortium of three companies, most notably the American oil major Chevron to implement the project.

“The Iraqi and Syrian people are one people in two countries,” Zaidi said according to INA, noting that “work to develop partnership and joint cooperation in various fields especially economic and social affairs, enhance security co-operation, unify positions on regional and international issues, and work to achieve peace and stability in the region”.

For his part, the Syrian president expressed his “great appreciation for the visit of al-Zaidi and his accompanying delegation,” stressing “the depth of bilateral relations and Syria’s keenness to achieve the highest levels of cooperation between the two countries”.



Al-Sharaa and al-Zaidi had previously met last September in New York on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly, where they discussed ways to strengthen political and security coordination and expand economic and trade cooperation.

World.title: Real Madrid apologise to Chinese people for Mbappe’s Mao ‘dictator’ remark
World.content:
Mocking Mao Zedong is taboo in China, which is a lucrative market for players and teams such as Kylian Mbappe’s Real.

La Liga club Real Madrid ⁠⁠issued an apology on Wednesday ⁠⁠after their French superstar Kylian Mbappe triggered a fierce backlash over his comments referring to the former Chinese leader Mao ⁠⁠Zedong as a “dictator”.

After apologies from Mbappe and La Liga failed to quell the negative response in China, La Liga President Javier Tebas set up a crisis unit ⁠⁠and met with Chinese ambassador Yao Jing.

The controversy highlighted the risks for athletes and brands in the lucrative Chinese market, where satire about Mao, modern China’s founding leader, who ruled the country from 1949 until his death in 1976, remains a social taboo.

“Real Madrid CF wishes to express its apologies to the Chinese people for any discomfort caused by the recent words of our player Kylian Mbappe,” Real said in a statement.

“Our club maintains a deep respect for China, its history, its culture and its citizens, as well ⁠⁠as for the millions of Chinese fans who ⁠⁠feel affection and admiration for Real Madrid,” the statement added.

Real Madrid game not on TV

China’s state-owned broadcasting platform Migu will not be showing Real Madrid’s La Liga game against Racing Santander on Sunday, while Chinese brands, including dairy companies Mengniu and Shanghai Milkground Food Tech as well as Eastroc Beverage, have ceased ⁠⁠all cooperation with Mbappe.

Migu is scheduled to show nine of La Liga’s 10 games this weekend, with Real Madrid’s match the only ⁠⁠one not covered. Migu did not immediately respond to a request for comment from the Reuters news agency.



La Liga moved quickly ⁠⁠to set up a crisis unit and reached out to Real Madrid, a significant move following years of strained relations between Tebas and the club due to a power struggle within Spanish football. Real Madrid recently called for Tebas’ resignation.

Both parties put aside their differences, acknowledging the potential immediate ⁠⁠and long-term financial repercussions of Mbappe’s comments. Following Real’s statement, sources at La Liga said Tebas was considering travelling to China to neutralise the threat of a huge financial loss for ⁠⁠Spanish football.

La Liga will also consider strengthening its institutional engagement with Beijing amid serious ⁠⁠concerns about a sharp drop in revenue, as Chinese state television awaits further gestures of reconciliation.

In a video on a French podcast that has since been taken down, Mbappe is heard discussing a humorous meme where his face had been photoshopped onto an image he described as “some guy – I think he’s a Chinese dictator”.

Fans have been creating memes superimposing Mbappe’s ⁠⁠face on images of military and political leaders to suggest that he has the power to influence decisions at the teams he plays for. Mbappe has been nicknamed “the dictator” in ‌‌the European press.

On Wednesday, when asked what China thought of Mbappe’s apology, foreign ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun said: “We take seriously the apology that ‌‌the ‌‌person has made.”

World.title: Ballon d’Or win will help keep Kane at Bayern, says Germany’s Matthaus
World.content:
Former World Cup winner Lothar Matthaus says relationship between Harry Kane and club Bayern Munich is ‘perfect’.

Share Ballon d’Or win will help keep Kane at Bayern, says Germany’s Matthaus on social media

Winning the Ballon d’Or will help persuade Bayern Munich striker Harry Kane to extend his deal with the German champions, former World Cup winner Lothar Matthaus said.

On Monday, Kane became the first Englishman to win the prestigious award – the top individual honour in the sport – since Michael Owen in 2001.

The England captain was prolific last season, scoring 61 goals in 51 games for Bayern across all competitions as the German side completed a domestic league and cup double. He was also a World Cup semifinalist with England, scoring six goals in the tournament.

“We are very happy to have Harry Kane in the Bundesliga. He is an international ambassador of football,” Matthaus, who won the award in 1990 after leading Germany to World Cup victory that year, said in an online media roundtable.

“Maybe he was dreaming to win the Ballon d’Or … but you have to play in a big club like Bayern. He found his peace in Munich and the right club with the right teammates.”

Kane, 33, joined Bayern in 2023 in a 100-million-euro ($111m) move from boyhood club Tottenham Hotspur, in search of silverware. He has since won the league twice and is in talks with Bayern over a new contract.

“I think he gets a bonus (for winning the Ballon d’Or); 36 years ago I got nothing,” Matthaus said. “But it is about more than money. It is a good moment to sign (a new deal) for Bayern. Bayern helped him get this Ballon d’Or.



“The relationship between Harry Kane and Bayern Munich is perfect, and with everything that has happened in the last three years, I think Harry will sign his contract for the next two, three years.”

Bayern, top of the Bundesliga standings, take on Magdeburg on Wednesday in the German Cup second round.

World.title: Tens of thousands flee Ethiopia fighting into neighbouring Kenya
World.content:
NewsFeed Tens of thousands flee Ethiopia fighting into neighbouring Kenya

Tens of thousands of people have crossed into Kenya, fleeing fighting between regional forces in Ethiopia’s Moyale town. Al Jazeera’s Malcolm Webb says many who arrive face hunger and limited medical care, as humanitarian aid cuts threaten relief efforts.

World.title: Photos: Spain high-speed train crash kills 30
World.content:
A high-speed train has slammed into the rear of another train that had stopped, derailing two carriages in central Spain and killing at least 30 people, authorities have said.

At least 80 people were injured in the crash that occurred early on Wednesday near Urda, in Toledo province, south of Madrid, the president of the Castilla-La Mancha region, Emiliano Garcia-Page, said, warning that the death toll could rise.

Spain’s Health Minister Monica Garcia said emergency workers were focusing on rescuing survivors and recovering bodies from the two most damaged carriages. She said the injured were being taken to several hospitals in the area.

In January, 45 people were killed in southern Spain when a train left the tracks and collided with an oncoming service. That crash was Spain’s deadliest since 2013, when 80 people were killed in a derailment.

World.title: Rivals in Israel Election Strike Tone of Triumph, but Outcome Is Far From Clear
World.content:
Shira Shapiro, right, a candidate for the Yashar party, meeting with Gadi Eisenkot at a roadside bomb shelter where her son died during the Oct. 7 2023, attack, near Reim, Israel, earlier this month.

Several people whose relatives were killed or taken hostage in the Hamas-led attack on Israel on Oct. 7, 2023, are running for office in Tuesday’s election, the first national vote since the assault, which shook the country’s foundations and ignited its longest war.

The October 2023 assault looms large over this week’s vote. There are sharp divisions over who was to blame for failing to prevent the worst military, intelligence and policy disaster in Israel’s history.

About 1,200 civilians and soldiers were killed that day, according to the Israeli authorities, and roughly 250 were taken hostage to Gaza. Many of the family members of hostages held by Hamas rose to prominence as they campaigned for their loved ones in television interviews and at nationwide protests.

Most of them called for Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu to take responsibility for the government’s failures of Oct. 7 and to prioritize negotiating the release of the hostages over continued fighting. Others supported Mr. Netanyahu’s right-wing government and urged it to keep up the military pressure on Hamas and Israel’s other enemies.

Parties from across Israel’s political spectrum have recruited candidates from what have become known as the Oct. 7 families. Here are some of the candidates with a chance to win a seat in Parliament:

Shira Shapiro is running with Yashar, the centrist party led by Mr. Netanyahu’s main political rival, Gadi Eisenkot. Ms. Shapiro’s son, Staff Sgt. Aner Shapiro, was on leave from the army on Oct. 7 when he attended the Nova music festival, one of the bloodiest targets of the Hamas-led attack. He took shelter in a crowded roadside bomb shelter and stationed himself by the entrance when gunmen attacked it. As the militants hurled grenades inside, Sergeant Shapiro repeatedly caught the grenades and threw them back out, until he was killed, according to surviving witnesses.

Zvi Mor, the father of a released hostage, Eitan Mor, is running as a candidate for the far-right party Religious Zionism, headed by Bezalel Smotrich. While Eitan was in captivity, Mr. Mor, an educator, founded a forum of right-wing parents of hostages and soldiers who opposed making deals with Hamas and pushed for Israel to defeat the group militarily.

Omri Ronen, a reserve soldier, is running with the left-wing Democrats, led by Yair Golan. His grandmother, Nira Ronen, was killed in her home in Kfar Aza, one of the border communities worst hit in the October 2023 attack, along with her Filipina caregiver, Angelyn Aguirre. Before Oct. 7, Mr. Ronen had been one of the leaders of a grass-roots group of reservists protesting the government’s plan to overhaul the judiciary. He said in a recent television interview that Mr. Netanyahu, whom he called “Mr. Oct. 7,” must go. “The word responsibility has meaning,” he said.

Rafael Ben Shitrit, a former mayor of Beit Shean in northern Israel, is in Yisrael Beitenu, a right-wing opposition party led by Avigdor Liberman. Mr. Ben Shitrit used to belong to Mr. Netanyahu’s conservative Likud party, but abandoned it after his son, Staff Sgt. Elroy Ben Shitrit, was killed in battle on Oct. 7 near the Gaza border. He has been an advocate for an independent state inquiry into what went wrong that day. Mr. Netanyahu has refused such an inquiry, and the opposition parties have pledged to establish one if they are elected.

Sharon Sharabi, also on Yisrael Beitenu’s list of candidates, is the brother of Eli Sharabi, a former hostage who was released from Gaza only to learn that his wife and two teenage daughters had been killed during the Oct. 7 attack. Another brother, Yossi Sharabi, was also taken hostage and killed after 100 days in captivity. Sharon Sharabi campaigned tirelessly for his brothers’ return. When Eli Sharabi was finally released, many Israelis were outraged over how emaciated he looked. “I was shocked,” Sharon said at the time. “I’d been told he would be thin, but I didn’t imagine how thin. It was extreme.”

Tali Gvili, running with Mr. Netanyahu’s Likud party, is the mother of Master Sgt. Ran Gvili, a member of a police counterterrorism unit who was shot and severely wounded in combat on Oct. 7 and then dragged into Gaza. His remains were recovered and returned to Israel in January 2026. The Gvili and Netanyahu families have become close, and the prime minister attended Sergeant Gvili’s state funeral, saying, “Our souls are bound with yours.”

Michal Hirsch Negri is running with Together, a joint slate led by right-wing politician Naftali Bennett and the centrist Yair Lapid. Ms. Hirsch Negri’s son Maj. Roee Negri was killed fighting in Kibbutz Be’eri near the Gaza border on Oct. 7.

Maj. Shahar Varon, a commander in the reserves, is another Together candidate. He fought that day in Kfar Aza, another border community, and later went to fight in Gaza. He was wounded in battle, then went back into Gaza to fight again. “There is life before October 7th, and there is life after,” he wrote recently, adding, “Our government disappeared that morning — but our people showed up instead.”

World.title: Live Updates: At Least 64 Killed in Train Crash in Spain, Officials Say
World.content:
Pinned

A high-speed passenger train rear-ended another on Wednesday morning near Toledo, Spain, derailing parts of both and killing at least 64 people, according to local emergency officials.

The death toll from the accident, which sent multiple carriages down an embankment, makes it one of the most lethal in the country’s history. The crash also comes after a deadly collision involving the same carriers on a southern line in January, which killed 46 people, stunned Spain and created deep doubts about the security of its once-vaunted rail system.

At least 58 people were injured in the crash on Wednesday, officials from the Castilla-La Mancha region said. That number and the death toll could both rise.

The cause of the crash was not clear.

In Spanish news reports, passengers who were in the crash described an awful impact that tossed people from a dining car, broke limbs and piled passengers atop one another. People crawled out of windows and lay in a nearby field, where local workers, who had heard the crash, rushed to help them with first aid kits and saw the first bodies.

The Adif, Spain’s rail authority, said the trains involved were a “Renfe train and another from the Iryo company, both covering the Madrid-Sevilla route.” Renfe, the national rail provider, reported that high-speed service from Madrid, the nation’s capital, to the southern region of Andalusia was suspended.

Initial reports suggested that the Iryo train was stopped on the tracks, and that the Renfe train barreled into it. Local news outlets reported that there were 397 passengers aboard the Renfe train and about 150 aboard the Iryo train.

Isaac Barrientos, a spokesman for the government’s transportation ministry, said initial reports indicated that two carriages of the Iryo train had derailed.

With early national elections set for the end of November, the crash had the potential to become an issue in an already bitter campaign about the competence of the left-wing government of Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez.

“Shocked by the serious train accident in Toledo,” Mr. Sánchez, whose office canceled all scheduled meetings, wrote on social media. “Emergency services are working on the ground to assist those affected and ensure their safety, in coordination with all the involved administrations. My affection, solidarity and support to all the victims and their families.”

The conservative opposition leader, Alberto Núñez Feijóo, quickly voiced his own concern as well.

“I am very concerned about the information we are receiving regarding another train accident,” he wrote on social media. “The priority now is to assist the victims and support their families. My full support goes to the emergency teams working on the ground.”

His Popular Party canceled all its campaign events around the country.

José Bautista contributed reporting from the scene of the crash.

World.title: Here’s the latest.
World.content:
news analysis

(From left) Yashar party leader Gadi Eisenkot and Israeli Prime Minister and Likud party leader Benjamin Netanyahu’s bid for victory could last for weeks before a party is in power. Amir Cohen/Reuters; Alexi J. Rosenfeld/Getty Images

The results of Israel’s pivotal parliamentary election will not be finalized at least until Thursday and it could be weeks until it is clear what kind of government will be formed and who will lead it. But some conclusions are already inescapable.

Arab citizens of Israel turned out to vote in record numbers. Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s Likud party gobbled up many votes that his right-wing and Orthodox Jewish coalition partners had expected would be theirs. And the pre-election polls failed to anticipate both phenomena.

Much could still change. But with most of the votes counted by Wednesday afternoon, here are some initial takeaways.

Netanyahu didn’t win, but Eisenkot lost.

Mr. Netanyahu’s coalition appears to have shrunk considerably from the 64 parliamentary seats that it won in 2022: The latest results show it with around 54, well short of a majority in the 120-member Knesset, or Parliament. But he could wind up in better position to form a government than his chief rival, Gadi Eisenkot.

Mr. Eisenkot, a former Israeli military chief of staff, had two goals in the election: to lead the Jewish opposition parties to an outright majority or at least get very close to one, and to make sure his own party, Yashar, got more votes than any other. He failed on both counts, the initial results indicate.

Reuven Hazan, a political science professor at the Hebrew University of Jerusalem, said that it had been hard to imagine better conditions for Mr. Eisenkot’s alliance ahead of the election. Mr. Netanyahu and his coalition were weighed down by anger over the Hamas-led Oct. 7, 2023 attacks and their failure to do more to free Israeli hostages; by anger over ultra-Orthodox Jewish draft-dodging in wartime; and by outrage over the government’s efforts to neuter the judiciary and allow growing settler violence against Palestinians in the Israeli-occupied West Bank, he said.

“The anti-Netanyahu camp had an election handed to them on a silver platter, and they still lost,” Mr. Hazan said. “Israelis have sent an ambiguous message: ‘We don’t really like the current government, but we don’t see a viable alternative.’”

Netanyahu’s coalition shrank, but he has options.

As votes were being counted on Wednesday afternoon, Likud was poised to be the largest party in the larger of the two blocs of Jewish-led parties, meaning Mr. Netanyahu could well be given the chance to form a government, Mr. Hazan said.

The long-serving Israeli premier may try to peel away some of Mr. Eisenkot’s putative partners in order to achieve a majority of 61 seats in Parliament. A number of them are as right-wing as he is, though all have more or less ruled out entering a Netanyahu-led government.

He could also try to form a national unity government with Mr. Eisenkot — perhaps with the assistance of President Trump, who has praised Mr. Netanyahu as a “warrior prime minister” and has made clear he wants Israel to join the United States in another round of war against Iran.

Perhaps the most mind-bending option available to Mr. Netanyahu, given that he ran a scaremongering campaign that demonized Arab lawmakers and stoked fears of Arab voter turnout, would be to recruit an Arab party to join him in a government. He nearly did so once before, in 2022.

“It could very well be that they become indispensable,” said Dahlia Scheindlin, a pollster and political analyst, said of Arab lawmakers. “And Netanyahu has certainly demonstrated his willingness to do anything to stay in power.”

The liberal camp still has a shot.

Speaking of Jewish opposition parties in isolation ignores the fact that, when Arab parties are included, Mr. Netanyahu’s rivals appeared headed toward a significant majority in Parliament, with about 66 seats to roughly 54 for the prime minister’s bloc.

“There is no need to go with the racist assumption that you need not count the Arabs,” said Gayil Talshir, a political scientist at the Hebrew University of Jerusalem who is advising the opposition.

That means the Knesset in effect will be controlled by the anti-Netanyahu opposition, regardless of who ends up being prime minister. If the vote breakdown roughly holds, Ms. Talshir said she expected Mr. Eisenkot and his Jewish and Arab allies to elect a new parliamentary speaker, begin repealing unpopular laws and at least try to form a government — perhaps including some combination of Arab and ultra-Orthodox lawmakers.

“I’m not saying it’s a good scenario to take the Knesset and not be able to form the government,” Ms. Talshir said. “It’s a disaster. But this is the hand they’re dealt, and they have to play it.”

Arab voters broke records but could face rejection.

Tuesday’s election appears to have had many losers. Mr. Netanyahu’s support shrank and Mr. Eisenkot came up short of his goal. The ultra-Orthodox parties were projected to lose seats, according to the latest returns, and two right-wing nationalist parties failed to make gains, despite four years in which they drove the Netanyahu government’s extreme policies in the West Bank.

The biggest ostensible winners were the Arab voters who voted in record numbers. But they could well wind up the most disappointed citizens of all, if the Jewish opposition leaders prove unwilling or unable to form a majority in an alliance with the Arab parties.

“They’re saying, ‘We believe in Israeli democracy, we believe in the system, we want to be part of the system, and we want to be treated better,’” Mr. Hazan said. “And if Netanyahu forms a government, they’ll get none of that.”

Omri Ronen, a reserve soldier, is running with the left-wing Democrats, led by Yair Golan. His grandmother, Nira Ronen, was killed in her home in Kfar Aza, one of the border communities worst hit in the October 2023 attack, along with her Filipina caregiver, Angelyn Aguirre. Before Oct. 7, Mr. Ronen had been one of the leaders of a grass-roots group of reservists protesting the government’s plan to overhaul the judiciary. He said in a recent television interview that Mr. Netanyahu, whom he called “Mr. Oct. 7,” must go. “The word responsibility has meaning,” he said.

Rafael Ben Shitrit, a former mayor of Beit Shean in northern Israel, is in Yisrael Beitenu, a right-wing opposition party led by Avigdor Liberman. Mr. Ben Shitrit used to belong to Mr. Netanyahu’s conservative Likud party, but abandoned it after his son, Staff Sgt. Elroy Ben Shitrit, was killed in battle on Oct. 7 near the Gaza border. He has been an advocate for an independent state inquiry into what went wrong that day. Mr. Netanyahu has refused such an inquiry, and the opposition parties have pledged to establish one if they are elected.

Sharon Sharabi, also on Yisrael Beitenu’s list of candidates, is the brother of Eli Sharabi, a former hostage who was released from Gaza only to learn that his wife and two teenage daughters had been killed during the Oct. 7 attack. Another brother, Yossi Sharabi, was also taken hostage and killed after 100 days in captivity. Sharon Sharabi campaigned tirelessly for his brothers’ return. When Eli Sharabi was finally released, many Israelis were outraged over how emaciated he looked. “I was shocked,” Sharon said at the time. “I’d been told he would be thin, but I didn’t imagine how thin. It was extreme.”

Tali Gvili, running with Mr. Netanyahu’s Likud party, is the mother of Master Sgt. Ran Gvili, a member of a police counterterrorism unit who was shot and severely wounded in combat on Oct. 7 and then dragged into Gaza. His remains were recovered and returned to Israel in January 2026. The Gvili and Netanyahu families have become close, and the prime minister attended Sergeant Gvili’s state funeral, saying, “Our souls are bound with yours.”

Michal Hirsch Negri is running with Together, a joint slate led by right-wing politician Naftali Bennett and the centrist Yair Lapid. Ms. Hirsch Negri’s son Maj. Roee Negri was killed fighting in Kibbutz Be’eri near the Gaza border on Oct. 7.

Maj. Shahar Varon, a commander in the reserves, is another Together candidate. He fought that day in Kfar Aza, another border community, and later went to fight in Gaza. He was wounded in battle, then went back into Gaza to fight again. “There is life before October 7th, and there is life after,” he wrote recently, adding, “Our government disappeared that morning — but our people showed up instead.”

World.title: Before the election, Netanyahu offered a grim economic forecast for Israel.

Shira Shapiro, right, a candidate for the Yashar party, meeting with Gadi Eisenkot at a roadside bomb shelter where her son died during the Oct. 7 2023, attack, near Reim, Israel, earlier this month.

World.title: Luxury cruise passengers stranded in Cambodia due to soaring fuel costs
World.content:
A luxury cruise ship on a years-long voyage around the world said it suspended operations due to extraordinarily high fuel costs, leaving passengers stranded in Cambodia.

The US-based operator of the Villa Vie Odyssey said it was working with passengers on disembarkation plans and "temporary living arrangements".

It is unclear how many were on board but the nearly 200m (656ft) vessel can carry up to 650 passengers. It departed Belfast in October 2024 for a "continuous voyage around the world".

Global fuel prices have soared since the Iran war started earlier this year. The ship's operator said the monthly fuel cost per cabin in parts of Asia has risen to as much as $8,000 (Â£6,000) from $1,800.

Villa Vie Residences said it had taken "significant steps to reduce fuel consumption, including slowing the itinerary and spending more time in port". But those measures turned out to be insufficient to "offset the extraordinary increase in fuel costs".

"Passing the full increase on to residents is not a realistic solution," it said.

The company would spend the next 60 days on "restructuring and recapitalisation", though "no outcome is assured", it said.

There were reportedly around 200 passengers on board when they were ordered to disembark in the Cambodian port city of Sihanoukville, a once sleepy beach town that has gained global notoriety in recent years as a hub for Chinese casinos and scam centres.

The Villa Vie Odyssey's voyage was expected to span 3.5 years and cover nearly 150 countries, according to its website.

Its departure had faced delays as the ship underwent repairs, leaving passengers stranded in Belfast for months and costing the company millions of pounds.

The ship was more than 750 days into its circumnavigation before announcing its suspension of its journey on Tuesday - which means its passengers would now be stranded in Cambodia.

Passengers Lanette Canen and Johan Bodin told the BBC they were informed by Villa Vie Residences' chief executive at 6am on Tuesday that they had to leave by 2pm on the same day.

The couple said passengers had known for some time about the company's financial difficulties. A potential investor had previously come onboard the ship to do due dilligence, but in the end it did not work out.

"Even then, we were still hoping a miracle investor would come through," they said. "Although there were signs that this would happen, we still felt disbelief when it became real. We were heartbroken. It felt like our dream had been crushed."

"There have been a lot of hugs and tears as residents support one another and process what has happened."

Another passenger Holly Hennessey said that the ship's passengers had earlier been asked to consider paying a fuel surcharge as global prices soared, and that their itinerary had been "severely curtailed".

Some people decided to disembark and travel on land, she said.

"It was not on my bingo card of places where I'd be spending a lot of time," Hennessey told the BBC from Cambodia.

"We're all in different hotels; there are a number of shipmates in the hotel that I'm in. We're just waiting."

Canen and Bodin said the location in Cambodia was "a difficult place to disembark" because of the distance to a major international airport.

World.title: Serbian shot dead after attacking officer outside Israeli embassy, minister says
World.content:
Serbian police shot dead a young man outside the Israeli embassy in Belgrade in the early hours of Wednesday after what authorities called a "terrorist attack".

The country's interior minister, Ivica Dacic, said the attacker had rushed at a police officer with two knives while shouting the phrase "Allahu Akbar". The officer sustained a minor knife wound to the face and shot the attacker.

Dacic said the suspect has not been identified, but he was a minor and Serbian citizen who was being monitored by security services as he was "known to be a supporter of the Islamic State".

Speaking to reporters outside the embassy, Dacic said an investigation is ongoing, but security services said the suspect had posted a picture of the Islamic State flag on his Instagram.

Dacic raised the country's terrorism threat level to "red alert" - the highest threat level â meaning stricter security checks and increased police presence at places like infrastructure facilities and areas where large crowds gather.

The interior minister said he had visited the injured police officer, who was reportedly doing well and did not need hospital care for his wounds.

Armed security personnel were seen standing guard outside the Israeli embassy on Wednesday morning.

Israel's foreign ministry confirmed in a social media post that no embassy personnel were injured and the mission was closed at the time of the incident.

This is the second such attack on Belgrade's Israeli embassy in less than three years; in June 2024, a man shot a police officer in the neck with a crossbow.

The officer who was shot survived the attack and shot dead the assailant, identified as a Serbian man who had converted to Islam.

Wednesday's attack comes just one day after elections in Israel.

World.title: Tanzania celebrates first natural gas discovery in more than 10 years
World.content:
Tanzania has announced a significant discovery of natural gas in the Mnazi Bay area in the south of the country - the first such find in a decade.

Energy Minister Juma Homera attended a ceremony at the Kasa-1X ST2 well, which is jointly owned by state-owned Tanzania Petroleum Development Corporation (TPDC) and French oil firm Maurel & Prom, to mark the occasion.

He said the estimated 223 billion cubic feet (6.3 billion cubic metres) discovery was a "major milestone" in the development of the small oil and gas sector in the East African nation.

The new well is expected to start production early next month and is intended to boost domestic supplies.

Tanzania has existing natural gas reserves of 57.54 trillion cubic feet.

World.title: Anger in Kenya over extradition hearing delay for ex-British soldier accused of murdering woman
World.content:
Wanjiru's niece, Esther Njoki, told the BBC that the family had learnt of the postponement through the UK embassy and had received no official explanation.

"We have exercised patience and endured uncertainty for years, but our patience is now being taken advantage of," she said in a statement.

"Agnes deserves justice. Her daughter Stacy deserves answers about what happened. And as a family, we deserve to be treated with dignity and kept informed about proceedings that profoundly affect our lives."

The family said it had already raised money and made arrangements to travel to the UK for the hearing, which was due to take place in three weeks.

It is now calling on the authorities to expedite the proceedings, warning that the latest postponement means the case will enter its 15th year without a trial.

The family said a UK court was expected next week to give the reasons for the hearing delay.

Wanjiru disappeared in March 2012 after spending an evening at a hotel in Nanyuki, about 200km (124 miles) north of the capital, Nairobi, where British soldiers were stationed for training.

Her body was found nearly three months later in a septic tank at the hotel. She had suffered stab wounds to her chest and abdomen and left behind a five-month-old daughter.

A Kenyan inquest concluded in 2019 that she had been unlawfully killed by one or two British soldiers.

In September 2025, a Kenyan High Court issued an arrest warrant for a British national after prosecutors presented evidence they said justified bringing murder charges.

Purkiss' lawyers said he intended to contest his extradition to Kenya.

He appeared at Westminster Magistrates' Court in February via video link, where he was further remanded in custody.

Last year, the then British Defence Secretary John Healey met Wanjiru's family during a visit to Kenya and pledged his government's support for efforts to secure justice.

The UK government has previously said it remains committed to helping the family, but would not comment on ongoing legal proceedings.

World.title: Ceasefire extended across Ukraine's Kherson region, officials say
World.content:
A ceasefire that began with the aim of getting food and medicine to the Russian-occupied Ukrainian city of Oleshky has been extended across the wider southern region of Kherson, according to sources.

Several thousand residents are trapped in the city with no access to food, water and electricity. On one side is the Dnipro river, while Russian forces are on the other and all the roads out are too dangerous.

However, no breaches of the truce that began early on Tuesday have so far been reported.

US First Lady Melania Trump, who helped broker the ceasefire along with Pope Leo XIV, said on Tuesday that the area involved had been expanded to provide "safe passage" for humanitarian convoys.

World.title: King acknowledges 'suffering of the past' as Caribbean tour begins
World.content:
King Charles III has begun his tour of the Caribbean by acknowledging the "great suffering of the past" as he faced calls for slavery reparations.

Speaking an event in the Bahamas celebrating local youth, the King said the country's culture was "born out of darkness", and it was "only right" to acknowledge historic injustices.

His nine-day tour will culminate in the Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting (CHOGM), where the King has confirmed leaders will discuss the region's legacy of slavery.

The visit, his first as monarch, comes in the wake of renewed calls from Caribbean nations for Britain to apologise for its role in selling enslaved people for profit.

Prior to the trip, Buckingham Palace said the King would not shy away from "colonial legacy" and the impact of the slave trade during his visit but, in line with the UK government position, he will not apologise for Britain's role in the slave trade or offer reparations.

Upon his arrival on Tuesday, the King met Governor General Dame Cynthia A. Pratt and its Prime Minister Philip Edward Davis, before speaking with members of the Royal Bahamas Defence Force as he inspected a guard of honour.

King Charles, wearing sunglasses and a grey suit, was then met with cheers as he arrived for his first engagement at a youth rally at Clifford Park - where he attended independence celebrations for the Bahamas as Prince of Wales in 1973.

The young people in the crowd had been given time off school for the event. "It's my first time seeing him in person out of TikTok so he's out there, it's cool," one student told the BBC.

A small group of protesters gathered close to the rally shouting "pay us what you owe us" and "return artefacts you've stolen."

The group of around a dozen protesters was kept outside the main venue as they called on the King to help change the UK government's position on apologising and offering reparations.

"He's a man of influence. The Crown still has influence. And if they do not do it then we will become a republic and we will turn our backs on England if you do not show respect to the former colonies," said one protester, Sharon Purcer-Cooper.

World.title: Dutch zookeeper dies after being mauled by leopard
World.content:
An experienced keeper at a Dutch zoo has died days after being mauled in a leopard enclosure, the safari park has confirmed.

The woman, who had worked at Beekse Bergen park for 40 years, was caring for two Persian leopards in an indoor facility when she was attacked on Saturday.

She sustained injuries to her head and neck and had emergency surgery, but the park confirmed her death on Tuesday.

An independent investigation will be launched into the incident, it added in a statement.

Announcing her death, Beekse Bergen - in the south of the Netherlands - said the keeper began her career there when she was 17 and had worked there on-and-off for four decades.

"Her passing has deeply affected us all, and our hearts go out to her family, friends, and loved ones. At this moment, our primary focus is on supporting her family and her colleagues," the statement added.

The two leopards, which are usually kept away from staff, had been brought inside due to bad weather conditions.

It is not clear exactly what happened in the enclosure because there are no CCTV cameras inside.

Local news website NL Times reported that despite her injuries she managed to alert colleagues via her walkie-talkie. She was then taken to hospital in a helicopter in a critical condition.

A park spokesperson told Omroep Brabant, a local media outlet, that the leopards were behaving naturally and they would not be euthanised.

"They are, and remain, predators."

Beekse Bergen said it would create a memorial location for guests and staff members to share their condolences.

World.title: Norway and Finland leaders hold rare call with Putin
World.content:
The leaders of Finland and Norway have held a joint call with Vladimir Putin - rare contact between the Russian president and European leaders.

Finland's President Alexander Stubb and Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr StÃ¸re said the aim of the call had been to "convey messages directly regarding future negotiations" towards peace. An end to the conflict in Ukraine "will not be achieved through silence," Stubb said.

Neither side suggested the needle had been moved on ending the war, which began when Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.

Although the Finnish leader said the conversation with Putin had been "frank and substantive," StÃ¸re added that there were "big differences in views" with Putin.

Several European leaders have recently shown willingness to engage with Russia directly, but both Stubb and StÃ¸re pointed out their initiative was taken in their capacity as neighbours of Russia, rather than on behalf of Europe as a whole.

"We've not set out to speak on behalf of anyone other than ourselves," StÃ¸re said.

Stubb added the call had been prepared in consultation with Ukraine and the US following a meeting between Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky, the Nordic leaders and US special envoy Steve Witkoff in Oslo last week.

The first trilateral US-Ukraine-Russia talks since the start of the year are tentatively planned for early November in Abu Dhabi.

Zelensky later confirmed Stubb and StÃ¸re debriefed him after the call and said he was grateful for their "active support", while his Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said the call had been "the right approach".

Finland and Norway, which border Russia, initiated the 90-minute call - held from Helsinki - to "discuss Russia's war of aggression against Ukraine and the diplomatic efforts to end the war and promote peace and stability in Europe", the leaders' offices said.

StÃ¸re added: "The war comes with enormous human and material costs... The suffering and destruction will impact generations."

The Kremlin said Putin told the leaders that "a just and lasting peace" would only be possible if Russia's interests were considered.

Putin also reaffirmed to the Nordic leaders what he views as the "root causes" of the conflict - his frequent shorthand for Ukraine's desire to exist as a sovereign state.

"A fair long-term peace settlement is possible only if Russia's legal interests are taken into account fully and unconditionally", Putin said.

All three parties reportedly agreed to continue their direct phone communication.

World.title: Nigeria’s Future Eagles thrash New Caledonia 7-0 to reach U-15 World Cup Round of 16
World.content:
Nigeria’s Future Eagles produced a dominant attacking display on Wednesday, thrashing New Caledonia 7-0 to reach the Tier C Round of 16 at the 2026 FIFA U-15 World Cup and Festival in Baku, Azerbaijan.

Oche opened the scoring in the first minute before Ijachi doubled Nigeria’s advantage in the 12th minute and struck again four minutes later.

Muhammad extended the lead in the 21st minute as Nigeria continued to overwhelm their opponents.

Ijachi completed his hat-trick in the 35th minute, while Muhammad scored his second goal four minutes later. Salu then found the net in the 40th minute to complete the emphatic victory.

The seven-goal haul provided a significant boost for the Nigerian youngsters as they turned their attention to the knockout rounds.

Future Eagles rediscover scoring touch

Nigeria entered the second phase after finishing third in Group AD with seven points from five matches, scoring 11 goals and conceding 10.

The Future Eagles opened their campaign with a 3-3 draw against South Sudan before playing out a 2-2 stalemate with Jordan. They subsequently drew 3-3 with The Gambia.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

Bassey’s side recorded their only group-stage victory with a 2-1 comeback win over Cyprus before sharing the points in a 1-1 draw against Pakistan in their final fixture.

Their third-place finish placed them in Tier C, where Wednesday’s convincing victory over New Caledonia has put them in contention for the tier’s title.

READ ALSO: Warri Wolves appeal NPFL sanctions over referee assault

Nigeria face Benin or Cuba next

The Future Eagles will face either Benin or Cuba in the Tier C Round of 16 on Thursday, 29 October, as they seek to maintain their momentum in the competition.

The 2026 FIFA U-15 World Cup and Festival features an eight-a-side format, with matches played over two 20-minute halves. Teams are grouped into six tiers based on their qualification-phase performances, with a winner emerging from each tier.

Nigeria will hope to build on their emphatic victory over New Caledonia and progress further in the knockout stage as they pursue the Tier C title.

World.title: CSOs identify stigma, poor facilities as barriers to HIV, TB, malaria treatment in Akwa Ibo
World.content:
Civil society organisations and health workers in Akwa Ibom State have identified stigma, cultural restrictions, inadequate health facilities and concerns about confidentiality as barriers limiting access to HIV, tuberculosis (TB) and malaria treatment.

They are calling for urgent government action to make healthcare more accessible to women and other vulnerable groups.

The stakeholders made the observations on Friday in Uyo at a one-day meeting to evaluate compliance with gender-responsive health policies in the state.

They called on the government to improve public awareness of available services, train health workers to treat patients without discrimination and equip primary healthcare centres to encourage service uptake.

They also called for consistent data collection to track HIV, TB and malaria cases and assess the implementation of policies designed to address gender-related inequalities in healthcare.

The meeting was organised by Lawyers Alert in partnership with Media Health and Rights Initiative of Nigeria (MHR) as part of efforts to strengthen accountability and promote gender-responsive policies in the state’s health sector.

Edidiong Enang, programme manager of Vitonia Lead Foundation, said cultural beliefs that discourage women from speaking up, economic hardship and institutional barriers continued to prevent women from accessing healthcare on equal terms.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

“We have cultural barriers that people believe that women are not supposed to speak up,” she said, adding that women who lacked economic independence often experienced delays in seeking healthcare.

Ms Enang said some health facilities were not sufficiently gender-friendly, while stigma could discourage women from seeking services even when they were available.

She said the project had strengthened the capacity of participating civil society organisations to engage ministries, departments and agencies, as well as public officials responsible for policy decisions.

She called for sustained advocacy to ensure that government institutions addressed the barriers and included women in healthcare interventions.

CSOs seek better-equipped health facilities

Participants said the government needed to do more than establish policies and build model health facilities, stressing that primary healthcare centres must also be adequately equipped to provide accessible and reliable services.

They called on authorities to intensify public sensitisation about available healthcare services and train health workers to be more accommodating and maintain patients’ confidentiality.

The organisations also stressed the need for consistent data on HIV, TB and malaria to improve case tracking and measure the effectiveness of interventions.

However, health workers from primary healthcare facilities said malaria treatment in the state was free when testing confirmed the infection.

They explained that the state’s policy required patients to undergo testing before treatment, noting that not every fever was caused by malaria.

Ubong Ekpo, representing the state Ministry of Health, said the government had intensified efforts to identify tuberculosis cases, including through house-to-house testing in rural communities.

He also said that the state had three sexual assault referral centres at Ikot Ekpene General Hospital, Iquita Hospital in Oron and Immanuel Hospital in Eket.

Mr Ekpo said the Ministry of Health is working closely with the Ministry of Justice on relevant interventions.

Akwa Ibom yet to assent to anti-stigma law

Enobong Akpan, project manager of the Akwa Ibom State Agency for the Control of AIDS, said the state had domesticated several HIV-related policies but was yet to have the governor’s assent to an anti-stigma law passed by the State House of Assembly.

PREMIUM TIMES’ investigation had shown how this has caused avoidable deaths and increased infections in Akwa Ibom State.

Mr Akpan said the bill had been received by Governor Umo Eno and forwarded to the Ministry of Justice for review before assent.

He commended Lawyers Alert for providing technical support to the state, particularly in reviewing its HIV workplace policy.

According to him, Akwa Ibom has policies covering HIV prevention, workplace protection, care and treatment, prevention of mother-to-child transmission, and key and vulnerable populations.

He said the state reviewed its HIV workplace policy last year with support from Lawyers Alert and was planning to unveil the revised document.

READ ALSO: Court remands man who killed girlfriend over alleged HIV infection

On tuberculosis, Mr Akpan said the state had policies on care and treatment, including for multidrug-resistant TB, describing the care and treatment policy as functional.

The discussions at the meeting pointed to the gap between having policies in place and ensuring that vulnerable people can access services without discrimination.

About the project

Lawyers Alert and MHR launched their Gender Equality Fund project in Akwa Ibom in October 2024.

The two-and-a-half-year initiative, supported through the Global Fund to Fight AIDS, Tuberculosis and Malaria in partnership with GSK and ViiV Healthcare, is being implemented in Akwa Ibom and Benue states.

Tagged “Law, Rights and Community Empowerment for Social Change in TB, HIV and Malaria Response,” the project seeks to strengthen women-led organisations and equip women leaders to demand accountability and advocate policies that address gender-related barriers to healthcare.

The Uyo meeting brought together government officials, health workers and civil society organisations to assess the implementation of gender-responsive policies, identify gaps in service delivery and clarify the responsibilities of institutions, health facilities and communities.

Participants said the findings should guide advocacy and practical action to make healthcare services more inclusive and accountable.

World.title: Reps propose road concession, toll gates to tackle Nigeria’s infrastructure deficit
World.content:
The House of Representatives has called for the concession of eligible federal roads to private investors and the reintroduction of toll gates on selected highways as part of measures to address the country’s deteriorating road infrastructure.

The call was made in a motion jointly sponsored by Esosa Iyawe (APC, Edo), Olusola Fatoba (APC, Ekiti), Abdulmaleek Danga (PDP, Kogi) and Uche Okonkwo (NDC, Anambra) during Wednesday’s plenary.

Presenting the motion, Mr Iyawe said the poor condition of several federal roads was largely caused by prolonged neglect, inadequate maintenance, insufficient funding and the pressure from heavy-duty vehicles.

He said the situation has led to avoidable accidents, loss of life, vehicle damage, higher transportation costs, and delays in the movement of people and goods.

Mr Iyawe, in particular, highlighted the condition of federal roads in Edo State, describing the state as a major transportation corridor linking the South-South and South-east with other parts of the country.

He identified the Benin-Lagos, Benin-Asaba, Benin-Warri, and Benin-Okene corridors as roads requiring urgent rehabilitation.

According to him, the poor condition of the roads has affected commercial activities, increased the cost of transporting agricultural produce and other essential commodities, discouraged investment and imposed economic hardship on residents, commuters and businesses.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

The lawmaker said relying on annual budgetary allocations to rehabilitate and maintain the extensive federal road network has not consistently delivered the required level of infrastructure renewal.

He therefore proposed using transparent Public-Private Partnership arrangements to attract private capital, technical expertise, and efficient project management for the rehabilitation, operation, and long-term maintenance of eligible federal roads.

He also called for the reintroduction of toll gates on selected rehabilitated highways, arguing that tolling could help private investors recover their investments while providing funds for routine maintenance and road safety operations.

“The reintroduction of properly regulated toll gates on selected rehabilitated federal highways could provide a sustainable mechanism for recovering private investment, financing routine maintenance, supporting road safety operations and generating revenue for the Federal Government,” the motion stated.

Mr Iyawe said toll gates could also create direct and indirect employment for host communities through toll administration, security services, traffic management, road maintenance and other businesses.

He further argued that strategically located toll plazas could serve as additional points for lawful security presence, intelligence gathering, emergency response and monitoring of vehicular movements when properly coordinated with security agencies.

However, he stressed that any tolling arrangement must be transparent, affordable and technologically efficient, with enforceable service standards to ensure motorists receive measurable improvements in road quality and safety in return for their payments.

He asked the House to urge the Federal Ministry of Works to develop a national framework for concessioning eligible federal roads to private investors under transparent PPP arrangements, prioritising roads requiring urgent rehabilitation and major economic corridors.

He also urged the Ministry, in collaboration with the Infrastructure Concession Regulatory Commission, the Federal Roads Maintenance Agency, and other relevant agencies, to assess the federal road network and identify roads suitable for concessioning, rehabilitation, operation, and long-term maintenance.

Mr Iyawe further called for the reintroduction of toll gates on selected federal highways after substantial rehabilitation and the establishment of clear concession agreements.

The lawmaker said toll charges should be determined through transparent economic assessments, public consultation and affordability considerations.

Lawmakers seconded the motion, and Ajang Iliya (APC, Plateau) adopted it without debate.

Speaker Abbas Tajudeen, who presided over the plenary, referred the motion to the Committees on Public Assets, Works and Finance for further legislative action.

The committees are expected to engage relevant agencies on the proposed framework and report to the House within four weeks for further legislative action.

World.title: Cybersecurity: EFCC strengthens digital systems to combat financial crimes – Official
World.content:
The Economic and Financial Crimes Commission (EFCC) says it is strengthening its digital systems and cybersecurity capabilities to combat increasingly sophisticated financial crimes.

‎EFCC chairman Olanipekun Olukoyede, represented by Nwanyinma Okeanu, deputy director, public affairs department of the commission, said this at the second edition of the International Cybersecurity Conference (ICSC) 2026 in Abuja on Tuesday.

‎The two-day conference has its theme as ‘Cyber Resilience in the Age of AI: Defending Minds, Networks and Nations’.

‎Mr Olukoyede said criminals were increasingly exploiting digital technologies to target thousands of people, move funds across borders and conceal their activities.

‎“For us in law enforcement, the message is clear: as crime evolves, our response must evolve with it,” he said.

‎He said the commission had embarked on a digital transformation programme to reduce manual processes, improve access to information, automate workflows and enhance operational efficiency.

According to him, the initiative has produced several digital platforms supporting the commission’s operations, including the e-Petition Platform, Enterprise Case Management System (ECMS), Fraud Risk Assessment and Management System, and Asset Management System.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

‎“Every new system and digital service creates opportunities, but it also introduces risks,” he said.

‎The EFCC chairman said the anti-graft agency was strengthening network and information security, improving security monitoring and access controls, and enhancing incident response mechanisms.

‎Momo Cyprus, the chairman of the Defence, Intelligence and Security Committee of the Liberian Senate, called for responsible use of AI to protect citizens, institutions and national security.

Mr ‎Cyprus, who represents Lofa County in his country’s senate, said AI offered significant opportunities to improve public services, expand education, accelerate research and empower African innovators.

‎However, he warned that the technology could also be exploited to spread disinformation, facilitate fraud and undermine public confidence in political institutions.

‎“Our task is not to fear technological progress, but to ensure that it serves humanity responsibly,” he said.

‎ The Liberian senator cited the 2026 African Cyber Threat Assessment Report by the International Criminal Police Organisation (INTERPOL), which highlighted the growing sophistication of cybercrime and the increasing use of AI by criminals.

‎He called for digital literacy, critical thinking, public awareness and responsible communication to help citizens identify and avoid online deception.

‎“We must encourage every citizen to pause, verify and act carefully before sharing information or responding to suspicious requests,” Cyprus said.

‎On defending networks, Mr Cyprus said governments, banks, hospitals, communication systems and energy infrastructure increasingly depended on secure digital networks to function effectively.

‎He said Liberia had taken steps to strengthen its cybersecurity framework through the Cybercrime Act of 2025 and the National Cybersecurity Strategy for 2025 to 2029 with ways of creating adequate implementation in mind.

‎The two-day conference brought together policymakers, cybersecurity professionals, law enforcement agencies and other stakeholders to discuss strategies for strengthening digital resilience in the age of AI.

(NAN)

World.title: ANALYSIS: The criminalisation trap in Africa’s responses to artisanal mining
World.content:
Thirty-seven boys and young men died in the custody of the Nigeria Security and Civil Defence Corps (NSCDC) in Minna, Niger State, last month. Accused of being ‘illegal miners’, they were arrested during raids by the Mining Marshals – a special NSCDC unit targeting illegal mining.

Yesterday, an investigative panel found they died of asphyxiation in ‘inhumane conditions’, calling the deaths preventable. Recommendations to compensate families, dismiss and prosecute the officers involved, and implement institutional reforms (among others) are significant, as they address the gravity of abuses and the need for holistic responses.

Such incidents are not unique to Nigeria, and offer a critical lens for examining recent human rights abuses at artisanal mining sites across Africa.

These sites are guarded by multiple actors, including state security, paramilitary outfits like NSCDC, private security, mercenaries and armed groups. Crimes they mete out against miners include trafficking, enslavement, extortion, sexual violence, child labour, forced recruitment and labour, arbitrary detention, torture and murder.

Artisanal miners and traders face not only abuses by government security forces, but also state failure to protect them from violations by non-state actors, including other miners.

In Central Africa, Institute for Security Studies research reveals that security forces in Cameroon, the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) and the Central African Republic (CAR) have perpetrated violence, including summary executions, against artisanal miners and mining communities. In the DRC, miners suffer abuse both from the Rwanda-backed M23 and private security guards.

South Africa’s zama zamas illustrate how illegal mining networks intersect with organised crime. Groups reportedly seize abandoned mines, extort other miners for protection, and steal gold from legal operations. Entangled in turf wars that inflame community conflict, these activities are compounded by alleged police corruption, limited enforcement capacity, and weak oversight of abandoned mines.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

The Krugersdorp gang-rape case highlights the severe security risks zama zamas pose. Similar patterns exist in the CAR, where the Séléka and Anti-Balaka profit from the country’s diamond trade, sometimes taking over mining sites.

Artisanal and small-scale miners (ASM) in Africa number roughly 13.2 million. There are 2.6 million in Central Africa alone, an increase of over 2,500 per cent from approximately 100,000 in 2013 – driven by a rising demand for mineral resources amid a surge in global commodity prices. Gold hit a record high of $4,000/ounce in 2025, with similar spikes in critical mineral prices.

Across Africa, ASM supplies substantial shares of mineral production, with an annual foreign exchange value of around $3 billion-$5 billion. ASM accounted for 32-41 per cent of Africa’s total gold production in 2022 and 52-74 per cent of global tantalum production between 2017 and 2023, underlining its significant role in the extractive economy.

The scale of ASM in Africa must also be understood in the context of low educational attainment and high unemployment. ASM appeals to young people with few livelihood options. For many, including out-of-school children, it’s a means of survival.

Regulatory gaps further expose miners to human rights abuses. Mining laws across Central Africa generally permit ASM, often within designated areas, and criminalise unlicensed activity. But artisanal miners struggle to obtain permission, facing bureaucratic delays, high administrative costs and complex permit procedures that leave many operating outside legal protections.

The state’s coercive implementation of regulations enables abuses at mining sites. And the criminalisation of ASM exposes miners to exploitation and violence by criminal elements, who commonly demand ‘taxes’, intelligence or ‘protection’ money in exchange for miners’ freedom to pursue their livelihoods. This coerced cooperation increases artisanal miners’ vulnerability, as criminals violate these agreements with lethal violence.

Without differentiating between survival miners and criminal networks, such transactional relationships can be misread as collusion, thereby legitimising security force targeting of miners.

The situation is exacerbated in countries like Chad and South Africa, where political elites and military personnel reportedly sponsor or engage in mining, employ artisanal miners, provide logistical support and receive gold in exchange for private protection. This creates conflicts of interest – and influences selective enforcement of regulations.

Many miners are driven by poverty. Criminalising ASM perpetuates their vulnerability, exposing them to unhealthy working conditions and exploitation, while governments penalise small-scale miners and not concession owners. It can also lead to unrest. In Ghana, some communities have resisted enforcement efforts, saying they threaten their livelihoods.

Criminalisation does not solve the problems posed by ASM; it merely drives miners underground, further exposing them to danger and exploitation, and fuelling crime. Crackdowns and lethal attacks against artisanal miners reveal a limited state understanding of ASM’s complexities, reluctance to confront entrenched mining interests, and inconsistent enforcement due to uncertainty over how to regulate it.

There are valid concerns about ASM’s economic, environmental, infrastructural and human security impacts in Africa and globally. However, purely coercive responses to this complex social phenomenon are counterproductive.

Recent events point to the securitisation of mineral wealth, state desperation to assert sovereignty over ungoverned spaces, minimal accountability and human rights protections, and environmental and governance failures. These dynamics suggest a tacit admission that mining regulations in resource-rich African countries have failed, while states continue to conflate ASM with illegal mining.

The October meeting in Accra on strengthening ASM across the continent was timely. It was attended by political and traditional leaders, the United Nations, the African Union, the private sector, media and international partners, and followed on from last year’s summit on the issue.

But authorities also need to recognise artisanal miners as partners in extractive economies. That requires legislative reforms that define ASM’s scope and protect artisanal miners from human rights abuses by rogue security and law enforcement agents and others. Where infractions occur, investigations and prosecutions should follow.

Countries should expand income-generating opportunities for youth to reduce recruitment into armed conflict and dependence on exploitative mining. That could include investing in industry-aligned vocational training, entrepreneurship, digital skills and creative industries that support their aspirations and economic independence.

Titilope F Ajayi is a Senior Research Consultant, and Oluwole Ojewale is a Senior Researcher in the Central Africa Observatory at the Institute for Security Studies (ISS).

(This article was first published by ISS Today, a Premium Times syndication partner. We have their permission to republish).

World.title: Court dismisses Nollywood actor’s N10bn damages suit against Wike’s aide, INEC
World.content:
The Federal High Court in Abuja on Wednesday dismissed a N10 billion rights suit filed by the Nollywood actor, Emeka Ike, against Lere Olayinka, spokesperson for FCT Minister Nyesom Wike, and the Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC).

Judge Salim Ibrahim, in a judgement, upheld the preliminary objections of the respondents on the grounds that the suit was incompetent and improperly constituted.

Mr Ibrahim also held that suit lacked proof for its claims.
