World.title: Kikuyu PCEA church loses 2.7-acre illegally acquired land
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

Justice Jacqueline Mogeni, in her verdict, said the land in contention was public property and its registration in the name of the said church was irregular and fraudulent. [Courtesy, EACC]

The Presbyterian Church of East Africa (PCEA) has lost its 2.7-acre piece of land to a school.

This is after the Environment and Lands Court at Thika established that the land under the church's Ruguthi Women's Guild was a school playground and was illegally allocated.

Presiding Judge Jacqueline Mogeni, in her verdict, said the land in contention was public property, and its registration in the name of the said church was irregular and fraudulent.

According to her, the land had been reserved for use as a playground by Kanyiha, Lusigetti and Njumbi Primary Schools.

The verdict follows a case filed by the Law Society of Kenya, with the Ethics and Anti-Corruption Commission (EACC) participating as an interested party.

In a statement on Monday, EACC's head of Corporate Affairs and Communication Stephen Karuga said the anti-graft agency presented evidence demonstrating that the land had been reserved for public use and therefore, any allocation to third parties was irregular. Justice Jacqueline Mogeni, in her verdict, said the land in contention was public property and its registration in the name of the said church was irregular and fraudulent. [Courtesy, EACC]

"Our investigations established that the land was set aside in 1957 by the former County Council of Kiambu for use as a school playing field," Karuga said, adding, "the investigations further revealed that there was no letter of offer or acceptance, no evidence of payment of rent rates and no proof that the Women's Guild had paid any consideration to the council for the land."

According to Karuga, the judgement safeguards a vital public facility used by more than 1,300 pupils, ensuring that the playground remains available for learning, sports and recreation for the current and future generations.

As a result, the judge said the allocation, transfer and registration of the land LR. NO KARAI/350 and subsequent issuance of a title deed in 2001 was unprocedural, illegal, null and void.

"An order of Mandamus is hereby issued directing the 3rd respondent, the Land Registrar, Kiambu Chief Land Registrar, to forthwith cancel and revoke the Title Deed and all register entries in respect of the land issued to the 1st respondent on Dec 6, 2001, or at any subsequent date," the Judge said.

The judge further ordered that the said parcel of land be handed over to the Board of Management of the two schools and the Education Ministry.

"An order of permanent injunction is hereby issued restraining the 1st respondent, whether by herself, her church officials, agents, servants, assigns or anyone claiming through her, from entering into, taking possession of, fencing, depositing construction materials upon, transferring, charging, developing or in any other manner dealing or interfering with the land," she ordered.

World.title: Sakaja protests release of 14 suspects linked to Eastleigh collapsed building
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

Sakaja demanded answers from Kamukunji Police on how the suspects were arrested in June but released on Sh50,000 bail without being charged in court. [GPS]

Nairobi Governor Johnson Sakaja has protested the release of suspects linked to the collapsed building in Eastleigh.

While pushing for the county to have prosecutorial powers, Sakaja demanded answers from Kamukunji Police on how the suspects were arrested in June but released on Sh50,000 bail without being charged in court.

Sakaja in statement posted on his X account (formerly Twitter) said City Hall had taken enforcement action against those involved after establishing change of user from a residential property to a commercial had been approved.

According to Sakaja, architectural plans required to authorise construction had not been approved.

The Governor said County officers arrested the suspects and handed them over to Kamukunji Police Station because county governments no longer hold prosecutorial powers they previously held.

“We enforced the law and arrested those involved. However, because we do not have prosecutorial powers, the suspects were handed over to Kamukunji Police Station. They were reportedly released on a cash bail of Sh50,000 without being taken to court,” Sakaja said.

“We want the police to explain why the suspects were released without being presented in court and why construction was allowed to continue. These are serious questions that must be answered,” he added.

A police occurrence book entry from Kamukunji Police Station indicates that 14 suspects were booked into custody on June 17, 2026, over the alleged offences relating to contravention of city planning laws.

Enforcement action and arrests were made severally by the county officials and most recently in July after failing to comply with the enforcement order below. However the suspects were released on a 50k bail at Kamukunji police on the very same day. Prosecution of the same was also denied. We have repeatedly asked for the resumption of the power to prosecute such violations of such county and county related laws after this was taken away from County governments in 2024 (one such letter to the office of the DPP is attached). Meanwhile, several such cases have either been rejected by prosecutors (who are independent of the County), dismissed by the justice system or have had minimal fines imposed. Fining a developer 50k for an illegal development with hundreds of millions without orders to stop and remove the offensive development is completely unreasonable. I raised this in the Senate a fortnight ago and we shall keep pushing for a review of this position. All of these instances, where enforcement action has been curtailed, blocked or interfered with, will be published to the public. October 25, 2026

The entry, recorded under OB No. 98/17/06/2026, names the suspects and states that they were booked by Nairobi City County officers before being placed in police cells.

A separate Kenya Police Service record indicates that 10 suspects were subsequently released on a cash bail of Sh50,000.

The entry, recorded at 9.44pm, states that the release was carried out on the instructions of the Officer Commanding Station (OCS), identified in the record as C.I. Onyapidi, through Corporal Awadh.

The record references receipt number 2039434 and states that the suspects left the station without complaints.

However, the documents do not, on their own, establish the specific charges against the suspects, the legal basis for the bail arrangement or whether they were subsequently presented in court.

The discrepancy between the 14 suspects recorded as booked into custody and the 10 named in the release entry also raises questions about the subsequent status of the other suspects. Sakaja demanded answers from Kamukunji Police on how the suspects were arrested in June but released on Sh50,000 bail without being charged in court. [GPS]

Sakaja said a June 2025 enforcement notice adds another dimension to the questions surrounding the property and the enforcement of planning regulations.

The notice, issued by Nairobi City County over alleged construction works undertaken without the required development permission, cited the Physical and Land Use Planning Act, 2019, and county by-laws.

It directed the recipient to stop the works and remove the development described as illegal, warning that the County could undertake the required action and recover the costs if the directives were not followed.

The notice also provided for an appeal to the County Physical and Land Use Planning Liaison Committee.

Sakaja clarified that approval to change a property’s use from private to commercial-cum-residential does not amount to approval of architectural plans authorising construction.

He said the County approved the change of use but did not approve the architectural plans, yet construction proceeded.

I have seen some people peddling a fake approval document alleging that the Eastleigh development was approved. It is telling that this is the same document that the Eastleigh developer used to get NCA approval. They allege that the development was approved in January of 2024. This is not true. The application for development as shown below was made in November of 2024, it could not have been approved in February of the same year. Also, there is a difference between a change of user approval and a development approval. The developer applied for change of use from residential to residential & commercial in August of 2024. Change of user was approved in October of 2024. Development approval has never been granted. The developer went on to build with impunity and without building approvals despite enforcement action by the county and arrests. — Sakaja Arthur Johnson (@SakajaJohnson) October 25, 2026

“If the building had been approved for construction, I would have named the officers who approved it so that action could be taken against them,” he said.

Sakaja, in his argument, said the current arrangement creates a gap between enforcement and prosecution, leaving counties dependent on other agencies after taking action against alleged offenders. Sakaja demanded answers from Kamukunji Police on how the suspects were arrested in June but released on Sh50,000 bail without being charged in court. [GPS]

Under his proposal, appropriately authorised county prosecutors would be able to pursue qualifying county offences through the courts, subject to the law and the constitutional authority of the Director of Public Prosecutions.

He said county prosecutors previously had a better understanding of technical offences involving planning, construction and other county regulations, enabling them to handle such cases more directly.

“We want to be able not only to enforce regulations and make arrests, but also to take offenders to court and prosecute them. When counties had prosecutorial powers, we had prosecutors who understood the nature and seriousness of county offences and could ensure that appropriate legal action was taken,” he said.

World.title: Pregnant woman rescued from collapsed Eastleigh building
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

Kenya Red Cross workers after rescuing a man who trapped in the rubble.

A pregnant woman was on Saturday evening rescued from the multi-storey building that collapsed in Nairobi’s Eastleigh estate on Friday, October 23 and rushed to the Kenyatta National Hospital (KNH) for treatment.

She is the second person to rescued as earlier in the afternoon the Kenya Red Cross society announced the rescue of a man from the ill-fated building.

The man was also taken to KNH for treatment with the society saying that the rescue followed hours of work put in by the search and rescue multi-agency team.

“After hours of painstaking work alongside multi-agency partners, our search and rescue teams in Eastleigh brought a trapped man out of the rubble,” said Red Cross.

The rescue comes even as the fate of six people who were reported missing on Friuday remains unknown with rescue teams still continuing with the search at the site of the collapsed building along Yusuf Haji Avenue.

The society said that 66 of the 67 construction workers who were at the site had been traced and accounted for but the search continues for people who may have been near the site of the collapsed building.

The development comes as police announced that they had launched a manhunt for the for the owner and contractor of a building.

Police spokesperson Muchiri Nyaga said that officers had launched a probe in collaboration with relevant bodies to establish the cause of the collapse and determine criminal liability.

“Any individual or entity found culpable of negligence or of violating building regulations will face the full force of the law,” he said in a statement.

Nyaga called on members of public to stay completely clear of Yusuf Haji Avenue and 9th Street to give access to heavy excavators, specialised canine units and rescue personnel to perform their duties.

Earlier Saturday, at least 31 families reported their relatives missing as coordinated rescue efforts entered their second day.

No deaths have been reported so far.

The National Construction Authority (NCA) on Friday evening identified the developer, contractor, architect and structural engineer listed for the collapsed building.

The Authority has faced scrutiny over its oversight role, as Nairobi Governor Johnson Sakaja said the project had failed to comply with construction guidelines.

He said the county had forwarded relevant information to the Directorate of Criminal Investigations for further investigation.

In a statement, the NCA said the building was registered on July 30, 2025, as a proposed development on 9th Street in Eastleigh.

It identified 9th Street Plaza Limited as the developer and Stromax Holdings E.A. Limited as the contractor.

Emmanuel Mwangi Maina was listed as the project architect, while Joseph Muturi Mugu was named as the structural engineer.

World.title: Several feared trapped in Eastleigh building collapse
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

Rescue efforts at the collapsed storey building in Eastleigh 9th street in Nairobi County. [Benard Orwongo Standard]

What was supposed to be a usually busy Friday afternoon in Eastleigh's 9th Street turned chaotic after an 18-floor building that was under construction came down, tumbling.

By Friday evening, rescue operations were still ongoing, with cries from people believed to have been trapped being heard from a distance as bulldozers and rescuers continued the search operation.

Two victims, a man and a woman, who were injured in the building had been rescued and rushed to hospital as the search continued.

Asha Jilo, one of the witnesses, said the building collapsed around 1:09 pm just after the afternoon prayers.

"Immediately after the building collapsed, we started contacting some people we know who work there, one of them was still available on the phone until around 3 pm, when his phone went offline," Jilo shared

On Fridays, Eastleigh is usually a hive of activities, being the main market day, but all the businesses were shut as police were battling rowdy youths, some of them believed to be opportunists.

The building, whose height was said to be about 15 floors, had not been cleared for occupation as required, raising questions about why the investors had allowed it to be taken.

It is said that the ground and first floors were already occupied by businesses, raising fears that the number of victims could be high. Rescue efforts at the collapsed storey building in Eastleigh 9th street in Nairobi County. [Benard Orwongo Standard]

At the time of the collapse, it is said that some construction workers were busy on the upper floors.

Governor Johnson Sakaja, who visited the scene after the collapse, was still gathering information about the building. The first priority was about saving lives.

“The building that collapsed is around 16 floors, and we have got information about the building, but what is more concerned right now is for us to save lives,” said Sakaja

Adding, “Equipment has already been mobilized, excavators and breakers, so we can be able to remove the big debris and save lives,’

The Governor said some developers engage qualified professionals to secure construction approvals before dismissing them and disregarding approved plans and safety standards.

He urged professional bodies to strengthen oversight, investigate such cases and take appropriate disciplinary action, stressing that developers must comply with approved designs, engage qualified personnel and obtain occupation certificates after safety inspections.

Rescue efforts at the collapsed storey building in Eastleigh 9th street in Nairobi County. [Benard Orwongo Standard]

Nairobi Regional Police Commander Issa Mohamud, who was at the scene, said that, according to reliable information, several people were trapped inside the debris, inside the big boulders, and the rescue effort is ongoing.

The city police boss said investigations will be carried out to ascertain who is responsible for any negligence.

“If there will be any death, that is negligence by murder. Whoever is the owner, whoever authorized the building, all of them will be charged properly. But that will come after thorough investigation is done,” he warned

Adding, “We will not excuse anybody on this matter. This has become now and then, and we will make sure that people face the law accordingly for any criminal negligence,”

World.title: Ruto hands over COMESA chairmanship, pushes for levy to fund regional programmes
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

President Ruto and Zimbabwean President Emmerson Mnangagwa during the handover of the Common Market for Eastern and Southern Africa chairmanship at the bloc’s 25th Summit of Heads of State and Government in Harare, Zimbabwe, on Thursday, October 22, 2026. [PCS]

President William Ruto has handed over the Common Market for Eastern and Southern Africa (COMESA) chairmanship to Zimbabwean President Emmerson Mnangagwa.

Ruto took over the one-year chairmanship from Burundi’s President Évariste Ndayishimiye at the 24th COMESA Summit in Nairobi on October 9, 2025.

His tenure focused on using digital technology to deepen regional integration, expand trade and promote inclusive growth.

He handed over the role on Thursday, October 22, during the 25th Comesa Summit of Heads of State and Government in Harare, Zimbabwe, where he urged the regional bloc to fast-track a market levy to finance its programmes and institutions.

“We cannot be ambitious in our plans and timid in our financing. Every programme we agree upon must be matched by the resources to deliver it. Otherwise, our communiqués will promise what our budgets cannot pay for,” Ruto said.

He urged the Comesa Secretariat to fast-track Article 168 of the COMESA Treaty, which provides for the Comesa Market Levy, as the organisation seeks sustainable and predictable financing.

The treaty establishes the levy to generate resources for financing the bloc’s activities.

Ruto said officials from finance ministries, central banks and other relevant agencies would meet to consider a draft COMESA Resource Mobilisation Strategy aimed at strengthening member states’ ownership of regional programmes and finding new ways to raise funds.

He called on member states to make financing central to their discussions, warning that the bloc’s institutions and integration agenda would depend on their ability to fund agreed commitments.

“Can we finance what we commit, and deliver what we finance?” he asked.

Ruto also urged African countries to channel more of their domestic financial resources into African institutions rather than leaving funds in foreign accounts while development projects lack capital.

He said Africa holds more than $4 trillion in domestic financial assets, arguing that regional financial institutions could mobilise more of these resources to support trade, infrastructure and development.

Ruto named the Trade and Development Bank (TDB), the African Trade and Investment Development Insurance (ATIDI) and ZEP-RE among the institutions that could mobilise capital for regional priorities.

He urged African governments to place more reserves with these institutions, finance more projects through them and support their bonds and guarantees.

The outgoing Comesa chairperson said the bloc needed stronger regional value chains and more trade among member states as global supply chains faced disruption and protectionism returned.

“Regional integration is no longer a dream we discuss. It is an economic and strategic necessity,” he noted.

Ruto said Comesa’s economic growth rose from 5.6 per cent in 2024 to 6.4 per cent in 2025, while inflation fell from 31 per cent to 13.2 per cent.

Exports among member states increased by 10.5 per cent to $14.7 billion, their highest level between 2020 and 2025, while exports to global markets rose by 6 per cent to $212 billion, he said.

He argued that African countries needed to process more raw materials locally instead of exporting them and importing finished products.

“To every partner who seeks our minerals, our markets and our young workforce, our offer is clear: invest with us, process with us, build with us,” Ruto added.

He called for partnerships based on mutual benefit and equal treatment, saying African countries should have a greater role in determining how their resources and markets contribute to economic development.

World.title: Judge certifies fresh bid to jail Sakaja, Charles Kerich over Sh76.7m debt as urgent
World.content:
Nairobi Governor Johnson Sakaja. [File, Standard]

The High Court has certified as urgent a fresh application seeking to have Nairobi Governor Johnson Sakaja, former Finance Executive Charles Kerich and two other county officials jailed over an alleged breach of a court-approved payment plan in a Sh106.7 million legal fees dispute.

Justice Francis Gikonyo certified the application by Kwengu & Company Advocates seeking to reinstate a three-month jail sentence previously imposed on Kerich and hold Sakaja, current Finance County Executive Committee Member Ibrahim Auma Nyangoya and Chief Officer for Finance Asha Abdi accountable for the alleged failure to pay Sh76.7 million.

World.title: Why Trump’s latest election warning is impossible to ignore
World.content:
When President Donald Trump signals he might not accept the result of an election, he’s worth taking seriously.

By now, in his fifth national election as Republican Party leader, Trump has an established MO. He spends months whipping up doubts about the voting system and the integrity of election officials while suggesting Democrats may cheat.

Then, he weaponizes the vortex of mistrust he created and implies before votes are counted that the election may not be fair.

A week from Election Day, it feels more like Groundhog Day.

Trump was asked Tuesday if he will accept the midterm election results, which could mean a tough night for the GOP, “whatever happens.”

This would hardly be a question for another other modern president. But Trump’s reply came with a caveat made all the more ominous by his past conduct: “I will, if they are honest elections, yeah.”

There’s a lot to be worried about here, beyond the equivocation of his answer. That’s because Trump effectively presents himself as the sole referee of the probity of an election. When he lost the presidential election in 2020, he falsely claimed fraud, despite multiple Republican officials, courts and even his own Justice Department proving there were no such irregularities.

An election worker processes mail-in ballots at the Los Angeles County Ballot Processing Center during California’s state primary election in the City of Industry on June 2. Patrick T. Fallon/AFP/Getty Images

Trump’s latest hedging over an election came in a threatening context. He’s spent much of this year trying to skew the midterms in the GOP’s favor by pushing a midterm gerrymandering effort in Texas and other states and by unsuccessfully demanding Congress pass a voter registration and ID law that critics say would disenfranchise millions of citizens.

And he recently ordered the Justice Department to sue to block certification of Alaska’s US Senate election if Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan loses, even though the Constitution grants a president no power to administer elections.

Trump insists that a separate candidate named Daniel J. Sullivan could confuse voters and that his candidacy is a Democratic conspiracy. Alaska’s Supreme Court has ruled the second Sullivan can legally run in the election.

In another preemptive strike, the DOJ on Friday ordered California to identify suspected noncitizens on voter rolls and set aside their mail-in ballots — warning that officials who knowingly count noncitizens’ ballots could face criminal liability.

A federal appeals court blocked that DOJ gambit.

In Alaska, Democratic challenger Mary Peltola has asked a judge to strike down the DOJ move before Election Day. But the administration’s maneuvering raises the possibility of a post-election showdown. And in contrast with 2020, when then-Attorney General Bill Barr rebuffed Trump’s accusations of expansive electoral fraud, the department seems less likely to contradict him this time.

President Donald Trump speaks at a midterm campaign rally at Port of Corpus Christi in Corpus Christi on October 27. Kent Nishimura/AFP/Getty Images

Why Trump’s remarks are so worrying

The scars of one of the darkest days in modern American history — January 6, 2021 — mean that Trump’s latest election maneuvering is particularly loaded.

Months before MAGA supporters smashed their way into the US Capitol, some beating up police officers, Trump had been poisoning their confidence in the 2020 election with remarkably similar language to that he used on Tuesday.

“I hope it’s going to be a fair election. If it’s a fair election … I am 100% on board,” Trump said in his first presidential debate against Joe Biden in September 2020. “But if I see tens of thousands of ballots being manipulated, I can’t go along with that.”

Four years later, when Trump was asked by Dana Bash at a CNN presidential debate whether he would accept the result of the election regardless of who won, he replied: “If it’s a fair and legal and good election — absolutely.”

Trump did not dispute the results in 2024. The reason is obvious: He won. Four years earlier he’d lost.

Trump’s serial election denialism in the absence of any widespread US election fraud raises the question of why he, alone among presidents, can’t accept the democratic reality that sometimes you lose elections.

One answer is that Trump has given plentiful evidence that he cares more about power than the principle that voters get to pick their leaders.

Another is that Trump has built a personal brand as one of life’s ultimate winners. This brittle veneer is incompatible with any perception of being a loser — one reason he still can’t admit he lost to Biden in 2020.

But what might he try to do if the election goes badly for Republicans this time?

Voters stand in line at an early voting location in a mall in Anchorage, Alaska, o, October 21. (AP Photo/Haven Daley) Haven Daley/AP

The DOJ’s intervention in Alaska implies a post-election legal campaign if Peltola tallies one of the four net gains that Democrats need for a Senate majority. Similar moves elsewhere cannot be ruled out.

Republican elected officials and attorneys general in key states can expect to come under withering pressure from Trump, if his failed bid to force GOP officeholders in Georgia to “find” votes in the 2020 election is any guide. There’s now no Barr equivalent to debunk potential claims of fraud. Current Attorney General Todd Blanche said on NBC’s “Meet the Press” in August that he could not pledge the department would always act independently of Trump.

On Sunday, Blanche said on CNN’s “State of the Union” the administration was doing nothing “improper” in Alaska and simply wanted to ensure the rightful person wins, saying, “President Trump is not trying to take over a state election in any way, shape, or form.”

But he vehemently rejected the idea that the president’s attempt to overturn the 2020 election justified any concerns about his remarks smearing the 2026 midterms: “It’s not a conversation about January 6.”

In 2020, America’s legal and constitutional guardrails held firm. But Trump is now less encumbered by aides ready to temper his most antidemocratic instincts.

Still, Democrats and state officials of both parties who oversee elections have had months to prepare for potential threats from White House officials and local MAGA operatives.

If Democrats win big, Trump may have less latitude to interfere. If the result is closer, it is possible that prolonged legal battles could deadlock the fate of the Senate for weeks. Hakeem Jeffries, the likely House speaker if Democrats win a majority, last week told CNN’s Manu Raju he assumed Republicans would “try to come up with any diabolical scheme to prevent November 3rd from being a free and fair election.”

President Donald Trump arrives to speak at a midterm campaign rally at Port of Corpus Christi in Texas on October 27. Kent Nishimura/AFP/Getty Images

And it’s not unprecedented for the seating of a new senator to be challenged, according to lawyer and elections expert Ben Ginsberg. “It is done really rarely. It rips apart the fabric of the institution of the Senate when it happens,” Ginsberg said on CNN’s special election coverage on Sunday.

Trump could have powerful incentives to challenge unfavorable election results, since Democrats are already planning a relentless campaign of investigations into the White House, the Cabinet and the Trump family’s financial dealings.

But would a lame-duck president with an approval rating in the 30s who’d just lost a major national election have the political juice to pull it off?

And Trump’s self-absorbed campaign posture has indicated little concern for vulnerable Republicans. He may simply care less when his name isn’t on the ballot.

The president seemed Tuesday to be at least contemplating a period of bitter cohabitation with a Democratic Congress. “Look, I have a strong veto. I hope that won’t be the case, but if it is, that has happened before with many presidents,” he said.

But Trump often follows through on his threats. And his latest electoral caveating shows he still thinks an election he loses must be unfair.

So it’s a good idea to take him at his word.

World.title: What is Israeli President Herzog’s role after results are out?
World.content:
Election night in Israel ends when all the votes are counted, but that is just the first step. Forming a government runs through the president of the state, who plays a pivotal role in post-election politics.

After the results are finalized, President Isaac Herzog will begin consultations with all the elected parties, asking each of them who they recommend to be prime minister. He then assigns the task of forming a government to the candidate he believes is most likely to secure a 61-seat majority. This is not necessarily the leader of the largest party, but the one he deems has a better path to a coalition.

When election results are clear, the choice can be obvious. If there is no clear winner or a deadlock, the president’s decision can be decisive for coalition negotiations.

After Herzog decides who gets the mandate, the assigned candidate will have 28 days – with a possible 14-day extension – to negotiate with other parties over cabinet posts, budget priorities and policy commitments.

The goal is simple: try to form a government. If that candidate fails, the mandate is passed to another candidate for another four weeks. If he fails as well, the Knesset gets a short window to put forward another candidate, and if it cannot then the country goes to another round of elections.

The current vote count shows neither Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu nor his primary rival Gadi Eisenkot with a clear path to a majority, enhancing Herzog’s role in the process even more. With neither side holding a clear majority, he may try to steer the two largest parties to form a unity government. Two weeks before the election, Herzog said he will do everything he can “to establish a stable government” and avoid another election.

World.title: Israelis are back to a familiar political deadlock that underscores deep rooted divisions
World.content:
Israelis woke up Wednesday to a familiar political deadlock, with neither Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s right-wing coalition nor the opposition winning a clear majority to form a government.

These results build on the unprecedented streak of political paralysis that has produced six elections in seven years. Between 2019 and 2022, the country voted in five rounds of elections as no side could secure a clear 61-seat majority in the 120-seat parliament and sustain a viable coalition, reflecting a country deeply divided over leadership and direction.

Netanyahu, Israel’s longest serving prime minister, is also the first sitting prime minister to be indicted for corruption charges. That has broadly shaped the country’s political map during his tenure, as most of the opposition parties have refused to work with him, pushing him deeper into a reliance on far-right and ultra-orthodox parties. Only in the 2022 election did he and his allies win a majority.

Relying on the support of nationalistic and religious parties, Netanyahu held his government together for its full four-years, the first time since 1988 a government had lasted its complete term.

Shortly after the government’s inauguration, it pushed for a sweeping judicial overhaul that was met with widespread liberal protests, that continued up until the October 7, 2023 Hamas attack on Israel, the greatest security failure in the country’s history, and a multi-front war that followed.

Once again, this vote was a referendum on Netanyahu’s leadership, but also about the country’s direction and identity. The results reinforce the deep divide and polarization between Israelis over democratic values, religion and state, military service and accountability.

World.title: Taking back the algorithm: Social media platforms are restoring users’ control of their feeds
World.content:
New York — As a new mom-to-be, my social media feeds have clocked me — funneling endless videos my way about pregnancy, nursery prep and birth stories, to the point of baby information overload. I needed a break.

I recently told my Instagram algorithm I’m no longer interested in seeing content about “pregnancy” or “birth,” although at least for now I’ve kept its suggestion to show me “newborn parenting hacks.”

Instagram this year expanded its feature that lets users provide this kind of specific feedback to tailor their feed. And across the social media ecosystem, platforms are increasingly offering similar options to give users greater control over what they see as they scroll.

It’s something users have been asking for after social platforms spent years leaning into relying on their own algorithmic recommendations to populate feeds.

In addition to Meta’s Instagram and Facebook, YouTube, TikTok and smaller social media upstarts like Divine have all recently rolled out features to let users tailor their main “For You” pages, or create custom feeds around specific topics.

“What we’ve really tried to focus on is: how can we recreate the sense of agency that you had when you were controlling the accounts that you followed, but in a world that still gives you the benefits of recommendations,” such as more easily discovering new content, Instagram’s Vice President of Product Tessa Lyons told CNN.

Advances in AI’s understanding of language make it possible for the platforms to process specific feedback from users about their interests and dislikes, rather than simply making guesses based on what users view and engage with.

“We’re able to do something we’re never able to do before, which is actually enable people to use human language… to say, like, I want to see more of this topic or less of this topic,” Lyons said, adding that previously, “we were not able to accurately enough understand that if you said ‘tennis,’ what the most relevant tennis content was.”

It’s a stark reversal from the approach major platforms had taken in recent years: replacing chronological feeds based on who users followed with algorithmic recommendations. The thinking was that — thanks to the huge volume of data social media companies collect about users through their activity on and off their sites — these platforms could predict better than users themselves what they’d want to see and what would keep them scrolling.

The shift may have been good for business, but users often lamented that lack of control, complaining that the recommendation algorithms could send them down rabbit holes of irrelevant or even toxic content. Platforms have faced particular scrutiny related to their sometimes harmful content recommendations for young people.

That user frustration has only ramped up over the past year as AI has played a growing role in mediating what people see across the internet, colliding with a wider populist backlash to AI, said Tim Weninger, a computer science and engineering professor at the University of Notre Dame who studies AI and social media.

“People have gotten fed up with AI feeding them stuff,” Weninger said. “They miss the old days … They just want to be able to follow what they follow and see the latest updates.”

Returning control to users

In 2022, Instagram brought back the chronological feed as an option with “following” and “favorites” feeds that would show users only content from accounts they opted to see, although the app defaulted to the main recommended feed each time a user opened it.

Then last June, TikTok introduced a “manage topics” feature that lets users tweak their main feed by adjusting how much content they want to see from certain categories — such as fashion and beauty, or health and fitness — on a sliding scale. The tool doesn’t remove certain topics from the feed altogether, but it does give TikTok’s algorithm a more direct signal on what users want to see.

TikTok also added “smart keyword filtering,” which removes from the feed any videos containing a keyword that a user has flagged, plus those containing similar, related keywords.

Months later, Instagram took the trend a step further by rolling out “your algorithm,” which lets users see which topics the app believes they’re interested in and add topics they want to see, as well as those they want to avoid. The feature, which was originally rolled out just for the Reels tab, now applies to the full Instagram app and recently expanded to Facebook.

The feature makes it easier for the app to adjust when users’ interests change quickly — for example, someone may no longer want to see wedding planning content after they’re married, or videos of their ex-boyfriend’s favorite band after a breakup, Lyons said. Her “your algorithm” selections currently include topics like “family rituals” and “Celine Dion.”

Instagram’s Vice President of Product Tessa Lyons said the app is trying to balance giving users more control over their feeds, while still offering them the benefit of recommended content they might not otherwise find. Elisa Schu/dpa/picture alliance/Getty Images

In the coming months, Instagram plans to prompt users to engage more with the feature, which is currently accessible via a button on the upper righthand side of the Reels tab.

YouTube last month announced its own “custom feeds” offering at its annual “Made on YouTube” product launch event, which lets users create dedicated tabs alongside the main feed tailored to specific needs or interests, such as workout videos or “late night ASMR.”

But these features may not necessarily enable social media users to prevent AI-generated content from popping up in their feeds. YouTube CEO Neal Mohan told reporters at the September event that separating AI-generated from human-made content is an “artificial distinction,” and that many videos combine both.

YouTube’s custom feeds feature, he said, is instead really about letting viewers “program their feeds” around certain topics and “dial up and dial down what you’d like to see, and you can change it throughout the course of the day.”

It remains to be seen exactly how these changes will impact users, Weninger said. While users may tell a platform that they want to see content on topics they enjoy, people are often more likely to view, comment on or share content that upsets or angers them, which could confuse the algorithms.

“If you say that you like soccer, and then you never actually watch a soccer video, then what’s the AI supposed to do?” he said. “People engage with things that make them upset and sad, that’s kind of part of our nature. Hopefully this will change that attitude a little bit.”

World.title: Egypt, Iran discuss regional de-escalation as risks grow
World.content:
Minister of Foreign Affairs, International Cooperation and Egyptian Expatriates Badr Abdelatty discussed regional de-escalation and crisis management with his Iranian counterpart Abbas Araghchi in a phone call on Tuesday, October 27, 2026.

Spokesperson for the Egyptian foreign ministry Nader Zaki said the two ministers reviewed options to manage escalating regional risks, as Abdelatty called on all parties to take responsibility for avoiding a broader conflict.

Abdelatty expressed full support for diplomatic efforts following recent meetings in Tehran to contain tensions.

The ministers also discussed expanding regional consultations between Iran and the “R4” ministerial group—comprising Egypt, Saudi Arabia, Pakistan, and Turkey—to coordinate joint actions and mitigate security threats.

World.title: Nile River supplies 98 percent of Egypt’s water-Irrigation minister
World.content:
Around 90 percent of Africa’s surface water lies within shared international basins, requiring strict adherence to international water law, data sharing, and prior consultation on transboundary projects, Irrigation Minister Hani Sewilam said Tuesday.

Speaking at Cairo Water Week during a session on the Africa Water Vision 2063, Sewilam noted that the Nile River supplies roughly 98 percent of Egypt’s total water resources.

He emphasized that national water security should not come at the expense of other basin nations, pointing to Egypt’s review of 36 downstream Nile projects.

Sewilam called for a unified African stance ahead of the 2026 UN Water Conference to secure sustainable financing and development.

World.title: PM directs study of investment opportunities to develop Capital Airport, surrounding area
World.content:
Prime Minister Mostafa Madbouly has directed the formation of a working group comprising the relevant ministries and authorities to examine submitted proposals and offers and prepare a comprehensive vision for developing the New Capital Airport and its surrounding area.

The group will also assess available investment alternatives to ensure optimal use of the area’s potential and assets and maximize its economic and development returns.

The directive came during a meeting held by Madbouly on Monday to review several proposals for developing the New Capital International Airport and the surrounding area. The meeting was attended by Minister of Finance Ahmed Kouchouk, Minister of Civil Aviation Sameh al-Hefny, Administrative Capital for Urban Development (ACUD) Chairman Khaled Abbas, Assistant Minister of Investment and Foreign Trade Saeed Arafa, and a number of officials.

Official spokesperson for the Cabinet Mohamed Adel said the meeting reviewed proposals to establish an integrated investment and logistics zone adjacent to the New Capital International Airport, designed to serve as a logistics hub hosting a range of economic, logistical and industrial activities.

He noted that several international investors had expressed interest in investing in the area, alongside proposals from investors to expand and develop the airport.

The proposed plans aim to attract further foreign direct investment and maximize the use of state-owned assets by creating an investment-friendly environment and providing the necessary incentives and facilitation measures for investors.

These efforts are intended to support the establishment of diverse projects that advance development in the New Capital, strengthen its position as an attractive destination for investment and economic activity, create additional job opportunities and promote economic growth.

World.title: Egypt urges regional states to join forces to avert further escalation
World.content:
Egypt has called on regional countries to join forces to find peaceful solutions to the ongoing crisis and prevent it from escalating into a more dangerous phase.

Foreign Minister Badr Abdelatty held separate phone calls with his Emirati and Saudi counterparts on Tuesday, October 27,2026 to discuss regional developments, growing risks of escalation, and efforts to resolve the ongoing crisis through peaceful means.

During his call with UAE Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Sheikh Abdullah bin Zayed Al Nahyan, Abdelatty stressed the need for regional countries to unite their efforts to reach peaceful solutions and bring all parties back to the political process.

This aims to prevent the crisis from escalating into a more dangerous phase amid the ongoing crisis, he added.

Meanwhile, Abdelatty and Saudi Foreign Minister Prince Faisal bin Farhan discussed the latest regional developments and efforts to contain the crisis amid rising risks of escalation. They underscored the need to advance political and peaceful solutions through dialogue.

Abdelatty and Prince Faisal also agreed to maintain close consultation and coordination both bilaterally and through the four-party ministerial mechanism comprising Egypt, Saudi Arabia, Türkiye, and Pakistan.

World.title: With Nearly $4 Billion Invested, ArcelorMittal Liberia Makes the Case for a Larger Industrial Future
World.content:
At Liberia’s international mining and energy conference, Chief Executive Michiel van der Merwe outlined plans for higher iron ore exports, shared railway access and a partnership intended to last decades.

MARGIBI COUNTY, Liberia — ArcelorMittal Liberia expects to export more than 20 million tons of iron ore in 2027, up from under five million tons in 2024, its chief executive said Wednesday, outlining an expansion that could substantially increase Liberia’s mineral exports and strengthen the infrastructure supporting its mining economy.

Speaking at the Liberia International Mining and Energy Conference and Expo, where the company is a platinum sponsor, Michiel van der Merwe said ArcelorMittal’s investment in Liberia was approaching $4 billion. That commitment, he said, extends across mines, railway operations, port facilities, power and social infrastructure.

His address presented the company’s next phase as both an industrial expansion and a test of what sustained cooperation between government and investors can deliver: higher-value mineral production, greater opportunities for Liberian workers and infrastructure capable of supporting additional mining companies.

“It is an investment in jobs, skills and local businesses,” he said. “Most importantly, it is an investment in Liberia’s future.”



The two-day conference, taking place October 28–29 at the Farmington Hotel, brings government officials, investors and industry leaders together to discuss the future of Liberia’s mining and energy sectors. For ArcelorMittal Liberia, it offered a platform to explain how two decades of investment could support a much larger operation in the years ahead.

Van der Merwe began with a simple numerical refrain: “One, Two, Three and Four.”

One company, he said, had reopened Liberia’s iron ore mining sector in 2011. Its commitment had continued for two decades, across three presidential administrations, with investment now approaching $4 billion.

The sequence framed a central argument of his speech: major industrial projects depend on relationships and commitments that endure beyond any single political administration.

Today, the company connects iron ore deposits in Nimba County with Buchanan Port through a railway that van der Merwe described as 245 kilometres long. Thousands of Liberians, he said, help operate that integrated system.

Its next stage of growth rests on the Phase II expansion and the commissioning of Liberia’s first large-scale iron ore concentrator, which he described as a milestone for both the company and the country.

The concentrator allows ArcelorMittal Liberia to process ore into a higher-value product for international steelmakers. Van der Merwe said that premium concentrate would serve existing steel mills as well as a new generation using technologies designed to reduce carbon emissions.

For Liberia, the significance reaches beyond the amount of ore leaving the country. Processing more of that material before export represents a step toward capturing greater value from its mineral resources and developing the technical capabilities required to sustain a more sophisticated mining industry.

Van der Merwe said the project also demonstrated Liberia’s ability to attract and carry out large-scale industrial investments that create employment, build local capacity and strengthen national infrastructure.

The production ambitions are substantial. After exports of under five million tons in 2024, the company expects to ship more than 20 million tons in 2027, he said. It is also planning for eventual growth to 30 million tons at the mines.

Those figures remain company projections. But they illustrate the scale of the transformation ArcelorMittal Liberia is seeking — and the importance of the railway and port facilities needed to move that production to market.

Van der Merwe said the company had invested $800 million to rehabilitate and expand the government-owned railway and port infrastructure. Its current railway expansion, he added, already supports the company’s planned future growth, allowing other operators to use surplus capacity temporarily.

The distinction between public ownership and private investment was a prominent part of his remarks. The assets belong to the Government of Liberia, he said, while ArcelorMittal has financed the rehabilitation and expansion needed to support its operations.

He also reaffirmed the company’s support for a railway serving multiple users.

“ArcelorMittal is fully committed to the desire of the three Presidential administrations that this Tokadeh to Buchanan Railway is a multiuser asset available for other companies to use,” he said.

According to van der Merwe, the Third Amendment to the company’s Mineral Development Agreement, ratified earlier this year, provides for access by other users, with the Liberian government deciding which additional companies may use the infrastructure.

He said prospective users would need to finance their own expansion requirements, building on the foundational investments ArcelorMittal has already made.

That approach places the company’s infrastructure spending within a broader development argument: an established railway and port system can provide a starting point for additional projects, extending the economic reach of investments originally made to support one mining operation.

Van der Merwe said operating arrangements discussed across three administrations over the past decade were now being formalized through the Rail Systems Operating Principles, known as the RSOP. Those principles, he said, include an independent company operating the railway beginning in 2030.

“The establishment of an independent rail operator marks a significant step in Liberia’s economic transformation,” he said.

He described the arrangement as a foundation for shared infrastructure that could open new mining opportunities, attract investment and accelerate national development.

He also expressed support for the government’s proposed creation of a National Rail Authority to oversee the development of additional railway corridors. ArcelorMittal, he said, wants the agreed operating principles for the Tokadeh–Buchanan railway recognized when that institution is established.

Beyond infrastructure, van der Merwe emphasized the importance of developing Liberian expertise.

The country’s mineral wealth, location and investment ambitions provide a basis for growth, he said. Turning those advantages into lasting prosperity requires collaboration among government, companies, investors and communities, alongside a sustained commitment to training Liberians.

That investment in people, he argued, would help ensure that future generations can lead and sustain the industries now being built.

His remarks linked the company’s expansion to a wider international opportunity. As economies develop and pursue lower-carbon technologies, he said, countries with strong resources, stable investment conditions and durable partnerships will be better positioned to compete.

For ArcelorMittal Liberia, the message was one of continued commitment: the concentrator, expanded logistics infrastructure and planned production increases form part of a relationship that the company expects to carry well into the future.

“No single company, government institution or investor can achieve all of Liberia’s goals alone,” van der Merwe said. “But together, we can create an environment where investment thrives, industries grow and communities prosper.”

He closed by returning to the time horizon behind the company’s investment.

“We’ve played this part for the last twenty years,” he said, “and we are ready to do so for another forty years or more.”

World.title: Liberia Tells COP17 That Biodiversity Pledges Mean Little Without Money, Tools and Local Buy-In
World.content:
Dr. Yarkpawolo said Liberia stands with the African Group on four priorities. First, he wants global targets paired with real implementation support. He said reviews of progress should look not only at conservation results but also at whether developing nations were given the means to deliver

By Selma Lomax, [email protected]

YEREVAN, Armenia – Liberia has told the global biodiversity summit in Armenia that wealthy nations must back their conservation promises with funding, technology and training, or the effort to halt nature’s decline will stall in the places that need help most.

The message came on Wednesday from Dr. Emmanuel King Urey Yarkpawolo, head of Liberia’s Environmental Protection Agency, who addressed the high-level segment of the 17th Conference of the Parties to the Convention on Biological Diversity. He spoke on behalf of President Joseph Nyuma Boakai, Sr.



Wildlife deaths as a warning

Dr. Yarkpawolo anchored his appeal in two recent cases at home. In Caldwell, a crocodile was killed by residents who feared for their safety. In Monrovia, a dolphin that had become stranded was reportedly killed on October 25, before fisheries officials could reach it.

He said the cases point to a shared failure: ordinary people have little guidance on handling dangerous or distressed animals, and the state lacks the means to respond quickly. The crocodile killing, he noted, reflected a real safety worry, while the dolphin’s death showed how thin the country’s emergency capacity is.

Protecting wildlife, he argued, cannot come at the expense of families’ security. Communities need to be equipped with knowledge and official backing so they never feel forced to choose between the two.

Four asks, aligned with the African Group

Dr. Yarkpawolo said Liberia stands with the African Group on four priorities. First, he wants global targets paired with real implementation support. He said reviews of progress should look not only at conservation results but also at whether developing nations were given the means to deliver.

Second, he called for biodiversity finance that is sufficient, predictable, timely and easy to reach. Liberia backs Africa’s push for a permanent financial mechanism answerable to the Conference of the Parties, with simpler application procedures and direct access for developing countries. Many African governments have complained that cumbersome funding rules slow projects and hamper responses to emerging threats.

Third, he pressed for stronger capacity and technology transfer. In Liberia, that would mean training wildlife emergency teams, expanding research and monitoring, equipping laboratories, and running public education campaigns in languages people actually speak.

Fourth, he urged fair sharing of the benefits drawn from biological resources, including digital sequence information, the genetic data increasingly used in research and commercial products. Liberia supports meaningful contributions from companies that use such data to the Cali Fund, a mechanism designed to channel benefits back to providers. Developing countries, Indigenous peoples and local communities, he said, should see real returns.

Dr. Yarkpawolo told delegates Liberia has already revised its national biodiversity targets and updated its National Biodiversity Strategy and Action Plan to match the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework, the 2022 accord aimed at halting and reversing biodiversity loss. He described the changes as a base for better coordination among government bodies, conservation groups, communities and foreign partners.

Yet he cautioned that rewriting policy will achieve little without money and sustained follow-through.

Liberia holds large stretches of what remains of the Upper Guinean forest, along with wetlands, rivers, coastal zones and marine habitats that support livelihoods and provide vital services. Those assets are under pressure from habitat loss, overexploitation and uneven enforcement.

Conservation beyond the environment ministry

The EPA chief also urged governments to weave biodiversity into agriculture, fisheries, public health and national development plans, rather than leaving the job to environmental agencies alone. Conservation, he said, is tied to public safety, education and economic opportunity.

He asked COP17 to deliver outcomes that strengthen awareness programs, emergency response systems and income opportunities that give communities a reason to take part in protecting nature.

In closing, he called for information to reach people before fear drives them to destroy wildlife, for help to arrive before threatened animals are lost, and for conservation to offer tangible value to ordinary citizens. He ended with a short line of solidarity: Liberia stands with Africa for action, accessible financing and fairly shared benefits.

His speech adds to a wider African call at the Yerevan talks for a global framework that acknowledges developing countries’ financial limits and ensures that communities living closest to natural resources share in conservation gains. Negotiations and high-level meetings are continuing.

World.title: Liberia: Davis Urges Financing Reforms to Unlock Liberia’s MSME Potential
World.content:
AfDB Consultant Calls for Credit Guarantees, Technical Support and Market Access to Close $1.03 Billion Annual Financing Gap

By Charles G. Lamadine, contributing writer

MONROVIA — Dr. James Francis Davis, a senior international consultant for the African Development Bank (AfDB), has called for comprehensive financing reforms to help micro, small and medium-sized enterprises (MSMEs) overcome barriers to growth, create jobs and compete in regional markets.



Speaking at the 7th Prosperity Africa Conference in Monrovia, Dr. Davis delivered a lecture on “MSME Financing: The Financial Gap,” highlighting the challenges confronting small businesses in Liberia and across Africa.

The conference brought together policymakers, chambers of commerce, development partners and private-sector representatives to explore ways to translate trade and investment opportunities into sustainable economic growth and employment.

Dr. Davis emphasized that although MSMEs play a critical role in employment and economic development, many continue to struggle with limited access to affordable financing, high collateral requirements and short loan repayment periods.

He highlighted an estimated annual financing gap of US$1.03 billion for MSMEs in Liberia and a broader financing shortfall of more than US$209 billion for small businesses across Africa.

Beyond access to capital, Dr. Davis argued that sustainable business growth requires a comprehensive support system that combines financing with credit guarantees, technical assistance, mentorship and access to markets.

He stressed that financing alone is insufficient to help businesses expand, underscoring the need for policies and institutional arrangements that enable entrepreneurs to develop viable businesses and compete effectively.

Linking Local Businesses to Regional Markets

Dr. Davis also highlighted the potential of the African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA) to expand opportunities for Liberian businesses through regional trade and value chains.

He called for stronger economic cooperation among African countries, allowing businesses in different markets to specialize in supplying raw materials, processing products, providing logistics and delivering financial services.

For Liberia, he identified agriculture, light manufacturing, logistics, technology and tourism as sectors with significant potential to support enterprise development, attract investment and generate employment.

He stressed that improving MSME financing must go hand in hand with efforts to connect local businesses to regional supply chains and emerging commercial opportunities.

Youth Entrepreneurship Financing

Dr. Davis also linked the discussion to Liberia’s Youth Entrepreneurship Investment Bank Management Company (YEIB-MANCO), an initiative funded by the AfDB and the Government of Liberia that targets 30,000 youth-led businesses.

He highlighted the importance of the initiative’s approach of combining training, incubation and financing to prepare young entrepreneurs for sustainable business operations.

According to the presentation, equipping entrepreneurs with the necessary skills and business support before providing financing can help address weaknesses that undermine the success of grant-funded and other small-business support programs.

Dr. Davis further emphasized the importance of infrastructure investment, arguing that roads should be viewed not merely as transportation projects but as economic corridors capable of connecting producers to markets, reducing business costs and stimulating investment.

He called for stronger coordination among government institutions, chambers of commerce and development partners to ensure that investment commitments translate into tangible economic opportunities and jobs.

Call for Stronger Banking Partnerships

Dr. Davis commended the Liberia Chamber of Commerce for advocating greater opportunities for local businesses, while urging commercial banks to work with credit guarantee funds to make financing more accessible to MSMEs.

He identified high interest rates, demanding collateral requirements and short repayment periods as major constraints facing Liberian entrepreneurs.

Partnerships between commercial banks and guarantee institutions, he suggested, could help reduce lending risks and improve access to credit for businesses that lack sufficient collateral but demonstrate viable growth prospects.

His presentation, described as interactive and practical, aligned with the conference theme, “MSME Financing at the Africa Prosperity Conference for Sustainable Development: Policy Reforms, Innovation, and Opportunities.”

The discussions underscored the importance of addressing financing barriers as part of broader efforts to promote inclusive growth, strengthen private-sector development and expand opportunities for young entrepreneurs.

For Liberia, closing the MSME financing gap will require more than increased lending. It will also depend on coordinated policy reforms, stronger financial institutions, business development support and improved access to domestic and regional markets.

World.title: Liberia: After CBL Pay Shock, House Turns on Executives
World.content:
MONROVIA – Liberia’s House of Representatives has ordered a sweeping review of salaries and benefits across government, days after a rare public disclosure of a senior official’s pay reignited anger over the cost of running one of the world’s poorest countries.

By Emmanuel Weedee-Conway

In a unanimous vote on Tuesday, the lower house of the national legislature instructed two of its committees, on Ways, Means and Finance and on Public Accounts, to examine the pay and perks of government officials and report back within two weeks. The motion was brought by Representative Alex S. Noah of Sinoe County.



Lawmakers argued that they are wrongly blamed for the country’s swollen wage bill, while ministers and the heads of state-owned enterprises earn far more.

The disclosure that lit the fuse

The vote came less than a week after Euphemia G.T. Swen-Monmia, President Joseph Boakai’s nominee for Deputy Governor for Economic Policy at the Central Bank of Liberia, appeared on October 22 before the Senate Committee on Banking and Currency for her confirmation hearing.

Asked about her pay, she did something Liberian officials rarely do: she gave the numbers. She testified that her monthly salary is US$9,000, that she receives around US$5,000 in cash benefits on top of that, and that her housing allowance should be about US$15,000. She has served in an acting capacity since August 12.

That amounts to roughly US$168,000 a year in salary and cash benefits before housing is counted. A civil servant on the government’s US$150 monthly minimum would need more than seven and a half years of uninterrupted work to earn what she receives in a single month.

Swen-Monmia is a career central banker who joined the bank in 2010 as a management trainee and rose to director of its Financial Markets Department. The controversy is not about her qualifications but about what her testimony revealed: pay at the top of Executive agencies is generous, and almost never made public.

No lawmaker cited her testimony by name during Tuesday’s debate. But the timing, and the focus of the two letters that triggered it, on officials earning more than US$5,000 a month, suggest the disclosure handed fresh ammunition to a chamber long cast as the main villain in Liberia’s debate over official pay.

‘We are suffering’

On the floor, several members described their own compensation as “peanuts” compared with Executive officials and argued the legislature deserves more because representatives serve larger numbers of constituents.

Representative Moima Briggs-Mensah of Bong County said a US$2,000 budget line meant for constituents’ school scholarships often never arrives, and that lawmakers lack the insurance enjoyed by Executive officials.

“We don’t even have Social Security benefits. We are suffering and people in the Executive are making mockery of us,” she said.

Representative Anthony Williams of Maryland County said lawmakers were being “falsely crucified” by the public while benefits such as fuel arrive months late.

“The Executive, especially SOEs are reaping the honey, while we are being falsely crucified,” he said, demanding that state enterprises disclose their gross and net pay and benefits to the House.

The numbers tell a different story

Lawmakers’ complaints sit uneasily with the figures. Senators earn US$8,000 a month each, according to the draft 2026 budget, and a bill to cut that to US$5,000, first introduced by Senator Abraham Darius Dillon in 2020, has stalled for years. In 2025, House members’ basic salary was put at roughly US$8,569 a month, with additional funding for security guards, drivers, cooks and other support staff.

The legislature as a whole has also grown more expensive. The draft 2026 budget gave lawmakers US$51.7 million, up from US$41.3 million in 2024.

That is in a West African nation of about 5.2 million people still rebuilding from 14 years of civil war that ended in 2003, whose national budget crossed US$1 billion for the first time this year. About half the population lives below the poverty line.

Meanwhile, front-line public servants struggle to get paid at all. Teachers’ U.S.-dollar pay has gone unpaid since October 2025, and nurses are demanding a monthly minimum of US$500.

A chamber in revolt

Tuesday’s vote follows weeks of turmoil inside the House over lawmakers’ own money. More than 40 members boycotted the legislature’s reopening session on October 9 in protest over unpaid benefits and allowances, including constituency visits, district projects, fuel and medical allowances. Calling themselves “Reformists,” they accused the chamber’s leadership of withholding benefits and legislative support funds.

The Senate faces its own scrutiny. A proposal from its Committee on Rules, Order and Administration, reported by FrontPageAfrica, seeks US$792,552 in the 2027 budget to raise salaries for 224 Senate staff, with some increases as high as 71 percent. The Senate has disputed the reporting and demanded a retraction; FrontPageAfrica stands by its story.

Two letters, two tones

The review was triggered by letters from two lawmakers who framed the problem very differently from their colleagues on the floor.

Representative Sumo Kollie Mulbah of Montserrado County asked the House to hold up the national budget until the Finance Ministry reports all salaries and benefits above US$5,000 a month for ministers, directors, county governors and commissioners. The central bank deputy governor’s testimony would place her nearly three times above that threshold.

Mulbah singled out housing allowances, fuel and phone-credit coupons, and overseas medical treatment on top of health insurance.

“While these elite benefits are sustained, critical national priorities like the increment of the minimum wage are continuously set aside,” he wrote.

Representative Musa Hassan Bility of Nimba County called for a special committee to review salaries, allowances, wasteful spending, duty-free privileges and tax exemptions across all branches of government, and insisted the legislature go first.

“We cannot continue to demand sacrifices from ordinary Liberians while protecting our own excessive privileges,” Bility wrote. “This must not be another selective exercise intended to embarrass particular officials for public applause.”

What to watch

The two-week deadline lands as the Executive prepares to send the 2027 budget to the legislature by October 31. The government projects total spending will fall to US$1.02 billion next year, meaning any gains for one group of officials will likely come at someone else’s expense.

The test is whether the committees follow Bility’s call to start with the legislature, or whether the review becomes, as he warned, a selective exercise aimed at the Executive. Liberians have heard promises of pay cuts before. A proposal to cut senators’ pay to US$5,000 has been on the table for six years without passing.

World.title: Liberia: Inside the Defense Bid to Overturn the Peter Bon Jallah Conviction
World.content:
A Liberian judge convicted a former national security aide of statutory rape and kidnapping but cleared him of gang rape. Four days later, his lawyers filed a motion arguing that the two halves of the ruling cannot both stand.

By Rodney D. Sieh

MONROVIA — When Judge Wesseh Alphonsus Wesseh Sr. delivered his verdict on Friday, October 23, he framed the case around three questions: whether the evidence supported a conviction for gang rape, for statutory rape, and for kidnapping. He answered no to the first and yes to the other two.



That split is now the battleground. On Tuesday, October 27, at 11:12 a.m., lawyers for Peter Bon Jallah, 63, a former special assistant to the director of Liberia’s National Security Agency (NSA), filed a motion for a new trial at Criminal Court “E” in Monrovia. The filing, received by Acting Clerk of Court Abraham Richards, asks the judge to set aside his own verdict.

The motion is the first formal test of a ruling that, by the court’s own record, states its conclusions on each charge without detailing how it weighed every witness and exhibit. That gap is what the defense is trying to exploit.

What the court decided

Jallah was arrested on January 7, 2026, after the mother of a 16-year-old boy complained to the police Women and Children Protection Section. The boy did paid chores at Jallah’s home.

A grand jury indicted Jallah and two unidentified men in February on charges of gang rape, statutory rape and kidnapping. The indictment alleged abuse at Jallah’s home on November 29 and December 24, 2025. It also alleged that on January 1, 2026, Jallah lured the boy with an offer of football boots, drove him to a building off Camp Johnson Road in central Monrovia, and held him there for three days while he and two other men abused him.

The two other men were never brought before the court. Jallah, who has denied all the allegations, chose to be tried by a judge rather than a jury.

The court acquitted him of gang rape, finding the prosecution’s evidence insufficient. It convicted him of statutory rape and kidnapping. Jallah was remanded to Monrovia Central Prison pending a pre-sentence report from the Ministry of Justice’s Bureau of Probation Services. No sentence has been imposed.

The prosecution’s case

According to the written verdict, the prosecution called 13 regular witnesses and six rebuttal witnesses. The defense called eight witnesses, including Jallah, plus three subpoenaed witnesses from the Ministry of Gender, Children and Social Protection, the mobile operator Orange Liberia and the John F. Kennedy Medical Center.

The state’s strongest scientific evidence came from Pascal Bavugirije of the Rwanda Forensic Institute, which analyzed exhibits after Liberia sent them abroad. He testified that DNA profiles from four clothing exhibits matched Jallah’s reference sample. Material collected from the alleged scene produced a mixed profile from unknown people that matched neither Jallah nor the boy.

The boy testified in August that he was assaulted three times, and the court admitted his police statement over defense objections. Investigators also told the court that phone records placed Jallah near one of the alleged scenes, contradicting his account that he had no contact with the boy.

The defense’s four arguments

The motion, signed by Counsellor G. Wiefueh Alfred Sayeh of the Law Offices of Sayeh & Sayeh, makes four main claims.

1. The kidnapping conviction contradicts the gang rape acquittal. The defense argues that the kidnapping charge rests on the alleged three-day confinement off Camp Johnson Road, the same episode at the heart of the gang rape charge. If the court found too little evidence that the gang rape happened there, the motion says, it cannot find that the boy was held there. It describes the conviction as “contrary to weight of the evidence.”

2. The court lacked jurisdiction over kidnapping. Criminal Court “E” is Liberia’s specialized court for sexual offenses. The motion argues it has no jurisdiction over kidnapping as a separate crime. This is a purely legal question, and if the judge or a higher court agrees, it could void that conviction regardless of the evidence.

3. Penetration was never proven. Under Liberia’s rape statute, penetration is an essential element. The defense points to three pieces of testimony:

* A JFK Medical Center doctor, called by the defense, testified that an examination under anesthesia shortly after the boy’s January rescue found no evidence of trauma. The hospital’s operative record lists the post-procedure diagnosis as “normal findings.” The motion says the prosecution offered no rebuttal.

* The Rwandan forensic examiner testified that DNA analysis cannot establish guilt or innocence and that his report did not show whether penetration occurred.

* A nurse examiner from the hospital’s One Stop Center for survivors of sexual violence, a prosecution witness, testified that she could not say the boy was not raped, adding that she was there only to report what she saw. The defense argues that statement does not prove rape and creates doubt that must favor the accused.

The motion goes further, accusing the judge of attributing the words “penetration” and “blunt object” to the nurse’s testimony when, it says, no witness used them.

1. The defendant did not get a fair trial. The motion alleges the judge remarked in open court that the prosecution was “asking weak questions.” It also says that after reviewing the defense’s Orange phone records, the judge on his own initiative subpoenaed Jallah’s records from a second carrier, Lonestar Cell MTN, over a defense objection that the court could not introduce evidence on the state’s behalf.

How strong are the arguments?

Each claim faces hurdles, and none has yet been tested by the prosecution’s response.

The medical findings do not settle the question on their own. Forensic medicine broadly recognizes that the absence of physical injury does not rule out sexual assault, particularly when an examination comes days after an alleged act. The prosecution can also point to the DNA findings and the boy’s testimony. A judge sitting without a jury is entitled to weigh credible testimony against an inconclusive medical record.

The kidnapping argument may be harder to dismiss. The acquittal on gang rape could reflect doubt about the two unidentified men rather than about the alleged confinement itself. Whether that distinction holds depends on reasoning the published verdict does not spell out.

The fair-trial complaint about the phone subpoena raises a recognized principle: a judge in an adversarial system is not supposed to build the prosecution’s case. How much weight the court gave those records is not clear from the verdict.

What happens next

Judge Wesseh must rule on the motion. If he denies it, the case moves to sentencing once the probation report arrives. The defense has already said it will appeal to the Supreme Court of Liberia, and the arguments in this motion offer a preview of that appeal.

The case has been closely watched in Liberia because of Jallah’s position close to the head of the country’s main intelligence agency, and because it tests how the courts handle sexual violence against children. It has already passed through two courtrooms, a failed prosecution bid to move the trial out of Monrovia, and a change of judge.

The Ministry of Justice, which prosecuted the case, had not filed a response to the motion as of Tuesday.
