World.title: They bought cabins to live on a cruise ship. High fuel costs got them kicked off in Cambodia.
World.content:
A residential cruise ship halted operations in Cambodia on Tuesday amid soaring fuel costs, leaving passengers in limbo after the U.S. company that operates it ordered them to disembark.

Florida-based Villa Vie Residences said in a news release that it was working to identify “temporary living arrangements” for people aboard The Odyssey, a 642-foot cruise ship that launched from Belfast, Northern Ireland, three years ago and promised passengers “an unparalleled lifestyle of luxury and exploration” as it toured the planet.

Cabins on The Odyssey were for sale or rent.

According to the company, the ship can accommodate 650 residents. A Cambodian official said Wednesday there were 203 passengers and 156 ​crew members on the ship. Some passengers had already departed on ​flights, while others were waiting in the port city of Sihanoukville, Long Dimanche, deputy governor of Preah Sihanouk Province, told media.

The ship is scheduled to refuel before leaving ‌Cambodia on ⁠Saturday, he added.

An executive with the company, Mikael Petterson, declined to provide additional details in an email to NBC News. In a release this year announcing the company’s second residential cruise ship, Petterson said The Odyssey was 85% sold.

The company said in Tuesday’s release that it had taken significant measures to reduce fuel consumption but that those steps had failed to offset the spike in costs.

Global oil prices have surged since the war with Iran began this year, disrupting the world’s flow of fuel. In recent days, oil prices have climbed to their highest levels in months.

The Odyssey in 2024. Peter Morrison / AP

“Passing the full increase on to residents is not a realistic solution,” the company said. “Our focus now is on supporting residents, crew, and employees while we work toward restructuring and recapitalization over the next 60 days. That work is ongoing, and no outcome is assured.”

Randy Cassingham, a resident on the boat, wrote in a blog post that he learned his journey was over after a company official posted a note on a message board for the ship shortly after 7 a.m. Monday.

The Odyssey was entering a “temporary lay up” period — indicating it would no longer be used — and everyone had to disembark by 2 p.m., the message said, according to Cassingham, who runs ResidentialCruising.com and didn’t immediately reply to an interview request.

Cassingham attributed the development to a “cascade of problems” that he would detail later.

Pamela Reckamp, who rented a cabin with her husband and disembarked this month, said in an interview that she wasn’t surprised that the ship’s journey was over.

Reckamp, 59, recalled having attended a meeting in early September at which a company official asked cabin owners to help them raise $1 million so they could leave Ha Long Bay, Vietnam.

“She said, ‘If we don’t get this money, we have about four days of the ship running,’” Reckamp recalled. “‘Then the lights will go off and the AC will go off.’”

When the ship’s financial issues were raised during another meeting a few weeks later, Reckamp recalled, a woman stood up and said she’d bought a cabin in August and hadn’t been made aware of the issues.

“I sold my house,” Reckamp recalled the woman saying. “I sold my car. I bought my home on this ship.”

Reckamp said she felt terrible for the residents and the staff, who she said were lovely.

“We dodged a bullet,” she added.

Villa Vie Residences didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment Tuesday night.

In a lawsuit filed last year, a company that bought a cabin on The Odyssey for $469,000 accused Villa Vie Residences of fraud, alleging it misrepresented its financial stability.

The company’s business model was not financially sound, the suit alleges, “but rather precarious.”

The plaintiffs are asking for a jury trial and unspecified damages of more than $100,000. Villa Vie Residences denied the allegations in the suit, which is ongoing.

Other cabins on the ship were available for significantly less money. Even though 85% of the ship was sold, the company said in 2024, prospective residents could still “secure their dream home starting at just $119,000.”

“When we launched Odyssey, we set out to prove that residential cruising wasn’t just possible — it was sustainable,” Petterson said in July.

World.title: Fed expected to hold interest rates steady as inflation tops midterm voters’ concerns
World.content:
The Federal Reserve is meeting in Washington this week, when it will consider whether to raise interest rates in an effort to tamp down on inflation.

The meetings come at a moment when rising prices are shaping large parts of the U.S. economy and inflation is set to play a key role in next Tuesday’s midterm elections.

Yet members of the bank’s interest rate-setting committee are widely expected to keep benchmark rates steady this month.

There are several reasons the Fed is unlikely to move on rates Wednesday. Most of them come down to a sense among top officials that the central bank shouldn’t rush into interest rate decisions — and that it definitely shouldn’t do so less than a week out from Election Day.

“Inflation remains above our goal,” Michelle Bowman, the Fed’s vice chair for supervision, said Oct. 14. “We have some time to wait and see how financial conditions evolve before we take more action.”

The Fed last raised rates by a quarter of a percentage point in September after a string of monthly inflation readings well above its target of 2% and no signs that prices were coming down anytime soon.

“The plain fact is that inflation is too high and has been for too long,” Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh said at the time.

Inflation figures for September, released this month, underscored Warsh’s point, with the annual inflation rate rising to 3.7% from 3.4% the previous month.

Some analysts believe Warsh and the Fed will be taking a risk if they vote to hold rates steady, given the trajectory of inflation.

“The case for skipping [a rate hike in] October is not terribly compelling,” analysts at Deutsche Bank wrote.

Fed officials, however, point to a core tenet of the dual mandate that Congress has assigned to the Fed, of promoting maximum employment while maintaining stable prices.

Specifically the “stable” part, which underpins the Fed’s famously slow and deliberative approach.

“I don’t feel urgent that ​we have to decide with a limited set of information,” San Francisco Fed President Mary Daly said in a recent interview. “I think we have the ⁠time that we need.”

Another guiding principle at the Fed that is most likely tipping expectations about Wednesday is its tradition of staying far away from politics.

If the Fed were to raise rates just days before the midterms, it could, at best, risk looking like a politically motivated decision. At worst, it could influence people’s votes.

“We could imagine that all else equal the Fed might prefer to stay out of the headlines for raising rates just ahead of a midterm election where affordability is the principal concern,” the Deutsche Bank analysts wrote.

Voters have repeatedly told pollsters that rising prices, especially in the housing and energy sectors, are their primary concerns as they cast their ballots.

With control of both the House and the Senate on the line in Tuesday’s election, voters are clear about whom they blame for the higher prices: President Donald Trump’s war in Iran and his global tariff regime.

The most recent NBC News poll found Trump’s approval rating at 27% for his handling of the cost of living and just 29% for his handling of the war with Iran.

Two-thirds of Americans said the soaring gas prices triggered by Trump’s Iran war were either a “very serious” or a “somewhat serious” problem.

Likewise, more than half of respondents said current economic conditions had caused them to change what kinds of groceries they buy.

All that adds up to a very difficult political environment for Trump’s fellow Republicans, who are struggling to balance their general support for him with how unpopular his policies have become with voters.

Even the Trump administration, which normally maintains an upbeat view about the economy and inflation, sounded concerned after the most recent inflation reading earlier in the month.

“This was a disappointing number,” said Kevin Hassett, director of the White House National Economic Council.

Asked by Fox Business hosts why voters had such negative views of the current economy despite higher spending, Hassett was unsure. “It’s a puzzle that we’re noodling about every day,” he said.

World.title: The former youth pastor leading one of the NFL’s best offenses
World.content:
When Nate Scheelhaase was promoted to offensive coordinator of the Los Angeles Rams last winter, he stepped into one of the NFL’s most auspicious jobs, and for a Super Bowl contender, no less.

Not bad for a former youth pastor.

Fresh out of college, Scheelhaase moved to Louisville, Kentucky, in 2014 to work with teenagers at Southeast Christian Church, one of the largest megachurches in the U.S. During that time, he regularly stopped by a few dozen high schools to visit with students. For two high schools’ football teams, he volunteered as a chaplain. The role entailed building trust, finding common ground and helping those he spoke with work for something bigger than themselves.

“An impactful year,” said Scheelhaase, 35.

It wasn’t the typical starting point for a career in coaching — because even though Scheelhaase had been a four-year starting quarterback at Illinois, he wasn’t initially interested in that career path at all.

Without intending to, though, Scheelhaase honed skills while he was a youth pastor that he says helped him rise quickly within the coaching industry.

“I would say that there’s a lot of carryover,” Scheelhaase said in an interview. “From a ministry standpoint, just being around people from all different walks of life, different journeys, being able to meet them where they’re at — that’s also a football locker room. That’s a staff locker room.”

Los Angeles Rams offensive coordinator Nate Scheelhaase during training camp at Loyola Marymount University this summer. Ric Tapia / Getty

The growth of sports in the U.S. is often a story of their crossover with faith. James Naismith, basketball’s inventor, is said to have believed he could better embody what it meant to be a Christian using sports than the pulpit. Many of football’s conventions, including the huddle, numbered jerseys and padded goalposts, came from Amos Alonzo Stagg, who had gone to Yale to study divinity and began coaching to fulfill a vision of “muscular Christianity.”

Careers in sports have often led to careers in religious roles. Rocky Seto won national championships at the University of Southern California and a Super Bowl with the Seattle Seahawks during 16 years on Pete Carroll’s coaching staffs. In Seattle, Seto’s role eventually evolved to include a weekly address delivered in front of the entire roster and staff. He obsessively prepared his material.

“How am I going to capture the whole room?” Seto said. “It’s basically convincing them that if you learn this, this is going to help us win, help us be better.”

That experience made him feel prepared to give his first sermon. It was 2017, and Seto had just left the Seahawks to become the pastor-in-waiting at Evergreen Baptist Church, in suburban Los Angeles. Standing in front of another packed room of congregants, Seto felt his new job’s mission mirrored that of his last one — to deliver hope.

“You come to church in some ways to take a peek into heaven for a moment, and then we break. It’s like a huddle, and then we break out to basically fulfill the Great Commission outside this building, right?” he said. “And so coaching is no different. The information has to be almost like, ‘This is the greatest thing you need to know.’”

As Scheelhaase’s career was ending in late 2013, all he knew was that he didn’t envision a future in coaching.

He had gotten married a few months earlier, and he had seen enough coaches get fired and hired to question raising a family in an industry with fleeting job security and a nomadic career path. Meetings with Illini alumni in corporate jobs in Chicago also failed to inspire him. Unsure what to do, Scheelhaase called Jason Epperson, a local pastor who served as Illinois football’s team chaplain.

Scheelhaase was a four-year starting quarterback at the University of Illinois. Michael Hickey / Getty

Epperson had just taken a job at Southeast in Louisville, where there was a youth pastor role open. The idea intrigued Scheelhaase, who had grown up outside Kansas City, Missouri, as a devout Christian. When he arrived at Southeast in early 2014, he was trying “to figure out different ways to just connect with people in the area and show them that I was interested in just who they were more than just what they were doing,” Scheelhaase said. “Which I think is always a good spot to start.”

Chris Burke, an ESPN baseball analyst who lived in the area, first noticed Scheelhaase because of his athleticism during pickup games inside Southeast’s gym. Other things about Scheelhaase soon stood out, too.

“He looked perfectly suited for that job,” Burke said. “You can tell he got a kick out of being around young people. He communicated well with them. He had the patience.”

When a local mother told Scheelhaase that her eighth grade son’s father had recently died and that she needed others to be there for her son, Scheelhaase gave him rides and went to practices. The son was Nate Hobbs, the future San Francisco 49ers defensive back whom Scheelhaase still describes as one of his closest friends.

Scheelhaase stopped by Trinity High School, a local powerhouse, with a “confident humility,” said Andrew Coverdale, Trinity’s offensive coordinator at the time, who is now the passing game coordinator at Kentucky. Scheelhaase didn’t expect students to listen to him just because he had been a college quarterback.

“As somebody who taught in high school for a long, long time, I can’t really emphasize enough that kids need every form of mentorship and positive adult presence they can have, because it is brutal to be a teenage kid right now,” Coverdale said. High schoolers are “just dealing with so much and carrying so much. And so I just think having a guy like that around that you can talk to, who has life experience that he’s willing to share in a really winsome way, it was just great.”

Scheelhaase spent a relatively brief year and a half in Louisville, but he said that time shaped him immeasurably. Scheelhaase, who now has three children, said spending time around church leaders and attendees gave him role models for how he wanted to act as a husband and a father. It also changed his career path.

While he was leading a chapel service for football players at Eastern High School in 2014, he gave what he thought was a compelling, relatable speech that pulled in his athletic background and life story. It was received, he said with a smile, by proverbial crickets.

Taking a seat, he was stunned to see the reaction when the school’s head coach stood up to deliver his own pregame speech.

“Everybody was on the edge of their seat,” Scheelhaase said. “And in that moment, I thought, man, there is a cool ability to impact as a coach. And it was probably the thing that triggered the thought of, man, what would it look like to be able to impact in that way and influence in that way.”

Scheelhaase celebrates against the Buffalo Bills at SoFi Stadium near Los Angeles on Oct. 12. Katelyn Mulcahy / Getty

By the start of the 2015 football season, Scheelhaase was at Illinois coaching running backs. Technically, he was new to the profession. Yet recruiting players to campus and developing them once they were on the roster didn’t feel any different, at its core, from how he’d worked to build trust in Louisville.

“You are going to ask people to do really hard things as a coach, things that are counterintuitive to what you want to do,” he said. “Stand in a pocket where you know somebody’s going to hit you in the side of your helmet. To be somebody who loves to catch the football, but you got to go and block. To be somebody that’s willing to do the dirty work, and you’re going to ask them to do it, and the only way I know how to do that is to connect with them on a deep level. They know I not only understand what we’re asking them to do, but I care and I see them in that. And so connection, fortunately for me, it’s how I’m wired. That’s the part I enjoy the most about my job. ...

“And there probably is an element of that’s what I enjoyed even about the job as a high school pastor in Louisville, too, is just connecting with people and seeing there’s oftentimes more common ground than you think.”

In 2023, he became a coordinator at Iowa State. A year later, he left to become an offensive assistant for Sean McVay and the Rams, which to some may have seemed like a backward step; his job revolved around using software to manually draw the plays McVay wanted called each week. In the NFL, however, just being around McVay is a career springboard: The last four Rams offensive coordinators are now head coaches, and Zac Taylor was drawing McVay’s plays before Cincinnati hired him as its head coach. In 2025, a full year before Scheelhaase’s promotion to Rams offensive coordinator, McVay had called him “a special coach” and “a rising star, without a doubt.”

Last winter, as Scheelhaase was interviewing for NFL head coaching jobs, he called interim Stanford coach Frank Reich to ask about the school’s opening. The two had more in common than football. After he retired from a long career as a backup NFL quarterback, Reich attended seminary and worked as a pastor before he became an NFL head coach.

He saw carryover between the two industries, too.

“In coaching or seminary or pastoring, there are a lot of hours,” Reich said in 2019.

The hours Scheelhaase put in in Louisville have paid off in ways he didn’t expect, he said. There, his life revolved around Sundays. In ways he could never have predicted, it still does.

World.title: Spain train crash leaves at least 64 dead in second major collision this year
World.content:
BARCELONA, Spain — At least 64 people were killed and 58 injured when two high-speed trains collided in central Spain on Wednesday, sending carriages careering off the tracks, in the second major accident on the same line in less than a year.

“We heard a massive roar, a truly enormous thud that went on for 10 seconds, as if the train were about to derail,” one passenger, Miguel, told Spain’s COPE radio, adding that he was traveling with several colleagues in the rear car of one of the trains.

“Through the right-hand window, we could see a wrecked train — I imagine it must have been the other one,” he added.

Pictures showed several carriages lying on their sides next to the tracks and others twisted at angles, their wheels sheared off. Debris was strewn around the scene of the accident in the countryside in the province of Toledo.

Passengers leave the crashed train. Cordon Press / Sipa USA via AP

As rescue teams continued to search through the wreckage ‌of ​the ‌derailed ⁠carriages, the Castilla-La Mancha ‌regional government said ‌64 people had been killed and 58 injured.

Earlier, the region’s President Emiliano García-Page said that at least 80 people were injured. Together the two trains were carrying more than 500 passengers.

Spain’s transport minister Oscar Puente said the crash ⁠occurred after a state-owned Renfe high-speed train was authorised ⁠to ​continue its ⁠journey despite an active red ⁠signal because ​of ⁠a stationary ‌train from private rail company Iryo on the tracks ahead.

Addressing ‌reporters in ‌Madrid, Puente said ⁠the red signal was issued due to a computer communications failure which automatically stopped ‌traffic. An erroneous ​decision was ‌made ⁠to restart the ⁠Renfe train, breaking protocol, he said.

Locals rushed to the scene of the accident, which has prompted a major national emergency response and raised questions about the safety and security of Spain’s high-speed rail infrastructure, which had previously been hailed as among the most sophisticated in Europe.

Esther Padilla, spokeswoman for the Castilla La Mancha region, told state broadcaster TVE that the trains were heading in the same direction from Madrid to Seville when one ran into the tail of the other, which had stopped on the line.

She added that some 397 people had been traveling on the Renfe train and 147 people on the Iryo train.

World.title: Flávio Bolsonaro leaves Brazil, lands in U.S. after election loss
World.content:
Brazilian Senator Flávio Bolsonaro and his family left the country on Tuesday after he lost Brazil's hotly contested presidential election over the weekend, and CBS News Miami reports they landed in Miami Wednesday morning.

Earlier, a senior State Department official told CBS News that Bolsonaro and his family would receive U.S. visas.

En route to the U.S., Bolsonaro, his wife and two daughters arrived in Argentina Tuesday night and hen boarded a private plane for a flight to Guayaquil, Ecuador, according to Argentinian officials and flight tracking data.

Bolsonaro, an ally of President Trump, departed Brazil for the U.S. after being defeated by incumbent President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva in Sunday's election.

A spokesperson for Bolsonaro did not respond to a request for comment. His campaign manager Rogério Marinho also refused to comment.

Silva said Tuesday it was "shameful" that Bolsonaro had fled Brazil.

"A person who sneaks out of their country must have something to hide," Silva said, per Agence France-Presse. "The act of leaving Brazil is shameful."

Bolsonaro's brother, Eduardo Bolsonaro, who lives in Texas, had publicly encouraged him to leave Brazil if he lost the election.

Bolsonaro has touted his relationship with Mr. Trump and visited the White House in May. The family connections go deeper: Brother Eduardo Bolsonaro was convicted in absentia in June of illegally lobbying the Trump administration and sentenced to four years in prison. A warrant was recently issued for his arrest.

Mr. Trump did not offer a full-throated endorsement of Bolsonaro in the runoff against Lula, as he has with some other right-of-center candidates in Latin America. But he suggested on Monday, without providing evidence, that Brazil's election was "rigged."

Flávio Bolsonaro speaks during a press conference following the runoff election in Brasilia, Brazil, on Oct. 25, 2026. Arthur Menescal / Bloomberg via Getty Images

Mr. Trump told reporters early Wednesday that said he approves of Bolsonaro coming to the U.S., though he had heard Bolsonaro was in Argentina.

"It would be OK with me," Mr. Trump said.

Bolsonaro's decision to leave Brazil came as a deadline for him to surrender his regular and diplomatic passports expired at noon Tuesday. It remained unclear whether he had complied.

"This is what the Bolsonaro family is like: Brazil is their second nation, the U.S. is the first," Lula said Tuesday, according to Reuters.

Bolsonaro was served with the order to surrender his passports Monday, a day after his stunning loss. Bolsonaro said he received it outside the home where his father, former President Jair Bolsonaro, is serving a 27-year sentence under house arrest for attempting a coup following his 2022 election loss to Lula. After his 2022 defeat, Jair Bolsonaro fled Brazil for Florida. He returned three months later.

The sealed Supreme Court order, viewed by The Associated Press, was issued Sunday. Bolsonaro has refused to concede defeat and has made unsubstantiated allegations of election fraud.

Lula, who turned 81 on Tuesday, received more than 64 million votes, compared with fewer than 60 million for Bolsonaro, a margin of nearly 4%.

World.title: At least 64 reported dead in high-speed train crash in Spain
World.content:
A high-speed train reportedly slammed into the rear of another train that had stopped in central Spain, derailing two cars and killing at least 64 people Wednesday morning, according to local authorities.

The regional government of Castilla-La Mancha told the Reuters news agency the death toll had risen to 64. Earlier in the day, 80 people were reported injured.

The crash occurred Wednesday morning in the province of Toledo, according to Spain's rail system operator ADIF. Rail service was suspended between Madrid, Ciudad Real and Andalusia.

Emergency services attend to the victims at the scene of a collision between two trains in Urda, Spain, on Wednesday, Oct. 28, 2026. Juanma Jiménez/AP

Padilla told state broadcaster TVE that the accident was between two high-speed trains heading in the same direction from Madrid to Seville and that one ran into the tail of the other while it was stopped, knocking two of its cars off the track. She said the cause of the crash was not known.

The accident involved a train from Spain's state-owned RENFE company and the private rail company IRYO. Trains from those two companies were also involved in a deadly crash in January.

Padilla said 397 passengers were in the RENFE train and 147 passengers were in the IRYO train.

Aerial view of carriages and first responders on the site of a collision between two trains in Urda, Spain, Wednesday Oct. 28, 2026. Guardia Civil/AP

The mayor of the nearby town of Urda, Manuel Galán, told Spanish state broadcaster TVE that passengers had been injured and that civil protection authorities had asked his town hall to prepare a sports pavilion to attend to passengers.

The regional president of Castilla La Mancha, Emiliano García-Page, wrote on X that he was on his way to the crash site.

In January, 45 people died in southern Spain when a train jumped the track and hit an oncoming train. The crash was the deadliest in Spain since a 2013 crash that killed 80 people. The January incident shook the confidence the European country has in its extensive high-speed rail network.

World.title: Serial killer Ted Bundy linked to another Utah girl's cold case murder
World.content:
DNA connects serial killer Ted Bundy to the death of a Utah teenager, authorities announced Tuesday, more than 50 years after her body was discovered by a hunter.

Bundy has been dead since 1989, but the tally of his confirmed victims continues to grow due to advances in DNA testing. He killed at least 30 women and girls in multiple states in the 1970s, and many more escaped or survived with injuries.

Investigators are satisfied that Bundy was responsible for killing 17-year-old Melissa Ann Smith in 1974, a death that had long been listed as a cold case, Summit County Attorney Margaret Olson said at a news conference.

Besides DNA evidence, Smith's death had the hallmarks of Bundy's "pattern, motive, means and opportunity," Olson said.

Investigators were able to close the cold case by making crucial DNA connections between Smith and Laura Aime, another Bundy victim whose case was resolved last April in Utah County.

A highly similar DNA profile linked to Bundy was found in evidence obtained from Smith's autopsy, Utah County Sgt. Mike Reynolds said.

"This case demonstrates the importance of preserving evidence," said Salt Lake County Sheriff Rosie Rivera.

Officials have been in touch with Smith's next of kin, none of whom still live in the area.

"With every case closure, may we stomp the memory of Ted Bundy out," Reynolds said.

Bundy was executed in 1989 by electric chair in Florida for the 1978 murders of two women at the Chi Omega sorority house at Florida State University.

Bundy killed at least 30 women and girls in multiple states in the 1970s, and many more escaped or survived with injuries.

In this 1977 file photo, serial killer Ted Bundy, center, is escorted out of court at the Pitkin County Courthouse in Aspen, Colorado. Ross Dolan / AP

Bundy was one of the nation's most prolific serial killers, with at least 30 women and girls' deaths linked to him in several states in the 1970s. In 2011, a vial of Bundy's blood — drawn in 1978 when Bundy was arrested in the death of a 12-year-old girl — was found in Florida. The full DNA profile was entered into the FBI's national database, giving investigators a shot at solving potential cases linked to Bundy.

His murders — which occurred in sorority houses, parks and elsewhere — set the nation on edge. Bundy's arrest drew widespread fascination, in part because many considered him to be charming and handsome.

Bundy gave a series of confessions in his final days, including to some crimes that were previously unknown to police. Not all of those cases have been confirmed.

It's not known when Bundy first began his attacks, but by 1974, young women — many of them college students — began disappearing in Washington state. Authorities were still investigating those cases when Bundy moved to Salt Lake City in September and began killing people in Utah, Idaho and Colorado.

Nancy Wilcox, a 16-year-old cheerleader in Salt Lake County, was believed to be one of Bundy's first victims in Utah, according to historian Linda Sillitoe. Wilcox disappeared on Oct. 2. High school senior Melissa Smith disappeared near the end of the same month. Deer hunters found her bludgeoned body, Sillitoe said.

World.title: Photos show record-breaking tides flooding homes, roads in California
World.content:
Photos show extensive flooding in some parts of Southern California amid record-breaking high tides that have swamped homes and highways.

The so-called king tide — the highest tides of the year caused by the full moon — reached 8 feet, 2 inches Tuesday in the Los Angeles Harbor, breaking a record set just the day before. The Pacific Coast Highway was inundated, and people in the area said water was coming up through the storm drains.

Linda Holle, who works at a marine fueling station in Newport Beach, told CBS News her office was flooded, and that she had never seen flooding like this before.

Experts say king tides during full moons in November and December could be even worse. If the king tide next month coincides with a winter storm and pounding surf, it could cause significant problems.

Cews work to repair a damaged boardwalk seawall at low tide, next to a protective sand berm in front of homes, some damaged by heavy surf, on Oct. 27, 2026 in Long Beach, California. Mario Tama/Getty Images

World.title: No clear winner in Israeli election as polls suggest stalemate
World.content:
No clear winner emerged in Israel's elections on Wednesday morning with the vote count still under way. Neither Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's coalition nor the opposition bloc, led by Gadi Eisenkot, secured a majority, according to exit polls on Tuesday night.

With 70% of votes counted, Netanyahu's Likud party has 20.6% and Eisenkot's Yashar party has 15.9%, according to official election data.

One or the other would need to obtain majority support in Israel's 120-seat parliament, known as the Knesset, in order to form a government.

On Wednesday morning, the head of Israel's main left-wing party called for his opposition allies to work with Arab parties to unseat Netanyahu.

"We must no longer accept Netanyahu's racist division between Jewish votes and Arab votes," Yair Golan said on X. "We have a responsibility. And we have an opportunity to form a government of change in partnership with Israel's Arab citizens."

Netanyahu dismissed the idea of partnership with Arab parties, instead calling on his allies to form a "right-wing, nationalist government."

"We must not endanger Israel and establish a government that relies on anti-Zionist Arab parties," Netanyahu said on Wednesday morning.

Israel's two Arab parties won more seats in parliament than in any previous election. That electoral success comes after what some Arab voters told CBS News was a difficult time for them in the country under the hard-right government of Netanyahu, prompting a historic turnout for the minority community.

Both Netanyahu and those opposing him have previously vowed not to form a government reliant on Arab parties, arguing it would endanger the country if they gain enough seats to influence Israel's engagement in its myriad conflicts. Arab citizens of Israel are around 20% of the population.

If the opposition breaks their pre-election vow — a common occurrence in Israeli politics — they could take power and remove Netanyahu. A central tenet of Netanyahu's election campaign was keeping the Arab parties out of power.

Another possibility given the current stalemate, analysts say, is a unity government between the pro-Netanyahu and opposition blocs without the Arab parties or the ultra-Orthodox. The question in this scenario is who would be prime minister or whether Eizenkot or Netanyahu could rotate out of the position.

This is the first election since the Oct. 7, 2023, attacks by Hamas, which authorities have acknowledged as Israel's most catastrophic security failure since the country's founding in 1948. Israelis headed to the polls with their country still fighting in the subsequent multifront war in Gaza, Lebanon and Syria, and after two direct rounds of conflict with Iran and Netanyahu advocating for renewed strikes.

For many Israelis, after three years of war on multiple fronts, the election is seen as existential, and voter turnout appeared to be high.

Netanyahu vs. the "change bloc"

Netanyahu, Israel's longest-serving prime minister and leader of the Likud party, is seeking to form another coalition similar to his current government, which relies on partnerships with ultranationalist and Jewish religious parties.

Netanyahu is telling voters that Israel's campaigns in Gaza, Lebanon and especially Iran, are ongoing, and he needs more time to finish what his government started.

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu speaks to supporters during a campaign event last week in Tel Aviv. Amir Levy / Getty Images

President Trump offered a full-throated endorsement of Netanyahu last week. He reiterated his administration's firm support for the war the two men launched jointly against Iran almost eight months ago, and warned that he could be disinclined to continue with it if Netanyahu doesn't hold onto power.

"If Israel has the wrong Leader, which would be anyone other than Bibi, America will have to do this work ourselves, and I am not inclined to do so," Mr. Trump wrote on Truth Social.

Running against Netanyahu is a diverse group of parties with different ideologies but one clear common denominator: They all want Netanyahu out of power.

The front-runner to lead the "change bloc," should its various parties collectively win enough seats to build a coalition, is former Israeli military chief Gadi Eisenkot, who leads the centrist Yashar party.

"The Israeli public has voted against Netanyahu's service as Israel's prime minister," Eisenkot said in a rally late Tuesday, according to Reuters. "A worthy leader would have accepted the people's non-confidence and announced today his retirement from politics."

Yashar party leader Gadi Eisenkot waves to supporters at a rally on Sunday in Tel Aviv. Erik Marmor/picture alliance/Getty

Eisenkot lost his son and two nephews while they were serving in the military in Gaza. He was part of the Israeli war cabinet for much of the first year of the Gaza war, working alongside Netanyahu. About half of his party's candidates in Tuesday's election are women, in stark contrast to the male-dominated Netanyahu coalition.

Eisenkot is framing himself as a humble veteran who wants to reunite Israel after years of division that he blames on Netanyahu.

What happens next?

In the event that neither bloc wins a clear majority in the Knesset, there are several paths forward to a new Israeli government.

One option is that parties or individual lawmakers could break election promises and switch sides, for which there is plenty of precedent in Israeli politics. There could be weeks of negotiating before a coalition is agreed on.

Another possibility is the change bloc, if it wins a significant share of the votes but not quite a majority, could seek to form a minority government. To do that, the parties just need to win more seats collectively than the other side, even if it's not more than the 50% of the 120 available.

Arab parties could give the change bloc that plurality by either voting in favor of a minority government, or just abstaining and not voting against its formation.

If there's a stalemate and neither side can build a coalition government, the country will have to hold new elections. There is plenty of precedent for that scenario, too.

Between 2019 and 2022, Israel held five elections due to electoral deadlock.

World.title: What's gone up even faster than gas or rent? The cost of caregiving
World.content:
What's gone up even faster than gas or rent? The cost of caregiving

toggle caption i Tyler Russell/Connecticut Public via Getty Images

As prices have ticked up in recent years, the cost to caregivers has skyrocketed. A study, released Wednesday by AARP, finds that family caregivers — people helping out disabled, chronically ill or elderly adults — now spend an average $11,508 out of pocket each year. That's roughly 60% more than just five years ago, and adds up to 31% of a caregiver's income, on average.

The increase during those years is more than twice the overall rate of inflation of 24%, as measured by the federal Bureau of Labor Statistics' Consumer Price Index.

What's driving the ramp-up? Food, housing and medical expenses are the biggest chunk, finds the study, which queried 2,538 family caregivers.

In other words, just the basics.

The bump in costs comes as family caregivers take on more care and more complicated medical responsibilities at home, says Megan O'Reilly, vice president of governmental affairs at AARP. "The more care that's needed, the more it costs."

Sponsor Message

And increased spending is only part of the story. The demands of caregiving often require people to reduce their working hours or quit work entirely, the survey finds. It's a double whammy: increased costs on top of lost income.

Increasing demands, falling income

Meghan Maher has seen that first-hand. Just seven weeks after the birth of her first baby, her mother was diagnosed with advanced cancer. Suddenly, Maher was a "sandwich" caregiver — parent and child needing her at the same time.

toggle caption i Maher family

At first, she tried to manage it all. She returned to her career in cancer research after maternity leave, but keeping up with the demands of work, her mom and her newborn son was too much.

She shrank her hours to part time. But even that wasn't manageable. There was no way to attend all her mother's appointments, coordinate her care, and also be available for big deadlines on the job.

She quit, and the family's income fell by half. Because her husband had a good job, they weren't struggling, but "it was definitely scary," she says now. As her mom got sicker her parents moved in, increasing the household expenses.

Sponsor Message

Soon after her mother's death in 2017, her father had a series of major complications from abdominal surgery and was critically ill for months. Maher needed to be by his side during hospital stays, advocating for him on a moment's notice, so now the family also needed to pay for child care. She estimates the cost at about $10,000 a year.

Her father eventually recovered, and the family was able to manage despite the difficulties. Many aren't so lucky.

About half of all family caregivers say they've made major financial sacrifices, according to the AARP report: Working more hours, cutting savings, or even drawing down on money put away for retirement.

More family caregivers, bigger bills

Many Americans deal with the cost of care, and more will in the future. About 63 million people now provide ongoing help for a family member or friend — roughly 1 in 4 adults. The need will likely grow: An estimated 70 percent of the people turning 65 today will need some form of help as they age.

Medicare does not pay for routine help either at home or in a facility, and that care is expensive. In 2025, 40 hours of in-home caregiving help a week ran about $72,792 a year, according to the insurance company Genworth, which conducts annual surveys of the cost of care. Skilled nursing costs an average of $115,000 per year for a shared room.

When Maher returned to work, she became a professional death doula. That means she helps clients with the emotional and practical challenges at the end of life. She's self-employed, so she can control her own schedule and limit the number of clients she serves. It allows her the flexibility to help her father as he ages. But her income is half what it would have been in her old career.

With the clients she helps, she sees other ways that care costs pile up. In Florida where she lives, it's routine for chronically ill people to hire an attorney in order to qualify for Medicaid, which unlike Medicare does foot the bill for long-term care. Even though they are eligible for the benefits, the paperwork is so complex that they wind up paying for legal help to navigate it. In Florida, she says, that runs about $6,000.

Sponsor Message

What she has seen and experienced motivates her to call attention to the caregiving crunch. In April, Maher testified before Congress at a special Senate committee on aging. "Caregiving has also reshaped my professional life," she said on the Senate floor. "The flexibility of self-employment comes with real financial and professional tradeoffs." She was invited by Daughterhood, an organization that offers support and resources for caregivers.

Family caregivers can access some public money, depending on where they live. All states pay some types of family caregivers through Medicaid. In California, for instance, more than 800,000 caregivers earn between $16.90 and $25 an hour for in-home work. Funds for these programs are likely to dwindle due to President Trump's big budget bill that cut nearly $1 trillion out of Medicaid funding over the next decade.

If the person who needs care is eligible for Veterans Administration benefits, they may also be entitled to financial help to cover the cost of caregiving. Like Medicaid, the rules are complex, and many family caregivers hire advocates to advise on eligibility and the application procedure.

More support on the horizon?

The cost of care hasn't been as visible as the cost of gasoline, food and healthcare, says AARP executive vice president Nancy LeaMond. She believes that will change. "When you see the number of people paying this kind of money, I think that'll be an impetus for action in the legislative arena."

In the last few years, Congress has introduced various proposals that could put some money back into the pockets of caregivers, such as allowing caregivers to spend money from their tax-sheltered health savings accounts on their parents' medical expenses. In some states, new rules are already a reality.

Six states now offer tax credits to family caregivers for expenses like retrofitting a home with grab bars or railings, usually between $1,000 and $5,000 a year. Two other states have more limited programs. Last year, two U.S. Senators introduced a bipartisan bill that would establish a similar $5,000 tax credit nationwide.

Sponsor Message

In 14 states and the District of Columbia, most employers are required to offer paid family and medical leave. Those policies include time off for caregiving for a family member. Another bill introduced into Congress would convert that into a national policy that would require up to 12 weeks of partly paid leave for some workers.

A third proposed federal law would protect the Social Security benefits of caregivers. Under current rules, a person who stops working in order to care full-time for family sees their future Social Security check shrink, because they are no longer earning credits toward retirement. This bill would change the law to continue awarding points to full-time caregivers.

"We spend a lot of time talking to members of Congress, and you can't raise this issue in a meeting without being interrupted by someone telling their own story," says LeaMond. "In time, I believe that will coalesce to support family caregiving."

Kat McGowan is an independent journalist covering adult caregiving who reports the series "What It Takes" for NPR.

World.title: Israel's election too close to call. And, the Ebola outbreak reaches grim milestone
World.content:
Israel's election too close to call. And, the Ebola outbreak reaches grim milestone

Good morning. You're reading the Up First newsletter. Subscribe here to get it delivered to your inbox, and listen to the Up First podcast for all the news you need to start your day.

Today's top stories

Midterm ad spending has surpassed a record $11 billion, according to Ad Impact. An NPR analysis found that candidates in four major Senate races spent more than $15 million on fundraising ads in the 2025-26 election cycle. Meanwhile, President Trump has been campaigning in tight races across states like Texas, Mississippi, and Kansas.

toggle caption i Elijah Nouvelage/Getty Images

🎧 Trump has not been sticking with his standard midterm pitch, which includes touting GOP tax cuts and attacking Democrats, NPR's Danielle Kurtzleben tells Up First. His jokes, including comments about Ohio Sen. Jon Husted's physique, entertain rally crowds but distract from the key issues the median voter cares about, like the economy and gas prices. Midterm turnout is usually low, but the GOP base still supports him, suggesting many MAGA votes are available, Kurtzleben says. But Trump needing to rally votes in very red states indicates a potential problem for his party.

The election in Israel is too close to call after voters turned out in record numbers to decide whether to keep Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu in office or oust him for an alternative. Netanyahu was in a tight race with his top rival Gadi Eisenkot, a center-right former military chief of staff. Final vote tallies may take time, and if no bloc secures a majority, it could take days or weeks for party leaders to form a governing coalition and determine the next prime minister.



Sponsor Message

🎧 Israelis went to bed thinking Eisenkot had the advantage, but by morning, Netanyahu pulled ahead, making the election too close to call, NPR's Daniel Estrin says. Election officials tell NPR that they expect to finish counting votes by tomorrow afternoon. The leading candidate will have six weeks to form a governing coalition, likely competing for support from defectors in each other's camps. Eisenkot could gain the majority of lawmakers' support in parliament, thanks to a strong showing from Arab-led parties eager to see him as prime minister. Eisenkot's camp is hesitant to form a coalition with Arab parties due to mistrust and demonization of Arab political leaders after the Oct. 7, 2023, attacks, Estrin says. He adds that both candidates don't have a clear path to a majority coalition.

The Federal Reserve typically combats inflation by raising interest rates. While prices are currently rising faster than average wages, investors don't expect a rate hike at today's meeting.



🎧 The Labor Department's latest cost-of-living report shows consumer prices rose 3.7% in September compared to last year. NPR's Scott Horsley says that marks a larger annual increase than the previous month. Fed policymakers raised interest rates in September, but investors believe the central bank will remain low-key ahead of Election Day and may increase rates again in December.

Sponsor Message

The Ebola outbreak has surpassed 10,000 people infected since its declaration in May, according to the latest figures from the Democratic Republic of Congo. This outbreak has spread faster than any in history. It is also the largest in geographic scope, spanning from Nigeria to Kenya, and is second in death toll with nearly 5,000 deaths. Around one-third of those who have died have been children.

On the ground

NPR

The results of the 2026 midterm elections will shape the final two years of President Trump's second term and serve as a precursor to the 2028 general election. This month, Morning Edition is reporting from six states that could change the balance of power in Washington.

With Election Day less than a week away, Morning Edition's Michel Martin went to the Midwest to hear from voters about what is important to them this midterm cycle. In Springfield, Ohio, the Trump administration has conducted an aggressive campaign to deport Haitian residents who have been living legally in the country with Temporary Protected Status. The administration revoked TPS for Haitians during Trump's second term. And in Michigan, Abdul El-Sayed has narrowly won the Democratic Senate nomination, a victory for the party's progressive wing. The swing state is important to both parties, which is why Trump and former President Barack Obama campaigned for their party's Senate candidate over the weekend.

Hear what voters in these two states had to say:

🎧 In Michigan, many voters expressed burnout as they worry about gas prices and healthcare.

🎧 Trump's tariffs are hitting Michigan households harder than any other state because many people depend on cross-border trade. But voters affected said the issue isn't so clear-cut.

🎧 Winning a statewide office in Michigan without Detroit is challenging, and El-Sayed didn't perform well there in the primary. Some Black Detroiters said they remain skeptical of him.

🎧 Some Springfield, Ohio voters said they are voting early because they are angry about the administration's treatment of Haitians.

Sponsor Message

Follow the reporting on Morning Edition, NPR.org, in the NPR app and in this newsletter.

The NPR App has all of NPR's election coverage in one place — from the biggest stories across the country, to the issues that matter close to home. Browse headlines, playlists, podcast episodes, videos and more, all on the 2026 Election tab.

Life advice

toggle caption i Juan Moyano/ Moment RF/ Getty Images

As the holidays approach and appointments and commitments begin to pile up, author Caroline Sylge recommends a "say no" retreat — a day dedicated to figuring out which obligations you want to decline in the coming weeks and months. While it may seem unconventional to devote an entire day to saying no, this approach can help create space for what truly matters to you. Sylge shared with Life Kit her suggested schedule for a "say no" retreat:

🙅 As soon as you wake up, list things you want to say no to. Identify the obvious tasks you want to avoid.

🙅 Take a break, then return to your retreat space and expand your "say no" list. Review requests, appointments, volunteer work and commitments for the coming days, weeks and months. Note the tasks you want to decline, and why.

🙅 After another break, review your list and start saying no. Start with a small win, like crossing off a demanding task. Next, focus on the tougher rejections that may involve saying no to someone you care about or work with.

For more guidance on a "say no" retreat, listen to this episode of NPR's Life Kit. Subscribe to the Life Kit newsletter for expert advice on love, money, relationships and more.

3 things to know before you go

toggle caption i Ella Mitchell/NPR

The latest installment of Sarah J. Maas' A Court of Thorns and Roses came out on Tuesday, prompting thousands of fans to attend midnight release parties at bookstores nationwide. A federal judge has temporarily blocked the Trump administration's plans to further change East Potomac Park, the municipal D.C. golf course that the president wants to turn into a championship-level venue.
