World.title: Why the Hispanic vote could sway the outcome of the U.S. midterm elections
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

While millions of U.S. voters have become only more entrenched in their party loyalties in the era of Donald Trump, the large and growing Hispanic community has instead bucked that partisan trend.

A willingness to cast ballots across party lines has made the roughly 39 million Hispanic eligible voters in the U.S. a crucial demographic at election time, courted equally by Democrats and Republicans.

They swung toward Trump in record numbers in 2024.

But if their current dissatisfaction with Trump's performance as president translates into votes in next Tuesday's midterms, the Latino community could potentially sway some crucial races and tip the balance of power in Congress toward the Democrats.

Latinos are the "swingiest" voters in the nation, says Javier Palomarez, president and CEO of the U.S. Hispanic Business Council, which advocates for the 4.5 million Hispanic-owned companies (small and large) across the country.

"We are a community that doesn't vote party, it votes person," Palomarez told CBC News. "You'll see Republicans willing to vote for a Democrat in the Hispanic community very often, and conversely Democrats willing to go for a Republican."

U.S. President Donald Trump travelled to Corpus Christi, Texas, for a campaign rally on Tuesday to try to boost support for Republican midterm candidates in the largely Hispanic districts of south Texas. (Eric Vryn/The Associated Press)

Trump increased his share of Hispanic voters in each successive election since 2016, garnering the highest percentage ever for a Republican presidential candidate in 2024, according to exit polls.

Yet the very issues that drove Hispanic support for Trump in 2024 — reducing the cost of living and tightening border security — could be the ones that hurt the Republicans in the 2026 midterms.

ICE tactics draw fire

Some Hispanic voters are focused on how Trump's decision to go to war with Iran triggered a sharp rise in the price of gas and diesel across the U.S.

Others are deeply concerned by the way Trump dramatically ramped up detention of undocumented Hispanics who've lived upstanding lives in the U.S. for years, rather than sticking to his pledge of deporting violent criminals.

In Texas, where Hispanics make up roughly one-third of eligible voters, disenchantment with Trump and the Republicans is palpable in the Latino-majority cities of the Rio Grande Valley.

CBC News shadowed a team of get-out-the-vote canvassers for LUPE Votes — an activist group whose name, La Unión del Pueblo Entero, translates as "union of all the people" — in the border city of Edinburg.

Canvassers with the activist group LUPE Votes prepare to knock on doors in the predominantly Hispanic city of Edinburg, Texas, with early voting under way in the U.S. midterms. José Ferrer, right, says his stepfather was detained by Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents and later deported. (Mike Crawley/CBC)

One of the canvassers, 24-year-old Jose Ferrer, said his stepfather was detained by Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) on Father's Day this year. The family found his truck abandoned at the side of the road and didn't hear from him for two weeks. He was deported to Mexico two months later.

"I'm not the only one getting affected, obviously," Ferrer told CBC News. His mother-in-law, a teacher, has described her students' parents being grabbed by ICE agents while waiting for the school bus.

ICE enforcement 'brutal' in south Texas: developer

The anger in the community over ICE tactics cuts across economic lines.

Mario Guerrero, a developer who voted for Trump three times because he considered him a very successful businessman, says immigration enforcement is one of the key reasons he'll vote Democrat on the midterm ballot.

"I believe in the American dream," Guerrero said in an interview at the site of a supermarket he's building beside a new housing development in Pharr, next door to Edinburg.

"The ICE enforcement that we've been seeing here in south Texas has been brutal," he said, adding that the job-site and roadside raids have scared off so many people from coming to work that the pace of construction projects slowed to a crawl.

Mario Guerrero, CEO of the South Texas Builders Association, oversees work on a grocery store his company is building on the edge of a residential subdivision in Pharr, Texas. (Mike Crawley/CBC)

"All of our workers are documented," Guerrero said. "The problem is [ICE agents are] apprehending, they're taking people with the proper documentation."

He believes the tactics will have midterm consequences for the Republicans, including "a turnout of Mexican Americans like they've never seen before."

Hispanic voting bloc defies generalization

Hispanic people now account for one-sixth of the eligible voters in the U.S., a larger group than Black Americans, according to data compiled by Pew Research Center.

But they defy broad generalizations as a voting bloc. They encompass devout Catholics, fiscally conservative entrepreneurs, working class immigrants-turned-citizens and college-educated Hispanics whose families have been in the U.S. for generations.

"We have seen over and over with data that we cannot put Latino voters in one category," said Dayana Iza, Texas director of Mi Familia Vota, a national organization that aims to build Latino political power.

She describes the group's work as helping Hispanic Americans "connect the dots" to understand how elections can have a tangible impact on their daily lives.

Álvaro Corral, an assistant professor of political science at the University of Texas Rio Grande Valley, specializes in the politics of Latino voters in the U.S. (Mike Crawley/CBC)

"That is what is really going to make a difference with how Latinos turn out for these midterms," Iza told CBC News.

"There are a lot of Latinos that still do not participate in this electoral process, and those are the folks that we're really trying to target."

Nuance on immigration, border security

But even if there is a notable shift away from the Republicans at the midterms, it won't necessarily mean that Hispanic voters are fully embracing everything about the Democratic Party.

Neither party has accurately reflected the nuanced position of the typical Hispanic voter on immigration and border security, says Álvaro Corral, political science professor at the University of Texas Rio Grande Valley.

He says that position combines strong measures to keep criminals from flowing across the border with a pathway to citizenship for undocumented migrants who've long worked in the U.S.

Instead, the Trump administration's approach "is really offending the sensibilities and morality of a large portion of the Latino voters," Corral told CBC News.

Palomarez, of the U.S Hispanic Business Council, says the Democrats "took the Hispanic vote for granted" and at the national level shifted "a bit too left for the Hispanic community's liking."

That leeriness about the Democrats can be seen in the campaigns of some of their own Hispanic candidates.

Bobby Pulido, left, campaigning recently at a seniors' activity center in McAllen, Texas. (Mike Crawley/CBC)

'Not Team Red. Not Team Blue'

Bobby Pulido, the Latino recording star who's trying to unseat incumbent Republican Monica De La Cruz in the 15th congressional district of Texas, downplays his party in his campaign ads and material.

"Not Team Red. Not Team Blue. Team You," says a slogan on the T-shirts worn by Pulido's campaign workers.

"Hispanics, they're not so partisan. It's very much, 'Are you gonna go fight for me?' That's what matters," Pulido told CBC News in an interview after he campaigned at a seniors' activity centre.

Still, Pulido says Hispanic Americans will punish Republican candidates in the midterms because they hate how ICE raids both separate families and disrupt the economy.

"When you add those two things, it's a very, very big explosion and you're going to see this Nov. 3."

World.title: At least 64 dead in crash between 2 trains in central Spain, authorities say
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

A high-speed train slammed into the rear of another train that had stopped, derailing two cars and killing at least 64 people on Wednesday in the province of Toledo in central Spain.

A high-speed train slammed into the rear of another train that had stopped, derailing two cars and killing at least 64 people on Wednesday in central Spain, the Castilla La Mancha regional government said.

Canada's Prime Minister Mark Carney said at least two Canadians were injured in the train collision, adding that the government is prepared to provide assistance.

"Our thoughts are with their families, the victims and their loved ones — in the days and weeks ahead,” Carney told reporters in Ottawa on Wednesday, adding that the federal government is ready to provide "any assistance" required.

Earlier Wednesday, the regional president of Castilla La Mancha, Emiliano García-Page, said that at least 80 people were injured and that the death toll "will surely rise" as rescue workers continue to search in the wreckage for survivors and bodies.

It was the second major train accident in Spain this year.

Spain's rail system operator ADIF said the crash occurred Wednesday morning in the province of Toledo. The accident was between two high-speed trains carrying hundreds of passengers and heading in the same direction from the capital Madrid to Seville in southwestern Spain, according to Esther Padilla, spokesperson for the Castilla La Mancha region.

One ran into the tail of the other that had stopped, knocking two of its cars off the track.

Padilla said that the cause of the crash was not known. Rail service was suspended between Madrid, Ciudad Real and Andalusia.

The crash, which occurred in a flat stretch surrounded by olive fields in between the towns of Urda and Los Yébenes, left one car shredded into bits of metal and other material, scattering debris down a gravel slope.

Spanish Health Minister Mónica García said that emergency workers were focusing on rescuing survivors and bodies from the two most damaged train cars. She said that the injured are being sent to different hospitals in the area.

"It was a high-speed impact, so we are expecting this to be a tragedy," García said.

The accident involved a train from Spain's state-owned RENFE company and the private rail company IRYO. It appeared the RENFE train rammed the IRYO train, Spanish media reported.

Passenger Ignacio Relaño was travelling on the RENFE train. He told state broadcaster TVE that the train had stopped momentarily on the line before it started again and then crashed into the IRYO.

"We all felt the train abruptly slowing down and then the impact," he said. "The car leaned to one side like it was about to tip over. I hit my nose, everything went flying, luggage, cell phones. Everything shook."

Padilla said that 397 passengers were in the RENFE train and 147 passengers in the IRYO train.

Trains from those two companies were also involved in a deadly crash in January.

IRYO, an Italian-owned company, said in a statement that it has "activated its security protocols and is closely working with authorities."

The spouse of a person who is missing is comforted near the site of the train collision on Wednesday in central Spain. (Violeta Santos Moura/Reuters)

The mayor of the nearby town of Urda, Manuel Galán, told state broadcaster TVE that civil protection authorities had asked his town hall to prepare a sports pavilion to attend to injured passengers.

A military emergency brigade was deployed to help emergency services, firefighters and police. Ambulances and medical helicopters made trips to and from the site, while unscathed survivors were put on buses.

Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez cancelled his agenda to focus on the crash. He wrote on X that he was "dismayed by the serious train accident in Toledo."

"Emergency services are working on site to attend to the affected passengers," wrote Sánchez, who faces a national election next month. "All my thoughts are with the victims and their families."

Latest crashes shake confidence in Spain's rail service

Spain's King Felipe VI and Queen Letizia said in a short statement on X that they were following news of the accident.

"We are deeply saddened and concerned by the train accident in Urda [Toledo]," the royal couple said. "We share in the grief of the families and loved ones of those who lost their lives, and we send our heartfelt support to the injured and all those affected."

European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said: "My heart goes out to the victims' families and loved ones. Today, Europe mourns with you."

Spain's soccer federation postponed all 24 Copa del Rey games scheduled on Wednesday.

The wreckage of Wednesday's crash reminded many of the aftermath of another train collision in January, when 45 people died in southern Spain after a IRYO train jumped the track and hit an oncoming RENFE train. That sent the first two cars of the impacted train plummeting down a four-metre slope.

That crash was the deadliest in Spain since a 2013 crash that killed 80 people.

The January incident shook confidence in the European country's extensive high-speed rail service.

PHOTOS | Dozens killed in Spain train collision:

Over recent decades, Spain has invested heavily in high-speed rail — which the country's railway union defines as rails for trains going 250 km/h and over — turning it into a world leader.

Spain has laid some 3,900 kilometres of such tracks over more than three decades for its 49 million residents. Only China, with 45,000 kilometres for its 1.4 billion people, has more high-speed track, according to the International Union of Railways.

Only recently did Spain open its rail network to private companies to compete against RENFE. IRYO started operating in Spain in 2022.

A spokesperson for Spain's train workers' union, Joan Rodríguez, said that the increased traffic brought by privatization has put extra strain on rail infrastructure.

"We are not convinced that the liberalization of the high-speed passenger rail service was matched by the necessary upkeep of the lines," Rodríguez told TVE. "I am not saying it was a determining factor [in the crashes,] but yes, the increase in use of the network is a factor to keep in mind."

World.title: Cruise billed as floating home suspends global voyage over fuel costs, stranding passengers
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

A U.S. cruise ship on an around-the-world voyage that touted its cabins as floating homes suspended its three-year voyage in Cambodia due to fuel costs, forcing hundreds of passengers to disembark.

The MV Odyssey set sail two years ago on a voyage to the seven continents marketed as combining long-term living at sea with global travel. Its operator had offered to "make the Odyssey your permanent home," with the purchase price of a suite for the lifetime of the vessel starting around $230,000 US, or about $323,000 Cdn.

For now, it is docked at the Cambodian port of Sihanoukville on the Gulf of Thailand, with no certain departure date.

The ship has been carrying 203 passengers, mostly Americans, along with 156 crew members, according to Cambodian officials. It has a 650-passenger capacity.

Its Florida-based operator, Villa Vie Residences, said monthly fuel expenses per cabin that historically averaged $2,527 Cdn have reached an estimated $8,425 to $11,234 in parts of Asia due to the war in Iran.

The company said it sought to reduce fuel consumption by slowing the itinerary and spending more time in port, but was unable to offset the surging costs.

The Odyssey, an around-the-world voyage that touted its cabins as floating homes, seen here in Japan in a press kit photo, has suspended its three-year voyage. (Odyssey/The Associated Press)

Traffic has been curtailed in the Strait of Hormuz since the Iran war began, squeezing supplies of all kinds of petroleum-based fuels, especially in Southeast Asia, and sharply increasing prices.

"We have been unable to continue carrying the resulting operating losses," Villa Vie Residences said in a statement issued Tuesday.

"Passing the full increase on to residents is not a realistic solution. Our focus now is on supporting residents, crew, and employees," the company said, while it tries to restructure.

"The company is working with residents to co-ordinate disembarkation and identify temporary living arrangements," it said.

Those on the ship had hoped to sail for years to come

Passengers, however, said they received no support and had to make their own arrangements after being given seven hours notice on Tuesday to disembark. Some were devastated and expressed hope a new company could rescue the venture so life at sea can continue.

Paul and Lynn Montoya, a retired couple from Wyoming, said they bought a window cabin and had expected to sail for years. They boarded the ship 17 months ago in Panama.

Passengers from the MV Odyssey, Paul Montoya, left, and his wife, Lynn Motoya, stand for an interview at the Independence Hotel in Sihanoukville, Cambodia, on Wednesday. (Heng Sinith/The Associated Press)

Paul praised the concept of residential cruising but said the shipowner lacked the expertise to make the business financially sustainable. While rising fuel costs had been cited publicly as the reason for the suspension, he said the company had already been struggling. Changes to itinerary, unreliable internet access and declining food quality had pushed many residents to leave the ship in recent months, he said.

Lynn said residents were repeatedly asked to contribute additional money for fuel and other expenses, including a fresh call to raise funds for fuel to get out of Cambodia. She said the crew members were also not paid.

"We were tired of every two to four weeks being asked for money for fuel, money for everything," she said. "We had hopes but they just kept sinking further and further into the hole through mismanagement."

The company could not immediately be contacted for comment.

For some, the venture was a worth risk taking

Yet for some, even the financial and logistical turmoil couldn't outweigh the extraordinary experience of travelling the world and living at sea.

Carol Larson, 69, and her sister Crystal Lavering, 72, occupied separate cabins aboard the ship for 18 months. The siblings, from California, described the suspension as heartbreaking, and hoped the cruise would be resuscitated.

"I hope there is a movement for the residents to buy the ship and I am hoping that goes through because it's a dream to live on the ship and I don’t want it to end," Larson said.

Lavering said her health improved during her time on the ship, and that she didn’t need to use a cane to walk anymore. "You come to this ship to live … it's just sad that it’s all over."

Larson bought her cabin for $168,000 Cdn, paid in installments, in addition to monthly maintenance fees, under a plan that had promised the possibility of living aboard for up to 15 years. She said she blamed U.S. President Donald Trump for the ship's woes as fuel costs spiked due to the Iran war, in addition to poor management. But she said she didn't regret her investment.

"Because it was a startup company, I believe that it was a risk. From the very first day, I said to myself that if it lasts a year, I can walk away and feel like I got my money's worth," she said. "I still feel that way. I feel blessed to have been part of the experiment of residential cruising."

Sisters Carol Larson, 69, left, and Crystal Lavering, both passengers from U.S. cruise ship MV Odyssey, speak outside the Independence Hotel in Sihanoukville on Wednesday. (Heng Sinith/The Associated Press)

The cruise began in Northern Ireland in 2024

The ship arrived in Sihanoukville last Friday and was scheduled to depart Wednesday, according to a statement from Long Dimanche, the deputy governor of Preah Sihanouk province. He said it was now expected to refuel and depart Cambodia on Saturday, but the ship's operator has not yet publicly confirmed any date.

Built in 1993 and operated under different names by several cruise lines over the years before being becalmed by the coronavirus pandemic in 2020, the Odyssey was bought by Villa Vie Residences in 2023.

Its current cruise, originally intended to last 3½ years, began in October 2024 in Belfast, where the ship had been refitted. A second cruise had been tentatively scheduled to end in August 2030.

World.title: Record amounts of Canadian cannabis seized as smuggling to Europe soars
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Hidden in a shipping container full of a family's household belongings. Stashed in crates cleverly built inside a facade of wooden fire briquettes. All neatly vacuum packed and labelled, and then shipped across the ocean.

Nearly a decade after it was legalized at home, Canadian-grown marijuana is being smuggled through Europe's largest ports, leading to record seizures and a call for Canadian officials to intervene.

According to Belgian customs officials, a record-breaking 21 tonnes of Canadian cannabis were seized in the port of Antwerp in 2025 alone, exceeding illegal exports from every other country in the world. That includes Morocco, until recently Europe's biggest supplier of illicit weed.

Officials told CBC News that smugglers are taking full advantage of Canada's decision in 2018 to legalize cannabis use to illegally ship it across the world and tap into the highly profitable European market. Criminals stand to make many more times in returns in Europe than what the same marijuana fetches at home.

"According to my information, it has to do with the policy of the Canadian government," Kristian Vanderwaeren, director general of the Belgian Customs and Excise, told CBC News in an interview in Brussels.

"And 320 million Europeans who have money to buy this … it's an immense market."

Europol, the EU's law enforcement agency, says the average wholesale price of a kilo of Canadian marijuana in a place like the Netherlands (where marijuana use is decriminalized, but technically illegal, as it is all over Europe) is about 4,100 Euros ($6,429 Cdn), and as much as 6,000 Euros (about $9,408 Cdn) in the U.K. Street prices would be even higher.

Kristian Vanderwaeren, director general of the Belgian Customs and Excise, says criminal organizations either earn a lot of money through smuggling or they don’t do it. (David Iacolucci/CBC)

In Canada, the wholesale price for a kilogram of dried cannabis is an average of $1,000 to $1,500 Cdn, according to the RCMP.

Vanderwaeren says he first noted the surge in 2024, and then seizures at the port spiked in 2025, prompting a "red alert." That’s when he contacted the Canada Border Services Agency (CBSA) for help in stemming the tide.

The port of Rotterdam, the largest in Europe, is also experiencing a surge in Canadian cannabis seizures this year.

CBSA confirmed intelligence indicates "a sustained increase in illegal export attempts since 2022, particularly to Europe" including Belgium, the Netherlands, Germany, France and others. In an emailed response to CBC’s questions, a spokesperson for the agency said such attempts are done "in cargo shipments, postal shipments, and smuggling by air passengers."

In 2025 alone, CBSA says its agents seized about 34 tonnes of cannabis products intended for export at maritime border points.

Still, Canada's policy is having a palpable impact in Europe, says Belgium's first-ever drug commissioner.

"This cannabis is sold in our Belgian streets but it's also going to the rest of Europe," said Ine Van Wymersch.

"This is a supply-driven market," she added.

"We see that criminal groups are taking advantage of a gray zone, that it is really hard for the Canadian government to mitigate and to regulate this whole new policy."

Legalization policies "sound very good in theory, but we have to take into account human behaviour," she said.

Belgian drug commissioner Ine Van Wymersch says information needs to be exchanged on both sides of the ocean to stop the smuggling. (David Iacolucci/CBC)

Van Wymersch, once Belgium's youngest public prosecutor, was appointed drug commissioner in 2023 to aid in the fight against rising drug crime. Brussels alone has seen a significant surge — 74 shootings so far this year, according to the Brussels-Capital region’s minister-president.

"The shootings we see and the explosions are overall mainly related to cocaine but also to cannabis," said Van Wymersch.

The violence has prompted a debate on whether Belgium may be devolving into a "narco state." Van Wymersch rejects that label, but in one indication of the severity of the situation, she is always protected by a security team.

"We can't be naive," she said. "These criminal gangs, they don't have any values.” To do her job, “there are some measures that need to be taken to protect me and my office."

Although drugs are also smuggled through Belgium's airports, most come via the port of Antwerp, officially called Antwerp-Bruges. It has long been considered a top cocaine gateway to Europe.

Smugglers are now using the same maritime lines, well-established criminal networks and logistics through Antwerp and Rotterdam to get Canadian marijuana to Europe, says Europol.

A drug sniffing dog searches a container during a customs control for drugs at the Belgian port of Antwerp-Bruges, on May 20, 2022. (Valeria Mongelli/AFP/Getty Images)

Europol gave CBC News exclusive insights on the movement of Canadian cannabis, including how criminal networks react when they encounter obstacles: "[They] will adjust, for example, by routing containers from Canada via the U.S. It is possible that cannabis from Canada destined for Europe could transit via the Caribbean."

"Smuggling is like surfing," said Vanderwaeren, the chief of customs. "You have to find the wave."

In other words, the criminal networks are swiftly adapting.

The surge in supply from Canada has meant Belgian seizures of marijuana at the port of Antwerp have for the first time overtaken those of cocaine.

CBC News is the first Canadian media organization to gain access to customs inspections at Antwerp, as well as a glimpse into some of the inventive ways smugglers tried to get Canadian cannabis through.

'Something was off'

One case concerned a container that arrived from Canada last February, ostensibly filled with the belongings of a family moving to France. Agents became suspicious when they spotted two juke boxes whose electrical innards had been removed, stashed among innocuous-looking household goods.

Once they opened the container, agents found packages of marijuana stacked inside the hollowed-out juke boxes.

Agents inspecting X-ray-like images of another container noticed an anomaly: What was supposed to be pallets-full of wooden briquettes for fires appeared darker at the edges.

This image supplied by Belgian customs shows juke boxes that had been stripped of all electronics and stuffed with Canadian cannabis. The machines were hidden in a container full of belongings from people who were moving from Canada to France. It arrived at the port of Antwerp in February. (Belgian Customs and Excise)

"My colleagues could see something was off," said communications officer Sara Van Cotthem.

They discovered that the briquettes were in fact a facade hiding crates that held vacuum-packed, one kilogram pouches of cannabis.

The port sees the equivalent of 13.5 million, 20-foot containers a year. Only one to two per cent of those containers are inspected, says Van Cotthem, using tools ranging from dogs, to scanners, to artificial intelligence and plain old intuition.

The rise in Canadian cannabis seizures has meant more scrutiny for Canadian containers than before, said Van Cotthem.

Sara Van Cotthem, a communications officer with Belgian customs, says officers undergo intensive training to learn how to spot suspicious shipments. (Brenda Witmer/CBC)

Any seized drugs are ultimately incinerated, she added. Finding the culprits is left to law enforcement in Europe and in Canada.

A recent example was a trial in Berlin that convicted ten men for smuggling marijuana from Canada to Germany, handing the three main defendants sentences ranging from six and a half to 15 years in prison. The judge ruled the three used a front company to move 1.1 tonnes of cannabis in shipping containers ostensibly carrying timber.

'Glocal' problem

Vanderwaeren says that since his appeal to Canada, he's noted a slight decrease in marijuana seizures in recent months, though the overall numbers remain high. He credits the CBSA’s ramped up efforts.

A letter of intent was subsequently signed between the heads of customs of Canada, Belgium, as well as France and The Netherlands, to cooperate on stymying smugglers.

However, Europol says the profitability of North American cannabis (due to its high potency and low production cost) coupled with the demand in Europe, "ensures that this illicit trade will likely persist and even grow." The profits will help fund other criminal activities, the agency added.

The CBSA says the RCMP is "aware of sophisticated transnational organized crime groups involved in the illegal cannabis market, including networks engaged in both illicit domestic distribution and international exportation."

The spokesperson added that Canada respects its obligations under international drug control treaties, and that the Cannabis Act regulates restrictions on import and export of cannabis. "Any other cannabis imports or exports … are prohibited."

Belgian officials are at pains to say they are not blaming Canada. But Vanderwaeren says that Canadians need to be aware of the unintended consequences of policies that are effectively "sponsoring criminal organizations" by enabling their huge profits.

Van Wymersch agreed, describing drug smuggling as a "glocal" problem — combining local and global — and so the solutions must be too.

"It will not help us to blame each other. Because we need each other," she said. "If we don't focus on the global level and we don't act on the local level, we will never come to something sustainable."

World.title: Meet the 'hell chicken,' a feisty little dinosaur who feasted on fruit
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

While other dinosaurs were crunching the bones of their prey in their powerful teeth, or slowly gnawing on leaves and twigs, Infernogallus jamesi may have been happily savouring nature's sweet delights.

The newly described creature — whose name translates to "hell chicken" — had a toothless beak and jaw structure that strongly suggest it ate a primarily fruit-based diet, according to a study published in Nature Communications ,

"This dinosaur was sort of a surprise to us because, for a long time, we didn't think dinosaurs were eating fruits," paleontologist Greg Funston, the study's lead author, told As It Happens host Nil Köksal.

In fact, if the study's authors are correct, that would make the hell chicken the first known frugivore dinosaur. Though some scientists caution that more evidence is needed to confirm the theory.

'Probably quite vicious'

Infernogallus jamesi was the turkey-sized dinosaur that lived about 66 million years ago, roaming the planet alongside the Tyrannosaurus rex and Triceratops.

It was a member of the Caenagnathid family, a group of bird-like dinosaurs with long beaks and feathered bodies. Funston described it as a cross between an emu and a parrot, and said it was "probably quite vicious in personality."

"Most people don't want to be stuck in a cage with a turkey," said Funston, an assistant professor at Stony Brook University in New York. "But it's not named for its mood or its bad behaviour."

LISTEN | Interview with paleontologist Greg Funston: As It Happens 6:32 Meet the 'hell chicken,' a feisty little dinosaur who feasted on fruit

Instead, the hell chicken gets its moniker from the Hell Creek Formation where its fossil was discovered in 2011. It's now a rocky area that spans much of the western U.S. and some of Canada. But back in the Cretaceous period, it was a lush forest filled with prehistoric creatures.

The finding is exciting because complete Caenagnathid fossils are rare, says paleontologist and author Riley Black, who wasn't involved in the study.

"I've been waiting for a fossil like Infernogallus for a long time," Black said in an email.

"Infernogallus is our first look at what a caenagnathid skeleton really looked like in life, and, even better, it's so strange that paleontologists might have to rethink how these dinosaurs were living."

A toothless beak and a human-like jaw

What's strange about the hell chicken's skeleton, says Funston, is its jaw.

Most dinosaurs, he said, had jaws that "chewed pretty much straight up and down." That gave herbivores the strength needed to consume prey, and allowed herbivores to chew through twigs, ferns, leaves and branches.

Not so for the hell chicken.

"Instead of pulling the jaws up and down, these muscles now would pull the jaws front to the back. This is a familiar motion for us. It's something we do when we're chewing," he said.

"This animal was chewing something relatively soft, but that needed a lot of manipulation and processing before it could be swallowed. To us, there's sort of only one thing that fits and that's fruit."

Scientists examined, scanned and reconstructed the skull of Infernogallus jamesi, a.k.a, the 'hell chicken.' (Submitted by Greg Funston)

If they're right, that would solve a mystery that has long plagued palaeontologists, he says.

About 130 million years ago, flowering plants began to emerge on Earth, replacing the cone-bearing plants that preceded them, and providing an abundance of fruit for animals to feast upon.

Birds — which are, themselves, dinosaurs — were early fruit adopters. Studies show evidence they've been eating nature's candy for at least 120 million years .

But until now, there's been little evidence that non-bird dinosaurs ate fruit, at least not as a dietary staple.

"For a long time, we were sort of struggling to see how dinosaur evolution matched up with this big change," Funston said.

Evidence 'circumstantial,' cautions scientist

But evidence the hell chicken was a fruit specialist remains, "for the moment, circumstantial," says Black.

"When we're looking at dinosaur skeletons, there's always tension between what a dinosaur could have done and what it actually did," she said.

"The beaky face of Infernogallus and the animal's size leaves little doubt that the dinosaur was plucking small morsels and eating relatively soft foods. But what?"

To be certain, she says, scientists would need to find direct evidence of fruit inside the creature's preserved guts — something easier said than done. A hell chicken would have to die shortly after eating, become fossilized, then be found relatively intact.

"Such finds are relatively rare, sometimes requiring exceptional circumstances and not a little bit of luck," she said. "That we have any gut contents for any dinosaurs is very fortunate."

Still, she says, the research is an exciting first step.

"The study will certainly feed further research and analysis on how plants and dinosaurs were interacting with each other," she said.

"Few things in paleontology are ever the final word on how an animal that's been dead for millions of years really lived. It's the questions that keep us looking and debating, and that's part of what's so wonderful."

World.title: Polls open across Manitoba for the 'wonderful opportunity' to vote in municipal elections
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Manitobans are headed to the polls in municipal elections across most of the province.

Voting locations are open from 8 a.m. to 8 p.m. for casting ballots for mayors (or reeves, as the head of council is known in many rural municipalities), councillors and school trustees in the majority of Manitoba's 137 municipalities .

A general municipal election happens every four years and always on the third Wednesday in October. The only exceptions are in Winnipeg Beach, Dunnottar and Victoria Beach, where elections were held July 24.

"It's a great day to go out and exercise your right to vote," said Sherwood Armbruster, the City of Winnipeg's senior election official.

Results for all of Manitoba will be updated as they are received from voting locations on the 2026 Manitoba municipal elections website shortly after polls close at 8 p.m., .

CBC Manitoba will also have coverage of the election online and on radio and television.

Voters wait in line at Bison Run School for the polling station to open on Wednesday morning. (Meaghan Ketcheson/CBC)

Tyler Wiwchar was first in line to cast his ballot at Bison Run School in the Waverley West neighbourhood of south Winnipeg, stopping on his way to work.

"I thought the first stop would be coming to vote as it it's an important thing to do — try to get there as soon as possible," he said. "Everyone should be able to have the opportunity to come vote and select someone that represents Winnipeg."

His choice was still being determined as he waited for the door to open. As Wiwchar did some last second research, he used a sports analogy for making a selection.

"Yeah, just like a hockey decision, a quick and quick and simple play," he joked.

Bola Osagie says she believes the people she voted for 'are good candidates that would move this area forward.' (Rudy Gauer/CBC)

Bola Osagie, who made her choice right after Wiwchar at Bison Run School, called it a privelege to vote.

“It's a wonderful opportunity to express what I wanna see done in the city," she said.

"I listened to them talk and I found out about the people I wanted to vote for and I believe that they are good candidates that would move this area forward."

For a look at the promises Winnipeg's mayoral candidates have made during the election campaign, click here.

The City of Winnipeg says the busiest times at polling stations are typically right when the they open and then again from 3 p.m. until close.

D on’t worry if you're still waiting to vote at the deadline. As long as you're in line, you'll be able to mark your choices.

But if you have the option consider voting during the quieter period between 9 a.m. to 3 p.m., when the process is likely a little quicker, the city says.

Winnipeg voters must be Canadian citizens, at least 18 years old on Oct. 28 and Winnipeg residents or property owners for at least six months (since April 28), the city says .

Eligibility to vote in municipal and school board elections can by found on the provincial government website. This includes eligibility for non-resident voters in municipal elections.

More choice

More Manitobans are getting a choice of who leads their communities than in 2022.

There are fewer acclamations compared to four years ago, the Association of Manitoba Municipalities said. U ncontested races are down to 30 per cent from 37 per cent in 2022.

At the same time, t he number of women candidates has increased to 340 this year from 289 in the previous election, the association said.

Incumbent mayors in several Manitoba communities, however, were acclaimed after no challengers registered to run. Those include Portage la Prairie, Winkler and Niverville.

Some places, like the Municipality of Cartwright-Roblin and the Rural Municipality of Argyle, saw their entire slate of council candidates acclaimed.

There's also more voting flexibility this year in Winnipeg, home to more than half the province's population. There are 184 polling stations and registered voters should have received a card letting them know exactly when and where to cast a ballot.

"The voters card is going to present not one, but two convenient locations," said Armbruster.

"We're also proud of the fact that we had a record number of advanced voters. More than 50,000 Winnipeggers have already cast their vote, which is 20 per cent higher than the previous record that was set four years ago."

If someone hasn’t received a voters card, they can call 311 to ask where their polling station is, or look it up on the city's where do I vote? web page.

"We always recommend you bring your voters notice if you have one. If you don't, bring one piece of valid government-issued photo ID with your name and current address," said Armbruster.

A list of accepted ID is available on the city's website .

World.title: Election denial has gone mainstream in the U.S. What does that mean for the midterms?
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Early on a Wednesday morning in October, a dozen people gathered in a wood-panelled room in Barry County, Mich., to be trained as poll workers for the U.S. midterm elections.

During the three-hour session, they were taught how to operate a vote-tabulating machine, check photo IDs and process absentee ballots.

But before the session began, Sarah VanDenburg, the clerk in this rural county, thanked them for "helping preserve our democracy."

As the clerk of Barry County, Sarah VanDenburg is responsible for staffing polling stations on election day. (Michael Drapack/CBC)

The 2026 midterms are taking place while an election denial movement, empowered by President Donald Trump, has spent months claiming these otherwise routine tasks are the source of rampant fraud.

And even though there is little evidence to support these claims, they’re being used as a pretext by election deniers — many now in positions of authority — to try to interfere in the voting process.

Trump himself has mused openly about invoking a national emergency measure to alter how votes are counted.

President Donald Trump greets Mike Rogers, a Michigan Republican candidate for Senate, left, on stage during a campaign rally in Port Huron, Mich., on Oct. 25. (Julia Demaree Nikhinson/Associated Press)

In Barry County, sheriff Dar Leaf has emerged as the loudest voice pushing conspiracies about how elections are run. For the past six years, he has been using his office to circulate claims that foreign nationals hacked voting machines in the county in 2020 to switch votes from Trump to Joe Biden.

More recently, Leaf has been trying to interrogate state election officials as part of a new investigation into claims Michigan’s voter rolls for the 2026 midterms are being deliberately inflated with non-citizens, even though studies have shown non-citizen voting is extremely rare.

"I have a duty to go out and investigate, and I'm not gonna back down," Leaf told CBC News during an interview at sheriff headquarters in Hastings, Mich.

VanDenburg says she tries to maintain a good working relationship with the sheriff, but his beliefs "can make things difficult."

I have a duty to investigate, sheriff says

Leaf is a prominent figure in the Constitutional Sheriffs and Peace Officers Association, which believes sheriffs have ultimate authority in their county and has encouraged its members to investigate unfounded voter-fraud theories.

"It's just getting the sheriffs woke up to what their duties are really supposed to be," Leaf said about the association.

Barry County Sheriff Dar Leaf, seen here at a 2024 Trump campaign event, said he would consider seizing ballots during the midterm elections. (Paul Sancya/AP Photo)

With help from his own deputies, Leaf tried to seize several voting machines in the county in 2021 and 2022 to prove his theory, only to be rebuffed by a judge and prosecutor who determined his claims had no merit.

In an unprecedented move last year, another member of the group, California sheriff Chad Bianco, seized 650,000 ballots from the 2024 election to probe claims of irregularities. A court ruled the seizure unlawful and ordered the ballots returned.

But the prospect of ballots, or voting machines, being seized by pro-Trump officials has alarmed elections observers, who worry such manoeuvres could disrupt oversight and make it difficult to verify results.

Asked if he would consider seizing ballots, Leaf told CBC News, "I would have to have a good reason to seize them. We'd probably seize and then go get a court order."

When election deniers are in charge

For decades, the U.S. Department of Justice monitored local compliance with federal election laws. But under Trump, election deniers now occupy senior positions in the department, which has aggressively sought evidence to support the president’s claims of widespread voter fraud.

For instance, the department is battling 30 states for access to sensitive voter information as part of an effort to find evidence of non-citizen voting.

Earlier this year, the FBI seized ballots in Fulton County, Ga., from the 2020 election. The Justice Department said it was investigating 'irregularities that occurred during the 2020 presidential election in the County,' even though Georgia’s votes in the 2020 presidential race were already counted three times. Each count affirmed Democrat Joe Biden’s win. (Mike Stewart/AP Photo)

The FBI and Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) have also been tasked with investigating voter fraud, even though most studies suggest it's a rare phenomenon .

Trump has used the premise of widespread voter fraud to justify his attempts to have the White House exert more control over elections and rewrite rules in his favour. Since returning to power, he has ordered the U.S. Postal Service to restrict mail-in voting and pushed Congress to pass a voter ID law that would have made it harder for millions of Americans to vote.

But the Constitution gives states, not the president, authority over elections. And courts, so far, have upheld that principle.

Can Trump call a national emergency?

The failure of these efforts, combined with polls suggesting the Republican majorities in Congress are in jeopardy, has led some in the election denial movement to urge Trump to take even more drastic measures, such as calling a national emergency.

Proponents of the measure argue voting machines are so vulnerable to foreign hacking that an emergency would be warranted on national security grounds.

WATCH | Joly says Canada 'absolutely not' interfering in U.S. election: Canada 'absolutely not' interfering in U.S. midterms, Joly says | Duration closed caption 1:19 Asked about the United States Ambassador to Canada Pete Hoekstra's comments about watching for Canadian interference in the U.S. midterm elections, Minister of Industry Mélanie Joly says 'we never do that and we never accept that also being done to us in Canada.' She says her recent visits to the U.S. were 'to attract investments' by American companies and she will continue to do so.

In an interview with Time magazine published earlier this month, Trump was asked about the possibility of declaring a state of emergency. "I don't rule anything out or in," he replied.

Lorenzo Sewell, a Detroit pastor with ties to the Trump administration and several Republicans in Congress, said calling a national emergency would allow the president to order states to stop using vote-tabulating machines and halt mail-in balloting.

Pastor of 180 Church Lorenzo Sewell delivers a benediction after President Donald Trump was sworn in at the U.S. Capitol in Washington, D.C., on Jan. 20, 2025. (Saul Loeb/Associated Press)

"But in terms of getting something like this, he needs people. He needs another January 6th, and that's what I'm advocating for, minus the violence," said Sewell, who spoke at Trump’s second inauguration and the Republican convention this summer.

Many legal experts say the idea is unconstitutional and almost certain to be blocked by the courts.

"Our entire constitution is based on the idea that the president has no power over elections," said David Becker, a former elections lawyer with the Department of Justice who now heads the Center for Election Innovation and Research.

Training 'democracy defenders'

State lawmakers and progressive voting-rights groups are nevertheless preparing for a wide range of scenarios on election day, including the prospect of confrontations with armed federal agents or pro-Trump crowds.

"It seems the rhetoric has become more violent," said Autumn Butler, deputy executive director of Michigan United, a Detroit-based social justice organization that's been training "democracy defenders" in de-escalation tactics.

Autumn Butler is deputy executive director of Michigan United, a Detroit-based social justice organization that's been training 'democracy defenders' in de-escalation tactics. (Michael Drapack/CBC)

She recalled how, in 2020, a crowd of Trump supporters attempted to disrupt poll workers counting mail-in ballots in Detroit.

"That's why we have our democracy defenders," Butler said. "These are the scenarios that we're thinking about and planning for."

VanDenburg, the Barry County clerk, is hoping her preparations will help prevent tensions from boiling over on election day.

She recently gave a presentation to the sheriff and his deputies about basic election day rules, such as who can enter a polling station (armed officers are not allowed).

Leaf welcomed the information, saying, "some of those things we've never been taught before."

Those working the polls in the county will mostly be people from the community, which VanDenburg says will lighten the atmosphere.

"You walk into the polling place and you feel warmth. You feel invited, which I think is very important for our voters to feel that way."
