World.title: Colombia’s government claims Petro exploited 48 women as president
World.content:
The administration chief of Colombia’s President Abelardo De la Espriella told Congress that former President Gustavo Petro hired at least 48 women who were “trapped and exploited” for presidential parties.

During a hearing, DAPRE director Carlos Andres Rios claimed that Petro had 48 women “working in the Presidency, who were unfortunately exploited through temporary work contracts.”

We’re going to prove this to the Colombian people: how, unfortunately, the Casa de Nariño was set up, organized, and designed not for governing, but for partying there every day, bringing women there and engaging in behavior we should not be engaging in—behavior that sets a bad example. DAPRE director Carlos Andres Rios

“Forty-eight women are already speaking with us about how, through a contract and an OPS, they were trapped and exploited in order to be with President Petro,” said Rios.

Former DAPRE director Angie Rodriguez, who was sacked by Petro in July, doubled down on her successor’s allegations and asked the former president to prove that the president managed a network of women, including child transvestites.

Were there transvestite children there? Answer me, Mr. President. Were there transvestite children there? I am asking you a question, and I have every right to ask it. Were there? And if there weren’t, uh… prove that what I am saying is a lie. Angie Rodriguez

Last but not least, far-right magazine Semana published an interview with a woman identified as Deicy Jimenez, who claimed she as hired by Petro after meeting him on an adult website.

Jimenez even told Semana’s former presidential candidate Vicky Davila she trafficked drugs for the former president when he was senator.

VD: What happened on the day you say you transported drugs for Petro? DJ: Yes, I was traveling, and he asked me as a favor to bring him some drugs. VD: Were you outside of Bogotá? DJ: Yes. VD: How do you recall that favor Petro asked of you? DJ: He asked me as the favor to bring him some drugs. VD: Did you buy them? DJ: Yes, I bought them somewhere. He gave me money. VD: Did he give it to you in cash or deposit it for you? DJ: In cash. VD: How much money? DJ: Three million pesos. VD: What kind of drugs did you buy? DJ: Cocaine. VD: Where did you buy it? DJ: I bought it from some people. I can’t say (publicly) their names or the location. VD: Is it a gang? DJ: Yes. VD: Did he know you were going to buy the drugs from that gang? DJ: Yes. VD: At that time, was he a senator or the president? DJ: A senator. VD: How did you bring that drug in? DJ: I brought it through the airport. VD: You mean, on a plane? DJ: Yeah. VD: Did you get on a plane with Petro’s drugs? DJ: Yes. VD: How were the drugs packaged? DJ: In bags. VD: Like individual doses? DJ: Yes. VD: And where did you hide the drugs? DJ: In my suitcase.

In a response, Petro denied having hired women for sex and claimed that the far-right attack were the result of authorities’ failure to sustain corruption allegations.

World.title: “Brazil and Colombia need each other,” says De la Espriella
World.content:
Colombia’s President Abelardo de la Espriella recognized the election victory of his Brazilian counterpart Luiz Ignacio Lula, who defeated far-right candidate Flavio Bolsonaro on Sunday.

In a post on social media platform X, the Colombian President said that “in the Colombian presidential campaign, President Lula openly supported Ivan Cepeda, and I won. In the Brazilian campaign, I supported Bolsonaro, and Lula won.”

“Neither does Lula decide for Colombians, nor do I decide for Brazilians. THE PEOPLE DECIDE! And when the people speak at the polls, their will is respected because it is sacred,” the president added.

Lula and I have major and profound political and ideological differences, but we agree on one fundamental point: Brazil and Colombia need each other. No other consideration can take precedence over the interests of our nations. Colombia and Brazil are sister nations, facing enormous shared challenges and opportunities.

President Abelardo de la Espriella

De la Espriella stressed that “we have much to do and much work to carry out for the benefit of our peoples” an ought to “fight against narco-terrorism and illegal mining, the protection of the Amazon, and the well-being of our citizens.”

Lula was the first leftist candidate and critic of US President Donald Trump to win an election, triggering celebrations among leftists throughout the continent.

De la Espriella, a US citizen, has been among the most fanatic among Trump supporter in trying to align his domestic policies to US foreign policy.

World.title: De la Espriella sacks interior minister after Congress bungles Colombia’s 2027 budget
World.content:
Colombia President Abelardo de la Espriella sacked Interior Minister Rodrigo Lara hours after Congress found a procedural flaw in the passed 2027 budget, which makes the law invalid.

In a post on social media platform X, De la Espriella briefly thanked Lara and announced he would be replaced by the ambassador to the Organization of American States, Alejandro Ordoñez.

The news surprised the interior minister, who suddenly left a congressional debate on a law to facilitate the demobilization of illegal armed groups after receiving a message on his phone.

Lara was apparently held responsible for the blunder of Congress, whose two houses approved the 2027 budget but with conflicting versions of an article on financial risk-coverage mechanisms for the Ministry of Finance.

By the time the error was detected, the budget debate had passed its October 20 deadline, forcing De la Espriella to issue a decree that would convert an older version of the budget bill into law.

The interior minister was the administration’s primary political liaison responsible for managing legislative procedure and whip operations in Congress.

Lara’s job was already under pressure after he failed to convince Congress to cede its presidency to the president’s candidate.

While Ordoñez returns from Washington, Justice Minister Ivan Cancino will assume the role of interior minister.

The incoming interior minister is an ultra conservative Catholic with ties to the Society of St. Pius X, which considers the modernizing reforms of the Catholic Church heresies and errors, and was declared in a schism with the church in June.

In Colombian politics and particularly among the opposition, Ordoñez is mainly remembered as the inspector general who illegally removed former President Gustavo Petro from his post as mayor of Bogota in 2013.

Petro was ultimately reinstated and would become president of the country in 2022.

World.title: Colombia’s Congress approves De la Espriella’s 2027 budget
World.content:
Colombia’s Congress agreed to increase the government’s 2027 budget despite promises by President Abelardo de la Espriella to reduce public spending.

Next year’s budget will be COP634.9 trillion, almost $204 billion, which is 16% more than last year’s budget and 10% higher than the proposal made by former President Gustavo Petro.

According to Finance Minister Miguel Gomez, the budget seeks to bring the State’s finances in line with reality.

The budget was approved in both the Senate and the House of Representatives with the support of De la Espriella’s government coalition.

The Historic Pact, the only leftist opposition party, rejected the budget and boycotted the vote.

On behalf of the national government, I would like to thank you all for your work over the past few months in passing the budget. I would also like to thank the opposition for the strength with which they defended their views. The message that Congress has sent today regarding the government’s economic policy is very important. It is the first step toward putting the country’s economy back on track toward growth, fiscal responsibility, and addressing the nation’s needs. Finance Minister Miguel Gomez

The budget seeks to reimpose the neoliberal model that had been abandoned by Petro and reduce public debt.

According to Green Party representative Jaime Raul Salamanca, who opposed the budget, funding for free higher education was cut in half from COP800 billion ($254 million) to COP400 billion (127 million).

“This cut raises concerns about its potential impact on the continuity and scope of this policy, which has enabled thousands of young people to enroll in public institutions of higher education,” said Salamanca.

The budget also cut the budget for the war crimes tribunal JEP, which could endanger the future of the peace process with the FARC and is opposed by the government.

World.title: De la Espriella announces “open, resolute, and patriotic struggle against wokeism”
World.content:
Colombia’s President Abelardo de la Espriella announced an “open, resolute, and patriotic struggle against wokeism” as part of his “cultural counterrevolution.”

During a visit to the Culture Ministry, De la Espriella described wokeism as “an ideological paradigm that aims to transform moral, cultural, and social foundations in the West, perverting values, family tradition, and national identity.”

According to the president, Culture Minister Paola Holguin was a general in the “cultural counterrevolution.”

Culture has an enormous capacity to shape society, and that is why the State has a moral, inescapable, and political duty to prevent cultural spaces from being taken over by social communism, which is atheist and an enemy to the fundamental values upon which the nation of Colombia is built. This is where that cultural counterrevolution will begin. President Abelardo de la Espriella

De la Espriella said that Holguin, the daughter of a reported money launderer, would lead the “Culture War” against the “extreme left,” which has “permeated all parts of society, particularly the cultural and academic spheres.”

I want to be clear about this: we are going to wage an open, resolute, and patriotic struggle against wokeism, which is nothing more than an ideological movement that aims to transform the moral, cultural, and social foundations of the West, corrupting values, family tradition, and national identity. President Abelardo de la Espriella

Earlier in the day, the National Museum removed all references to members of the exterminated Patriotic Union party, slain guerrilla leader and presidential candidate Carlos Pizarro, and the struggle for the rights of Colombia’s LGBT+ community.

References to Colombia’s former guerrilla movements was “terrorism apology, which is “exactly what we have come to confront” in an attempt to “recover pride for Colombian culture.”

Atheists, the Pizarro family and gay rights activists rejected the president’s attempts to remove them from mainstream culture.

World.title: Colombia’s first lady promises transparency over earthquake donations
World.content:
Colombia’s first lady, Ana Lucia Pineda, vowed to reveal how much money she collected and spent in response to the August 10 earthquake that affected hundreds of thousands of people.

Amid mounting public pressure about where the money had gone, Pineda went on the morning program of public television channel Nuestro Caribe to promise that her foundation, Luz y Sonrisas, will take its finances public on Friday.

Carrying a white folder, the wife of President Abelardo de la Espriella stressed that “in the foundation’s accounts rest all, absolutely all of the monies from the donations we received during the ‘Colombia One Single Heart’ campaign” that was announced on August 12.

“A lie is not going to tear down the truth of who I am or what I represent, or how my children recognize me,” said Pineda.

Luz y Sonrisas was one of three NGO’s that were promoted by the De la Espriella government to collect contributions for victims of the earthquake.

Pineda’s foundation was the only one that could receive contributions from abroad.

Earlier in the week, news program Noticias Uno revealed that her foundation that was founded on July 7 lacked the tax exemption that would allow it to accept donations, a process that usually takes months.

In a press statement, tax office DIAN subsequently said that it had granted the tax exemption to the first lady and that she could legally accept financial contributions.

Pineda did not say how much money she had received, but said that she stopped supporting the initial relief efforts “because the humanitarian aid was sufficient, it was huge.”

The first lady vowed she had saved the donations for the reconstruction phase “because I have also taken the initiative to build and return to the victims a house that is durable for the families who lost everything.”

World.title: Colombia’s opposition takes to the street to protest De la Espriella
World.content:
Despite intimidation attempts by the national government and the police, tens of thousands of people took to the streets throughout Colombia to protest the far-right government of President Abelardo De la Espriella.

The protest had been organized by social organizations, labor unions and the country’s largest opposition party, the Historic Pact.

Opposition leader Ivan Cepeda, who joined the protests in Bogota, told a reporter that the government is “exercising a mafia-style rule in the service of the worst elements of Colombian politics—the drug trade.”

Contrary to what De la Espriella is saying, this is not a government that opposes drug trafficking; it is a government that supports the drug trafficking cartels, the paramilitaries, and the ultra-conservative forces that want to destroy people’s rights, the democratic advances made by President Gustavo Petro, and the progress achieved by the popular movement over the past four years. Senator Ivan Cepeda

“That’s why we’re here; we won’t allow people’s rights to be violated or trampled upon,” said the senator.

Hours ahead of the protest, the president signed off on a decree that changed the police response to protests and accused the organizers of being “instigators of evil” who “seek to once again cause chaos.”

Human rights organizations denounced that the security forces put snipers on the roofs of buildings in Bogota and in Cali, a helicopter flew over the heads of the protesters.

The protests sought to test the waters for an even larger “national strike” that is set for November and shut down parts of the country in 2021.

“We are only warming up,” warned Cepeda, who has yet to recognize De la Espriella as Colombia’s legitimate president after losing the elections in July.

World.title: Colombia’s national strike organizers “are instigators of evil,” claims De la Espriella
World.content:
Colombia’s President Abelardo de la Espriella called labor unions and social organizations who organized anti-government protests for Wednesday “instigators of evil” who “seek to once again cause chaos.”

In an address to the nation, De la Espriella stressed that the security forces were instructed to allow peaceful protests, but warned the protesters that “if they intend to set Colombia ablaze, they will face the determination of the tiger and his government to do what is lawfully required—which is to defend the lives, honor, and property of all Colombians.”

Wednesday’s protests are a preparation for a national strike that is set to take place in November and is supported by the country’s political opposition to the far-right government.

According to the president, “those who are promoting the strike and seeking to use it to once again cause chaos and destabilize the government are the very same people who left the country bankrupt, on the brink of a blackout, with the healthcare system in intensive care, energy sovereignty compromised, and public resources plundered and looted.”

“They are instigators of evil, not fighter for freedom,” said De la Espriella.

If they intend to set Colombia ablaze, they will face the determination of the tiger and his government to do what is rightfully required—which is to defend the lives, honor, and property of all Colombians. President Abelardo de la Espriella

The president stressed that he would be signing a decree that regulates public protests in an attempt to avoid the chaos that erupted during massive strikes in 2019 and 2021 an killed 80 people.

De la Espriella additionally is expected to present an “anti-terrorism stature” to Congress, which could see the prosecution of protest organizers on terrorism charges, according to opposition leaders and security experts.

World.title: Adderstone builds on the foundations of hangar success with new Stanley House contract
World.content:
Adderstone builds on the foundations of hangar success with new Stanley House contract

28th Wednesday, October 2026 - 10:28 UTC Full article

M. Wallbank (Managing Director), G. Vatamanu (General Foreman) and Natasha Greenland (General Manager), Adderstone Co. (Falkland Islands) Ltd, outside the newly completed FIGAS hangar, Port Stanley.

Adderstone Construction (Falkland Islands) Limited, part of the Newcastle-headquartered property and construction group, has been awarded a further contract by the Falkland Islands Government, shortly after completing the redevelopment of the FIGAS aircraft hangar in Port Stanley.

The redevelopment gives the islands' air taxi service a hangar built for the long term, keeping communities connected to schools, farms and medical care.

Work is now underway on Adderstone's next Falkland Islands Government contract: upgrading residential amenities at Stanley House. Built in 1878, it is one of Stanley's oldest and most prestigious buildings, and since 1981 it has been where children from the islands' farms and settlements live while they attend secondary school. Children on remote farms,some more than 200 miles from Stanley, are taught at home by travelling teachers until secondary school age. At that point, many move to Stanley and board at Stanley House if their families live too far away to travel each day.

Both projects reflect Adderstone's growth strategy in the Falklands: long-term investment in the infrastructure and buildings that matter to island communities. Stanley House plays a role in island education every bit as vital to daily life as the hangar itself.

Martyn Wallbank, Managing Director of Adderstone's Falkland Islands division, said: “We see our relationship with the Falkland Islands Government as a lasting one, and it rests on doing what we say we'll do. We said we'd deliver on the hangar, and we have. We'll deliver Stanley House in exactly the same way.”

Colin Summers, Director of Public Works, Falkland Islands Government, said: “Adderstone delivered the hangar project on time and to the required standard, and that performance speaks for itself.

“We’re building a longer-term partnership with our delivery partners, including Adderstone, focussed on the essential infrastructure and upgrades that make a genuine difference to life on the islands.

“The FIGAS hangar and Stanley House are examples of that, and we hope there are many more in the future.”

Natasha Greenland, General Manager for Adderstone's Falkland Islands division, added: “I've lived here my whole life, and my family's been here for generations before me.

”That’s why both of these projects matter so much to me - and to families here. They’re about keeping islanders connected to each other, and now, giving children from across the islands a better place to call home while they get their education. That means the world to me, and it’s exactly why we’ll make sure we get this one right too.”

Adderstone's Falkland Islands division is part of a wider Group with operations across the UK and internationally, spanning affordable housing, civil engineering, construction, commercial property management and fit-out.

World.title: Flávio Bolsonaro leaves Brazil despite a court ban and the US will grant him a visa
World.content:
Flávio Bolsonaro leaves Brazil despite a court ban and the US will grant him a visa

28th Wednesday, October 2026 - 09:17 UTC Full article

A State Department official confirmed that visas would be issued for the senator and his family

Senator Flávio Bolsonaro, defeated on Sunday by Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva in the presidential runoff, left Brazil with his wife and two daughters despite a Supreme Federal Court order barring him from leaving the country, and the US State Department confirmed it will grant them visas. According to the newspaper O Globo, he arrived in Miami on Tuesday night.

A State Department official confirmed that visas would be issued for the senator and his family, without specifying the type. Mexican lawyer Simón Levy, who is close to President Donald Trump, said Washington had authorised political asylum, which the US government has not confirmed. His brother Eduardo Bolsonaro lives in Florida, having moved to the United States in 2025, and faces a final arrest warrant in Brazil after being sentenced to four years and two months in prison for coercion in the case against their father.

Judge Alexandre de Moraes had given Bolsonaro 24 hours to surrender his passports as part of an investigation into alleged money laundering through online betting companies, which also involves a lawyer friend of the senator. The deadline expired at 11 a.m. on Tuesday and the Federal Police cancelled his ordinary and diplomatic passports. His exit route has not been officially confirmed. Argentina’s National Migration Directorate, after inspecting a private plane at Iguazú airport highlighted by the press, said its paperwork was in order and that no flight plan including the Bolsonaro family had been submitted. Argentine presidential spokesman Adrián Ravier said there had been no request for asylum.

On Monday, Bolsonaro had said he would hand over his passports and defend himself against “this farce”, and that his place was “beside the Brazilian people”. That same day, Supreme Court Judge Flávio Dino ordered the Federal Police to investigate possible foreign financing of his campaign, following complaints about contributions from Rockbridge Network, a network of US conservative donors founded by Vice President JD Vance, and alleged manipulation of social media algorithms. The senator is also under investigation over his links with banker Daniel Vorcaro, jailed over the Banco Master case.

“A citizen who sneaks out of his country must owe something. Leaving Brazil is shameful,” Lula said on Tuesday at a celebration of his 81st birthday. “He could have stayed here and shown that the accusations were not true,” he added.

Bolsonaro never formally recognised his defeat, although his Liberal Party accepted the result. His father, Jair Bolsonaro, also travelled to Florida after losing the 2022 election, two days before Lula’s inauguration, and stayed there until late March 2023. Lula will begin his fourth term on January 5, 2027.

World.title: Trump suggests Venezuela become the 51st US state and elect a governor
World.content:
Trump suggests Venezuela become the 51st US state and elect a governor

28th Wednesday, October 2026 - 03:36 UTC Full article

“We’re bringing out a lot of oil for ourselves, a lot. It will become a prosperous country, and who knows? Maybe someday soon it will become a prosperous 51st state. That’s possible,” Trump said

US President Donald Trump suggested on Tuesday that Venezuela become the 51st US state and that its citizens elect a governor instead of a president, at a rally at the port of Corpus Christi, Texas, where he announced the arrival of the first shipment of one million barrels of Venezuelan oil obtained under an agreement between Washington and Caracas.

“We’re bringing out a lot of oil for ourselves, a lot. It will become a prosperous country, and who knows? Maybe someday soon it will become a prosperous 51st state. That’s possible,” Trump said, standing beside an oil tanker at an event backing Republican candidates a week before the November 3 midterm elections. “Let’s make it. Let’s make it the 51st state. And instead of a president, we’ll have an election for a governor. How about that? You know, they have a lot of oil.”

The president thanked Venezuela for a relationship he described as “very, very good” and presented the shipment as “a historic win that gives us control over a massive part of the world’s oil supply”. The crude, which Trump described as free, will be refined in Texas, including in Corpus Christi. “Billions and billions of dollars are now being invested by the biggest oil companies,” he added.

It is not the first time Trump has raised annexing Venezuela. In February he said it could become the 53rd state, after Canada and Greenland, and in August he shared a map of the country in the colours of the US flag with the caption “51st state”. Acting President Delcy Rodríguez has rejected the idea on several occasions; in July she said Venezuela has more than two centuries of sovereignty.

The remarks come amid close cooperation between the two governments. After the US military operation on January 3 that removed Nicolás Maduro from power, now jailed and on trial in New York, Washington recognised Rodríguez’s government, lifted sanctions on her and her brother, National Assembly President Jorge Rodríguez, and in August sealed an oil agreement giving it majority control over a significant share of Venezuela’s reserves. The State Department has said that under the roadmap negotiated with the opposition, Rodríguez should leave the presidency vacant in 2027, although the presidential election still has no date.

The rally came two days after opposition leader María Corina Machado returned to Venezuela after nearly ten months abroad. Trump said he hoped Machado “is safe”, and Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Washington had urged Rodríguez to allow her return. The acting president called the opposition leader’s arrival a “show”.

World.title: Latin America’s energy inflation reaches its highest level in a year
World.content:
Latin America’s energy inflation reaches its highest level in a year

28th Wednesday, October 2026 - 03:30 UTC Full article

The study, based on data from the statistics institutes and central banks of member countries, shows energy inflation exceeded the previous high for the period, 8.03% in June

Annual energy inflation in Latin America and the Caribbean accelerated to 8.33% in August, its highest level in twelve months, and pressure on fuel prices continued in September and October, when diesel prices matched petrol for the first time, according to a report by the Latin American Energy Organization (OLADE) published by the Energy Report website.

The study, based on data from the statistics institutes and central banks of member countries, shows energy inflation exceeded the previous high for the period, 8.03% in June. Overall inflation in the region rose from 4.17% in July to 4.43% in August. The report links the acceleration to the resumption of hostilities between Iran and the United States in July, after a fragile ceasefire in June.

Diesel has risen faster than petrol. In August, its regional average price rose 2.5% to US$1.31 per litre, almost four times the increase in petrol, which rose 0.6% to US$1.38. In October, both fuels reached US$1.41 per litre, the highest level of the year. Since February, diesel has risen 26% compared with 18% for petrol, and the report expects it could overtake petrol in the coming weeks. Its rising cost has a particular impact on freight and passenger transport, farm machinery and the distribution of goods.

WTI crude averaged US$83.90 per barrel in August, US$97.31 in September and around US$98.29 in October. The report warns that the pass-through of crude prices to fuel is asymmetric: international increases are passed on quickly, while decreases are reflected with a delay or only partially, due to inventories, retail margins, taxes, subsidies and local price stabilisation mechanisms.

World.title: Argentina: opposition asks Milei to clarify whether Bolsonaro left Brazil through the country
World.content:
Argentina: opposition asks Milei to clarify whether Bolsonaro left Brazil through the country

28th Wednesday, October 2026 - 03:20 UTC Full article

Milei backed Bolsonaro during the campaign and repeatedly called Lula a “thief” and a “jailbird”

Argentine opposition lawmakers on Tuesday demanded that Javier Milei’s government report whether Brazilian Senator Flávio Bolsonaro, who left Brazil despite a court ban and travelled to the United States after his election defeat, crossed through Argentine territory. The National Migration Directorate said it has no record of the senator entering the country.

“There is no record of any entry by Flávio Bolsonaro into the Argentine Republic,” the agency said in a statement. It explained that after press reports of a private plane at Puerto Iguazú airport, in the Triple Frontier area with Brazil and Paraguay, it inspected the aircraft and its crew and “found that the company’s paperwork is in order and no flight plan including the Bolsonaro family was submitted”. Presidential spokesman Adrián Ravier said there had been “no request for asylum”. The route by which Bolsonaro left Brazil has not been officially confirmed.

Peronist Senator Juliana Di Tullio said the government, through Interior Minister Diego Santilli, “must explain whether Bolsonaro used our border and our territory to escape from Brazil”. Left Front deputy Myriam Bregman called on the authorities to clarify “whether Bolsonaro, Milei’s fugitive friend, passed through Argentina”. Socialist deputy Esteban Paulón filed a formal request for information in the Chamber of Deputies asking the executive to state whether there are records of the senator’s entry or exit and whether the country received notice of the court restrictions placed on him.

Milei backed Bolsonaro during the campaign and repeatedly called Lula a “thief” and a “jailbird”, prompting Brazil to recall its ambassador in Buenos Aires for consultations in July. The Argentine government has not congratulated the Brazilian president on his re-election and, according to El País, confirmed it will issue no official statement on the result.

The case revives a precedent that has already strained bilateral relations: in recent years, dozens of people charged or convicted over the January 8, 2023 storming of the seats of the three branches of government in Brasília have settled in Argentina, according to media in both countries.

World.title: Brazil investigates whether Flávio Bolsonaro left the country via Argentina after his defeat
World.content:
Brazil investigates whether Flávio Bolsonaro left the country via Argentina after his defeat

27th Tuesday, October 2026 - 16:32 UTC Full article

Judge Alexandre de Moraes ordered Bolsonaro, who is under investigation by the court, to surrender his ordinary and diplomatic passports within 24 hours and barred him from leaving the country

Brazil’s Federal Police are checking with Argentine authorities whether Senator Flávio Bolsonaro, defeated by Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva in Sunday’s presidential runoff, left the country across the Argentine border, after he failed to hand over his passports within the deadline set by the Supreme Federal Court. His campaign and the Argentine government deny that he has left Brazil.

Supreme Court Judge Alexandre de Moraes on Monday ordered Bolsonaro, who is under investigation by the court, to surrender his ordinary and diplomatic passports within 24 hours and barred him from leaving the country. In a video posted on social media, the senator said Federal Police officers served him notice “in the middle of the street” as he left the Brasília home of his father, former president Jair Bolsonaro, and he agreed with his lawyers to hand over the documents on Tuesday morning. The deadline passed without police confirming the handover, and the passports were cancelled, according to the Brazilian press.

Argentine newspaper Infobae reported early on Tuesday that Bolsonaro had entered Argentina at Puerto Iguazú, in the Triple Frontier area, at around 2 a.m. using his national identity card, valid for travel between Mercosur countries, in order to continue to the United States on a private plane. According to the newspaper, it was a Gulfstream G400 owned by Argentine company Baires Fly, which requested immigration clearance for four passengers and three crew. Records on the Flightradar24 platform show the aircraft flew from Buenos Aires to Puerto Iguazú on Monday night.

Federal Police sources quoted by the newspaper Metrópoles said Bolsonaro had not passed through any official Brazilian border checkpoint, though they acknowledged it is possible to cross the border without being checked. His campaign’s general coordinator, Rogério Marinho, denied he had left the country, and the Argentine government also rejected the report. Since Tuesday morning, his allies had been unable to reach him, according to a columnist for the UOL news portal.

His brother Eduardo Bolsonaro, who has lived in the United States since 2025 after being convicted by the Supreme Court of coercion in the case over their father’s coup attempt, said on Friday that Flávio should leave the country if he lost. The senator refused to recognise Lula’s victory and later said he would “organise the opposition”. US President Donald Trump said on Monday, without offering evidence, that the election looked “rigged”.

World.title: A judge appointed by Jair Bolsonaro rejects his son’s case for annulling the election
World.content:
A judge appointed by Jair Bolsonaro rejects his son’s case for annulling the election

26th Monday, October 2026 - 13:39 UTC Full article

“Even before all these circumstances, we took all the necessary measures and were entirely successful. I repeat: there was no change resulting from the court ruling,” Nunes Marques said

The president of Brazil’s Superior Electoral Court, Kassio Nunes Marques, who was appointed to the Supreme Federal Court by former president Jair Bolsonaro in 2020, said on Monday that the extension of voting hours did not change the result of the runoff won by Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva. Senator Flávio Bolsonaro, the former president’s son, had cited the extension in refusing to recognise his defeat and calling for the election to be annulled.

“Even before all these circumstances, we took all the necessary measures and were entirely successful. I repeat: there was no change resulting from the court ruling,” Nunes Marques told a press conference.

On Sunday night, Bolsonaro called it “unacceptable” that Supreme Court Judge Cristiano Zanin, whom he called “Lula’s lawyer” for having defended him in the Lava Jato cases, ordered at 5.01 p.m., when polls were due to close, an extension of voting until 7 p.m. “There is a lot to clarify before Brazil recognises this outrage that has just happened,” he said. “I will never know how many votes I could have had.”

Zanin ordered the extension at the request of Lula’s coalition, which reported a lack of buses to carry voters in cities such as Salvador and São Paulo. Bolsonaro’s campaign, for its part, had asked the electoral courts to extend voting in municipalities affected by rain, flooding and power cuts in states such as Minas Gerais and Rio Grande do Sul. The measure applied only to polling stations still open; those that had closed at 5 p.m. did not reopen and followed the usual counting procedure.

Lula won with 51.78% of valid votes against Bolsonaro’s 48.22%, a margin of about 4.4 million votes. There is no record yet of the senator’s campaign having filed a formal challenge.

World.title: Debt, inflation and a hostile Congress: the economic challenges of Lula’s fourth term
World.content:
Debt, inflation and a hostile Congress: the economic challenges of Lula’s fourth term

26th Monday, October 2026 - 13:29 UTC Full article

Public debt has risen by more than ten points during the current term and exceeds 82% of GDP, driven by growing mandatory spending

Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva will begin his fourth term as Brazil’s president on January 1 with an economy that has grown more than expected and record-low unemployment, but with fiscal imbalances that markets punished heavily on Monday, the first trading day after his re-election. The dollar rose more than 12% at one point to 5.60 reais, the Ibovespa index triggered an automatic trading halt at the open and long-term interest rates jumped almost two points.

The reaction reflects investors’ bets on a victory by Senator Flávio Bolsonaro, who promised sharp spending cuts. On Friday, the dollar had closed at 4.99 reais and the Ibovespa at 205,082 points, close to the record it reached after the first round. Analysts agree that the president’s first test will be the make-up of his economic team and his fiscal framework. These are the five main challenges he faces.

Debt

Public debt has risen by more than ten points during the current term and exceeds 82% of GDP, driven by growing mandatory spending, which leaves less than 8% of the federal budget for adjustable items. Lula has at times played down concerns over debt, arguing that stronger growth will solve the problem. His team has pledged to keep the current fiscal rules, which cap spending growth and set primary surplus targets, but meeting them will be harder given the commitment to raise the minimum wage above inflation, which also increases pension costs, and the new benefits announced during the campaign.

Inflation and interest rates

The Central Bank has cut the Selic rate five times in a row to 13.75%, but annual inflation exceeded the 4.5% tolerance ceiling in September, against a 3% target. The Monetary Policy Committee meets on November 4, and the real’s depreciation complicates further cuts. Lula proposes lowering rates through greater fiscal discipline without touching social programmes, while most economists argue a faster decline would require spending cuts.

Household debt

According to credit agency Serasa, nearly 84 million Brazilians and 9.3 million companies are behind on payments, a record attributed to high interest rates. The government is preparing new relief measures, such as buying distressed mortgages from banks at a discount and forgiving tax debts for small business owners, which analysts see as temporary relief.

A hostile Congress

Bolsonaro’s Liberal Party will hold the largest bloc in both the Chamber of Deputies and the Senate, in the most conservative Congress since the return to democracy. That will hamper the government’s plans to cut tax exemptions and the approval of appointments to the Central Bank, regulators and the Supreme Court, which were already difficult during the current term. Bolsonaro, moreover, does not recognise the result and has said he will seek to annul the election.

Tax reform

The new value-added tax, approved in 2023, takes effect in January, but the government has yet to set its effective rate, which independent analysts put at around 28%. The government also postponed during the campaign a bill for a selective tax on products harmful to health or the environment, such as tobacco and alcohol.

World.title: Protesters file complaints with Attorney General’s Office alleging torture at hands of Jalisco state police officers
World.content:
“I stopped breathing because they were suffocating me.”

“They subdued me with water, and four or five men came over and grabbed me by each of my limbs and by my hair. Then they said all sorts of things to me: ‘You fucking bitch, you whore, you don’t know what’s going to happen to you.'”

Those are the words of two women who allege they were tortured by Jalisco state police officers during an Oct. 11 protest in Guadalajara to demand clean tap water.

Adriana Gabriela Arreola Dueñas, a lawyer and leader of a collective called “Access to Health, Justice and Education,” and Daniela Álvarez Zepeda, a medical doctor, are among around 10 people who have filed complaints with the Federal Attorney General’s Office (FGR) alleging that they were tortured and unjustly detained by police in Guadalajara on Oct. 11.

The two women recounted their traumatic experiences at a press conference on Monday. Their allegations, and those made by other protesters, are under investigation by the Jalisco Attorney General’s Office (FGE). The FGR has not publicly said whether it has commenced its own investigation.

In addition to the FGE, the National Human Rights Commission is investigating the events in Guadalajara on Oct. 11. It said in a statement that it was investigating “possible violations of human rights during a protest for access to potable water in Guadalajara,” where water contamination is a long-running problem.

Police used tear gas and water cannons against protesters gathered outside Casa Jalisco, the official residence of Jalisco Governor Pablo Lemus, a representative of the Citizens Movement party. Officers are also alleged to have physically and verbally abused demonstrators. Dozens of people were hurt and at least 39 people were arrested during the protest.

Arreola alleges she was suffocated, partially stripped and kicked in the head

Arreola filed a complaint with the FGR on Oct. 14. She alleges that both she and her 19-year-old daughter were victims of police brutality on Oct. 11.

On Monday, Arreola said that three female police officers grabbed her while she was protesting at Casa Jalisco. She said the officers attacked her, verbally abused her and told her to shut her “snout.”

Arreola said that officers pulled down her pants within the grounds of Casa Jalisco, leaving her semi-naked. She said that one officer kicked her back while she lay on the ground partially clothed. Arreola also said that officers used her own scarf to tie her hands together behind her back. She said police yanked her by her hands to force her to stand up, injuring her shoulders in the process.

Arreola also said that officers sat and jumped on her back, leaving her breathless.

“I stopped breathing because they were suffocating me,” she said.

Arreola also said that a person dressed in civilian clothing — possibly a plainclothes police officer — kicked her in the head.

Álvarez: ‘All we wanted was clean water’

Álvarez, the doctor, said Monday that she was “grabbed” by police officers after she was hit with a water cannon outside Casa Jalisco on Oct. 11. Like Arreola, she said she was subjected to verbal abuse.

Álvarez, who filed a complaint with the FGR on Oct. 15, said she suffered a neck strain and bruises during her violent arrest. She also said that officers took her phone and broke her bag.

Álvarez said that she and other protesters weren’t trying to make any political point when they took to the streets to protest on Oct. 11.

“All we wanted was clean water,” she said.

Detention inside the Casa Jalisco compound

Both Álvarez and Arreola said they were held in a small room inside the Casa Jalisco compound after they were detained. All told, around 40 people — some with bloody injuries — were allegedly held in the room for hours.

During the protesters’ detention, police officers allegedly threatened to “disappear them.” One officer allegedly said they would be taken to a place “where no one will find them.”

Álvarez said that one young woman began to “convulse” inside the “five by five meter” room.

“As a doctor, I tried to go over to her, at least to put her in a safe position. [But] they wouldn’t let me approach,” she said.

Álvarez said that paramedics arrived to assist her, but the woman started convulsing again.

“Police said she was faking, they laughed at her,” she said.

José Francisco Salazar González, a lawyer and academic at the University of Guadalajara, described the small room inside the Casa Jalisco precinct as a “torture center” where there was a “suspension” of detainees’ human rights.

Governor Lemus was apparently not at his official residence when the acts of police brutality and torture were allegedly committed.

Transfer to an FGE lockup

Arreola and Álvarez said that they and other detained protesters were eventually transferred to a Jalisco Attorney General’s Office facility where they were placed in cells. They said they were held in cold conditions and had no access to their phones.

It was not until Tuesday, Oct. 13, that Lemus announced that all the people detained during the protest on Oct. 11 had been released.

He conceded that authorities made “serious mistakes” during the protest. He said those mistakes “must be investigated and punished.”

Arreola, Álvarez and others are calling for Lemus and Jalisco Security Minister Juan Pablo Hernández González to be investigated.

‘It wasn’t me’: Hernández denies he gave an order to use force against protesters

Asked last Thursday who gave police the order to use force against protesters at Casa Jalisco, Hernández responded, “Yo no fui” (It wasn’t me).

” … We have several statements from police officers and commanders; three of the latter are involved, they’ll probably receive a sanction,” the security minister said.

Roberto Alarcón Estrada, the Jalisco government’s strategic security coordinator, told reporters that the names of police commanders who issued orders to use force against protesters couldn’t be disclosed. He said that the disclosure of their names could place them at risk of retaliation by protesters detained on Oct. 11 and/or their family members.

For his part, Jalisco Attorney General Salvador González de los Santos said that the FGE didn’t send any personnel to assist the police operation during the Oct. 11 protest in Guadalajara. The news magazine Proceso reported that his statement was “relevant” given that there have been allegations that officers dressed in civilian clothing were present during the police “intervention” at Casa Jalisco.

On repeated occasions, President Claudia Sheinbaum has denounced the alleged torture committed by police in Guadalajara on Oct. 11.

“How is it possible that in 2026, there is still torture of young people by police?” she remarked at her morning press conference on Oct. 14.

“… We, who came from the fight against [government] repression, cannot allow there to be police forces in Mexico that repress and torture,” Sheinbaum said.

With reports from Proceso and La Jornada

World.title: With Day of the Dead less than a week away, Mexico City’s cempasúchil production hits record heights
World.content:
The Mexico City area has achieved a record production of 10 million cempasúchil plants — a Mexican variety of marigold that is important for Day of the Dead celebrations — marking a 53.8% increase over last year’s cultivation figure, Mayor Clara Brugada announced last week.

The bright orange flowers were grown by producers on chinampas (artificial islands) in the southern Xochimilco borough of the capital, with support from the city government, which contributed over 8 million pesos (US $428,100) to directly support 597 producers.

The government provided technical assistance, distributed pots, compost and seeds, and carried out work to prepare cultivation areas, rehabilitate roads and provide harvesting facilities.

Growing flowers each year provides vital revenue to rural communities and contributes to the preservation of chinampa gardens and conservation land.

People are advised to purchase plants with a Green Seal, an image indicating that the cempasúchil flowers were grown on conservation land in Mexico City and guaranteeing sustainable production. The flowers are being sold in all 16 boroughs of Mexico City, including markets in Xochimilco, with plants priced at 15 to 30 pesos (US 80 cents to $1.60).

Xochimilco’s head of government, Cirse Camacho, thanked the Mexico City government for its support of the district’s producers, and emphasized the importance of the contribution to the recovery of the region’s agricultural sector following flood damage.

Mayor Brugada also highlighted the free cultural events being held across the city over Día de Muertos (Day of the Dead) weekend, from Oct. 30 to Nov. 2, including the giant offering in the central Zócalo square, which will showcase a more than 30-meter-tall Catrina figure accompanied by 100,000 cempasúchil plants from the conservation area. A cempasúchil trail will also be set up in Chapultepec Park.

Visitors are also encouraged to go to Xochimilco to see performances of La Llorona or to join the Día de Muertos celebrations in the borough’s neighborhoods, where various cultural traditions will be on display over the weekend, including six theatrical performances at the piers, as well as activities in downtown Xochimilco.

With reports from El Economista and Excelsior

World.title: Rural Michoacán residents lead researchers to previously undiscovered dinosaur footprints
World.content:
Residents who spotted unusual marks in a streambed in the Michoacán countryside have helped lead researchers to at least 50 dinosaur footprints.

Mexico’s National Institute of Anthropology and History (INAH) announced the discovery Monday, hypothesizing that the tracks were left by three types of dinosaurs: large meat-eaters possibly belonging to the tyrannosaur family, smaller raptor-like predators and duck-billed plant-eaters.

The footprints were found in San Juan de los Plátanos, a small lime-growing community in Apatzingán — a municipality of 126,000 in the sizzling lowlands of Michoacán’s Tierra Caliente region.

Raymundo Cervantes Barriga, a paleontologist with INAH’s Michoacán center, inspected the site, where footprints cover about 40 square meters (430 square feet) of sedimentary rock beside the stream.

They measure 12 to 48 centimeters (about 5 to 19 inches) long and up to 30 centimeters (12 inches) wide. Researchers believe additional tracks could extend beyond the area surveyed.

Based on their size, shape, depth and toe impressions, Cervantes tentatively linked the tracks to three dinosaur families known to have roamed Mexico — but it’s too early to say definitively if some of them are, say, T. rex footprints.

The number of species remains undetermined. Researchers say further paleontological analysis is needed to refine those identifications.

Cervantes placed the animals in the Late Cretaceous, which lasted from about 100 million to 66 million years ago, when he said the region had bodies of water where dinosaurs came to feed.

Specialists began documenting the site last week. They have collected rock samples and are making molds and using photographs to create detailed models of the footprints.

The tracks could help researchers study how dinosaurs moved, their travel directions and possible interactions among species, archaeologist José Luis Punzo Díaz said in an INAH press release.

The discovery would bring Michoacán’s recorded dinosaur footprint sites to four, according to INAH, which has registered just over 30 nationwide.

San Juan de los Plátanos is a community of about 1,300, roughly 145 kilometers (90 miles) southwest of Morelia, the state capital.

The Apatzingán area has struggled with organized crime and violence, but it is also known for its lime orchards and its Tierra Caliente regional cuisine, namely morisqueta, a paella-like dish of white rice served with beans and tomato-chile sauce, often topped with cheese or meat.

There is also an airport in Apatzingán. Pablo L. Sidar National Airport used to have regional commercial flights but now serves general aviation.

With reports from Expansión and Gaceta UNAM

World.title: Following Gelman controversy, President Sheinbaum moves to keep Mexico’s masterpieces in the country
World.content:
As the controversy surrounding the prestigious Gelman Collection’s return to Spain continues, President Claudia Sheinbaum intends to strengthen the Federal Law on Monuments and Archaeological, Artistic and Historical Zones (LFMZAAH) to prohibit the permanent export of protected works.

A preliminary draft of the decree protecting and conserving Mexico’s cultural heritage was published on Oct. 15.

The decree seeks to eliminate contradictions between the existing Monuments Law, which does not contemplate a restriction on exports, and multiple presidential decrees declaring national artistic monuments and prohibiting private owners from exporting works by specified artists.

It would explicitly prohibit the “definitive export of goods owned by private individuals that have been declared artistic or historical monuments under the jurisdiction of the National Institute of Fine Arts and Literature (INBAL).”

The proposal empowers INBAL to investigate, protect, conserve and restore such works in the possession of private individuals to guarantee the right to culture above the right to private property.

To date, 10 separate presidential decrees have declared the works of Diego Rivera, David Alfaro Siqueiros, José Clemente Orozco, Octavio Paz, Remedios Varo, Frida Kahlo and María Izquierdo as national heritage.

However, there are exceptions. The works of Diego Rivera and José Clemente Orozco can be definitively exported if they go to museums.

As for Frida Kahlo’s works, the permanent export of her easel paintings, graphic works and technical documents in the hands of private individuals and within Mexican territory has been prohibited since 1984.

As many of Kahlo’s works were already outside the country when the decree was issued, and as the exact location of some remain unknown, it is “essential to safeguard the pieces still in the country,” the new proposal asserts.

Sheinbaum’s proposal is time-sensitive as the Supreme Court is set to take up a challenge to the 1984 Kahlo decree filed by the owner of the painting “Self-Portrait with Medallion.”

There is precedent to countermand these decrees. In 2010, collector Andrés Blaisten obtained an injunction against the prohibition of the export of the works of María Izquierdo and that specific decree was declared unconstitutional.

If the Court resolves the matter before Sheinbaum’s reform is enacted, it must determine if its ruling applies only to the 1984 decree and if it only applies to the party filing the injunction.

And if it rules in favor of the decree, it must explain why it deviated from the 2010 decision, while also raising the constitutional question of how a presidential decree supersedes a law passed by Congress.

The tension between property owners and heritage laws has become palpable in recent months thanks to the Gelman collection controversy, which involves the transfer of 160 of its 300 works to Banco Santander in Cantabria, Spain.

With reports from El Sol de México and El País

World.title: MND Local BCS: Port protests, tourism challenges and million-dollar fish in Los Cabos
World.content:
On Wednesday, Oct. 21, as 175 fishing boats streamed out of the Cabo San Lucas Marina during the iconic shotgun start of Bisbee’s Black and Blue — aka “the world’s richest fishing tournament” — a group of protesters lined the shore.

But they weren’t protesting the tournament. In fact, crew aboard some of the fishing boats participating in the tournament were among those displaying signs of peaceful protest. At issue was a new schedule of dock fees from the Cabo San Lucas Marina, already considered the most expensive in Mexico.

Why tourism service providers are protesting in Cabo San Lucas

View this post on Instagram A post shared by Susana Zatarain (@susanazatarain)

The Cabo San Lucas Marina is no stranger to drama. On Apr. 11, 2024, the government-owned Administración del Sistema Portuario Nacional (ASIPONA) seized control of the port from IGY Marinas — which had managed it for the previous 20 years — stating that the latter’s permit had expired, and that they now had a 50-year concession to the marina granted by Mexico’s Secretariat of the Navy (SEMAR).

But IGY Marinas’ parent company, MarineMax, has disputed the legality of these actions in Mexican courts, claiming that the takeover of the marina itself was illegal, and that renegotiation clauses in its operational contract weren’t properly honored.

Two years later, however, ASIPONA remains firmly in charge, despite complaints about the lack of cleanliness and infrastructure improvements around the marina, and outrage at the new fee schedule — the reason for the recent protests — which raises the rates for various dock fees by a reported 200% to 500%.

The charge of uncleanliness is undeniable: “The marina is currently full of trash and smells bad,” said tourism service provider and protester Javier Ontiveros, per El Sudcaliforniano. “It lacks security services, and the ground is uneven — I’ve even seen elderly people fall while disembarking from cruise vessels. We are asking that a portion of the revenue collected be allocated toward infrastructure maintenance.”

But it’s the massive fee hikes themselves, published on the first of this month and made without any consultations with tourism service providers, that are the most distressing to locals.

The squeeze continues for tourism service providers

This has not been a banner year for tourism in Los Cabos. Through September, international air travelers — the most valuable type of tourist to the local economy — are down by 8.4%. But that only tells part of the story.

For five straight months, the number of international air travelers has plummeted: decreasing by 10.5% in May relative to the same month in 2025, 14.2% in June, 16.6% in July and August, and 14.7% in September.

Since each of these high-value tourists is expected to spend US $1,157 on average, the 294,800 fewer international tourists that have flown into Los Cabos this year relative to last year represent a loss to the local economy of about US $340 million.

This is important context for the recent protests, since tourism service providers who have made less money this year are now being asked to pay substantially more for operating costs.

Another exciting Bisbee’s tournament in Cabo San Lucas

Despite the backdrop of protests, Bisbee’s Black and Blue delivered another memorable tournament, with 175 teams competing for a US $7.4 million purse. As it turned out, an overwhelming amount of that money would go to just one team.

Although it was their first time in the tournament, Team Contango’s Spartan’s Revenge caught the first fish brought to the scales on the first day of fishing: a 491-pound blue marlin boated by team member Kevin Miranda after a 2.5 hour fight. The fish was immediately worth $US 1.9 million due to daily jackpots.

“It was the best day on the water ever,” said Miranda’s teammate, George Kypreos, per Bisbee’s. “It was sunny and beautiful and the water was flat. We were like on a yacht (a 60’ Viking). We saw a few other boats in the distance, but we were pretty much alone. And that was the big one for everybody!”

One qualifier, one big winner

But after three days of fishing, when no other team could beat the standard set by the 491-pound blue, or even muster a qualifying marlin, life got better and better, and the fish became worth more and more money: US $5,629,300, to be exact; or the largest single payout in the 46-year history of the event.

In total, 38 qualifying marlin were caught during the tournament, but 34 of them were released. And of the four brought to the scales, three failed to meet the 300-pound minimum limit.

“El Niño certainly did a number on us, fishing-wise,” explained the tournament’s director, Wayne Bisbee. “But in true Bisbee’s fashion, the teams had fun and I’d like to thank all of them for fishing with us again. Congratulations and well done to Contango’s Spartan’s Revenge for a nice marlin and for setting the payout record for that catch.”

Chris Sands is a writer and editor for Mexico News Daily, and the former Cabo San Lucas local expert for the USA Today travel website 10 Best and writer of Fodor’s Los Cabos travel guidebook. He has also contributed to numerous other websites and publications, including The San Diego Union-Tribune, Marriott Bonvoy Traveler, Forbes Travel Guide, Porthole Cruise and Travel, and Cabo Living.

World.title: Mexico’s exports soar on AI-driven electronics demand, but oil deficit continues to grow
World.content:
The value of Mexico’s exports increased almost 40% year over year in September and rose more than 30% in the first nine months of 2026, according to data published on Tuesday by the national statistics agency INEGI.

Mexico’s exports were worth US $77.79 billion in September, an increase of 37.9% compared to the same month of last year. It was Mexico’s third-highest monthly export total on record, after July and August of this year.

In the first nine months of 2026, Mexico’s exports were worth $627.19 billion, an increase of 30.4% compared to the same period of 2025. The value of Mexico’s exports in the January-September period was just $37.6 billion less than the total for all of 2025, which was a record high of $664.8 billion.

It is practically guaranteed that the value of Mexico’s exports will exceed the 2025 total in the January-October period of 2026.

INEGI’s latest trade data also shows that Mexico’s outlay on imports in the first nine months of the year increased 27.5% compared to the same period of 2025 to reach $617.94 billion.

Consequently, Mexico recorded a trade surplus of $9.25 billion between January and September. Mexico is thus on track to record a trade surplus for a second consecutive year after recording deficits between 2021 and 2024.

Mexico’s strong export growth in 2026 has been driven by a surge in sales of non-automotive manufactured goods — especially computer and electronic equipment — to the United States, where an AI-driven data center boom is underway.

Meanwhile, Mexico’s oil exports have declined this year and its petroleum imports have increased significantly, putting the country on track to record its largest ever petroleum deficit (see below).

Non-auto exports surge 53% in September, rise 46% so far this year

Manufactured goods accounted for 93.5% of the total value of Mexico’s exports in September.

The full breakdown of INEGI’s export data for September — including year-over-year increases — is as follows:

Exports of manufactured goods were worth $72.77 billion, an increase of 39%.

Exports of non-automotive manufactured goods were worth $56.34 billion, an increase of 53%. Within that category, Mexico’s exports of electric and electronic equipment and devices increased 94.7%.

Exports of manufactured automotive goods (including vehicles) were worth $16.43 billion, an increase of 5.7%.

Mining sector exports were worth $1.93 billion, an increase of 66.8%.

Petroleum exports were worth $1.8 billion, an increase of 9.6%.

Agricultural exports were worth $1.28 billion, an increase of 4.6%.

The full breakdown of INEGI’s export data for the first nine months of 2026 is as follows:

Exports of manufactured goods were worth $578.59 billion, an increase of 31.7%.

Exports of non-automotive manufactured goods were worth $436.64 billion, an increase of 46%.

Exports of manufactured automotive goods were worth $141.96 billion, an increase of 1.3%.

Mining sector exports were worth $16.6 billion, an increase of 74.1%.

Petroleum exports were worth $16.35 billion, a decline of 0.2%.

Agricultural exports were worth $15.64 billion, a decline of 2.4%.

Spending on imports on track to set a new record in 2026

Mexico imported goods worth $78.4 billion in September, an increase of 33.1% compared to the same month of last year. Spending on imports in the first nine months of the year — $617.94 billion — was just $46 billion less than Mexico’s total outlay in 2025, which was a record high of $664.06 billion.

Data on imports in the first 10 months of 2026 will almost certainly show that Mexico’s spending in that period exceeded the record set last year.

The full breakdown of INEGI’s import data for the first nine months of 2026 — including year-over-year increases — is as follows:

Imported non-petroleum goods were worth $575.9 billion, an increase of 28.2%.

Imported petroleum products were worth $42.03 billion, an increase of 19.4%.

Imported intermediate goods (including non-petroleum and petroleum products) were worth $497.04 billion, an increase of 33.4%.

Imported consumer goods (including non-petroleum and petroleum products) were worth $77.14 billion, an increase of 9.9%.

Imported capital goods were worth $43.76 billion, an increase of 4.8%.

Mexico’s oil trade deficit exceeds $25 billion

As noted above, Mexico’s oil exports were worth $16.35 billion in the first nine months of 2026, a year-over-year decline of 0.2%. In the same period, Mexico imported petroleum products worth $42.03 billion, a year-over-year increase of 19.4%.

Consequently, Mexico recorded an oil trade deficit of $25.68 billion between January and September. That amount is higher than the $25.55 billion oil deficit Mexico recorded in 2025.

If Mexico’s oil deficit continues to increase in the final three months of 2026, as expected, it will record its highest oil deficit on record.

INEGI’s data indicates that Mexico is still a long way off achieving its goal of self-sufficiency for fuel, including gasoline. The country’s outlay on petroleum-based consumer goods — i.e., fuel — in the first nine months of 2026 increased 27.7% year over year to reach $14.04 billion.

The energy-focused publication Factor Energético reported that the increase in imports of petroleum-based consumer goods “warrants special attention due to its potential impact on supply and the domestic market’s exposure to international prices.”

Mexico spent $27.99 billion on petroleum-based intermediate goods between January and September, a year-over-year increase of 15.7%.

With reports from El Economista, Expansión and Factor Energético

World.title: Government invests US $60M to restore polluted, drought-impacted Lake Pátzcuaro
World.content:
As part of the Plan Michoacán for Peace and Justice, the National Water Commission is investing 1.1 billion pesos (US $60 million) in the Lake Pátzcuaro Sanitation Plan, in order to restore the environmental health of one of the most emblematic bodies of water in Mexico.

Lake Pátzcuaro — a popular vacation region and an international landmark — is home to a rich biodiversity, including endemic species of birds, fish and other aquatic organisms.

Visitamos la obra de rehabilitación de la Planta de Tratamiento de Aguas Residuales en Quiroga, Michoacán. https://t.co/0yz5XQzAzJ — Claudia Sheinbaum Pardo (@Claudiashein) October 25, 2026

It is a central part of a region in western Mexico comprising archaeological, historical, recreational and cultural sites linked to the heritage of the Indigenous Purépecha peoples, lending identity, sustenance and life to the communities that surround it.

However, agricultural, industrial and domestic activities — especially the excessive use of fertilizers and pesticides and the discharge of untreated wastewater — have seriously degraded the water quality in the lake.

Six wastewater treatment plants are being renovated — in Las Garzas, Janitzio, San Pedrito, Quiroga, Tzintzuntzan and San Andrés Ziróndaro — and four new plants are being built — in San Juan Tumbio, Ihuatzio, Tzurumutaro and Quiroga.

More than 116 kilometers of sanitary sewer lines are being reconditioned and 10 area wetlands will be rehabilitated. Conagua will also oversee dredging and hydrological restoration to help reduce pollution in Lake Pátzcuaro.

These actions will be complemented by the removal of water hyacinth and a reforestation project, as well as the construction of terraces in the surrounding hills to contribute to the environmental recovery of the basin.

President Claudia Sheinbaum, who spearheaded the clean-up plan, toured the Quiroga Wastewater Treatment Plant on Saturday, thanking the workers involved in the rehabilitation projects. She also praised the Michoacán government for its effort to recover the springs that supply water to the ecosystem.

“The conservation of this ecosystem is fundamental for the communities of the region,” she said, adding that her administration will continue to support projects aimed at recovering Michoacán’s natural resources.

Luis Roberto Arias Reyes, the director of Conagua’s Michoacán office, said the Sanitation Plan will directly benefit more than 142,000 residents of the municipalities of Pátzcuaro, Tzintzuntzan, Quiroga and Erongarícuaro by providing more efficient hydraulic and sanitary infrastructure for wastewater management.

In a press release, the Michoacán government said the Lake Pátzcuaro clean-up project will generate economic growth for the Indigenous communities of the islands of Janitzio, Tecuena, La Pacanda and Yunuén, as well as for lakeshore towns such as Urandén and Huecorio, which depend on fishing and tourism as pillars of their economy.

With reports from ContraRéplica, El Sol de Morelia, La Jornada and Cambio de Michoacán

World.title: 8% salary increase among ’12 actions in 120 days’ promised by IMSS director: Tuesday’s mañanera recapped
World.content:
Listen to this article

Sheinbaum’s mañanera in 60 seconds

🏥 Robledo presents 12-action plan for IMSS: IMSS director Zoé Robledo presented a plan of “12 actions” to be completed in 120 days in response to protests by IMSS workers. It includes an 8% salary increase, the transition of almost 11,000 temporary workers into permanent positions, the hiring of 2,500 specialist doctors and the provision of more than 18,000 additional beds and gurneys. The plan also promises “guaranteed” medicines and medical supplies, a program to clear the surgical backlog and the “strengthening” of emergency departments.

IMSS director Zoé Robledo presented a plan of “12 actions” to be completed in 120 days in response to protests by IMSS workers. It includes an 8% salary increase, the transition of almost 11,000 temporary workers into permanent positions, the hiring of 2,500 specialist doctors and the provision of more than 18,000 additional beds and gurneys. The plan also promises “guaranteed” medicines and medical supplies, a program to clear the surgical backlog and the “strengthening” of emergency departments. 🇧🇷 Sheinbaum recounts “very emotional” call with Lula: The president said her Monday phone call with Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva was brief and that the reelected Brazilian president was “very happy, very excited” about the response from Brazilians at the ballot box. Sheinbaum said she invited Lula to visit Mexico and he invited her to go to Brazil. The two agreed to talk again to set a date and agenda for the visits.

The president said her Monday phone call with Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva was brief and that the reelected Brazilian president was “very happy, very excited” about the response from Brazilians at the ballot box. Sheinbaum said she invited Lula to visit Mexico and he invited her to go to Brazil. The two agreed to talk again to set a date and agenda for the visits. 🗳️ Sheinbaum rejects claims Morena is to blame for INE problems: A day after endorsing Guadalupe Taddei’s resignation as National Electoral Institute (INE) president, Sheinbaum reiterated her call for a comprehensive audit of the electoral authority. She pushed back on journalist Carlos Loret de Mola’s claim that “Taddei is Morena,” saying: “Don’t come and tell us… that Morena is the problem.” Sheinbaum noted that Taddei was elected INE president in 2023 by the Chamber of Deputies.

Why today’s mañanera matters

Improving Mexico’s public healthcare system is one of the various challenges faced by the Sheinbaum administration, which has now been in office for almost 25 months. Deficiencies in the system have been brought into sharp focus this month by protesting workers from the Mexican Social Security Institute (IMSS), Mexico’s largest public healthcare provider.

At President Sheinbaum’s Tuesday morning press conference, IMSS general director Zoé Robledo presented a plan aimed at improving conditions in IMSS hospitals and for IMSS workers, whose demands have included higher pay, the hiring of additional healthcare personnel in order to ease excessive workloads and an end to shortages of medicines and medical supplies.

The plan is the federal government’s most comprehensive response to IMSS workers’ complaints and demands. Its presentation came four days after the government unveiled a new initiative aimed at resolving long-running problems related to the supply and distribution of medications.

Whether the government’s latest initiatives significantly improve conditions in IMSS healthcare facilities and satisfy workers remains to be seen. Medicine shortages have persisted despite government efforts to address the problem through initiatives such as the establishment of a “mega-pharmacy” in 2023 and the creation of a distribution scheme called “Rutas de la Salud” (Health Routes) last year.

Also of note at today’s mañanera were Sheinbaum’s remarks about her telephone conversation on Monday with Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, who was reelected on Sunday.

The president indicated that she will travel to Brazil at some point in the not-too-distant future.

A key focus of face-to-face talks between Sheinbaum and Lula would likely be the fledgling partnership between Mexico’s Pemex and Brazil’s Petrobras that is aimed at boosting oil production in the Gulf of Mexico.

Robledo presents 12-action plan for IMSS

Early in the press conference, Robledo presented a plan for IMSS healthcare facilities consisting of “12 actions” to be completed in a period of 120 days starting today.

He said that the actions in the plan “stem from what the [IMSS] workers themselves told us” and are needed.

The 12 “actions” of the plan Robledo presented are as follows:

An 8% salary increase for IMSS workers.

The transition of almost 11,000 temporary workers into permanent positions.

The hiring of 2,500 specialist doctors.

The provision of 100 pieces of high-tech medical equipment to IMSS hospitals.

The provision of 2,917 other pieces of medical equipment to IMSS hospitals.

The provision of more than 18,000 additional beds and gurneys to IMSS hospitals.

The commencement of a “permanent maintenance” program.

The “guaranteed” provision of medicines and medical supplies.

The “complete” provision of medications in IMSS pharmacies.

The commencement of a program aimed at clearing the surgical backlog in IMSS hospitals.

The provision of specialist medical appointments in December. (Robledo explained that appointments scheduled for December have commonly been rescheduled to January or even February.)

The “strengthening” of emergency departments, including via the hiring of additional personnel.

Sheinbaum recounts ‘very emotional’ call with Lula

Sheinbaum told reporters that her telephone conversation with Lula on Monday was “very emotional.”

“As you can imagine, he is very happy, very excited about the response from the people of Brazil” in Sunday’s election, she said.

🇲🇽🇧🇷Claudia Sheinbaum y Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva preparan un encuentro entre México y Brasil. La presidenta reveló que sostuvo una llamada telefónica “muy emotiva” con el presidente electo brasileño, en la que ambos intercambiaron invitaciones para visitar sus respectivos países. “Fue una llamada breve, lo invité a que viniera a México… me invitó a que fuera a Brasil”, contó Sheinbaum. Acordaron una segunda conversación para definir la fecha del encuentro. 🗞️Israel Aldave | @Radio_Formula — Azucena Uresti (@azucenau) October 27, 2026

“It was a brief call and I invited him to come to Mexico and he invited me to go to Brazil,” Sheinbaum said.

“We agreed to talk at another time to confirm and to set a date and agenda for these visits,” she said.

Sheinbaum rejects claims that Morena is to blame for problems at the INE

A day after endorsing Guadalupe Taddei’s decision to resign as president of the National Electoral Institute (INE), Sheinbaum reiterated her call for a comprehensive audit of the electoral authority to be carried out.

Taddei resigned amid allegations that lucrative INE contracts were improperly awarded to companies controlled by a businessman with whom she has a close personal relationship.

After advocating “constant audits” of the INE, Sheinbaum rejected claims that the ruling Morena party is responsible for improper conduct at the INE.

“Don’t come and tell us, like [journalist Carlos] Loret de Mola did yesterday, that Morena is the problem,” she said.

Sheinbaum highlighted that Taddei was elected INE president in 2023 by the Chamber of Deputies.

Taddei’s election occurred via sortition — also known as selection by lottery — as none of the candidates for president of the INE had the support of the required two-thirds of lawmakers in the lower house of Congress. At the time of her election, questions were raised about her family links to both the government and Morena.

In an El Universal column published on Monday under the headline “Taddei is Morena,” Loret de Mola described Taddei as a “morenista” and effectively accused the INE of favoring the ruling party under her leadership.

By Mexico News Daily chief staff writer Peter Davies (peter.davies@mexiconewsdaily.com)

World.title: France Weighed Social Media Shutdown
World.content:
CRS riot police, France’s national riot-control force, on Boulevard Voltaire in Paris on 6 October 2026. Photo: Jules*, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

Published Wednesday, 28 October 2026, 9:30 a.m. ET (2:30 p.m. Paris) · Source: French Interior Ministry, CGT union, Rio Times reportingFrance’s government has weighed cutting off social networks and even mobile internet to stop a third weekend of street violence, according to reports.

Officials have neither confirmed nor denied it, and nothing was switched off.The story sits at the heart of the Europe political crisis, in which France faces its worst unrest in years.

For readers in the United States, it is a test of how far a democracy will go to control protests.

Key Facts Report: Officials asked phone operators how to block social networks or mobile data; no cut happened.

Officials asked phone operators how to block social networks or mobile data; no cut happened. 24 October: 410,000 marched, says the Interior Ministry; the CGT union says more than 800,000.

410,000 marched, says the Interior Ministry; the CGT union says more than 800,000. Arrests: 1,314 on 24 October, about half the total from the 17 October riots.

1,314 on 24 October, about half the total from the 17 October riots. Next: Protests on Saturday, 31 October; a national strike on Thursday, 5 November.

This story is part of our coverage of the europe political crisis. Dates, times and how to follow it are in our guide. Latest: French Senate Backs Seizing Rioters' Benefits

What the Reports Say

Reports on 27 October said the prime minister’s office asked France’s big phone operators to be ready to block X, TikTok, Instagram and Snapchat. The Interior Ministry reportedly also asked how mobile internet could be cut during the protests.

Officials from the prime minister’s office and two ministries neither denied the move nor the existence of the letter. The reports rely partly on anonymous sources, and no public order has been issued.

No cut happened on the weekend of 24 and 25 October. Cutting mobile data would also break card payments and emergency calls, which makes a full shutdown hard to carry out.
