Monday, 2 November, 3:45 a.m. ET: Nigeria Stanbic IBTC Bank PMI — October data is due with no forecast, following a previous reading of 56.4. The figure will indicate whether private-sector activity is holding up amid detention and security concerns.

Background: Africa: The New Scramble — why the world’s powers are competing for the continent.

Frequently Asked Questions

What happened in Nyala, Sudan, on 28 October 2026?

A drone strike on Tangong Market in Nyala, South Darfur, killed more than 100 civilians and set parts of the market ablaze. A separate drone attack on an electricity substation disrupted power across parts of Khartoum, Omdurman and El Gezira, affecting drinking-water stations.

How large is the current Ebola outbreak in Africa?

Africa’s latest Ebola outbreak has exceeded 10,000 confirmed cases with nearly 5,000 deaths, most of them in the Democratic Republic of Congo. Cases have also been reported in Kenya and Nigeria, with Congolese health authorities describing the DRC as the principal source of regional spread.

Why were 33 detainees found dead in Nigeria’s Niger State?

An inquiry attributed the deaths of 33 detainees to overcrowding, poor ventilation, heat stress and dehydration. The detainees had been held on suspicion of illegal mining, but investigators reportedly found that the mining sites were licensed.

What is the situation at the Ethiopia–Kenya border?

Approximately 36,000 people crossed from Ethiopia into Kenya to escape fighting around Moyale, according to the UN Refugee Agency. Kenya is managing this displacement while also monitoring 98 Ebola contacts still in quarantine.

World.title: International News: Flávio Bolsonaro arrives in United States after Brazilian officials cancel passport
World.content:
International News: Flávio Bolsonaro arrives in United States after Brazilian officials cancel passport

By Zoila Palma: Flávio Bolsonaro, the defeated presidential candidate in Brazil’s recent election, has arrived at Opa-locka Executive Airport near Miami, Florida, following days of speculation about his whereabouts.

His arrival comes after he lost a runoff election to incumbent President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, BBC reports.

Bolsonaro emerged from the first round of voting in early October with 47% of the vote but was defeated by Lula in the runoff. He subsequently indicated that he intended to challenge the election results, raising political tensions following the closely watched contest.

Before his arrival in the United States, Brazil’s Supreme Court had ordered Bolsonaro to surrender his passports as part of an ongoing investigation into alleged money laundering.

Bolsonaro, who has denied the allegations and has not been charged in connection with them, reportedly failed to surrender the documents by the deadline, prompting authorities to cancel his passports.

His whereabouts became the subject of widespread speculation after he stopped making public statements and his lawyers reportedly said they did not know where he was.

The U.S. State Department had confirmed that visas would be issued to Bolsonaro and his family, allowing them to enter the United States.

World.title: International Organization for Migration, U.S. Embassy and Passport Department collaborate on document fraud detection training
World.content:
International Organization for Migration, U.S. Embassy and Passport Department collaborate on document fraud detection training

By Zoila Palma: The International Organization for Migration (IOM), in collaboration with the U.S. Embassy and the Belize Nationality and Passport Department, is conducting practical training aimed at strengthening Belize’s capacity to detect fraudulent travel documents and identity fraud.

The training focuses on equipping frontline officers with the knowledge, tools and practical skills needed to examine travel documents and verify identities as fraudulent techniques become increasingly sophisticated.

The initiative is expected to strengthen border security by improving officers’ ability to identify fraudulent documents encountered at Belize’s borders. Effective document examination is also essential in efforts to combat irregular migration, human trafficking, migrant smuggling and other forms of cross-border crime.

This is supported through the European Union-funded Regional Integration and Border Management Project, implemented by IOM.

World.title: Government of Belize to introduce “Cost of living” plan
World.content:
Government of Belize to introduce “Cost of living” plan

By Zoila Palma: During cabinet’s meeting on October 27, 2026, cabinet reviewed and discussed a paper entitled “Addressing the Rising Cost of Living/Affordability.”

The objective of the paper was to present practical, short-term fiscal, policy and regulatory measures that would mitigate immediate cost-of-living pressures for Belizean households, particularly low- and middle-income families affected by food price increases, fuel costs and housing/rent costs.

A statement from the Government of Belize noted that specific measures and decisions were adopted, which will form the basis of a Cost of Living Plan that will be finalized and approved by Cabinet at its next meeting.

The proposed measures will be implemented initially for the period November 2026 to March 2027.

World.title: Blue Creek couple injured after gas tank bursts into flames
World.content:
Blue Creek couple injured after gas tank bursts into flames

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): A Blue Creek Village couple suffered burn injuries after a gas tank caught fire at their home on Monday afternoon.

Police say that around 12:00pm on October 26, a 31 year old woman was washing and drying clothes in a concrete washroom about 10 feet from the family’s two storey house when a plastic table fell onto a gas tank connected to the dryer, causing gas to spray out.

She called for help, and her 28 year old husband, a nurse, rushed in and tried to shut the valve. Before he could, the tank burst into flames, burning his arms and hands.

He ran outside, while his wife took cover in a small bathroom inside the washroom. The fire quickly spread through the washroom and reached a red Chevrolet pickup parked about five feet away, which was completely destroyed.

The husband was treated for burns to both arms and the right side of his face, while his wife suffered burns to her arms and legs. Neither injury is considered life threatening.

The value of the property destroyed has not yet been determined.

World.title: Thieves make off with two ladders valued at $600 in Orange Walk
World.content:
Thieves make off with two ladders valued at $600 in Orange Walk

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): A 56 year old labourer of the Belize Corozal Road, Orange Walk Town, says two ladders were stolen from her yard.

The woman told police that around 9:30pm on Sunday, October 25, she went outside to bring in her clothes and noticed that two silver eight foot ladders were missing.

She said she asked her son whether he had used them, and he said no.

The ladders are valued at $600.

There is no video footage in the area, and no suspects have been identified. She has requested court action.

World.title: Trial Farm woman says partner broke into home and stole tools and wheelchair
World.content:
Trial Farm woman says partner broke into home and stole tools and wheelchair

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): A 50 year old woman of Temash River Street, Trial Farm Village, Orange Walk District, has reported that her common law husband damaged her property and stole several items from her home.

The woman told police that around 3:00pm on Sunday, October 25, she was in Belize City with her daughter when a neighbour called and sent her video footage that allegedly showed her partner damaging a $100 surveillance camera mounted in front of her house.

She returned home around 8:00pm, where she said she saw him outside the house.

When police responded, they found the burglar bar door open and the door bolts damaged.

Missing from the house were a weed eater, a power washer, a tile cutter and a boxed wheelchair, with a total value of $885.

The woman said she did not give anyone permission to take the items. She told police the man had left his house keys inside.

Scenes of Crime personnel processed the scene. Police are searching for the man, who is wanted for damage to property and theft.

World.title: Earn an MBA for under US$10,000: Edinburgh Napier session happening today
World.content:
Earn an MBA for under US$10,000: Edinburgh Napier session happening today

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): Belizeans looking to take their careers to the next level have a golden opportunity today. Edinburgh Napier University is hosting an information session in Belize City this evening, Wednesday, October 28.

The session will be held at The Great House, The O.U.R.S Café and Lounge, 13 Cork Street, from 6:30pm to 8:00pm.

Attendees will get an inside look at the university’s Global Online programmes, including its highly regarded MBA and MBM. Both can be completed in as little as 18 months, or extended up to four years if needed, for under US$10,000, with flexible pay as you go instalments.

The credentials carry serious weight. Edinburgh Napier’s Business School holds AACSB accreditation, placing it in the top five percent of business schools worldwide. Its online programmes are also formally recognized by Belize’s Ministry of Education, Culture, Science and Technology.

Beyond business, prospective students can explore the BSc Computing (Top up), BSc Nursing Studies (Top up), MSc Data Engineering and MSc Transport Planning and Engineering, as well as BA Business Management (Top up) with specialisations in Marketing, HRM, Hospitality, Finance and Sustainability, and the BA Business and Enterprise (Top up).

It is not too late to reserve your spot. Email [email protected], call 1 239 444 4399 or join a live chat at www.seidegrees.com.

World.title: Belize stays partly wet with showers focused mainly offshore and in the south
World.content:
Belize stays partly wet with showers focused mainly offshore and in the south

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): Belize is in for a variably cloudy Wednesday, with showers and light rain expected to shift across different parts of the country during the day.

According to the National Meteorological Service, a gentle and somewhat moist northwesterly airflow is prevailing over the country.

Showers or light rain will continue mainly offshore this morning before developing over some central and southern areas later today.

Tonight, most of the shower activity is expected over southern Belize and some offshore areas.

Temperatures will remain warm during the day but cooler overnight.

Coastal areas will reach a high of 87°F, falling to 76°F tonight. Inland temperatures will peak at 89°F before dropping to around 68°F, while the hills will see a high of 77°F and a low of 65°F.

Marine conditions will be light chop to choppy, with north to northwesterly winds of 5 to 10 knots and waves between two and five feet.

The outlook for Thursday and Thursday night is for variably cloudy skies with isolated showers or light rain possible mainly over southern areas.

Forecasters say tropical cyclone formation is not expected over the region during the next 48 hours.

Today’s low tide was at 5:40am, followed by a high tide at 11:57am. Another low tide is expected at 4:51pm and a high tide at 10:54pm.

The sun rose at 5:49am and will set at 5:22pm.

The forecast was issued by forecaster Crystal Rosalez.

World.title: Holness points to sabotage
World.content:
A woman walks past these Hurricane Melissa-wrecked buildings in Black River, St Elizabeth, last Friday. Today marks the first anniversary of the Category 5 storm that inflicted heavy damage on sections of the island. (Photo: Garfield Robinson)

Prime Minister Dr Andrew Holness has signalled that changes are coming to the public sector as there are individuals deliberately delaying or derailing government programmes. As such, he said the country should prepare for a shake-up in how the public service operates.

Holness said he was increasingly concerned that some public officers were obstructing the Government’s plans, warning that it could no longer be “business as usual” as Jamaica continues to recover from Hurricane Melissa.

“I don’t usually speak in extreme terms, and there are some subjects that it is better not to speak about them. But more and more I’m coming to the conclusion that there are persons in the public sector who are determined to, again, to use the very harsh word, sabotage. And I don’t say it lightly, they delay, derail policies, programmes, and initiatives of the Government. I see you, [and] I’m preparing the country to expect these changes, as it cannot be business as usual,” he said.

The prime minister was speaking at a special press briefing at Jamaica House on Tuesday during which he outlined plans to reduce government spending and improve the delivery of public services as the country faces the continuing cost of hurricane recovery.

While announcing further spending restrictions, Holness said the Government would also examine how ministries, departments, agencies, and public bodies operate, with the aim of removing duplication, improving coordination, and speeding up decisions.

He indicated that personnel changes would form part of that process, particularly where leadership, capacity, or performance needed to be strengthened.

Holness said the changes were necessary to ensure that the public service could respond more effectively to the country’s needs, especially as the Government tries to move recovery projects forward while controlling expenditure.

“Government must be reset and reorganised to meet the needs of our country. Government must be frugal and disciplined in its use of public resources, agile in its decisions, and responsive to the people it serves,” he said.

The warning comes as the Government intensifies its efforts to redirect funds towards hurricane recovery, including an additional $9.65 billion for the Restoration of Owner and Occupant Family Shelter (ROOFS) programme.

Holness said the Government could not meet every demand without making difficult choices, and that savings would have to be found in some areas to finance higher-priority needs.

“If I have to find $9.65 billion for the ROOFS programme, some things will have to be cut elsewhere,” he said.

Among the measures announced on Tuesday was an immediate pause on the purchase of motor vehicles for public officials until March 31, 2027, alongside a review of Government property leases and restrictions on hotel retreats and end-of-year celebrations.

The measures build on a moratorium on non-essential official overseas travel announced last week, scheduled to remain in effect until March 31, 2027.

Holness said greater financial restraint must be matched by improvements in how public institutions work, arguing that Government leaders and senior officials must make priorities rather than attempt to satisfy every demand at once.

He said the Government would be expected to make changes to its systems and procedures, while warning that officials who delay or derail its programmes could not expect the existing arrangements to continue unchanged.

World.title: Sagicor delivers double boost to Melissa-hit schools
World.content:
Little London High School grade 11 student Alyssa Hinds (second right) presents a plaque of appreciation to Christopher Zacca (second left) — president and CEO of Sagicor Group Jamaica Limited, and chairman, Sagicor Foundation Jamaica — in recognition of the organisation’s support. Sharing in the moment are Latoya Harris Ghartey, executive director, National Education Trust; and Garfield James, principal, Little London High School.

SAGICOR Foundation Jamaica on Monday handed over restored facilities at two schools damaged by Hurricane Melissa last October and announced the allocation of an additional $30 million to support further school restoration.

The $30 million, the foundation explained, will build on the record $152 million raised through the 2026 Sagicor Sigma Corporate Run, which surpassed its $150-million fund-raising target.

“Last year, following the hurricane, Sagicor allocated $200 million to national recovery efforts, separate from and in addition to the funds raised through the Sagicor Sigma Corporate Run. I am pleased to share that $30 million of that allocation will support additional school projects, helping to fast-track restoration and return more children to safe, welcoming spaces,” Sagicor Group Jamaica President and CEO Christopher Zacca said during the handover at Little London High School in Westmoreland.

The foundation said that restoration works, at a combined value of approximately $50.4 million, have been completed at Little London High and Mayfield Primary and Infant School in St Elizabeth.

Approximately $22.2 million was invested at Mayfield Primary and Infant School while approximately $28.2 million funded restoration and infrastructure works at Little London High School. The projects addressed priority sections damaged by the hurricane rather than complete school-wide refurbishments.

The two schools are among five selected to benefit from the 2026 run. Work at the remaining beneficiaries — Hopewell High, Green Pond High, and Salt Marsh Primary and Infant — is nearing completion, the foundation said in a news release.

The foundation also said it will work with the Ministry of Education and the National Education Trust (NET) to identify additional schools with the greatest need for restoration support.

On Monday, Zacca credited the public’s support for helping turn the fund-raising effort into completed improvements.

“The real value is a student focusing on a lesson instead of a leaking roof, a teacher working in a safe space, and parents sending their children to school with greater peace of mind. After the year these communities have endured, that stability means everything,” the release quoted Zacca.

“When we asked Jamaica to ‘Run for the West’, people answered the call. They registered, donated, volunteered and supported because they understood that getting our children back into safe and functional schools had to be part of the recovery of western Jamaica. Today, we can actually see what that generosity has accomplished. These improved spaces mean students and teachers can focus again on what matters most — teaching, learning and building a better future,” Zacca added.

Sagicor Foundation board member Brigette Azan said restoring schools is ultimately about protecting opportunity for Jamaica’s children.

“Education remains one of the greatest tools we have for creating opportunity. Not every child starts life with the same advantages or resources, but every child deserves the opportunity to learn, discover their talents, and fulfil their potential. That is why getting our students back into safe, welcoming schools matters so much,” Azan said.

Latoya Harris Ghartey, executive director of NET, said the completion of the projects demonstrates what can be achieved through purposeful partnerships centred on students and their education.

“When we first began this process, the priority was clear: identify the schools where the need was greatest and help get our children back into safe spaces where they could learn and thrive. NET was pleased to work with the Sagicor Foundation from those early stages, supporting the process of identifying the beneficiary schools and the areas requiring attention. Seeing the work completed at Mayfield Primary and Infant School and Little London High School is especially meaningful because, ultimately, this is about ensuring that the disruption caused by Hurricane Melissa does not become a lasting barrier to our children’s education,” Harris Ghartey said.

World.title: Kranium: A ‘glitch in the dancehall matrix’
World.content:
Kranium recently returned to New York for a performance at Sony Hall after a four-year absence.

“I am a glitch in the matrix.”

For Kranium, the statement is more than a catchphrase. It is his unapologetic assessment of a career that has challenged conventional thoughts about what it takes to establish oneself in dancehall, particularly the long-held assumption that an artiste must be physically based in Jamaica to remain connected to the culture and build a successful career.

Born in Jamaica, but based in New York, USA, for much of his professional journey, the Nobody Has to Know hitmaker has established an international presence while operating outside the island’s borders.

And while he is not seeking recognition for changing the game, he believes the evidence of his impact is already there.

“I don’t just feel that way; I know it for a fact,” Kranium told the Jamaica Observer when asked whether he considers himself among the artistes who helped change perceptions about where a dancehall career can be built.

“The facts and the history are there: I took dancehall music and cemented myself as a household name while living outside Jamaica. Unfortunately for those who withhold that information it is already written: Kranium is a glitch in the matrix,” he added.

It is a confident position, but one Kranium believes his body of work supports. Attributing his success to more than just overcoming geographical barriers, the entertainer shared that he has had to tap into his creativity while ensuring he remained authentically himself.

“I didn’t feel like I had to work twice as hard. What I had to do was create authentic, quality music and be real with myself,” he said.

That commitment to authenticity has helped Kranium to cultivate a catalogue that includes songs that have received gold and platinum certifications across three major markets.

For him, those milestones are both a measure of achievement and an incentive to keep pushing.

“Seeing them gives me more motivation to take things to the highest level at my own pace,” he said. “Most importantly, seeing them on my wall reminds me that I am a very talented artiste. It gives me all the validation I need.”

He also sees room for Jamaican music to compete more forcefully on the international stage, provided the ambition extends beyond simply being successful within the genre.

“Yes, I think we can compete at the highest level once we understand that we need to be the best in the school, not just the class,” he said, indicating that geography is not the defining factor in whether a song travels. He explained that the quality of the music and the way it is introduced to audiences matter more than an artiste’s physical location.

“I know how to make authentic music. Even if I were under a rock, if the song is a hit, it will take off with the right juggling,” he said. “I think you can still stay connected as long as you remain true to the culture and understand the importance of paying attention to the current state of dancehall.”

His comments take on added significance against the backdrop of his recent return to New York for a performance after a four-year absence.

The city has played a significant role in his development as an artiste, making the occasion more than another date on an international schedule. The timing also coincided with the anniversary of his first album, We Can, achieving gold certification, creating what he described as the right moment to reconnect with the market.

“Now was the right time to return because everything aligned — the anniversary of my first album, We Can, going gold and, most importantly, the fact that I hadn’t done a show there in four years,” he said.

For Kranium, the performance felt like a homecoming, and he approached it with the intention of making the night memorable for the audience. From the energy of the show to his choices of fellow performers, he was deliberate about how the experience unfolded.

“It felt like a homecoming. That’s why I worked so hard to make sure the show stayed active all night, right down to who I wanted to share the stage with,” he said.

The return also signals that he intends to maintain that connection without over-saturating the market. While he recognises the value of appearing regularly before an audience, he is mindful of the balance between being present and overdoing it.

“There’s a fine line between being in the market frequently and overdoing it. But, for sure, it won’t take that long for me to hold another event there,” he said.

World.title: NOT SO SWEET
World.content:
THE price of bread, biscuits, buns, and drinks could come under fresh pressure as Jamaican manufacturers face the prospect of paying more for refined sugar once a new refinery in Belize begins supplying the Caribbean market.

Major food and beverage producers, including Wisynco, Lasco and ice-cream maker Caribbean Cream, have raised concerns that changes to regional import arrangements could make it more expensive to buy the sugar used in products consumed by Jamaicans every day.

Manufacturers fear that once the Belize refinery begins supplying the region, they could lose the duty waivers that allow them to buy refined sugar from outside Caricom at world market prices. They would then have to weigh the Belize supplier’s price against the cost of overseas sugar carrying a 40 per cent import tariff.

Wisynco Group Chairman William Mahfood said the potential increase would affect businesses across food manufacturing, with consequences for consumer prices.

“Legally, we can’t really challenge it, so the only thing I think we can do is push the Government to lobby for a reduction in the CET,” Mahfood told the Jamaica Observer, referring to Caricom’s common external tariff.

He said Belizean suppliers had indicated that they were proposing a 40 per cent increase in refined sugar prices, arguing that the tariff protection would leave Jamaican manufacturers with little room to find a cheaper alternative.

“These trade regimes were not intended to have, you know, penalties, which is really what it is…,” Mahfood said. “It’s effectively like Jamaicans are being penalised so that an investor can put a refinery in Belize.”

Mahfood argued that reducing the tariff would allow manufacturers to continue buying sugar from other suppliers without facing the full 40 per cent duty.

“If the CET goes down, it changes the whole dynamic and it gives us the ability then to import refined sugar from wherever and we’ll pay the duty,” he said.

“It won’t have as significant an impact on the cost of the finished product as a 40 per cent price increase.”

An increase in the cost of sugar would not automatically produce an equivalent increase in the price of bread, biscuits or drinks. The effect would depend on how much sugar a product contains, other production costs and how much of the increase manufacturers and retailers pass on.

But the ingredient’s use across food and beverage manufacturing means the concern extends well beyond the three companies that spoke with the Business Observer.

Lasco’s James Rawle said the company had been discussing the matter with the Jamaica Manufacturers and Exporters Association (JMEA), but had received no formal notification about future sourcing arrangements.

“The major concern that Lasco has, you know, and I would imagine that this is shared by sugar users, is that we are all sourcing sugar on the world market at the world market price,” Rawle said.

He explained that waivers have allowed manufacturers to import refined sugar without paying the external tariff because regional producers have not been able to supply their requirements.

“We haven’t received anything like samples or anything like that from the proposed suppliers from Belize,” he added.

Asked whether the concern was about the inconvenience of changing suppliers, Rawle was direct.

“How it’s going to impact price.”

Caribbean Cream Chief Executive Officer Christopher Clarke raised similar concerns at the ice cream maker’s annual general meeting on Monday, saying additional approvals or changes to duty-free access could increase costs, extend purchasing lead times and complicate production planning.

“Our principal concern is whether changes in regional sourcing arrangements could limit our access to competitively priced sugar from alternate suppliers,” Clarke said during his presentation.

In the question-and-answer session, he added: “The concern is being forced to supply from one place, while right now, as it is now, we have the option to buy it from anywhere we want to.”

Caribbean Cream has not yet quantified the potential financial impact.

More than price

In an interview with the

Business Observer, JMEA representatives Kamesha Turner and technical consultant Joy Angulu said manufacturers also needed certainty about when the refinery would begin supplying them and time to test its sugar.

Turner said the changing timetable made purchasing decisions more difficult for businesses that arrange their supplies well in advance.

“The timeline for this refinery continues to be a moving target. So even that within itself creates some uncertainty for businesses,” she said.

During the interview, the JMEA representatives explained that obtaining samples was an essential part of preparing for a change in supply.

“The quality of your sugar will affect the quality of your product,” Angulu said, explaining that manufacturers would need to conduct product trials and stability testing.

The association said higher sugar costs could also weaken the competitiveness of Jamaican exports. Manufacturers selling overseas must compete with producers that may still have access to ingredients at lower world market prices.

“We can’t just look at Caricom as being a protectionist market because we’re now playing in a global landscape where we have to ensure that our products are competitive,” Turner said.

The association is working with Jamaican Government ministries on its position ahead of regional trade discussions.

“We are in dialogue with Foreign Affairs and Minister of Finance to put together the position,” Turner said.

The regional case

Caribbean Sugar Refinery (CSR) is being developed at the Santander complex in Belize to expand the region’s capacity to produce refined sugar.

The Caricom Private Sector Organization (CPSO), which supports the project and another refinery investment in Guyana, estimates that the region imported more than US$150 million worth of refined sugar from outside Caricom in 2024. It argues that processing more of the region’s raw sugar within the Caribbean would reduce dependence on external suppliers and strengthen regional production.

CSR has said regional refining capacity could improve supply stability and strengthen manufacturers’ ability to compete with producers outside Caricom.

In a September statement, the company said tariff waivers for refined white sugar would remain in place until April 1, 2027, allowing customers time to adjust while commissioning, quality assurance and distribution arrangements were completed. It said full commissioning was expected in the fourth quarter of 2026.

A report on an August stakeholder meeting, published in the Private Sector Organisation of Jamaica and VM Group’s September economic bulletin, said CSR intended to use the international London No. 5 refined sugar price as its reference, with logistics, payment terms and other commercial details negotiated with customers. The report also said the company was open to local warehousing and established distributors serving Jamaican buyers.

The JMEA said a proposed transition discussed with regional stakeholders would begin with manufacturers sourcing 30 per cent of their refined sugar regionally and 70 per cent from outside Caricom. The regional share would rise gradually to 70 per cent by the fifth year.

Those proportions remain a proposal. The association said they had been discussed at stakeholder meetings but had not yet been settled through Caricom’s Council for Trade and Economic Development (COTED), which makes decisions on tariff arrangements.

“So we’re not sure how they plan to move forward with that,” Angulu said.

World.title: ON THE BRINK
World.content:
Jamaican football superstar Khadija Shaw (Photo: AFP)

KHADIJA “Bunny” Shaw has long been one of Jamaica’s brightest stars. However, her historic achievement at the women’s Ballon d’Or has strengthened the belief that she deserves greater global recognition, with the dream of becoming the world’s best player closer than ever before.

Reggae Girlz superstar Shaw finished third in the Ballon d’Or Féminin rankings on Monday at the awards ceremony in London. She finished behind winner Alexia Putellas of Spain, who claimed her third hold on the award, while compatriot and former Barcelona teammate Ewa Pajor finished second.

Shaw, the only Jamaican and fourth non-European player to finish in the top three in the award’s history, had an incredible 2025/2026 season with Women’s Super League (WSL) and FA Cup champions Manchester City, where she finished with 35 goal contributions including 21 goals in 22 games to win her third-straight WSL golden boot.

The reigning WSL Player of the Season, Professional Footballers Association (PFA) Player of the Year and Football Writers Association (FWA) Footballer of the Year joined male superstars Erling Haaland and Kevin De Bruyne as the only Man City players to finish in the top three.

Women’s football writer with The Guardian in the UK, Tom Garry, told the Jamaica Observer that Shaw’s third-place finish shouldn’t be underestimated.

“The mere fact that she made the top three despite not playing Champions League football last season, said a lot about how revered she is and how immensely well-regarded she is across the world,” Garry said. “Almost every colleague I interact with in the media considers Shaw to be the best out-and-out central number nine in the world.”

Since joining City in 2021, Shaw has established herself among England’s elite, scoring 127 goals in 146 appearances in all competitions.

However, some in the sport believe she hasn’t received the level of recognition she deserves in the UK and wider Europe for her performances, particularly when compared with other top players.

Sports reporter and presenter with UK football outlets Hayters TV and FourFourTwo, Ayisha Gulati, who covered Monday’s Ballon d’Or ceremony, believes the lack of recognition is no fault of Shaw’s and expects that to change in the near future.

“I think there have been times when Bunny Shaw has been overlooked, although some of that comes down to the wider landscape of women’s football,” Gulati told the Observer. “Barcelona have been the dominant force in the women’s game in recent years, with global superstars like Alexia Putellas and Aitana Bonmatí attracting a lot of attention and dominating conversations about who the best players in the world are.”

“By comparison, Manchester City haven’t been competing in the Champions League in the same way, while Jamaica are not a leading nation in international football. Those factors can influence how much global exposure a player receives, regardless of their individual quality. But Shaw’s performances and the individual awards she has collected make it increasingly difficult to overlook her.”

Garry also believes Shaw warrants far greater appreciation on the international stage.

“I do think she is sometimes overlooked, and that is probably because so much emphasis is placed on performances at senior international level and especially at major international tournaments such as a World Cup and — through no fault of Bunny’s — that means the players who are part of more successful international teams are naturally getting more credit. That’s a shame, because Bunny and — for example, Ewa Pajor of Poland or Melchie Dumornay of Haiti — deserve more awards than they get.”

Shaw described being named the third-best player in the world as a “huge honour”. She finished 24th in the 2023 rankings before climbing to 15th in 2024.

Gulati and Garry believe her performances in Man City’s European campaign, along with her exploits at FIFA World Cup could be key to her bid to lift the prestigious golden ball.

“The Ballon d’Or is an individual award, but team success and performances in high-profile matches has a big influence on how players are perceived,” Gulati said “Manchester City must compete deep into the Champions League and delivering in those decisive knockout games would give Shaw an even bigger platform to showcase her ability. Internationally, Jamaica qualifying for and performing well at the next World Cup would also help, however, that is not entirely within her control and she can only do so much.”

Garry said, “Realistically, in 2027 she would either need to be part of a Champions League-winning side with Manchester City or a Jamaica side that goes into the latter stages of the Women’s World Cup, or perhaps if she was able to win the Golden Boot for the most goals at the World Cup, regardless of how far Jamaica progressed overall. The former will be very difficult because Barcelona are the heavy favourites for the Champions League.”

Next month, Shaw could cap off an already remarkable year by helping the Reggae Girlz secure a third-straight World Cup appearance when they battle Costa Rica in the quarter-finals of the Concacaf W Championship in Texas.

It will be the 50th senior cap for Shaw, who has 67 international goals to her name, including seven so far in 2026.

World.title: New power players at Elite
World.content:
Lewis founded the Ideal Group of Companies, which includes Ideal Betting Company Limited, Ideal Finance Corporation Ltd, Ideal Portfolio Services Co. Ltd, Ideal Securities Brokers Limited, Resource in Motion Ltd, Ideal Global Investment Company Limited, Ideal Group Corporation Ltd, Resource Assets Ltd, Donwis Limited, Children’s Health, Education and Wealth Foundation.

THE mystery surrounding the recent shake-up in ownership at Elite Diagnostic Limited has been partly cleared, with two St Lucia-registered companies emerging as its largest shareholders following weeks of heavy trading that raised questions about a possible takeover of the Junior Market-listed company.

Resource Assets Limited (RAL) and Navy Inc. now hold 49.80 per cent and 20.96 per cent, respectively, of Elite’s issued ordinary shares, according to a disclosure issued on Monday by the company’s secretary, Cube Corporate Support Limited. Together, the two companies account for 70.76 per cent of Elite’s issued shares, although neither has disclosed any arrangement to exercise control jointly.

RAL has been linked to Jamaican businessman and investor Donovan Lewis, whose investment interests extend across several companies listed on the Jamaica Stock Exchange. However, the latest disclosure does not independently identify Lewis as RAL’s beneficial owner.

The announcement follows several weeks of speculation over who had been acquiring large blocks of Elite shares after a series of transactions between July and October significantly altered the company’s ownership structure.

The transactions attracted attention earlier this month after Elite disclosed that a review of shareholder records showed a single investor holding more than 50 per cent of its issued ordinary shares between October 2 and 6. The holding subsequently fell to approximately 38 per cent, raising questions about whether the temporary majority position triggered an obligation to make a takeover offer to remaining shareholders.

Under the applicable takeover rules, an investor acquiring 50 per cent or more of a listed company’s voting shares may be required to make an offer to other shareholders unless an exemption applies.

Monday’s disclosure confirms that RAL held 49.80 per cent of Elite as at October 23, just below the 50 per cent threshold.

In response to enquiries from Elite, both RAL and Navy Inc indicated that they had acquired their shares as long-term investments and had no immediate intention of purchasing additional shares.

“It acquired its shares for long-term investment purposes and with a view to enhancing shareholder value,” the shareholders stated in their responses to the company.

Both entities also advised that they were not acting in concert with any other person concerning their Elite shareholdings and that their voting rights were not subject to any agreements.

Elite Diagnostic, which listed on the JSE Junior Market in February 2018, provides medical imaging services, including MRI, CT scans and X-rays. The company is chaired by Steven Gooden, while Marjorie Miller serves as general manager.

Lewis’S investment interests

The reported connection between RAL and Lewis has drawn attention to the businessman, who has built sizeable investments across several Jamaican listed companies.

Lewis, founder of the Ideal Group of Companies, has investment interests spanning banking, financial services, food manufacturing and distribution.

Through Resource in Motion Limited (RIM), he has accumulated significant holdings in GraceKennedy Limited and Salada Foods Jamaica Limited, according latest public data.

RIM holds 57.98 per cent of Salada Foods, while the original shareholding analysis places Lewis’ combined connected interest, including holdings through other companies and accounts, at 78.69 per cent.

His investment interests also extend to NCB Financial Group Limited, where the original analysis puts his combined holdings at 2.86 per cent. Lewis previously served on the board of National Commercial Bank Jamaica Limited between May 2002 and January 2011.

RIM has also increased its investment in Scotia Group Jamaica Limited, acquiring another 3,036,379 shares between May and July 2026. The transactions brought its reported holdings to 43,075,177 ordinary shares at the end of July.

Based on the revised acquisition consideration of J$75 per share being offered by Scotiabank Caribbean Holdings Limited, that holding would be valued at approximately J$3.23 billion.

The amount represents an estimate based on RIM’s last reported shareholding and does not establish its final entitlement under the transaction, which would depend on its holdings and the applicable terms of the offer.

While Lewis’ existing portfolio gives the reported RAL connection added significance, the extent of his interest in Elite cannot be independently established from the company’s latest shareholder disclosure alone.

Questions remain over Navy Inc

The identity of the beneficial owner of Navy Inc, Elite’s second-largest shareholder, also remains unclear.

According to information cited in the original shareholder analysis, Navy Inc was incorporated in St Lucia on November 7, 2024, with Foster Capital Inc serving as its registered agent.

Elite has not publicly identified the individuals ultimately controlling Navy Inc, although the company said it had sought information from its substantial shareholders regarding their holdings and intentions.

“The information above was provided to the Company by the shareholders concerned. The company has kept the Jamaica Stock Exchange and the Financial Services Commission informed of these matters,” Elite stated.

The unusual trading activity for the otherwise thinnly traded stock and limited information available to investors have also prompted public criticism.

Mayberry Group Limited Chairman Christopher Berry raised concerns on social media platform

X on October 12 about the movement of large blocks of Elite shares and what he regarded as information gaps affecting minority shareholders.

“Over 50 per cent of Elite has been sold, no takeover bid, stock exchange refusal to provide market [the] top 100 to market, information gaps, minority shareholders buying and selling without material information,” Berry wrote.

The concerns followed transactions involving several of Elite’s former major shareholders, including Excel Investments Inc, which had held 24.53 per cent of the company as at June 30, and NCB Capital Markets Limited, which had held 18.68 per cent.

Elite has maintained that it has kept both the JSE and the Financial Services Commission informed of the changes in shareholdings.

The company’s audited results for the financial year ended June 2026 showed revenue increasing two per cent to $867.29 million, while net profit declined 14 per cent to $27.60 million. The company has also been investing in new equipment and premises as part of efforts to expand its diagnostic services.

Elite’s annual report is due on October 28, while its first-quarter report is expected by November 14.

World.title: Get ready to ‘Shop the Sales’ as TSO returns this weekend
World.content:
Jamaica Observer Senior Lifestyle Editor and Takes Style Out (TSO) conceptualiser Novia McDonald Whyte is flanked by Jamaica Observer Managing Director Dominic Beaubrun (right) and designer Robert Young at the launch of TSO 2026 at the newspaper's headquarters in St Andrew on Tuesday, October 27, 2026. (Photo: Naphtali Junior)

It promises to be a shopping bonanza this weekend as the Jamaica Observer Takes Style Out (TSO) returns for its 17th iteration, encouraging consumers to ‘Shop the Sales’.

The three-day shopping event from October 29 to October 31 will feature steep discounts and a special guest appearance by Trinidadian designer Robert Young of ‘The Cloth’.

Young was present at the launch event at the Jamaica Observer’s Beechwood Avenue headquarters on Tuesday, alongside the newspaper’s Senior Lifestyle Editor and TSO conceptualiser Novia McDonald Whyte, and a specially invited group of TSO sponsors and participating realtors.

TSO began as a direct offshoot out of the first Fashion’s Night Out in New York in 2009, created to get people shopping again after the economic downturn in 2008.

Even though Fashion’s Night Out in New York ended, the local event, committed to providing a night of genuine discounts to Jamaicans, has endured.

“When we talk about a sale, we’re talking about 50 per cent, 60 per cent, 70 per cent off, not 10 per cent and 20 per cent,” McDonald-Whyte explained.

“Fashion’s Night Out ended, but we continued, because it proved to be an economic booster in Jamaica,” she shared.

The scope of the event was emphasised by chief operations officer at Jamaica Electronic Transfer Services Limited (JETS Limited), Natalie Samuels Buckle.

“What I can say is that Takes Style Out is well embraced by the Jamaican shopping public. From where I sit, we see that Takes Style Out is a Richter-scale shopping event,” she explained.

JETS, the company behind the multilink debit card network which connects financial institutions across the country, is a key sponsor of the event alongside the National Commercial Bank (NCB) and Island Car Rentals.

Edmundo Jenez, Chief Executive Officer of JETS, maintained that retail has been recovering post Hurricane Melissa, driven by customers.

“We found that customers have been quite resilient. They’ve been able to bounce back, and we’re seeing it, just as we’ve mentioned before, the numbers are there,” he shared.

NCB Vice President of Payment Services and Digital Channels, Danielle Cameron Duncan emphasised the country-wide effect that the event has on the Jamaican public.

“Each sale is an opportunity to build a relationship, and each positive experience is a reason for a customer to return. That is what makes Takes Style Out valuable. It brings attention to businesses across Jamaica and gives them a platform to show customers what they can do,” she explained.

Cameron Duncan acknowledged the bank’s position in the consumer framework locally, including at Takes Style Out, noting that NCB processed over a trillion transactions for its merchants in the last financial year.

Emphasising the individuality and creativity of Jamaican style, Marketing Manager of Island Car Rentals Kerry Ann Harrison lauded the event.

“Takes Style Out is more than an event; it is an opportunity to celebrate individuality, to spotlight Jamaican talent, encourage creativity and to remind us that style belongs to everyone who has the confidence to own it,” she said.

Special Guest Robert Young also spoke to the Observer about fashion and individuality.

The mind behind fashion brand ‘The Cloth’, Young describes himself as an artist working with clothing. His pieces have been displayed at the Smithsonian National Museum of African Art, Washington, DC, the Museum at FIT, New York and Savvy Contemporary, Berlin.

In commenting on fashion microtrends defined by the rapid-fire TikTok algorithm, from ‘clean girl’ to ‘old money’, Young commented on style and individuality, as well as its wider reflection of a people.

“I don’t have a style,” he said with a laugh, adding that “Style exists. Style is definable by the person. But also as a perception… We have to find our own style and slowly find it as Caribbean people. And that has to be decolonised…We have to find our own language to describe it. We have to find something else other than the word ‘style.’”

He urged Caribbean people to question the reasons behind why certain things become relevant and assess the catalysts of certain laws surrounding what is acceptable fashion in the region, from the way hair is groomed to what we wear.

“We have to ask, what do these styles represent, and why are we attracted to it?” Young shared,

Retailers in the room included Fontana Pharmacy, Onya’s Kloset, Dunns Electrical, Moda Home Goods, Haven Beauty House, Loud Fashion, Ammars, Sakred, SOHO, Signature Styles, and Clarks Original. The general consensus from the specially invited retailers was that the event serves as a good lead-in to the Christmas shopping season.

“Our customers really, really appreciate it, We have up to 50 per cent [discounts], and we’ll honour all three dates… overseas, they look for Black Friday. In Jamaica, we look forward to Takes Style Out,” Karen Smith D’Aguilar, of Signature Styles Clarks Originals, said. “We really, really appreciate Observer.”

Anne Chang of Fontana Pharmacy shared that the company even extends the sale by one day due to popular demand.

This year’s event will be supported by dozens of stores and businesses. The full list of merchants offering discounts will be published in the Jamaica Observer newspaper on Thursday.

World.title: WATCH: Jamaicans divided over proposed 20-year minimum sentence for gun crimes
World.content:
KINGSTON, Jamaica — Jamaicans have expressed mixed reactions to a proposal by the National Security Council (NSC) to increase the mandatory minimum sentence for gun crimes from 15 to 20 years, with some welcoming the move as a crime-fighting measure while others believe the penalty is too harsh.

Observer Online took to the streets to gauge public opinion on the proposal, which was announced Sunday by the NSC, chaired by Prime Minister Andrew Holness.

The proposal has already drawn criticism from the Opposition People’s National Party (PNP), with Opposition Spokesperson on Justice, Zuleika Jess, arguing that it was put forward “without adequately addressing the legislation’s flaws”.

The existing 15-year mandatory minimum sentence under the Firearms (Prohibition, Restriction and Regulation) Act, 2022, has also faced scrutiny from members of the legal fraternity, who have raised concerns about its broad application and staged demonstrations calling for legislative reform.

Speaking with Observer Online, some individuals supported the proposed increase, arguing that tougher penalties could deter individuals from possessing illegal firearms and help curb gun violence.

“Twenty year minimum, 20 years. It’s a bit harsh, but I feel like the Government is working a way to try to reduce crime because there’s a lot of fatality with gunman and all of them things…” one respondent said.

Another agreed, suggesting that the prospect of spending two decades behind bars could discourage illegal firearm possession.

“I think it’s appropriate because if you know you’re going to get sentenced to 20 years for having illegal firearms, [would] you put yourself in that position? No, I agree with it,” she said.

Another Jamaican encouraged those interested in owning firearms to pursue legal avenues rather than risk facing criminal penalties.

“Gun is a thing weh protect you and thing. Some man use it fi do wrong thing, some use it fi do the right but sometimes you can get right out of wrong same way. You have to just get your thing license, go to the proper place and look bout your thing. If you love gun so much, prefer you have a gun license or if you wah really be a gunholder, go inna the force or go join the JDF or police,” he said.

However, not everyone was convinced that a longer mandatory sentence was justified.

One respondent described the proposal as excessive, raising concerns about the consequences for young people who may become involved in firearm-related offences without having committed a violent act.

“I believe that it is excessive. I’m thinking that 20 years of someone’s life is like a half of their lifetime. What time would you get for one mistake? Especially if it’s a situation where you did not commit a crime, as in murder anyone or shoot up anyone or even use a firearm. Suppose it’s a situation where your teenager or young adult was caught up in bad company. It’s a harsh penalty. Your entire future is lost in 20 years,” she said.

(Video by: Llewellyn Wynter)

World.title: EU set to scrap ‘associate member’ status offer for Canada
World.content:
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney delivers a speech in the hemicycle of the European Parliament in Strasbourg on September 17, 2026. | Jean-Christophe Verhaegen/AFP via Getty Images

A group of countries including Germany, Italy, Greece and France all objected to mentioning associate membership in a joint EU-Canada statement.

BRUSSELS — EU countries have dropped the idea of offering Canada "associate member" status in the 27-member bloc, opting instead for softer language promising "ever closer association" ahead of a landmark EU-Canada summit, according to the latest version of the draft statement, seen by POLITICO.

A group of countries including Germany, Italy, Greece and France all objected to mentioning associate membership in a joint EU-Canada statement to be issued in Montreal, the diplomats said.

European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen had originally proposed "associate membership" for Canada in her State of the European Union speech in September, catching some EU countries off-guard.

World.title: Healey targets Brits’ energy costs, raids banks in first budget
World.content:
Around 20 million households will be targeted for the energy payment “directly into people’s bank accounts to deal with rising energy bills,” Healey said. The scheme comes with a £2.6 billion price tag — and will arrive against a grim backdrop. Annual household energy bills are expected to rise by around £450 in January because of higher global gas prices.

Since coming to power as a self-styled “cost-of-living government” earlier this year, Burnham and Healey have tried to offer a raft of targeted, small-scale policy interventions to show that the government has a grip on rising costs — without spooking the financial markets.

Other measures unveiled Wednesday include the scrapping of standing charges on Brits’ gas bills, a hike in the minimum wage and a new tax-free allowance for poorer pensioners.

On the revenue-raising side, Healey has opted to target Britain’s banks.

While praising their “huge contribution” to the economy, the chancellor will hike an existing surcharge on bank profits by three percentage points, taking it to 6%. The increase will last for 15 months starting in January.

The tax on the banks was widely expected despite major pushback from the banking sector. It has been pared back compared to previous reports that the surcharge could hit 8%, with accompanying documents vowing that the measure “will not be extended.”

World.content:
Share on LinkedIn

Wie opportunistisch agiert Alice Weidel an der Parteispitze? Geleakte E-Mails aus den Jahren 2015 bis 2017 offenbaren einen radikalen Kurswechsel im Umgang mit Björn Höcke und zeigen detailliert, wie aus scharfer Distanzierung und Parteiausschlussforderungen ein strategisches Bündnis mit dem extremen Flügel wurde.

Die brisanten Dokumente werfen zudem ein neues Licht auf illegale Wahlkampfspenden aus der Schweiz und die Frage, wann Weidel wirklich davon wusste. Gleichzeitig vollzieht sie in der Russlandpolitik eine bemerkenswerte Wende, die sie an die Seite von Tino Chrupalla rückt. Warum dieser Kurs selbst in rechten Medien und Teilen der eigenen Fraktion für heftigen Widerstand sorgt, ordnet diese Recherche ein.

Ein abschließender Blick nach Sachsen-Anhalt zeigt eine drohende Zerreißprobe für die dortige CDU-Fraktion. Sollten Abgeordnete wie Guido Heuer bei der Abstimmung über den AfD-Kandidaten Ulrich Siegmund ausscheren, könnte das der Partei einen unerwarteten strategischen Triumph bescheren.

Den Artikel von Frederik Schindler bei WELT zum Thema AfD-Leaks gibt’s hier: Einmal zu den Aussagen von AfD-Mitbegründer Albrecht Glaser über Björn Höcke und zur Warnung Weidels vor dem Verlust der bürgerlichen Mitte.

„Inside AfD“ ist der POLITICO-Podcast über die umstrittenste Partei des Landes. Trotz Radikalisierung und Beobachtung durch den Verfassungsschutz wächst die AfD weiter. Wie ist das möglich? Was treibt ihre Anhänger, Strategen und Gegner an? Wie funktioniert das Innenleben der Partei? Und was bedeutet ihr Aufstieg für das politische System Deutschlands?

Antworten liefern immer mittwochs Pauline von Pezold von POLITICO und Frederik Schindler von WELT — unaufgeregt, aber kritisch.
