World.title: UK’s Healey cracks down on VAT-shirking online sellers
World.content:
Previously, these marketplaces only had to collect VAT on behalf of overseas sellers and not domestic ones. Some overseas sellers then exploited this gap to avoid paying the tax by registering as U.K. based companies.

The government launched an eight-week consultation into extending VAT online marketplace liability in June, after mounting pressure from retailers.

Amazon estimated that up to £3.2 billion of sales across online retailers in the U.K. are made by sellers avoiding VAT collection — costing the Treasury hundreds of millions each year in lost revenue.

The move to close the loophole brings Britain closer to approaches adopted in Switzerland. The European Commission is also due to review its marketplace VAT collection rules next year.

Monica Ariño, director of U.K. public policy at Amazon, said: “This is an important step towards closing a loophole exploited by bad actors and creating a level playing field for the thousands of UK small businesses that sell in our store. We look forward to continuing to work with HM Treasury and HMRC to make the changes effective, practical and fair.”

World.title: Berlin startet KI-Überwachung am Kottbusser Tor
World.content:
KI analysiert fortlaufend Bewegungsmuster

Wie das aussehen soll, demonstriert die Polizei gleich selbst. Draußen unter den Kameras führen Statisten eine Auseinandersetzung vor, drinnen in der Polizeiwache schlägt das System Alarm. Auf einem zuvor schwarzen Monitor erscheint das Videobild. Ob die Polizei tatsächlich eingreift, entscheidet der Beamte am Monitor.

Die KI analysiert das Videomaterial fortlaufend auf bestimmte Bewegungsmuster. Dafür abstrahiert sie die abgebildeten Personen vereinfacht zu einer Art „Strichmännchen“ und wertet deren Bewegungen aus. So soll sie etwa Schläge, Tritte oder eine am Boden liegende Person erkennen. Hält das System eine Situation für auffällig, schlägt es Alarm.

Die Darstellung als „Strichmännchen“ betrifft allerdings nur die Analyse durch die KI. Bei der Vorführung in der Polizeiwache zeigt sich: Die Beamten sehen nach einem Alarm das normale Videobild, auf dem Personen zu erkennen sind. Auf Nachfrage erklärt Polizeidirektionsleiter Markus van Stegen, die Beamten bekämen „natürlich richtige Bilder“ zu sehen, weil sie für ihre Entscheidung „das Maximum an Information“ benötigten.

Auch Spranger räumt in der Fragerunde ein, dass ihre vorherige Darstellung – die Bilder blieben anonymisiert – so nicht richtig gewesen sei. Die Videoaufnahmen werden zudem für 28 Tage gespeichert. Zeigen sie eine Straftat, können sie für die Strafverfolgung gesichert und als Beweismittel genutzt werden.

Wie treffsicher ist die KI?

Die Daten bleiben nach Angaben der Polizei in Behördenhand. Die Aufnahmen werden in einem Rechenzentrum der Berliner Polizei gespeichert. Polizeipräsidentin Barbara Slowik Meisel zufolge werden sie verschlüsselt und nach BSI-Vorgaben gesichert.

Offen ist allerdings, wie treffsicher die KI im Alltag sein wird. In Hamburg haben sich 99 Prozent der von der KI ausgelösten Situationen als Fehlalarme erwiesen. Der Polizeidirektionsleiter erwartet in Berlin deutlich bessere Ergebnisse. Man habe sich bewusst für ein anderes System entschieden: „Wir sind sehr überzeugt von der Auswahl, die wir getroffen haben.“

World.title: Zelenskyy defends leaders of Finland and Norway over Putin talks
World.content:
Speaking to reporters Tuesday, Zelenskyy praised the two Nordic leaders for their help, saying he had a “positive” view of them. “We really have very good relations with these countries. They truly help,” Zelenskyy said.

The Ukrainian leader said Putin had been taken out of diplomatic isolation last year when U.S. President Donald Trump met him in Alaska. “Since Alaska, Europeans have also been in contact with Russia,” Zelenskyy said. “They just haven’t done so as openly as the leaders of Norway and Finland.”

Everyone understands that there have been contacts “at the national security adviser level and between intelligence agencies,” as well as talks that only emerged after they had happened, he said.

“Here, though, everything is completely out in the open: discussions in advance, a full briefing, and transparent objectives. Finland and Norway are showing that they want to open another channel of communication, so that Europe can receive information not only through the United States and Russia can hear certain things directly,” Zelenskyy added.

The question of whether — and how — Europe should talk to Putin is a sore subject for officials and diplomats among Ukraine’s allies in the EU and beyond.

On Tuesday, Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen said she was “very skeptical” about the Finnish-Norwegian joint call and Swedish Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson said peace must come through “strength” rather than “appeasement” of Russia.

World.title: Eurovision confirms candidates for 2027 — but 2 EU countries are still on the fence
World.content:
The Eurovision Song Contest logo is seen as people arrive for the semifinal of the competition in Vienna on May 12, 2026. | Tobias Schwarz/AFP via Getty Images

Ireland, the Netherlands and Iceland will once again boycott the competition next year.

Spain and Slovenia are still undecided about whether to compete in next year’s Eurovision Song Contest, after they boycotted this year’s edition over Israel’s participation.

The European Broadcasting Union, which organizes Eurovision, announced Wednesday that national broadcasters from 36 countries would take part in next May’s contest, which will take place in Burgas in eastern Bulgaria.

Five countries staged an unprecedented boycott of the 2026 contest due to Israel’s war in Gaza — sparked by the Oct. 7, 2023 Hamas attack on Israel — and the resulting humanitarian crisis it triggered.

World.title: At least 64 people die in major Spanish train crash
World.content:
Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez said he was “dismayed” by the accident and sent his “solidarity and support” to the victims and their families. He said emergency services were working at the scene to help those affected and ensure their safety.

Opposition leader Alberto Núñez Feijóo of the People’s Party said he was “very worried” about reports of a new rail accident and that the priority now was to help the victims and support their families.

Santiago Abascal, leader of far-right Vox, also offered condolences to the victims’ families but turned his message to the government. “I will not rest until this government, which is a criminal organization, sits in the dock to answer for its crimes,” he said on social media.

The accident led the government, the PP, the PSOE and the left-wing Broad Front to cancel their main pre-campaign events ahead of the Nov. 29 general election, with Vox as the exception. Abascal said he would not “use mourning to silence the complaints” in an interview Wednesday morning.

European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen offered her condolences on X, saying she had received the “devastating news” from Toledo and that “Europe mourns with you.”

The Adamuz accident drew sharp criticism of Sánchez’s government, with the PP accusing it of failing on rail safety and demanding that Transport Minister Óscar Puente answer for it. Sánchez, who stood by Puente, was later grilled in the Spanish parliament over the government’s response.

This is a developing story.

World.title: Satellites the size of drinks cans: Young engineers take on a space challenge in Uzbekistan
World.content:
Building a satellite usually takes years, specialist facilities and substantial funding. But at an airfield outside Uzbekistan's capital, Tashkent, young engineers from 15 countries faced a different challenge: building a miniature satellite model small enough to fit inside a drinks can, then sending it into the sky.

 

Their creations, known as CanSats, carried sensors, electronics and communications systems designed to collect measurements during flight. Launched aboard rockets and released to descend by parachute, they offered students a chance to put their engineering skills to the test without ever leaving Earth's atmosphere.

A miniature CanSat satellite Euronews

Unlike conventional satellites, CanSats do not enter orbit. Instead, they simulate selected functions of a space mission under real flight conditions.

Teams spent several days assembling electronics, configuring sensors and programming their devices at Turin Polytechnic University in Tashkent before preparing them for launch. The programme brought together 50 international participants and more than 100 students from Uzbekistan.

From design to flight

During the descent, the challenge was to keep the CanSats operating independently while their sensors collected measurements and their communication systems transmitted data to ground stations.

One Uzbek team added a camera to its device alongside sensors measuring temperature and air pressure, attempting to transmit live video during the flight.

“The main challenge here is to make sustainable telemetry. It should connect the ground station and the CanSat itself,” Ahmadkhon Latipov told Euronews.

The devices also stored information onboard, allowing teams to recover data even if communication with the ground station was interrupted.

Baris Beynek, an instructor from Istanbul Technical University, said this reproduces a fundamental part of real satellite operations.

“In the real satellite project, there is a satellite which sends the data to ground station and also stores inside, which we also do,” he said.

After landing, teams recovered their devices and analysed the information recorded during flight. This allowed them to compare their calculations with the actual performance of the electronics, sensors, communications and parachute systems.

According to the organisers, 14 teams competed in the final stage, with Team Nebula taking first place, followed by Pegasus and Sky Lab.

Space skills beyond satellites

The competition formed part of the fifth international CanSat training workshop, organised by Uzbekistan's space agency, Uzcosmos, the Islamic World Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization (ICESCO), and Turin Polytechnic University in Tashkent.

Dr Muhammad Sharif, an adviser for science and environment at ICESCO, said the growing use of satellite technology is creating demand for skills beyond traditional aerospace engineering.

He highlighted Earth observation, satellite communications and artificial intelligence, alongside applications in agriculture, food security and climate monitoring.

The programme also puts international teamwork at the centre of the engineering challenge.

“They need to use their own skills, and they need to cooperate with other people,” Beynek said. “In space, international cooperation is the most important thing.”

The CanSat participants group photo Euronews

For Uzbekistan's space agency, the programme is also an opportunity to train young specialists for the country's developing space sector.

Muhiddin Ibragimov, Deputy Director of Uzcosmos, said that involving young people in space technology is essential, stressing that even the most advanced projects depend on having the right skills and teams.

World.title: Germany and Japan strengthen economic ties as global tensions rise
World.content:
It is a meeting of the leading representatives of two of the world's largest economies. On his first visit to Japan the German chancellor Friedrich Merz has met Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi.

 

Takaichi and Merz issued joint statements on economic security and future technologies. These are intended to strengthen and better align cooperation between the two countries in these fields.

Side swipes at China and the US

Although China and the United States were not explicitly mentioned in the joint statement or in subsequent remarks, the message appeared to contain indirect criticism of both countries. Beijing and Washington have repeatedly used their economic policies as a means of exerting pressure on partners and rivals.

"Both heads of state and government expressed their deep concern about the growing use of economic coercion, for example through arbitrary export restrictions and retaliatory measures affecting critical raw materials. They also rejected non-market-based measures and practices that lead to overcapacity and market distortions and thereby undermine our economic security and resilience," the joint statement said.

The two nations have said they intend to step up their cooperation in monitoring and assessing supply chains, to prevent economic dependencies from being abused as a tool of pressure. They are also examining closer collaboration in key sectors such as critical raw materials, semiconductors, batteries, electric cars, industrial AI, robotics, pharmaceuticals and wind power.

On critical raw materials, Merz and Takaichi welcomed the signing of a joint declaration of intent. At the same time, they announced plans to broaden the supply base and improve the substitutability of rare earths in the automotive industries of both countries.

Japan has faced supply bottlenecks for rare earths after China restricted exports of several important raw materials. In November Takaichi addressed Japan's parliament, stating that Japan could intervene militarily in the event of a crisis over Taiwan. Beijing regards the democratically governed island as part of its own territory.

Takaichi and Merz also agreed to establish a high-level dialogue on artificial intelligence and to work more closely together on protection against cyberattacks. Both areas are gaining importance for the Japanese government as AI-driven cybercrime is rising sharply in the country.

In their joint statement, the two leaders both voiced concern about the situation in the East and South China Seas. They rejected unilateral attempts to change existing conditions by force or coercion – wherever in the world they may occur. They also underlined the importance of peace and stability in the Taiwan Strait and called for a peaceful resolution of the conflicts between China and Taiwan.

The shared goals of Japan and Germany

In view of rising geopolitical tensions, Germany and Japan are expected to intensify their cooperation with allies and like-minded states. Both sides reaffirmed their commitment to freedom, democracy, fair trade, the rule of law and human rights.

Military cooperation in the Indo-Pacific is also to be further expanded. One example is the first-ever participation of German armed forces in the Japanese-American military exercise "Keen Sword" this year. The drills, which run until Thursday, are taking place at several locations in Japan, particularly in the sea and airspace around Okinawa, where China has stepped up its military activities in recent years.

At an economic forum in Tokyo on Wednesday morning, Chancellor Merz called for the creation of a new political alliance to strengthen rules-based global trade. The alliance is intended to defend and further develop trade based on international agreements. At the same time, it could "provide political impetus and also respond jointly when the rules-based order comes under threat".

Germany plans to invest two billion euros in artificial intelligence and high-tech by 2029. Japan is aiming for around 18 billion euros in private investment in these areas by 2040.

Germany only at the beginning of diversifying its partners

During his time in Japan, Merz also visited the start-up Kyoto Fusioneering. It is considered a flagship project of the German-Japanese high-tech partnership thanks to its cooperation with Siemens Energy. The goal of the collaboration is to generate electricity from nuclear fusion.

The Japanese government is promoting the strategically important semiconductor industry with extensive state subsidies.

Germany is guided by EU requirements stating that by 2030 no more than 65 percent of critical raw materials should come from China. But the diversification of partners - that is, the reduction of dependencies on Beijing, which is the declared goal of the chancellor’s Asia trip - is still in its infancy.

On Thursday, South Korea is on the agenda at the end of the chancellor’s Asia tour. At his meeting in Seoul, in addition to bilateral economic relations, security issues and cooperation on future technologies such as artificial intelligence are to be discussed.

World.title: South Korea fines Google, Apple for pushing app developers onto their payment systems
World.content:
South Korea's media and telecommunications regulator on Wednesday ordered Google and Apple to pay a combined 63.7 billion won (€42.7m) accusing them of exploiting their grip on app stores to push developers towards their own payment tools and of stalling app reviews.

 

The two US companies have faced similar penalties elsewhere, including in the EU.

The Korea Media and Communications Commission (KMCC) fined Google 42.9 billion won (€28.7m) and Apple 20.8 billion won (€13.9m) after an investigation that began back in August 2022.

It found that both firms had broken a 2021 law that stops app store operators from making developers use a specific payment system, a rule that South Korea was the first country in the world to put into force.

On paper, Google and Apple allowed developers to offer other payment systems inside their apps. However, they charged a 26% commission on those payments, only slightly below the 30% they charge for their own systems, and held back some features, which the commission said left developers with little real choice.

Payments through external websites were also blocked altogether.

The regulator also found that the companies held up app reviews without properly explaining the reasons to developers, or saying when the reviews would restart.

Apple was also found to have charged South Korean developers more than those elsewhere between 2015 and January 2023, as it calculated its commission on prices that included value-added tax.

FILE. A model iPhone Duo is displayed outside the Apple Store on Fifth Avenue on its launch day in New York, 23 Oct. 2026 AP Photo/Ryan Murphy

Both companies must now let South Korean developers place links to outside payment options in their apps and improve how they review apps. They have one month to submit plans and three months to make the changes.

Commission chair Kim Jong-cheol said he hoped the sanctions would bring real change to the market, reiterating that South Korean law would be applied equally to domestic and foreign companies.

Google and Apple have not yet reacted publicly to the decision.

A familiar fight in Europe

The case echoes battles in the EU, where the Digital Markets Act (DMA), a law setting rules for the biggest online platforms, prohibits so-called gatekeepers from stopping developers directing users to cheaper deals.

In April 2025, Apple was fined €500 million by the European Commission under the DMA for blocking such steering on its app store, a decision it has appealed.

In August this year, following what it called close collaboration with the Commission, Apple announced new EU terms taking effect on 1 October.

They cut its standard commission on in-app purchases to 26% from 30% and set a 15% rate when developers send users elsewhere to complete a purchase.

Meanwhile, Google was fined €890 million by Brussels in July, including €430 million for restricting developers on Google Play from pointing users to cheaper purchase options.

It has since changed some of its fees and terms on Google Play, which the Commission is still assessing, and has appealed the fines.

World.title: More than half of pilots say they flew while tired as trust in reporting systems remains low, survey finds
World.content:
Fear of negative consequences and a lack of trust in reporting systems are among the barriers that prevent pilots from declaring themselves unfit to fly due to fatigue, according to a new survey by the European Cockpit Association (ECA).

 

The ECA identified head nodding, struggling to keep their eyes open, impaired alertness and microsleeps — brief, involuntary episodes of sleep — as signs of fatigue that can affect pilots on the flight deck.

More than half of pilots surveyed said they had flown while tired, while over 76% reported experiencing at least one microsleep on the flight deck in the previous four weeks, highlighting concerns about fatigue management in aviation.

Conducted by aviation consultancy Baines Simmons, the survey gathered responses from 7,200 pilots across 32 countries.

More than half of respondents reported that at least once in the previous three months they had operated a flight before realising in hindsight that they should have declared themselves unfit to fly due to fatigue.

The most commonly cited barrier was concern about management’s reaction, reported by 47% of pilots. A further 44% said they did not want to draw attention to themselves, while 35% were reluctant to inconvenience their employer.

“When pilots fear career consequences, fatigue goes unreported and the risk returns to the cockpit,” said ECA Board Director Captain Coen George.

Fatigue can result from acute sleep loss, long or demanding flight duty periods or repeated inadequate recovery time between duties.

The report highlights the particular dangers of cumulative fatigue, which can build up over time. Pilots may find it harder to recognise the resulting impairment in advance than the effects of short-term sleep deprivation.

Despite widespread awareness of fatigue risks, the problem remains underreported in the aviation industry.

While 82% of pilots knew how to submit a fatigue report, only 12% said they trusted the reporting system, and just 11% reported that fatigue submissions had led to operational changes to improve safety.

Half of respondents said fatigue risks at their airline were either poorly managed or not managed at all.

Fatigue is a known problem

Fatigue among aircrew is not a new concern. Aircrew fatigue was identified as one of the most consistent and prominent safety concerns in the European Union Aviation Safety Agency (EASA) report published in June 2026.

It linked fatigue to several operational and socio-economic factors, including flight scheduling, short-notice roster changes and the use of commanders’ discretion to extend flight duty periods beyond their scheduled limits.

EASA highlighted the need for targeted safety initiatives to improve reporting quality and awareness and foster a workplace culture where personnel can declare themselves tired without fear of reprimand.

World.title: UK budget: Here’s five key takeaways from the Chancellor’s speech
World.content:
Britain's economy will grow slightly faster than forecast this year before slowing in 2027, finance minister John Healey said on Wednesday as he presented the government's annual budget.

 

Gross domestic product (GDP) is estimated to grow by 1.2% in 2026, Healey said, up from a government estimate of 1.1% issued shortly after the start of the US-Iran war.

He told parliament that GDP growth would slow to 1.0% next year, down from the 1.6% growth forecast for 2027 by Labour in early March.

Here are some of the key takeaways from his speech:

UK to lift tax rate on bank profits

Britain's Labour government will increase a surcharge on profits earned by banks operating in the country to help offset soaring energy bills.

The additional corporate tax rate will double to 6% to finance a one-off subsidy to millions of households struggling with higher energy costs, Healey told parliament.

Energy support to households

The Chancellor said the government would hand out a direct payment of £100 to 20 million households to help with soaring energy bills.

The measure is designed "to take the pressure off in the coldest months and see people through to the spring", Healey said, as gas and electricity prices surged largely because of the Middle East conflict.

First-time buyer ISA changes

Healey announced that a First-Time Buyer ISA will replace the Lifetime ISA.

He also said the changes to the ISA penalty would mean buyers would receive at least their original contributions back if the property costs more than the purchase limit.

“For every young person who is working hard, saving what they can, and dreaming of their first home, I’m taking action.

“I’m announcing that a first-time buyer ISA will replace the lifetime ISA. From today, I’m dealing with the ISA penalty, so that if the home you want costs more than the limit, you will get back at least what you put in,” he said.

Adjusted triple lock and new care service

The chancellor confirmed changes to the triple lock, a measure that ensures the value of the state pension rises each year in line with whichever is highest: inflation, average wage growth or 2.5%, and the creation of a new national care service.

“This will save £15bn a year by the end of the 2030s, £50bn by 2050,” he said.

A rising state pension and a national care service would work together to support older people when they needed it, “taking the burden off families, taken the burden off our NHS,” Healey added.

Business rates to be retained locally

Healey further outlined plans to devolve tax revenues, calling it a "roadmap to fiscal devolution".

He announced that "100% of business rates will be retained locally by the end of the decade".

"From next year, 20% of business rates revenue will go to mayors," he said, and from 2028 "a share of income tax receipts will go to mayors as well".

World.title: Pictures show rescue efforts after deadly Spain train collision
World.content:
Images from the scene show the devastation left by a collision between two high-speed trains near Urda, in the province of Toledo, central Spain, which has killed at least 64 people and injured dozens more.

 

More than 500 passengers were travelling on the two trains, operated by Spain's national rail company Renfe and private operator Iryo.

Emergency crews launched a major rescue operation, working to free passengers from the wreckage of derailed carriages and treat the injured.

The photographs capture the aftermath of the crash and the rescue efforts on the ground.

World.title: Trump rolls back methane rules for US oil and gas industry
World.content:
US President Donald Trump announced on Tuesday plans to significantly ease restrictions on methane emissions from oil and gas producers, targeting regulations aimed at limiting the release of the potent greenhouse gas.

 

The regulations were introduced under former Democratic President Joe Biden's administration.

"Tonight, I'm officially terminating Biden's expensive and unnecessary methane regulations to save consumers and energy producers $45 billion," Trump said at the rally in Lubbock, Texas.

Trump told a cheering crowd that the move would "unlock vast quantities of Texas natural gas." Texas is the largest fossil fuel-producing state in the United States.

The Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) had previously estimated savings of $45 billion (around €39 billion) earlier this month, but provided no detailed breakdown of the figure,

"Americans must be able to afford to heat their homes in the winter and fill up their car and drive to work," said EPA administrator Lee Zeldin. "They can't do that when the people producing the energy are weighed down by unnecessary burdens."

Methane's impact on global warming

Methane, the main component of natural gas, is the second-largest contributor to global warming after carbon dioxide, accounting for roughly a third of the rise in global temperatures since pre-industrial times, or around 0.5°C.

Although methane traps significantly more heat than carbon dioxide, it remains in the atmosphere for just seven to 12 years, compared with hundreds of years for CO₂.

According to the International Energy Agency (IEA), the United States is the world's largest source of methane emissions from oil and gas production, followed by Russia.

World.title: Biometrics, AI and digital passports: Europeans ‘most cautious’ about travel technology, IATA survey finds
World.content:
European travellers are the “most cautious” when it comes to adopting digital travel technology, according to the International Air Transport Association (IATA) 2026 Global Passenger Survey.

 

With results based on more than 10,000 responses from 200 countries, the survey found that Europeans are the least willing, at 70%, to share biometric data for airport processes. This is compared to the global average of 78%.

Of all the regions, Middle Eastern and African travellers showed the most willingness, at 84% and 82% respectively.

European travellers are also less enthusiastic about using a digital passport for online check-in, with 79% expressing interest, compared with 84% globally.

Concerns about data handling may explain this caution. Overall, 59% of respondents said they worried about data breaches. While 49% were concerned about their information being shared with other organisations and 41% cited a lack of clarity on how their personal details are handled.

Despite these concerns, IATA found that biometrics have become a “mainstream” part of the travel experience, with 58% of passengers overall reporting having experienced biometrics at least once in the past 12 months. This is up from just 34% in 2022.

“More passengers are experiencing biometrics during their travels. They like it and want more," Nick Careen, Senior Vice President, Operations, Safety and Security at IATA, said.

“That’s good news because the benefits are substantial – smoother journeys for passengers and more efficient, secure processes for governments and airlines.

"To make biometrics the norm for international travel, governments must agree a framework for issuing and accepting secure digital passports – or Digital Travel Credentials."

IATA found that as many as 82% of respondents would share a digital passport with an airline at booking and after payment to receive personalised services, including information on visa requirements.

Also, 82% would use a smartphone combining a digital wallet, digital passport and loyalty cards to book, pay and navigate airport processes at departure and arrival.

Is AI changing the way we travel?

AI is becoming a more prominent tool for people’s travel plans.

The survey’s findings point to 49% of travellers saying they have used AI for their planning. This includes 21% who have used it to search for flights to a specific destination, while 19% say they used it to look for the cheapest flights. Lastly, 17% of respondents used it for their travel inspiration.

"People are using AI to plan their travel,” Careen added. “It’s important for airlines not only to ensure their offerings show up in AI, but also to develop convenient links to convert an AI conversation into a real booking.”

Immigration rules are a barrier to travel

Despite new technologies designed to make journeys easier, immigration requirements remain a growing barrier to travel – discouraging as many as 43% of global travellers from visiting a destination, up from 33% in the 2025 survey.

This is the case for 52% of African travellers – more than any other region. Comparatively, entry requirements discouraged 38% of Europeans.

For those put off by immigration requirements, 53% said the process was too complex, while 17% were discouraged due to cost, and a further 17% because of privacy.

For a quicker experience, however, 86% said they would be likely to share immigration information digitally before departure. While 45% would prefer to complete immigration procedures before arriving at the airport, and 60% saying they would prefer to have their visas processed online, compared to 25% who would prefer the application be done in person at a consulate or embassy.

"Passengers want to apply for visas online and complete immigration procedures before they reach the airport,” Careen said. “E-visas can deliver that, but airlines can only verify them efficiently if governments use common standards.

“More than 100 countries issue e-visas, yet there is little consistency in how they are checked. The tools to fix that already exist, and governments should adopt them."

World.title: Egypt's mahrganat music: from the streets to five-star hotels
World.content:
Born in Egypt’s working-class neighbourhoods, mahraganat music is loud and raw, and these days it is practically impossible to escape. But for the artists behind it, mahraganat is more than just party music: they see it as the latest chapter in Egypt’s rich musical history.

Advertising

In this third episode of the season, we travel to the Egyptian capital, Cairo, to discover the origins of a genre that has become the soundtrack to urban life, despite receiving no official airtime.

Mahraganat evolved from shaabi: music by the people, for the people. Although it rose to prominence during the revolution of 2011–12, it has since become less overtly political.

It remains the music of happiness, partying, joy and celebration.

Its fast rhythms and loud beats may be a far cry from the golden age of Egyptian music, but mahraganat has been on the scene since the early 2000s and it isn’t going anywhere any time soon.

We trace its origins and evolution as we speak to one of the godfathers of the movement, his musical partner and a specialist in the genre.

Mid-East Junction is produced by RFI's English-language service. This episode was mixed by Vincent Pora.

World.title: Spain train crash caused by operator 'inexplicably' telling driver to resume journey despite red signal, transport minister says
World.content:
Skip next section Renfe train was told to continue journey despite red signal, transport minister says

10/28/2026 October 28, 2026 Renfe train was told to continue journey despite red signal, transport minister says

The Renfe high-speed train that crashed into another stationary train had been told to continue its journey "as normal" despite the fact that all trains on the section of track in Toledo province had been told to stop, Spain's Transport Minister Oscar Puente has said.

Puente told a press conference at the ADIF control center in Madrid that the control system at the train station in Urda had failed due to a computer error.

That failure meant that a 63-kilometer section of track had no control system, which triggered an automatic stop, or "red signal," for all rail traffic on the parts of the track affected.

Operators at the control center ADIF, the company that is responsible for managing and maintaining Spain's railway infrastructure, took over communications.

"At 8:36 a.m. the Renfe train was told to resume its journey 'with normality'," Puente explained, a decision he described as "inexplicable."

He said that between that time and the moment of impact at 8:53, the Renfe train had traveled about 25 kilometers (15.5 miles), likely reaching a speed of over 100 kilometers (60 miles) per hour.

During the press conference, Puente refused to respond to questions about whether he would resign in the wake of the crash, saying his attention was on clarifying the circumstances that led to the crash and supporting the victims.

World.title: Is Iran headed to war or peace after Mecca alliance meeting?
World.content:
Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Turkey have taken their latest peace push directly to Tehran. Officially, it was to avert a new military escalation, but their diplomatic outreach can also be seen as a warning to Iran.

Amid rising fear that the US and Israel are preparing to launch new attacks on Iran after the US midterm election on November 3, three major Middle Eastern powers delivered a coordinated diplomatic message directly to Tehran.

Pakistan's army chief Asim Munir, Saudi Defense Minister Khalid bin Salman and Turkish intelligence chief Ibrahim Kalin all traveled to Iran to meet Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian and senior officials in Tehran this Monday. The three envoys serve as representatives for the Mecca defense pact — a military alliance of Islamabad, Riyad and Ankara, which was officially set up this summer.

Saudi Arabia said ⁠the ⁠trip aims to open negotiating channels and "prevent the return of military escalation." Details on the agenda, however, remain scarce.

Iran conflict: Could a new phase of the war be imminent? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

A senior Pakistani official cited by the Reuters news agency said the talks focused on building a regional non-aggression network, in addition to US-Iran talks, Houthi rebels' attacks on Saudi Arabia, the Strait of Hormuz and the US naval blockade.

Another official said Pakistan's Munir presented Iran with a solution to the conflict that would offer something both to Washington and Iran, with the three Mecca states and Qatar acting as mediators. The source told Reuters US President Donald Trump previously gave Munir the go-ahead to try diplomacy.

Tehran presents the meeting as a success

Iran hailed the "very positive atmosphere" during the Tehran talks, even though no breakthroughs were officially announced.

"Very good discussions took place between us," Mohsen Rezaei, head of Iran's Supreme National Security Council, told state television. "I feel that a new atmosphere is emerging in the region."

Rezaei argued that regional security should be built by countries in West Asia themselves and without outside intervention.

A day later, Rezaei reportedly met Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei. Iranian state media said Khamenei called for protecting Iran's interests and maintaining Tehran's conditions for ending both the war and the current state of "neither war nor peace."

Meanwhile, Iran's President Masoud Pezeshkian travelled to Moscow for the Gas Exporting Countries Forum, where he met Russian President Vladimir Putin and Qatar's Emir Sheikh Tamim bin Hamad Al Thani, with Pezeshkian and the emir also discussing the war and the Strait of Hormuz.

These and other diplomatic contacts were framed by Tehran as evidence that the US is unable to diplomatically isolate the Iranian regime.

Are Turkey and Pakistan closing ranks with Saudi Arabia?

The united front presented by the three nations in Tehran, however, can also be seen as a show of force for the new Mecca defense alliance. It comes as the Saudis grow increasingly wary of the attacks on Saudi infrastructure launched by the Iran-allied Houthi militants.

Egypt ready to back Saudi Arabia's war against Houthis To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Under the terms of the Mecca agreement, an outside attack on one of the member states is to be regarded as an attack on all of them. The visit also came on the same day as Egypt's parliament agreeing to give military help to Ryad and take "all necessary measures" to help Saudi Arabia defend itself, in addition to the looming threat of the US and Israel.

"The presence of the three senior representatives at the same time sent the message that these countries are acting as a bloc," Babak Dorbeiki, a London-based political analyst and former official at Iran's Strategic Research Center, told DW.

Saudi Arabia has long been regarded as Iran's archrival in region. It has used its enormous wealth to counter Iran's influence, and now it can, at least in theory, also count on Pakistan's nuclear capability, and Turkey's conventional military strength.

At the same time, Dorbeiki argued that the Mecca pact is primarily designed for deterrence rather than offensive war. And having a defense pact does not mean its members want to fight Iran.

Dorbeiki believes the message from the bloc could therefore work in two directions: it can provide mediation, but continued escalation could also alter that position.

Ryad pushing for a 'diplomatic solution'

Saudi Arabia faces the most immediate dilemma. Further Houthi attacks damage its infrastructure and economy, but a wider war with Iran could threaten the investment and development projects at the heart of Riyadh's economic strategy.

"For Saudi Arabia, both the current situation and a war with Iran carry serious costs," Dorbeiki said. "Its preferred route is, therefore, a diplomatic solution."

What now for Saudi Arabia after Riyadh airport attack? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Moreover, Pakistan has spent months mediating between Washington and Tehran and has important relations with both. A direct conflict would also distract Islamabad from its long-standing security concerns involving India.

Turkey is a NATO member, but Dorbeiki says direct military support for Iran against the United States is highly improbable. The fact that Ankara sent intelligence chief Ibrahim Kalin rather than its foreign or defense minister also suggests a cautious approach.

Iran pursues diplomacy while preparing for fighting

Ali Asghar Shafieian, media advisor for Iran's President Masoud Pezeshkian, also rejects the perspective that the Mecca pact representatives were trying to present Tehran with an ultimatum.

He told DW that the three countries may also have wanted to demonstrate their own growing coordination, while showing that Iran remains part of regional diplomacy.

"You cannot conclude from this meeting alone that it was an ultimatum before an attack," Shafieian said.

He also noted that Iran, just like the US and Israel, could prepare for the possibility of further conflict while maintaining negotiations.

Mediator or enforcer? Pakistan's role in the Middle East To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

"Just as they use the opportunity to strengthen their military and defensive capabilities, Iran does the same," he said.

Shafieian said an agreement remains possible if Iran's political standing and what Tehran describes as its national dignity are respected.

Diplomatic game continues

Analyst Dorbeiki argues that Iran is following a familiar strategy of extending negotiations while avoiding real-world commitments.

The Houthi rebels are central to Tehran's calculation.

Tehran has not publicly offered the kind of guarantees over Houthi attacks that Riyadh would want. Dorbeiki believes Iran could seek to trade influence over such the attacks for concessions such as an end to US military pressure and broader steps toward ending the war.

The only apparent outcome of the Tehran meeting is to keep talking. For Iran, that might be enough of a signal that it is still a diplomatic partner rather than an enemy.

Edited by: Shamil Shams

World.title: Gen Z protests in Germany: Is France-style violence looming?
World.content:
Young people in Germany will take to the streets this weekend to demand education and action on climate change. Politicians warn that the protests could become violent, as in France, but the situations are different.

As politicians in Germany look ahead to the coming weekend, many fear that cities across the country could witness the kind of violent unrest that recently shook France. An initiative known as "Gen Z regelt" ("Gen Z sorts it") has launched a social media campaign calling for demonstrations in 23 cities nationwide.

"Gen Z" broadly refers to the generation born between 1995 and 2010. Many feel that their parents' generation has done too little to combat climate change and has allowed the gap between rich and poor to widen ever further. At the same time, they are concerned about their educational prospects and future opportunities.

CDU: 'We must prevent scenes like those in France at all costs'

In France, what began as largely peaceful protests recently spiraled into serious unrest. Cars were set alight in several towns, while in Limoges the town hall was torched. In Lille, Lyon, and Toulouse and elsewhere, police deployed tear gas, leading to numerous arrests.

Many politicians, particularly within Chancellor Friedrich Merz's center-right Christian Democratic Union (CDU), are warning of similar scenes this coming weekend.

Alexander Throm, the CDU parliamentary group's domestic spokesperson, told the daily Handelsblatt newspaper: "Scenes like those in France must be prevented at all costs."

France protests continue despite police crackdown To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Concerns over internationally coordinated far-left extremists

In Throm's view, far-left groups and criminals from immigrant communities could "hijack" the demonstrations. "An ominous alliance is emerging, particularly in Berlin," he warned.

Marc Henrichmann, also of the CDU, chair of the Bundestag's parliamentary oversight panel for the intelligence services, also expressed concern: "The far-left extremist scene is internationally connected and coordinated." He said that violent far-left activists now even cross national borders to engage in looting and acts of violence elsewhere.

But Sebastian Koos, sociologist at the University of Konstanz whose research focuses on youth and protest movements, told DW that he does not expect Germany to experience unrest on a scale comparable to that seen in France, even though events in the neighboring country helped spark the protests now being planned across Germany.

Koos: 'Not driven by anger as in France'

Koos sees key differences between young people in the two countries. "Unlike in France, these protests are not driven by the same level of anger," he said. "They have been planned, officially registered and carefully organized. The website, in particular, places strong emphasis on peaceful protest and repeatedly stresses a non-violent approach."

At the same time, the sociologist does not rule out the possibility that extremist groups could exploit the authorized demonstrations to stir up unrest: "It is certainly very important for the police and public authorities to be well prepared."

Quentin Gärtner, 19, studies biotechnology in Heidelberg and served until November of last year as secretary-general of the Federal Student Conference, which represents around 7.5 million school students in Germany.

"What unites us is that we have run out of patience with the education system. Many young people are deeply frustrated," he told DW. "The performance of German school students continues to decline, teaching positions are constantly being cut, and in many cases school buildings have seen little or no meaningful investment for years."

Alexander Throm of the CDU has warned against far-left extremist violence Image: Christoph Soeder/dpa/picture alliance

Greens express understanding for the protests

For Gärtner, the discontent reflects a broader problem with parliamentary democracy in Germany and many other Western countries.

"Politicians want to win elections. They focus on the groups that matter most to them electorally rather than on the future and the long-term sustainability of their policies," he said.

"And in our aging societies, older people and the baby boomer generation are the groups that carry the most political weight."

Opposition parties in Germany have also voiced understanding for the concerns of younger people. Speaking to Germany's public broadcaster ZDF, Green Party co-leader Felix Banaszak said: "The intergenerational contract is no longer working. Older generations have driven the climate into a dead end."

He argued that the social welfare system was also reaching its limits and that rents had become unaffordable. According to Banaszak, the only thing the state seems to offer young people are the letters sent to 18-year-olds asking them to consider joining the military. Germany is currently desperate to expand the Bundeswehr and is considering reintroducing national service.

By Tuesday, around 134,000 people had registered on the "Gen Z regelt" website to take part in the protests planned for the coming Saturday. With several days still to go before the demonstrations, that number could rise further.

This article was translated from German.

World.title: Israel election: Netanyahu-led bloc in slight lead with more than 80% of votes counted
World.content:
Skip next section President Herzog says it's imperative 'to avoid another round of elections'

Herzog voted in Jerusalem with his wife early on Tuesday Image: Ronen Zvulun/REUTERS

President Isaac Herzog, who will have a key role in choosing someone to try to put together the next government, has urged all parties to "come with an open mind" when the time for negotiations comes.

"I will receive the official election results next week," Herzog said. "I wil then begin the process of the consultations here, hearing from each and every fraction, asking questions, and holding discussions."

Typically the president chooses the leader of the party with the most votes to try to form a government although he is not required to follow this convention. That nominee then has 42 days to try to set up a working coalition.

"One thing must be clear, and I said this before the elections too," Herzog said. "We must do everything we can, certainly after yesterday, to avoid another round of elections. So I expect everyone who comes here to come with an open mind."

Between April 2019 and November 2022, Israel had five general elections in rather rapid succession amid similar difficulties either forming or maintaining coalition governments.

World.title: Can we regrow damaged seagrass meadows?
World.content:
Seagrass protects coasts, shelters thousands of species and stores CO2. But some 30% of this valuable ecosystem has disappeared since the late 19th century. Can we bring it back?

Half a dozen divers are navigating the cold waters of the Baltic Sea off the coast of Dahme, a small beach town in northern Germany. Keeping the roots intact, conservationists carefully lift shoots from a donor meadow of seagrass and place them in a bag.

They only take a few shoots from each spot, which will be planted where the conservationists hope to regrow another meadow. They've already picked out a prime area for the young plants, which need sandy sediment, shelter from waves and currents and sufficient light and oxygen to thrive.

The scientists see the work as critical. Myriam Spicka, who heads the NGO Seagrass Conservation, says she has "seen the changes" in the more than 30 years she's been diving. And she is not the only one who has witnessed the destruction.

How seagrass is becoming a green building material To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Scientists estimate that around 60% of the Baltic coast's seagrass meadows have disappeared.

"That's the bad news," said marine ecologist Thorsten Reusch from the GEOMAR Helmholtz Center for Ocean Research Kiel . "The good news is that the decline has stopped."

Why should we care about seagrass?

Underwater seagrass meadows feed and shelter fish, crabs, shellfish and many other species. They improve water quality and slow waves, helping protect shores from erosion. And they store carbon in the seabed about 30 to 50 times faster than forests.

Around 70 species of seagrass can be found along the coasts of more than 150 countries. Some grow just below the surface, others at depths of 60 meters or almost 200 feet.

On patrol with Mallorca's 'seagrass police' To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

"Some countries have far more seagrass, particularly in the Indo-Pacific," said Reusch. "There, it can play a major role in their carbon balance."

But the value of seagrass goes beyond carbon storage. Its meadows in the Baltic are among the sea's most valuable habitats. They shelter wildlife, stabilize the seabed and act as natural filters by trapping particles and nutrients.

How can seagrass be replanted on a larger scale?

Planting individual seagrass shoots is painstaking work so people like Reinhard Helbig are trying to make it easier.

Through ZosteraTec, the start-up he co-founded, he helps restore marine habitats, including seagrass meadows damaged by offshore activity, such as wind farm construction. His work begins on the beach.

"Stormy weather helps us. Waves and currents wash seagrass out of the seabed. A day or two later, it washes up here, still fresh," he said.

The pressed strand of seagrass with biodegradable thread makes it easier to plant on longer stretches along the ocean floor Image: DW

The collected shoots are grown and multiplied in ZosteraTec's aquaculture. Several months later, the marine saplings are laid on a plant support. A specially developed machine binds the planted strands with biodegradable thread. The resulting lengths can be laid on the seabed with less diving work.

"We plant here on land to cut down on underwater work. That means fewer dives, and we can do the painstaking work on shore," Helbig said.

Could planting seeds be a solution?

Researchers at the Geomar Helmholtz Center in Kiel are also testing new ways to restore seagrass across larger areas, including using seeds.

Marine ecologist Esther Thomsen reaches into an aquarium tank and pulls out a flowerpot containing seagrass.

"Ten percent of the plants in our meadows produce seeds. You can clearly see the seeds sitting inside the seed pod," she said.

"The big advantage of restoring meadows from seed is greater genetic diversity. And in the future, we should be able to sow seeds over much larger areas," explained Thomsen.

Together with replanted shoots, seeds can help regrow underwater meadows Image: DW

Reusch from Geomar said they currently "think the most promising way to grow meadows that can withstand climate change is to plant individual shoots as a foundation, then sow seeds between them to increase genetic diversity."

It takes time to see results

Whether a planting mission is successful is revealed months or even years later.

Thomsen and her colleagues are visiting the first seagrass meadow planted in Germany's Baltic waters in 2021. The divers count shoots, check how densely they grow and record how the meadow has developed.

They then compare it with the donor meadow that supplied the plants. Only that comparison reveals whether the new crop has merely survived or is beginning to function more like a natural one.

"We've just checked the seagrass meadow, and it's really dense. We counted lots of shoots per square," Thomsen said. "It's looking really good."

This article is based on a Global Us video report.
