World.title: At least 64 people killed in Spain as 2 high-speed trains collide
World.content:
COLLISION. Emergency teams work at the scene of a collision involving two high-speed trains near Urda station in Toledo province, Spain, on October 28, 2026.

'We heard a massive roar, a truly enormous thud that went on for 10 seconds, as if the train were about to derail. Through the right-hand window, we could see a wrecked train,' says a passenger traveling with several colleagues in the rear car of one of the trains

URDA, Spain – Rescue workers in Spain on Wednesday, October 28, were scouring the wreckage for more bodies at the crash scene where at least 64 people were killed when two high-speed trains collided, in the second deadly railway accident in the country this year.

Evacuated passengers streamed along a road near the scene, some splattered with blood or with their wounds bandaged, others wheeling suitcases and being given water by volunteers who said it had been donated from neighboring towns.

Hundreds of ambulances, funeral home vans and helicopters were parked next to a train with several carriages sitting on an elevated section of track while twisted metal, broken panels and wreckage could be seen strewn across an embankment beneath the line where at least three carriages had plunged.

Miguel, a passenger traveling with several colleagues in the rear car of one of the trains, described to COPE radio the moment of the accident.

“We heard a massive roar, a truly enormous thud that went on for 10 seconds, as if the train were about to derail. Through the right-hand window, we could see a wrecked train,” he said.

A person briefed on the disaster said a train operated by private consortium Iryo stopped near Toledo on orders from infrastructure manager ADIF due to a signal fault.

A train operated by Renfe then struck the stationary train at high speed, causing several carriages of both trains to derail, the person said.

Renfe said in a statement that after a being authorized to continue its journey, its train had crashed into the Iryo train that had remained stationary “for reasons we don’t know.”

“The Renfe train continued on its way as instructed, and a collision occurred. The exact sequence of events, the traffic conditions and the circumstances of the impact will have to be established by the investigation,” Renfe said.

There was no immediate response to a Reuters request for comment from Iryo or Adif. – Rappler.com

World.title: Alex Eala advances to Toray Pan Pacific quarterfinals after besting Talia Gibson
World.content:
Eala is now set to face Russian player Diana Shnaider, who previously defeated her in the second round of the Ningbo Open in China

MANILA, Philippines – Alex Eala pulled off a thrilling win over Australia’s Talia Gibson, 4-6, 6-2, 6-0, in the Toray Pan Pacific Open round of 16 match in Tokyo, Japan, on Wednesday, October 28.

Eala had gotten off to a rough start after losing the first set to her World No. 38 opponent, 4-6. It had been smooth sailing in the succeeding sets, 6-2, 6-0, as she was able to contain Gibson by a large margin.

“I think really staying in the match [and] never giving up,” Eala explained in a post-game interview when asked what the key to her victory was.

“The first set was difficult, and I had my chances, so I knew that if I kept my concentration I would have more chances.”

This is not the first time the two players went head-to-head. Eala and Gibson had previously played against each other at the IXXVII Open Generali Ciudad de Palma del Rio round of 16 in June 2023, and then in the ITF W25 Aldershot GB Pro Series round of 16 in August 2023. The Filipina won both matches.

The Filipina tennis star will now face Diana Shnaider of Russia in the quarterfinals on Friday, October 30.

Just before Eala made her Toray Pan Pacific Open debut, she had suffered a second-round exit at the hands of Shnaider at the Ningbo Open in China on October 22. – Rappler.com

World.title: [Mind the Gap] In chaotic US midterm polls, Filams are running
World.content:
Filipinos running across statewide and local races find themselves navigating an American political system increasingly resembling tactics they thought they had left behind

It’s hard not to feel that this November 2026 US midterm elections is a déjà vu of cheating in Philippine elections.

“Dinaya!” is usually the first word a losing candidate shouts in the Philippines: “I got cheated!” President Donald Trump seems to have taken this script to heart, casting a shadow over the forecasted “Blue Wave” that could flip Congress to Democratic control even before the first ballot is counted.

Even if Trump’s unfounded claims of voter fraud are overwhelmed by a huge Democratic turnout, many fear that Republicans in Congress, out of loyalty to Trump, may try to block Democrats from assuming the majority.

Echoing the “doomsday scenario” espoused by US Attorney General Todd Blanche — delaying the count or refusing to certify results if they favor Democrats — Trump has directed the Justice Department to block certification of the coming Senate election in Alaska if Republican incumbent Dan S. Sullivan loses by a narrow margin. The New York Times reported that the justice department cited flimsy concerns about confusion with another candidate whose name is similar to Sullivan’s.

Their efforts to project a narrative of widespread noncitizen voting is also relentless, even using as bogeymen the 11 individuals the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) who were arrested in California on October 16 for allegedly illegally registering to vote. Election experts have raised questions as to whether the charges could be trusted to be accurate, citing similar accusations being disproved elsewhere in the country.

‘Dagdag-Bawas’

Remember when Gloria Macapagal-Arroyo called “Hello, Garci!” to pad her votes during the 2004 presidential election against the late Fernando Poe Jr.? Trump seems to have taken a page from that “Dagdag-Bawas” playbook by questioning voter registrations, challenging mail-in ballots and raising the possibility of hacking voting machines.

“My thought was they could keep it in their back pocket to invalidate any election results they don’t like,” a former Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) official told ProPublica, which reported that DHS has asked CISA to “secretly acquire a voting machine and hack it.”

With early voting underway, shaving off Democrat votes is in play, with software glitches delaying nearly 600,000 voter registrations in Texas. In Nashville, Tennessee, Dolly Parton’s sister, singer Stella Parton, claimed she had to correct her ballot multiple times, saying a voting machine repeatedly selected Republican gubernatorial candidate Marsha Blackburn when she tried to vote for Democrat Jerri Green.

Guns, goons, gold

While a seasoned “trapo” in the Philippines rolls a ₱1,000 note in a folded T-shirt to buy votes, Trump is dangling $5,000 to voters and billions in federal aid to farmers affected by tariffs if Republicans keep control of Congress.

While hired armed goons in the Philippines steal ballot boxes, Trump has threatened to send heavily-armed ICE agents and National Guard troops to polling places, raising fears of intimidation among immigrant and minority voters. Though we are hopefully far from the impunity of an “Ampatuan massacre,” the shocking, pre-dawn DHS raid on Representative Ilhan Omar’s home three weeks before election day smacks of the same tactic in eliminating his political enemies.

Amid this chaos, Filipino candidates running across statewide and local races find themselves navigating an American political system increasingly resembling tactics they thought they had left behind.

This year’s crop includes California Attorney General Rob Bonta, seeking reelection; Assemblymember Jessica Caloza, fighting to retain her 52nd District seat; and Cerritos City Councilmember Mark Pulido, campaigning for the 67th Assembly District in the California state legislature.

In Daly City, Councilmember Rod Daus-Magbual is running for reelection, joined by Tony Bayudan in what is often celebrated as the “Pinoy Capital” of the United States, where Filipinos make up a full third of the population. In Southern California, Artesia Councilmember Melissa Ramoso is defending her seat while Los Angeles City Controller Kenneth Mejia seeks a second term.

The Filipino political footprint extends beyond California.

In Nevada, Assemblymember Erica Mosca is seeking reelection. In New York, Assemblymember Steven Raga is running for State Senate in Queens, while Georgia State Representative Marvin Lim is running unopposed.

Across the Pacific, Hawaii — the first state to elect a Filipino governor in US history with the landmark 1994 election of Benjamin Cayetano — has its own growing crop of FilAm candidates. State Senator Joy A. San Buenaventura is seeking reelection in Puna, joined by State House candidates including Tess Abalos, Travis Bumanglag, Danny Degracia, Diamond Garcia, Greggor Ilagan, Darius K. Kila, Rose Martinez and Julie Reyes Oda.

At the county level, Tyler Dos Santos-Tam is seeking another term on the Honolulu City Council, while Kauanoe Batangan and Addison Bulosan are running for county council seats on Maui and Kauai.

It’s time for us to walk precincts, man phone banks and donate to our kababayan running for office.

We immigrated to the United States to escape the feudal dynasties, vote-buying and the “Guns, Goons and Gold” of traditional Philippine politics. Now it’s time to push back and make sure those tactics don’t follow us here.

So, don’t forget to vote. If voting in person, carefully review your selections before submitting your ballot to make sure the machine properly records your choice.

If voting by mail, don’t wait until November 3 to mail your ballots to prevent the understaffed US Postal Service from throwing them away if they don’t get picked up on Election Day.

In one of the most consequential elections in modern history, our mission this November is not only in supporting our kababayan to win — it is a front-line battle to make sure our votes are counted, and defend them if need be. – Rappler.com



Oscar Quiambao is a former reporter for The Philippine Daily Inquirer who now lives in San Francisco.

World.title: What’s hindering us from progress in our power generation, transmission, and distribution segments?
World.content:
Editor’s note: This content is sponsored by AboitizPower and was handled by BrandRap, the sales and marketing arm of Rappler. No member of the news and editorial team participated in the publishing of this piece.

With high electricity prices, vulnerable infrastructure, and critical supply, it can be difficult for Filipinos to have an optimistic outlook not only for our energy industry’s future, but also even just for the present. Did you know that in the Visayas alone, there have been nearly 130 yellow and red alerts since January 2026?

“Nagkakaroon tayo ng red and yellow alerts. Maraming kadahilahan. Maaaring kinapos ang supply, may mga planta na nasira, o kaya naman ay may mga planta na nasa construction nga pero na-delay din ang pasok,” said Atty. Francis Saturnino “Nino” Juan, chairperson and CEO of the Energy Regulatory Commission (ERC).

(We have red and yellow alerts. There are many reasons behind this. It may be from a lack of supply, broken power plants, or probably power plants that are under construction but got delayed in deployment.)

Juan said this in the panel discussion “Energy for Progress: Strengthening the Vital Links of our Energy System”, where he was joined by Energy Secretary Sharon Garin and Prof. Rowaldo “Wali” Del Mundo, who is the associate dean of the College of Engineering in the University of the Philippines (UP) and the UP System’s vice president for development.

Moderating them was Ruth Yu-Owen, the energy committee chairperson of the ECCP (European Chamber of Commerce).

“Energy for Progress” is part of Rappler’s “Powering Up” roundtable discussion, done in partnership with Aboitiz Power Corporation and the ECCP.

Critical monitoring

There is a perfect fuel mix fit for the Philippines, according to Energy Secretary Garin, but notes that it is an “evolving formula” that contains a mix of renewable energy, as well as baseload (steady and more affordable, like coal) and mid-merit sources that can fill up the gaps left by variable and intermittent supply.

“The technologies change faster than our policies, so we keep catching up. And now what we’ve done is do a super simulation to have some projections, get a super computer with super people from DOE and the rest of the industry so we can calculate what to expect in the next 10 years,” quipped Garin.

There’s also a need to create new regulations and even revisit the Philippine Grid Code, Juan added, on account of new technologies coming into the grid.

“Nakapaloob kasi din diyan ’yung [energy] reserve requirements natin, so tinitingnan kung ano na ba ’yung sufficient na reserve. Anong klase na ’yung reserve na dapat papasok? So ito ang mga sinosolusyunan natin ngayon.”

(It also houses our [energy] reserve requirements, so we get to check what kind of reserve is sufficient. What kind of reserve should we integrate? So these are the things we are trying to solve right now.)

Meanwhile, Del Mundo stressed the need to catch up on project delays, especially as demand for electricity continues to grow. It can be recalled that the Department of Energy has been calling out projects that failed to meet their development commitments.

“Electricity supply interruptions send ripple effects to other sectors of the economy, and this ultimately leads to economic losses,” the Philippine Institute for Development Studies said.

Making energy affordable

In terms of alleviating the cost of power, Del Mundo also emphasized the importance of strategic procurement on the part of distribution utilities for both the short-term and the long-term, with the latter serving as more of a signal for power producers to build more future capacity.

But even then, Del Mundo observed that there were long-term contracts that didn’t result in new capacity.

Instead, these were crafted for existing power plants, making it uncertain that there is available capacity in the long run. Del Mundo said that there’s too much dependence on the existing power plants, suggesting the need for more alignment when it comes to procurement in the distribution sector.

Empowering the innovative Filipino spirit

During the first episode, Garin also highlighted Filipino innovation as a big anchor in building more energy capacity – like through agrivoltaics, or growing vegetables under solar panels, to balance out the demand of both for arable land.

Some forms of makeshift solutions have also come out of the Philippines being a climate-vulnerable nation, like what Garin recalled during her visit to a location that experiences floods: The people raised the pole mount of the solar panels.

The Philippines itself, as an archipelago, invites the need for innovation and exploration.

“Because of this, very expensive [and weak] ang ating transmission[…] So kung ang ating power generation ay magiging embedded, ibig sabihin, distributed… Bawat island, may adequate supply[…] so yung ating interconnection ay hindi natin kailangan problemahin na, “Kailan natin i-u-pgrade [o] lalakihan?” Ibig sabihin, importanteng ma-interconnect natin para ma-hold lahat nung mga island together para sa stable na operation,” Del Mundo said.

(Because of this, our transmission is very expensive and weak. So if our power generation will be embedded, meaning distributed… Each island, there’s an adequate supply, so we don’t need to stress about our interconnection in terms of, “When do we need to upgrade or expand?” This means it’s important to interconnect so the islands will be held together for a stable operation.)

Improving and modernizing electric cooperatives

Electric cooperatives should also be improved in terms of their capacity-building and infrastructure, Garin said.

The far-flung areas served by these cooperatives shouldn’t be forgotten, the panel maintained, with Juan adding that the consumers’ best interest should always come first.

For Del Mundo, an option could be combining multiple electric cooperatives into just one entity per region to produce scale and, ideally, improve overall performance and power rates.

World.title: Dela Rosa again presses SC to reverse ruling on ICC arrest warrant
World.content:
Dela Rosa’s camp says the 'armed and dangerous' tag and P50-million bounty for his arrest place his right to life in 'present and serious danger'

MANILA, Philippines – Senator Ronald “Bato” dela Rosa has again pressed the Supreme Court to reverse its earlier ruling and stop the use of an International Criminal Court arrest warrant against him.

In a manifestation on Tuesday, October 27, Israelito Torreon, dela Rosa’s lawyer, asked the SC to urgently rule on a pending motion for reconsideration they filed in June, seeking to reverse a May court decision that denied their plea for a temporary restraining order or a status quo ante order to stop the implementation of the ICC arrest warrant.

A status quo ante order simply means a rewind or the court wants things returned to how they were before a disputed action happened, while it decides the case.

Dela Rosa’s lawyer argued that the enforcement posture surrounding the senator had “escalated” while the motion remained unresolved. It cited supervening events, including the Department of the Interior and Local Government’s (DILG) declaration of the senator as “armed and dangerous” and the P50-million bounty offered for his arrest.

“Taken together, these are not stray remarks of individual officials. They constitute an announced executive enforcement program: an official ‘armed and dangerous’ designation, a ₱50-million capture bounty from public funds, a dedicated task force, Special Action Force deployment, and express presidential support, all directed at the arrest of a sitting senator of the Republic for surrender to a foreign tribunal, while the legality of that very act is pending before this Honorable Court,” the manifestation reads.

Voting 9-5-1, the SC previously denied Dela Rosa’s request for a TRO, saying he had “no clear and unmistakable right to be protected.”

The tribunal also noted that the Senate had provided the lawmaker with protective custody, preventing his arrest and the implementation of the ICC warrant.

“Hence, Senator Dela Rosa’s claimed invasion of his purported rights is more imagined than real,” the SC said.

Dela Rosa’s camp said the recent pronouncements from the executive branch placed the senator’s right to life in “present and serious danger.”

“No court has found Petitioner Dela Rosa to be armed and dangerous. In law enforcement practice, the designation signals to operating units that armed resistance should be anticipated, which is precisely the setting in which lethal force is most likely to be used,” it said.

“Coupled with a bounty and a declaration abandoning restraint, the designation places Petitioner dela Rosa’s right to life under Article III, Section 1 of the Constitution in present and serious danger,” the lawyer added.

ICC drug war case

The ICC Pre-Trial Chamber I issued a warrant against Dela Rosa in November last year due to his role in former president Rodrigo Duterte’s drug war.

He was Duterte’s first police chief who implemented the bloody anti-drug campaign which human rights organizations said took the lives of nearly 30,000 people.

The ICC named him a co-perpetrator in the case. It added that those involved “controlled a structure of power” which enabled them to “direct and control the actions” of those who carried out drug war killings.

In November, the ICC warrant was still sealed. It was only made public on May 11, after Dela Rosa, following months of absence in the Senate, showed up to back Senator Alan Peter Cayetano’s election as Senate president. For three days, Dela Rosa sought refuge inside the Senate building until a shooting chaos, which was allegedly triggered by his mistah, Senate sergeant-at-arms Mao Aplasca, ensued on the night of May 13. Hours later, Dela Rosa escaped from the Senate at around 2:30 am. He was accompanied by his political ally, Senator Robin Padilla.

Dela Rosa has since stayed out of public view. – with reports from Jairo Bolledo/Rappler.com

World.title: FACT CHECK: Castro spoke about Rodrigo Duterte, not Marcos, in spliced drug-use clip
World.content:
The original clip is from a September 11 briefing in which Castro cited former president Duterte's admissions of drug use. The viral clip was edited to replace Duterte's name with Marcos'.

Claim: Palace Press Officer Claire Castro said President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. admitted to using marijuana and abusing fentanyl because it felt like “cloud nine.”

Rating: ALTERED

Why we fact-checked this: A Facebook post by “Wilfredo Villacastel Orencejr,” published on October 24, carries the claim. Its caption reads, “Ay naku, Ante Claire binubuking mo na yung boss mo, Ante.”

(Oh, Auntie Claire, you’re exposing your boss, auntie.)

The video shows Castro speaking in a supposed interview, with a breaking news label overlaid on top. In the clip, Castro says, “Inamin mismo ni Pangulong Marcos Jr. na siya’y gumagamit ng marijuana, at inamin niya rin na ang paggamit niya ng fentanyl ay inabuso niya dahil masarap daw ang pakiramdam, cloud nine.”

(President Marcos Jr. himself admitted that he uses marijuana, and he also admitted that he abused fentanyl because it supposedly felt good, cloud nine.)

As of writing, the video has garnered over 709,000 views, 11,000 reactions, 1,300 comments, and 5,600 shares.

The facts: Castro did not say Marcos used marijuana or abused fentanyl. The viral clip altered what she said during September 11 press briefing in New Delhi, where she was referring to former president Rodrigo Duterte.

In the genuine clip, Castro was asked to respond to Vice President Sara Duterte’s accusation that Marcos was an “addict.” She said: “Inamin mismo ni dating Pangulong Duterte, pangulo na siya, na siya’y gumagamit ng marijuana. At inamin niya rin na ang paggamit niya ng fentanyl ay inabuso niya dahil masarap daw ‘yung pakiramdam, ‘cloud nine’ ang feeling.”

(Former president Duterte himself admitted, while already in office, that he used marijuana. He also admitted to abusing fentanyl because he enjoyed the feeling, describing it as being on “cloud nine.”)

The viral clip replaces Duterte’s name with “Pangulong Marcos Jr.” (President Marcos Jr.) and omits the phrase “pangulo na siya” (when he was already president).

GMA News reported Castro’s original remarks, which match the Presidential Communications Office transcript and RTVM livestream on September 11.

No credible report shows Marcos admitting to using marijuana or abusing fentanyl.

Duterte’s original remarks: Duterte acknowledged using fentanyl in December 2016, saying he took it for a spinal injury from motorcycle accidents but had exceeded the prescribed dose. He denied being addicted, saying he used it only when prescribed.

In a 2017 Davao City speech, he recalled using an entire fentanyl patch instead of cutting it into four pieces, saying it made him feel “on cloud nine,” the phrase Castro later repeated. He later told critics he had made up the fentanyl story.

In 2018, Duterte said he used marijuana to stay awake during official functions, later calling the remark a joke. Both statements were made while he was president, as Castro said.

Drug-use feud: Castro’s press briefing was a response to the Vice President’s accusation that Marcos was an “addict.” Duterte made the statement at her September 11 arraignment in Quezon City.

The accusation against Marcos is not new. Senator Imee Marcos made a similar claim at a rally in November 2025, which Malacañang rejected, citing a negative drug test.

Rappler also published a fact-check of a similar manipulated clip falsely attributing the remarks to Marcos, along with several other fact-checks debunking his alleged drug use:

– Cyril Bocar/Rappler.com

Efren Cyril Bocar is a journalist from Llorente, Eastern Samar who graduated with a degree in English Language Studies at the Visayas State University. Cyril is also a graduate of the Aries Rufo Journalism Fellowship of Rappler for 2024.

Keep us aware of suspicious Facebook pages, groups, accounts, websites, articles, or photos in your network by contacting us at factcheck@rappler.com. Let us battle disinformation one Fact Check at a time.

World.title: Goodbye, SPNEC: MVP rebrands Leviste’s solar firm, lines up P5-B deal
World.content:
A new name, five more solar businesses, and a possible "re-IPO," but Meralco's makeover can't quite banish Leviste's past or the P10.34-billion headache that comes with it

Manuel V. Pangilinan is giving Leandro Leviste’s old solar crown jewel quite the makeover. First, shed the SPNEC name. Next, bring in nearly P5 billion worth of other renewable energy businesses.

And perhaps, pitch the shiny new thing to stock market investors all over again.

SP New Energy Corporation (SPNEC) is now officially MGEN Renewables Inc., (MGENR) after securing Securities and Exchange Commission approval on Monday, October 26; its stock ticker is also set to change to MGENR.

Officially, the renaming is part of the Meralco group’s broader rebranding strategy. Conveniently, it also removes a reminder of Solar Philippines, the controversial empire Leviste built before Pangilinan’s group took control.

And there’s quite a history behind SPNEC.

FROM SPNEC to MGENR. This Rappler diagram shows the ownership of the rebranded solar company as of September 1, 2026 and before the proposed share swap. Diagram by Raphael Reyes/Rappler.

Leviste made his fortune assembling landholdings and securing solar development rights that attracted deep-pocketed investors, including Pangilinan himself. Industry sources that Rappler spoke with describe the young billionaire as a talented “flipper.”

But getting the rights to build solar farms and actually getting them built are two different businesses.

The Department of Energy (DOE) terminated 33 contracts tied to Leviste’s wider Solar Philippines group, covering around 11,400 megawatts of proposed capacity, and sought around P24 billion in financial obligations. His camp disputes the claims.

While much of the P24-billion mess relates to Leviste’s other companies, SPNEC is dragged into this too.

In a December 23, 2025 letter seen by Rappler, Energy Secretary Sharon Garin terminated the service contract for SPNEC’s 280-megawatt Santa Rosa Nueva Ecija 2 project and demanded P10.34 billion.

The DOE cited missed work-program commitments, an unrenewed performance bond, and missing documents, including a feasibility study and proof of land rights. Most of the demand came from P12.38 billion in work-program commitments, less P2.04 billion credited for reported accomplishments.

MGEN insists SPNEC is legally separate from Solar Philippines and not liable for the wider group’s P24 billion obligation. But it acknowledges that Santa Rosa belongs to SPNEC and says that it invoked force majeure over transmission delays and sought reconsideration.

Separately, Leviste and his mother, Senator Loren Legarda, face graft and plunder complaints involving solar contracts awarded to Leviste-linked companies. Both deny wrongdoing.

Leviste himself has kept his distance from his now Meralco-controlled company, resigning from the board in January and cashing out P3-billion worth of shares, leaving his holding company with an 11.51% stake.

New name, new MGENR

So, what’s next for MGENR?

On Tuesday, October 27, MGEN Renewables’ board approved a proposed P4.98-billion deal to take in stakes in five solar businesses from its controlling shareholder, MGEN Renewable Energy Inc., another Meralco subsidiary.

The companies have interests in operating solar plants across Luzon:

Greenergy for Global Inc. – 52.7-megawatt solar plant in Isabela

Greentech Solar Energy Inc. – 19.8-megawatt solar plant in Nueva Ecija

CACI Power Corporation – Linked to an 80.1-megawatt solar plant in Rizal

Nuevo Solar Energy Corporation – 68.7-megawatt solar plant in Ilocos Norte

PowerSource First Bulacan Solar Inc. – 55-megawatt solar plant in Bulacan

Instead of paying cash, MGEN Renewables will issue around 3.1 billion new shares to its controlling shareholder. If completed, the share swap deal would strengthen Meralco’s control while further diluting Leviste and other investors.

Then comes the more intriguing possibility, a “re-IPO” targeted for March 2027.

Since Leviste already took SPNEC public in 2021, this would be another share offering in the now bigger company under Meralco’s control, rather than a second listing. Nothing has been finalized.

This time, there’s more to show investors. Its P200-billion MTerra Solar project began commercial operations in August, while MGEN Renewables forecasts P774 million in profit for 2026, reversing a P4.1-billion loss in 2025.

The group also plans to invest up to another P7.815 billion in Terra Solar, subject to lender and investor approvals. – Rappler.com

World.title: #CourageON: Highlights from #MoveCebu 2026
World.content:
Rappler’s civic engagement arm MovePH brings #MoveCebu to the University of San Carlos, gathering over 200 people during the public forum to define what a liveable city should be

Last week, Rappler’s civic engagement arm MovePH brought #MoveCebu to the University of San Carlos, gathering over 200 people during a public forum to define what a liveable city should be.

To solidify our long-term commitment to campus journalism and civic engagement, we proudly signed memoranda of understanding with the University of San Carlos, and the University of the Philippines Cebu.

Rappler multimedia reporter John Sitchon, who reports on Cebu and the Visayas region, joined us as we worked directly with participants. You can check out these stories to read more about what happened during the roadshow:

Taking advantage of the momentum generated by the forum, we dove into focused workshops with 35 newly-trained Movers, and leaders from Cebu’s civil society groups to bridge reporting with civic organizing.

Our Movers who chose the civic mobilization track pitched bold, ground-level initiatives tackling community realities across Cebu province.

For example, participants designed action plans to address food safety at the Colon Night Market. Some Movers want to address the lack of housing for displaced families in Minglanilla. One Mover hoped to champion the rights of people with dwarfism.

Meanwhile, Movers who wanted to specialize in community journalism pitched stories tackling gut issues in Cebu, like substandard flood control projects, child labor, and how neighborhood carinderias navigate inflation to keep meals affordable.

Our civil society and academe partners matched this energy during our Partners’ Huddle, where they decided to prioritize four crisis clusters: Ecological, Governance, Services, and Displacement. Together, partners committed to lobbying local councils to prioritize environmental policy over profit, conducting citizen audits, raising awareness of and tackling the energy crisis plaguing Cebu, and fighting for humane relocation sites and protected municipal waters for fishing communities.

Movers and partners are already coordinating on next steps in the Padayon Cebu chat room on the Muni app. To be part of the action, you can join the chat room by downloading the Rappler app for free. If you would like to support Rappler’s Cebu coverage, we hope you consider becoming a Rappler+ member. Rappler+ is our premium membership program that allows you to experience the best of our journalism, while supporting our work. You can join Rappler+ here. – Rappler.com

World.title: China’s Monroe Doctrine and Its Strategic Blunder in Myanmar
World.content:
The United States has its Monroe Doctrine, which asserts American preeminence in the Western Hemisphere, placing Latin America within its sphere of influence. Over the past three decades, China’s rapid economic growth and military expansion have transformed it from a regional power into a global superpower. It is therefore unsurprising that Beijing would seek to establish a similar sphere of influence over neighboring Southeast Asian countries.

Myanmar holds particular strategic importance for China. Through Rakhine State, Beijing can access the Indian Ocean, bypassing the strategically vulnerable Strait of Malacca during a crisis. Myanmar also possesses substantial deposits of rare earth elements essential to modern technologies. Furthermore, the China-Myanmar Economic Corridor (CMEC) is one of the six major economic corridors under China’s Belt and Road Initiative (BRI).

Yet in pursuing these geopolitical objectives, China appears to be missing the forest for the trees. Its decision to prop up Myanmar’s military junta at the expense of democratic forces represents a serious strategic miscalculation—a bet on the wrong horse. Following a widely discredited sham election, the junta has attempted to rebrand itself as a civilian government under former junta chief Min Aung Hlaing, with a ruling party dominated by military officers and loyalists. Such a regime is ill-equipped to deliver what China needs: a stable, secure and predictable neighbor capable of supporting its long-term economic ambitions through the BRI and its broader maritime strategy.

The culprit behind an unstable neighbor

Since the 2021 military coup, Myanmar has become increasingly unstable, while ethnic resistance organizations (EROs) have expanded their territorial control. Ironically, many resources and infrastructure projects China hopes to develop now lie in territories controlled by EROs and People’s Defense Forces (PDFs). Rare earth deposits are concentrated in Kachin State, where the Kachin Independence Organization (KIO) exercises substantial control. The Chinese-backed Kyaukphyu deep-sea port, a strategic gateway to the Indian Ocean, lies in Rakhine State, where the Arakan Army (AA) has established extensive territorial control. Significant stretches of the China-Myanmar gas pipeline also pass through areas where resistance forces operate in Magway and Mandalay regions.

So far, PDFs and EROs have shown considerable restraint in refraining from attacking these strategic assets. This reflects, in part, their desire to earn Beijing’s goodwill and demonstrate their ability to safeguard Chinese investments.

An unreliable partner turning to criminality

Myanmar’s economy has deteriorated sharply under the weight of military expenditure, corruption, nepotism and mismanagement. The junta is in no position to fulfill its commitments under numerous bilateral economic agreements with China, particularly because it cannot guarantee security in project areas. Worse, the regime has allowed scam centers to proliferate, with some military officers reportedly maintaining close ties to the warlords operating them. Many centers, particularly in northern Shan State, have targeted Chinese citizens. Despite repeated requests from Beijing, the military failed to take effective action.

Operation 1027, launched by an alliance of ethnic armed organizations, proceeded with Beijing’s tacit approval after the Myanmar National Democratic Alliance Army (MNDAA) framed it partly as a campaign against scam operations. Among those subsequently handed over to China was Bai Suocheng, a former lawmaker from the military-backed Union Solidarity and Development Party.

Beyond its inability to provide stability and security, Min Aung Hlaing’s regime is hardly a trustworthy ally. He has repeatedly sought to balance competing powers against one another and could readily turn against China if doing so served his interests. His efforts to court Western goodwill were evident in a recent TIME magazine interview, a low-profile U.S. delegation visit to Naypyitaw in September and the expensive hiring of Washington-based lobbying firms to advocate on its behalf.

Previously, Min Aung Hlaing courted Russia to counterbalance China’s influence, only to turn back toward Beijing when Moscow could not meet his needs. Beijing should think twice before entrusting its long-term strategic interests to a regime whose loyalty is conditional and whose survival is increasingly uncertain.

Why the opposition is a more reliable partner

Many EROs have concluded that genuine autonomy, security, and prosperity are unattainable under military-dominated rule. They increasingly see their future in a federal democratic union. For decades, these organizations understood that none could defeat the military alone. They also recognize that their battlefield successes since 2021 would have been far more difficult without the nationwide Spring Revolution, which fundamentally transformed the country’s political landscape.

This convergence of ethnic resistance and the broader pro-democracy movement has created an unprecedented opportunity. In March 2026, the movement took a significant step forward with the formation of the Steering Council for the Emergence of a Federal Democratic Union (SCEF). It brings together influential resistance actors, including the KIO, KNU, CNF, Karenni National Progressive Party (KNPP), Committee Representing Pyidaungsu Hluttaw (CRPH), and National Unity Government (NUG). A few months later, the federal units of Sagaing, Mandalay, and Magway joined the initiative.

The SCEF combines political leadership and military coordination within a common framework. It seeks not merely to defeat the junta but also to lay the institutional foundations for a future federal state. For China, this emerging coalition offers an alternative to continued dependence on a weakening military regime.

The assumption that China cannot tolerate a flourishing democracy in its neighborhood oversimplifies Beijing’s strategic interests and Southeast Asia’s political realities. China already maintains important economic and diplomatic relationships with democracies such as Japan, South Korea and India. Myanmar is comparatively small, and any government emerging from the current conflict will have compelling geographic and economic reasons to maintain constructive relations with its powerful neighbor. A federal democratic Myanmar has no inherent reason to be antagonistic toward Beijing.

Myanmar’s democratic forces are also learning that the West is unlikely to sustain its strategic attention. The Trump administration included Myanmar among the countries subject to a full travel ban, while its dismantling of USAID disrupted American assistance. Washington’s reported attempts to reengage clandestinely with the junta have further frustrated the democratic movement.

In contrast, the NUG has adopted a pragmatic approach toward Beijing. Its 10-point Position on China, released on January 1, 2024, explicitly commits to safeguarding Chinese investments and cooperating with China against online scams and human trafficking. Democratic forces thus recognize the importance of maintaining a workable relationship with their powerful neighbor.

A strategic opening for Beijing

China’s ambition to achieve national rejuvenation and modernization by the centenary of the People’s Republic of China in 2049 requires long-term strategic thinking rather than short-term political expediency.

By recalibrating its Myanmar policy, Beijing has a rare opportunity to earn the goodwill of the Myanmar people at a pivotal moment. Supporting a political settlement that recognizes the aspirations of ethnic nationalities and democratic forces would not undermine China’s interests. On the contrary, it could help establish the stability, security, and predictability Beijing has long sought.

China should therefore engage constructively with the SCEF and other credible democratic stakeholders rather than continue to prop up a failing junta. Such engagement could protect Chinese investments, improve regional stability and strengthen Beijing’s international standing.

The underlying principle of a Chinese Monroe Doctrine—a regional sphere of influence shaped by strategic interests—is understandable as a geopolitical ambition. But achieving that ambition requires choosing partners wisely. If China wants to secure its long-term interests in Myanmar, supporting the forces capable of building a stable federal democratic union would be a far more prudent investment than backing a military regime marked by declining territorial control, economic mismanagement and uncertain loyalty.

Than N. Oo is a co-founder of advocacy group Free Myanmar and writes frequently about Myanmar’s political developments.

World.title: Nationalist Regime Supporters Turn Against China Over Northern Shan
World.content:
Staunchly nationalist supporters of the Myanmar military are growing wary of the regime’s increasing dependency on China on all fronts, voicing rare criticism of the way Chinese money and influence are being allowed to shape their country.

It was the question of northern Shan State that finally galvanized this resentment among the pro-military crowd.

Many nationalists believe that China enabled Operation 1027, the offensive by an alliance of three ethnic armed groups that dealt a serious blow to the Myanmar military in 2023-24. They staged protests at the time accusing Beijing of interference, and the sentiment has recently resurfaced over what they see as the “Sinicization” of borderlands that the regime has lost in northern Shan.

“We accept them making investment in our country. But supplying arms and funds to ethnic armed groups to capture towns and interfering in our government is unacceptable,” a nationalist told The Irrawaddy. “Public opinion must be voiced openly.”

The renewed criticism comes after the Shan State Joint Action Committee (SSJAC)—an ethnic coalition comprising the Shan State Progress Party/Shan State Army (SSPP/SSA), the Shan Nationalities League for Democracy (SNLD), and a Shan militia group—issued a statement on Oct. 23 accusing Kokang’s Myanmar National Democratic Alliance Army (MNDAA) of imposing Chinese language in schools, granting land rights to foreigners, and erasing local traditions in territories it seized during Operation 1027. The MNDAA swiftly rejected the allegations as unfounded.

Earlier this month, Shan civil society organizations released an open letter warning that the MNDAA’s cultural and administrative practices threaten ethnic coexistence and the stability of the China–Myanmar border.

Ta’ang civil society groups similarly condemned the MNDAA in April after it seized Kutkai Township, where ethnic Ta’ang communities form the majority.

At the peak of Operation 1027, China pressured armed groups to agree ceasefires with the regime in northern Shan, but since then has allowed them to consolidate their quasi-autonomous administrations there rather than handing back all the territory they had gained to the regime.

No other armed group has been able to consolidate administrative control as rapidly as the MNDAA, which analysts say would be impossible without Beijing’s backing.

Regime supporters were initially silent about this perceived Sinicization, but started to voice concerns when exiled independent media widely covered Chinese border encroachment in northern Shan areas controlled by the MNDAA. The regime warned domestic outlets not to publish stories that could damage bilateral ties, but the concerns persisted.

The pot seems to have boiled over when Chinese Special Envoy Deng Xijun in mid-October recommended “high-level autonomy” for ethnic monitories. His remark was interpreted in different ways across Myanmar’s political circles, stirring debate over China’s intentions.

Along Myanmar’s eastern frontier, three armed groups are widely regarded as being under heavy Chinese influence, the others being the United Wa State Army (UWSA) and the National Democratic Alliance Army (NDAA). The latter two have upheld ceasefires with the Myanmar military for nearly four decades, and in return they exercise de-facto autonomy in their fiefdoms, serving as effective buffers that insulate China from Myanmar’s instability.

Under the 2008 Constitution, the MNDAA’s Kokang—with a population of fewer than 200,000—is a self‑administered zone, but that covers only Laukkai and Kongyan townships east of the Salween River. But after Operation 1027, the MNDAA reorganized both that original enclave and newly captured areas into four districts: Laukkai, Kutkai, Hsenwi, and Monekoe. Governance in these territories increasingly mirrors administrative practices seen in Beijing, raising alarm not only among staunch nationalists but also among some lawmakers.

“We don’t like it when a powerful neighbor interferes in our sovereignty,” one MP remarked. But he admitted, “The Myanmar government is not in a position to shut out China. We don’t have that strength, and we are deteriorating in every aspect.”

Democracy activists, for their part, accuse Beijing of propping up the military since the coup, reaping political and economic benefits. The exiled leader of the Democratic Party for a New Society, Hnin Hnin Hmwe, said the regime itself is starting to worry about its over-reliance on China.

“China has pushed its interests so far that even the regime is beginning to feel constrained,” she said. “At the same time, China maintains ties with revolutionary forces. China is shrewd to keep the balance.”

World.title: Resistance Forces Inflict Heavy Losses on Regime Troops in Indaw
World.content:
A Myanmar junta offensive to reclaim territory in Sagaing Region’s Indaw Township near the Kachin State border has suffered heavy losses in resistance ambushes, resistance sources said.

Dozens of junta troops were killed and many, including a tactical commander, were reportedly captured by pro-democracy forces.

Troops from two regime Tactical Commands advancing south from Indaw town toward Wuntho and Tigyaing were ambushed by resistance forces on October 4. According to reports, the regime units buried the bodies of dead soldiers in local villages, and one Tactical Command lost contact with its base.

The regime retook control of Indaw town and the Mandalay-Myitkyina road from resistance forces at the end of April. However, it is still conducting clearance operations in the area.

On October 4, roughly 700 troops from Indaw, led by Colonel Kyaw Win Tun, deputy commander of the 33rd Light Infantry Division (LID), advanced south and split into two Tactical Commands: Tactical Command 331, led by Col. Myo Thein, and Tactical Command 332, led by Col. Kyaw San Win.

Both were ambushed by resistance forces, sparking fierce clashes and prompting the regime to bomb the area from the air, Indaw Revolution (IR), a local news information page, reported on Monday.

IR reported that locals found the bodies of 50 regime soldiers near Nanthe Village and cremated them on October 23. Other soldiers’ bodies were spotted near villages on the Indaw-Tigyaing road, it said.

“Eyewitnesses reported over 50 dead bodies. More than 20 [regime soldiers] surrendered, and it is initially understood that a tactical commander was among them,” a source close to the resistance forces told The Irrawaddy.

Intense clashes were reported between regime troops and resistance groups—including the civilian National Unity Government’s People’s Defense Force (PDF), the Kachin Independence Army, the All Burma Students’ Democratic Front and allied groups—on October 25 and 26.

Zin Yaw, a military defector and military analyst, told The Irrawaddy that both Tactical Commands had suffered heavy losses.

“Tactical Command 332 led by Col. Kyaw San Win lost communication with the base for 48 hours,” Zin Yaw said.

The troops led by Col. Kyaw San Win advanced along the Indaw-Tigyaing road and ended up near Ma Au Kone Village, which is 23 km south of Indaw town.

According to the reports, some regime soldiers were captured by or voluntarily surrendered to resistance forces.

However, The Irrawaddy couldn’t independently verify the situation, and there has been no official statement from resistance forces or the regime yet.

Madaya Myohman force, which is under the command of the Mandalay PDF and is believed to have taken part in the ambushes, stated that the regime’s 33rd LID faced heavy losses on Monday.

The clashes and bombing in the area forced residents of at least 35 villages in Indaw and Wuntho townships to flee their homes, according to a source close to the resistance.

World.title: Myanmar Migrant Applications Plunge at Thai CI Centers Amid Boycott
World.content:
The number of Myanmar migrant workers applying for Certificates of Identity (CI) in Thailand has dropped sharply in the past few days following the launch of a social media campaign against the CI process, according to migrant groups and agents.

The Myanmar regime opened five Thai hubs on October 14, offering migrant workers CI required for residency and work. In exchange, workers must comply with a new Labor Ministry mandate to remit 25 percent of their wages through official channels and pay 2 percent annual tax.

The number of registered Myanmar workers in Thailand rose to nearly 3 million as of November 2025, but a significant population remains undocumented.

Many migrants say that as low-wage workers they can barely afford CI application fees, while the regime’s mandatory 6,000-baht remittance rule adds an extra layer of cost.

Labor activists say the boycott is also being driven by reluctance to legitimize the regime or help fund its ongoing military attacks on civilians.

Migrants launched the online campaign on Oct. 18, calling on the Thai government to grant them residency-work permits without CI documents.

Regime Labour Minister Maung Myint slammed the campaign on Oct. 20, insisting the new process was meant to ease CI registration for workers in Thailand. He claimed that around 1,500 workers had used the new centres in the first few days. However, migrant workers groups and agents said applications have plunged as the campaign gains momentum.

“Very few workers are applying for the CI,” Khaing Gyi of the Aid Alliance Committee, which assists migrants, told The Irrawaddy on Tuesday.

“Normally, the CI centre in Samut Sakhon alone receives over 1,000 CI applications daily,” he said, adding that the hub has gone quiet in the past few days.

He estimated that at least 500,000 workers are due to apply for their CI, but few are showing up at centers.

Labor activists said workers were also delaying CI renewal because of the cost.

“Migrants’ income levels vary,” Naing Aung Aung of the Arkan Worker Organization in Thailand told The Irrawaddy. “Some took loans to pay for passport and visa issuance. They don’t have extra savings.”

He said the regime’s remittance scheme is unviable given it can easily be bypassed by bribing corrupt officials. Applicants can secure a CI without evidence of remittance for a fee of 1,500 baht, according to labor activists and agents.

Experts note the new policy benefits the cash-strapped regime while piling financial burdens on low-paid workers and cutting remittance lifelines for their families at home. They argue that instead of restrictions and punishment, workers should be offered incentives to remit money through official channels.

Under the current scheme, Myanmar workers lose at least 5,000 kyats for every 100 baht they remit via regime-endorsed channels. While official channels offer 125 kyat per baht, informal markets offer upwards of 130.

The Labour Ministry continues to push the new scheme, projecting that 2026 inflows will match last year’s total of US$ 5.6 billion. Annual remittances have more than doubled since 2019, driven by the mass emigration of workers escaping the turmoil and economic collapse that followed the 2021 coup.

World.title: Hostage Diplomacy: How the Myanmar Junta Is Weaponizing Jailed Aung San Suu Kyi
World.content:
As the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN)’s November summit approaches, the Myanmar junta—desperate for international recognition—has made a series of minor concessions regarding access to jailed civilian leader Aung San Suu Kyi.

Highlighting the regime’s ongoing atrocities against civilians, observers and anti-regime groups have warned that the regime’s moves are merely a ploy to win resumption of full participation in ASEAN and ease international pressure.

Since the 2021 coup, the Myanmar regime has been barred from attending high-level ASEAN summits for failing to comply with the bloc’s peace plan, which calls for the immediate cessation of violence against civilians and the opening of a dialogue among all concerned groups, among other things.

Aung San Suu Kyi was allowed to meet with ICRC representatives in Naypyitaw on August 3, and to receive books and a diplomatic letter from King Charles on October 19. The jailed Nobel Peace Prize laureate was also permitted to talk with her youngest son, Kim Aris, on October 22, for the first time in the five years since her arrest.

Domestic and regional observers warn that the regime has started using Aung San Suu Kyi as a political bargaining chip to gain access to the bloc’s upcoming summit.

“The regime led by the sham president Min Aung Hlaing has been trying to scam the world by using hostage diplomacy,” said Debbie Stothard, founder and coordinator of the Alternative Asean Network on Burma.

She cited another recent instance of hostage diplomacy, in which the junta jailed 78 Filipino trafficking victims who had escaped from scam centers. Instead of repatriating them, the regime used the victims as a bargaining chip in negotiations with Maria Teresa Lazaro, the Philippine foreign secretary, who was forced to request the release of her compatriots during a visit to Naypyitaw in January, then thank the internationally-isolated regime for freeing the jailed Philippine nationals.

An ASEAN humanitarian delegation led by the bloc’s special envoy Maria Teresa Lazaro is scheduled to visit Myanmar for two days starting Wednesday.

The tactic was used again with the detention of U.S. citizen Adam Castillo, which allowed the regime to secure engagement with the U.S, Stothard said. A delegation of U.S. officials visited Naypyitaw to secure Castillo’s release.

“The regime continues to use its hostage diplomacy by … dangling Aung San Suu Kyi to secure normalization of relations with ASEAN,” she said. “ASEAN and the international community shouldn’t be easily scammed this way. They shouldn’t be normalizing relations with a gangster who is the architect of genocide and war crimes.”

Thailand welcomed the U.S. engagement with the regime and expected discussions to be held at the upcoming ASEAN summit in Manila on how to proceed with the Myanmar issue, Foreign Minister Sihasak Phuangketkeow told media on Friday.

The minister, who is working to improve relations between ASEAN and the military regime, commented that the regime’s granting of permission for Aung San Suu Kyi and her son to speak represented a positive development.

Further evidence of the regime’s concerted effort to secure ASEAN’s recognition and support can be seen in Naypyitaw’s recent decision to form an ASEAN Affairs Committee to communicate and cooperate with the bloc.

Foreign Minister Tin Maung Swe, who chairs the committee, said it was formed to foster additional channels of engagement with ASEAN. The regime is currently engaging regional neighbors on a country-by-country basis according to priority levels, he added.

Coup leader-turned-president Min Aung Hlaing has been engaging with the U.S., and in recent months has visited ASEAN members Laos, Thailand, Cambodia, Vietnam and Malaysia.

David Gum Awng, deputy foreign affairs minister of the civilian National Unity Government (NUG), told The Irrawaddy he shares the view that the regime is using Aung San Suu Kyi as a political bargaining chip to secure Min Aung Hlaing’s attendance at the upcoming ASEAN summit.

“Civilian leader Daw Aung San Suu Kyi is entirely innocent and is merely a political hostage unjustly detained by the regime for political reasons. Allowing her to receive books and gifts sent by King Charles and permitting a 20-minute phone call with her son is purely a political transaction by the regime,” he said.

He said the regime’s recent moves are a political ploy, despite some ASEAN member countries’ characterization of them as a positive development, and warned that “ASEAN needs to see this reality.”

Mon Mon Myat, lecturer at the Department of Peace Studies at Thailand’s Payap University, remarked that the junta’s apparent relaxation regarding access to the jailed civilian leader “might include hopes of being allowed to attend the ASEAN summit. It appears they urgently need both international recognition and assistance. On the other hand, they might be pushing for this out of fear of becoming more isolated on the international stage if the ICJ ruling comes out later this year.” The International Court of Justice is considering a genocide case brought by The Gambia against Myanmar over the military’s persecution of the Rohingya minority in Rakhine State.

The regime’s charm offensive may be having some effect. Former Japanese Prime Minister Fumio Kishida said in an exclusive interview with Nikkei Asia on October 12 that Japan should assist in Myanmar’s reintegration into ASEAN. For the time being, however, ASEAN as a bloc is upholding its summit ban, citing the failure to honor its peace plan. Known as the Five-Point Consensus, the plan established over five years ago in Jakarta includes calls for an immediate end to violence and the holding of dialogues. Both coup president Min Aung Hlaing and his rubber-stamp parliament have formally rejected the plan. Meanwhile, the regime continues its five-year campaign of airstrikes, shelling and village burnings.

The NUG’s David Gum Awng said ASEAN must clearly and decisively call out the regime’s total failure to implement the peace plan. He warned that bilateral engagement with the junta by individual member states is emboldening the regime’s war crimes against civilians, rather than applying necessary pressure.

“While ASEAN member states may have different views on the country’s crisis, there must be definite consequences if the junta fails to comply with the agreements. Without clear repercussions for their defiance, the regime has absolutely no incentive to cooperate,” he added.

Citing the junta’s ongoing attacks on civilian targets, Stothard noted that hostage diplomacy is a smokescreen for the regime’s continued brutality against its own people.

“ASEAN and the international community should not be engaging or dancing with a regime that has turned Burma into a transnational crime hub, created the worst humanitarian crisis in the region, and will negatively impact ASEAN for years to come,” Stothard said.

World.title: The Fatal Flaw in China’s Myanmar Policy is Economic Collapse
World.content:
While Beijing’s military‑centric approach — backed by its “three bottom lines” — defines China’s Myanmar policy, the ground reality shows that civil war is not the only source of instability. Alongside the widening conflict, Myanmar’s foundations are being shaken by a deepening economic crisis with historical echoes. The collapse of General Ne Win’s Burma Socialist Programme Party regime four decades ago was not triggered by battlefield defeat, but by economic breakdown — a reminder that today’s regime faces the same danger.

Deepening economic crisis

When Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi visited in August 2024, the junta was facing not only military setbacks but also severe inflation marked by surging commodity prices. Thanks to Chinese financial assistance, inflation eased after his trip and the kyat stabilized at around 4,000 per US dollar. But it plunged again after military-staged elections early this year and now hovers near 4,600 per dollar.

Starved of hard currency, the junta restricted imports and choked off border trade. The cost of fuel and cooking oil surged, followed by staples such as rice, eggs, and onions, as well as household electronics and medicines. Vehicle prices soared, and black markets reemerged. Domestic manufacturing, agriculture, and livestock industries — reliant on imported technology, seeds, feed, fertilizers, and medicines — were hit hard, while foreign investment also dwindled.

As the kyat weakens, commodity prices are surging again and shortages are widespread. This is not merely a policy miscalculation: the junta channels all foreign currency into military spending, compounding the economic crisis. Without an end to war, the economic crisis cannot be fixed.

Corrupt state apparatus

Another major issue is systemic corruption in the bureaucracy. Graft grew steadily under military rule from 1988 to 2010 but was restrained somewhat by public oversight during the 2010–2020 reform period. But since the 2021 coup, the entire machinery of government — from Min Aung Hlaing and the top brass down to the lowest ranks — have exploited power for personal gain.

Legal restrictions and licensing requirements have become tollbooths for bribery. Payment is required for import permits, ID cards, passports and the right to travel at home or abroad. Importers routinely pay bribes, while ordinary people face extortion by soldiers and police on the streets. This endemic corruption has also facilitated the boom in narcotics production and online fraud gangs.

Narcotics and online scams

Myanmar is among the world’s largest producers of heroin, methamphetamine, and synthetic drugs, with output now rising annually as officials, soldiers and police turn a blind eye in exchange for bribes.

Online scam syndicates previously confined to borderlands are now spreading inland. Evidence from Karen State and northern Shan’s Kokang shows that gangs are relocating under the protection of military‑linked MPs, administrators, border guards, police, and senior officials. Even as criminal syndicates elsewhere in northern Shan are dismantled, Muse—the only border town Naypyitaw still controls thanks to China—remains an online scam hub, highlighting the regime’s complicity in cyber-fraud.

In other words, the economic crisis is not a standalone problem, but deeply intertwined with systemic corruption, narcotics production, and scams.

Poverty and social collapse

Illicit revenues from narcotics and scam syndicates have flooded Myanmar, fueling inflation and driving property values to unsustainable heights. Ordinary citizens are bearing the brunt as the country’s economic crisis deepens. Chinese loans cannot solve this problem.

The persistent civil war, combined with entrenched corruption and criminality, rampant inflation, and worsening shortages, has created a dire situation. While a handful of elites hoard wealth, most of the population struggles to afford basic food, leaving Myanmar society fractured and unstable.

A UNDP report released on October 8 revealed that one in three Myanmar citizens — over 17 million people — are already experiencing multidimensional poverty, with another 19 million at risk. In total, about 37 million people, or 68 percent of the population, are either poor or vulnerable to poverty.

Years of conflict, displacement, economic collapse, and climate shocks have devastated housing, healthcare, education, and livelihoods, worsening deprivation.

China’s other Myanmar headaches

Beyond these crises, China must also reckon with four other problems.

First is anti‑China sentiment — which is rising not only among resistance forces but also within the regime itself. Resistance anger is fueled by Beijing’s support for a failing military regime, not hostility toward Chinese people.

For the regime, however, anti‑China sentiment remains a core worldview. In times of political, economic, or military crisis, the Myanmar military often resorts to Burman nationalism, routinely stoking anti‑China and anti‑Muslim prejudice. In this way, it diverted public anger over rice shortages in 1967 by orchestrating anti‑Chinese riots. Today, the regime sponsors ultranationalist groups such as Ma Ba Tha to sustain this narrative.

Propping up the regime offers China no protection from Naypyitaw’s deep-seated disdain. This hostility is not incidental but fundamental; Beijing will be forced to confront it again and again no matter how much support it provides.

Second, the regime’s corrupt apparatus continues to protect online scam syndicates, undermining China’s efforts to suppress them.

Third, the regime has closed key border trade gates including Muse and Chinshwehaw once worth billions annually to China. At a time when Chinese goods are cheaper than Japanese or Western equivalents, the border-trade shutdown is a major loss. Meanwhile, talk of opening trade routes with India has alarm bells ringing in Beijing.

Fourth, the regime is seeking to reestablish relations with the United States. While China might accept restoration of normal diplomatic ties, anything deeper would be difficult for Beijing to tolerate given its red line over Western engagement with ethnic armed groups.

‘Three bottom lines’ collapse

China’s policy goal is stability in Myanmar. But by betting on the Myanmar military to deliver it, Beijing has tethered itself to failure. The regime’s reliance on force over negotiations, corruption over the rule of law, entanglement with narcotics and scams—coupled with economic breakdown—guarantee perpetual instability.

Despite Beijing’s support, Myanmar remains mired in conflict and crisis. The “three bottom lines” have not been upheld: civil strife is intensifying, ASEAN engagement is faltering, and international powers are finding new entry points.

China’s core objective — stability in Myanmar — remains unfulfilled.

World.title: Malaysia to Seek Clarification Over Reports of Detained Myanmar Returnees
World.content:
KUALA LUMPUR—Malaysia will seek clarification from Myanmar over reports that hundreds of migrants recently returned to the country are being held in military detention, Foreign Minister Mohamad Hasan said on Monday.

Malaysia in late September sent back around 1,500 Myanmar nationals as it launched a scheme that rights groups say may endanger migrants by returning them to the war-torn country.

Kuala Lumpur said the group agreed to “voluntary” repatriation from detention centers amid an uptick in anti-migrant sentiment in Malaysia.

Myanmar pledged “safe and dignified” returns for its citizens displaced abroad, after criticism from the United Nations and rights groups.

Mohamad told parliament on Monday that Malaysia’s charge d’affaires in Myanmar would investigate the allegations and learn the condition of those reportedly detained.

“If there is news that the 300 people are still being detained, we will ask the Myanmar government to explain to us,” he told parliament in response to a lawmaker’s question.

“We will ask the Myanmar government to ensure that the assurances it gave us are honored,” he added.

Myanmar news outlet the Democratic Voice of Burma reported on Thursday that more than 400 ethnic Rakhine residents who returned from Malaysia earlier this month “remain in military custody” after arriving in Yangon.

They were among a group of 1,476 returnees who arrived by ship outside Yangon, the first of 5,000 that Kuala Lumpur says Myanmar agreed to take back amid the anti-migrant sentiment in Malaysia.

An additional 3,524 people are expected to be repatriated in a second phase.

The UN has warned conditions in Myanmar, which has been consumed by civil war since a 2021 military coup, mean safe homecomings cannot be guaranteed as required under international law.

Myanmar’s coup leader turned president Min Aung Hlaing has been a pariah in many capitals abroad since the putsch, but Malaysian Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim invited him for talks about returning Myanmar migrants earlier this month.

During the visit, Min Aung Hlaing said migrants from his country held in Malaysian detention centers will be returned home “as soon as possible”.

“We will take those verified nationals back as soon as possible,” he told a joint news conference with Anwar.

The opaque repatriation scheme has been criticized by rights monitors, some fearing ethnic Rohingya may be sent back to a country where they have experienced persecution that rights experts say amounted to genocide.

World.title: Tokayev’s Ambitious Construction Push Draws Optimism, Questions Over Implementation
World.content:
ASTANA — President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev’s announced plans for a sweeping infrastructure overhaul and long-term energy security have drawn reactions from Kazakh analysts, who see opportunities for economic growth alongside questions about how the government will turn ambitious proposals into lasting results.

In his Oct. 28 state-of-the-nation address, Tokayev outlined plans to allocate approximately 6.5 trillion tenge ($14.2 billion) from the National Fund through 2029 to modernize infrastructure, including new hospitals, schools, transportation networks and public utilities. He also proposed designating 2027 as a year of nationwide construction.

“Our country is entering a new historical cycle. At this turning point, we must critically reassess all national plans and strategies,” said Tokayev in his nearly one and half hour long address.

The address also called for considering a strategic uranium reserve to secure supplies for the country’s planned nuclear power plants for the next century.

Ambitious construction drive

Financial analyst Andrei Chebotarev framed the president’s emphasis on construction as part of a broader effort to reshape the country’s economy and society.

Writing on his FINANCEkaz Telegram channel, Chebotarev said the address appeared to frame construction as more than the development of roads, hospitals and logistics hubs.

“This isn’t just about building infrastructure, roads, and logistics hubs, both ground-based and air-based,” Chebotarev writes.

According to him, the concept also extended to strengthening economic opportunities, public institutions and civic responsibility.

He noted that construction could create employment and open opportunities that had previously been unavailable, particularly as Kazakhstan seeks to develop its economy amid rapid technological change.

“We have rolled up our sleeves and are building not a new Kazakhstan, not an old one, but our own Kazakhstan,” he added.

Olga Kaldybayeva, chief expert at the Public Opinion Monitoring Department of the Kazakhstan Institute for Strategic Studies, emphasized that expanding infrastructure alone would not guarantee better living conditions.

In an analysis published following the address, she noted that the effectiveness of urban development would depend on coordinated planning, efficient management of resources and investment in human capital.

According to figures from the Bureau of National Statistics cited by Kaldybayeva, Kazakhstan’s urban population reached approximately 13.2 million, or 64.2% of the total population, as of Sept. 1.

Almaty, Astana and Shymkent together accounted for approximately 38.7% of national GDP in 2025, she added.

“A city’s development is directly linked to the growth of human capital. Access to quality education, healthcare, modern jobs, and public spaces influences residents’ opportunities for professional development and self-fulfillment,” she explained.

“There is a reciprocal relationship here: a well-developed urban environment helps unlock human potential, while skilled and proactive residents become the most important resource for the city’s own economic and technological development. Therefore, investments in urban infrastructure should also be viewed as investments in human capital,” she said.

Kaldybayeva also highlighted Tokayev’s instructions to develop medium- and long-term plans for major cities and introduce digital twins of urban infrastructure, virtual models that can help authorities assess the condition of utility networks, anticipate demand and improve planning decisions.

She also stressed that the benefits of urban development should extend to surrounding regions and rural communities, rather than remain concentrated in Kazakhstan’s largest cities.

Questions of long-term planning

While the infrastructure agenda drew an optimistic interpretation from Chebotarev, energy analyst Askar Ismailov raised questions about the implementation of another proposal: the creation of a strategic uranium reserve.

Tokayev described a proposal to establish a state strategic uranium reserve as worthy of serious consideration, saying it could cover the needs of Kazakhstan’s nuclear power plants for the next century.

Ismailov, founder of PACE Analytics, pointed to Tokayev’s 2022 instruction to examine the construction of large oil storage facilities in the Atyrau Region. In a post on the PACE Analytics channel, Ismailov said the Energy Ministry and KazMunayGas national oil company subsequently deemed the project economically unjustified, favoring greater flexibility in oil export routes instead.

He questioned whether a similar argument could eventually be used against the proposed uranium reserve.

The concern comes as Kazakhstan seeks to expand nuclear power generation. In his address. Tokayev suggested considering beginning the construction of the Balkhash nuclear power plant next year and accelerate the agreement on the development of the second plant.

Social justice

Political analyst Gaziz Abishev identified social justice as another central theme of the address, highlighting the president’s proposals to reconsider the distribution of social benefits and increase the tax burden on wealthy citizens.

In a comment on his Telegram channel, Abishev said that Kazakhstan faces growing pressure to balance social expectations with limited budget resources.

He suggested that declining returns from oil revenues and fiscal constraints make reductions in some government expenditures unavoidable. In his view, the priority should be ensuring that assistance reaches citizens who genuinely depend on state support.

Tokayev instructed officials to thoroughly examine changes to the social assistance system, test new approaches through pilot projects and assess their effectiveness before expanding them nationwide.

Abishev also supported the proposal to consider higher tax rates for wealthy individuals, describing progressive taxation as an established practice in many countries, including France and Germany. He said Tokayev had raised this issue back in 2019.

“Kazakhstan’s market economy allows people to monetize their talents, their labor, and their initial social status. This is not the case everywhere. Even in many liberal countries, high incomes are taxed at extremely high rates,” he added.

Human capital development

Anastasiya Matyukh at the Kazakhstan Institute of Public Development also drew attention to education, human capital development and social responsibility in ensuring the success of economic reforms.

Matyukh stressed that Kazakhstan’s modernizing economy requires more than technically qualified specialists. It also needs people capable of critical thinking, adapting to new technologies, taking initiative and assuming responsibility for their decisions.

She described education, professional development and the cultivation of civic values as strategic investments in the country’s long-term competitiveness.

Reflecting on Tokayev’s call for a new public ethic, Matyukh emphasised that institutional reforms and technological advances alone cannot fully improve living standards without corresponding changes in social behavior.

World.title: Trade, Connectivity and Diplomacy: What’s Next for Turkic Cooperation
World.content:
ASTANA — As the Organization of Turkic States (OTS) prepares for its Oct. 30 summit in Ankara, experts say its expanding ambitions in trade, transport, energy and security present Kazakhstan with both opportunities and challenges, particularly in turning political commitments into economic gains while preserving its independent foreign policy.

For Kazakhstan, translating political commitments into practical economic benefits, strengthening regional connectivity and maintaining independent foreign policy priorities will be central to the organization’s development, experts told The Astana Times.

“The OTS should not be viewed as a new geopolitical bloc or a zero-sum alternative to other regional organizations,” said Gabit Zhumatay, professor at the School of Law and Public Policy at Narxoz University.

“Its greatest potential lies in complementing existing frameworks and expanding the strategic choices available to its members. For Kazakhstan, the real opportunity is to transform Turkic solidarity into greater economic resilience, stronger regional connectivity, and greater diplomatic influence, while preserving its strategic autonomy,” he said.

The summit, hosted by Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan under the theme Turkic Century: Unity in Language, Thought and Deed, will review cooperation in political, economic and humanitarian fields.

Türkiye will assume the OTS chairmanship from Azerbaijan, with leaders expected to adopt the Ankara Declaration and discuss the organization’s institutional development, including the appointment of a new secretary general.

Institutional expansion and implementation priorities

Zhanibek Arynov, an assistant professor at Nazarbayev University, described the OTS as one of the most active regional institutions involving Kazakhstan, following an expansion of its activities over the past five to six years. Its agenda now covers trade, investment, transportation, energy, education and cultural exchanges, supported by additional agreements and dialogue mechanisms.

According to Arynov, Kazakhstan’s approach remains pragmatic, with participation focused on areas that correspond to its national interests. The growing number of initiatives has provided additional opportunities for cooperation, although the organization’s limited resources and institutional capacity could affect their implementation.

“However, the resources of the OTS are very limited. When you spread these limited resources across multiple issue areas, the effectiveness and depth of cooperation might suffer. Instead of constantly widening the scope of cooperation, the OTS members should be paying more attention to the depth of those collaborations, to the implementation of those commitments,” Arynov told The Astana Times.

Zhumatay similarly highlighted the need to translate institutional development into economic outcomes. Initiatives involving the Turkic Investment Fund, innovation, digitalization and regional infrastructure could contribute to Kazakhstan’s economic diversification, although their effectiveness depends on financing, institutional coordination and the distribution of benefits among participating countries.

Different national priorities within the OTS

The organization’s members share an interest in expanding cooperation but differ in their expectations concerning its political, economic and security dimensions. These differences influence the prospects for common positions on sensitive international issues and the pace of institutional development.
