World.title: Nelson ute theft: Nicholas Tripp jailed after dangerous police chase
World.content:
A tradesman opening a gate to his yard turned to find a stranger at the wheel of his ute, who then sped off in the vehicle.

Disqualified driver Nicholas Tripp led police on a chase from Nelson, where he weaved through dense traffic, to Wakefield, 30km south, where he stopped at a dairy to buy tobacco.

He hoped to get to Christchurch, Judge Bruce Davidson said while sentencing Tripp on Wednesday.

Tripp evaded police at the dairy, then ran rampant through the village of Wakefield, pulling open car doors and yelling at drivers to get out.

In one instance, he tried to open the door of a vehicle as the driver grabbed it and pulled it shut, then screamed: "Help me, help me, the police are gonna get me".

The 34-year-old with an "extensive list of previous offending" over 14 years was sentenced in the Nelson District Court to 22 months in prison on 11 charges.

Nelson District Court. (File photo)

Most sprang from his "offending spree" on June 17, which resulted in multiple victims, police said.

Tripp had earlier pleaded guilty to charges of unlawfully taking a vehicle, attempting to take a vehicle, unlawfully interfering with a vehicle, driving while disqualified on a third or subsequent time, two burglary charges including one over $5000, driving dangerously, theft and assaulting a female.

'Seized opportunity'

On the morning of June 17 this year, a landscaping firm worker parked his ute at the entrance to the company's yard in central Nelson.

Tripp, who has convictions for driving while disqualified on two occasions and driving while suspended on four occasions, was nearby and found the ute running while the driver got out to unlock the entrance gate.

Tripp, who was on intensive supervision for earlier offending, got in the vehicle and sped off, police said.

He "impulsively seized the opportunity" to get in the vehicle and drive off, Judge Davidson said.

The worker called police and tracked the vehicle via a company GPS tracking app.

Tripp threw away the worker's cellphone stored in the vehicle's drinks holder as he sped south, thinking it might stop the ability to track his movements.

"Your driving was very dangerous, including that you overtook a truck laden with fuel and were undertaking other vehicles," Judge Davidson said.

As Tripp reached State Highway 6 south of Richmond he went through a busy intersection and overtook a road contracting firm's fuel truck, narrowly missing it as he passed, police said.

He then undertook a vehicle and continued south before overtaking another vehicle, forcing three oncoming vehicles to take evasive action and pull to the left to avoid a collision, police said.

Tripp passed officers waiting for him at a site before Wakefield and continued to undertake other southbound vehicles as he entered the village.

Stopped for tobacco

He stopped outside a local dairy and bakery, went in and asked for a packet of tobacco.

As the staff member turned her back, Tripp reached through a plastic barrier, took a cigarette lighter and hid it in his pocket.

He then reached under the barrier and grabbed the staff member by the arm as she held the tobacco.

Unable to get the tobacco, he took another lighter instead, police said.

As he went to get back in the ute he saw a police officer approaching and began running away, discarding the stolen items in a bush and tossing his wallet into a boat parked nearby, police said.

Tripp then spotted another ute parked on the roadside, with the driver at the wheel.

Police said Tripp banged on the driver's door before trying to pull it open, but the driver held the door and pulled it shut.

Tripp then screamed at him, "Help me, help me, the police are gonna get me", before running off when he saw the officer in pursuit.

He spied another vehicle parked nearby and punched the driver's window multiple times in an attempt to break in.

The officer caught up with Tripp and told him he was under arrest.

But Tripp ran off again and into a nearby property through an open gate.

He got into a vehicle parked there and while rummaging for the keys, the officer opened the driver's door.

Tripp climbed out the passenger side and ran to another property where he tried to get into a vehicle, but it was locked.

Another vehicle on the property was unlocked, so he got in, rummaged through a purse on the front seat and fled on foot again as police closed in on him.

Tripp tried one more car before police stopped him. Another officer had arrived at the scene by then and Tripp was arrested.

Defence lawyer Fleur Oback said Tripp was sorry and had admitted his actions early.

She said background factors in his life warranted credit in sentencing, and he had been in custody since his arrest for the equivalent of nine months.

"It's given him significant time for sober reflection," she said.

Tripp told the court he was sorry, but was stressed at the time.

"Sorry for overtaking that vehicle. It was very foolish," he said.

Police prosecutor Mary Hewlett said it was serious offending, conducted while Tripp was under the influence of an undetermined substance.

Judge Davidson said Tripp appeared to have limited insight into the risk posed to members of the public, including multiple road users.

From a starting point of two and a half years in prison, Tripp received 22 months, with leave to apply for home detention if he could demonstrate a "sea change in attitude", including accepting proper treatment for substance abuse.

He received a further disqualification from driving for a year.

* This story originally appeared in the New Zealand Herald.

World.title: Diamonds avoid clean sweep in Constellation Cup
World.content:
The Diamonds have defeated the Silver Ferns 68-58 in front of a sold-out crowd of 9,471 at John Cain Arena to avoid a Constellation Cup clean sweep.

Despite falling to an overall 3-1 series defeat, the victory gives Australian fans hope ahead of the team's title defence at the 2027 Netball World Cup.

Both sides were only separated by a single goal at the half-time break, 32-31, before the hosts outscored the Commonwealth Games gold medallists in the second half, 37-26.

The result extends the Diamond's 11-year undefeated record against New Zealand in Melbourne.

Ferns coach Noeline Taurua and captain Karin Burger hold the Constellation Cup. (Getty: Daniel Pockett)

New Zealand head coach Noeline Taurua made 19 changes to her team throughout the game to try and slow down the Diamonds in attack.

Australia, meanwhile, were unchanged for the entire 60 minutes.

A new shooting combination between Sophie Garbin and Georgie Horjus looked promising for the Diamonds. Together, the pair finished with an overall accuracy of 91 per cent.

It was the first time Horjus has got a proper chance at goal attack. She was named in that position on Sunday for game three but quickly had to slot back into wing attack following a finger injury to Kate Moloney on the first centre pass.

Horjus was named Player of the Match for her efforts inside the circle on Wednesday night.

Despite being 12cm shorter than her direct opponent Karin Burger, and 20cm shorter than goal keeper Kelly Jackson, she was not spooked by their wingspan or height.

Georgie Horjus shoots during game four of the Constellation Cup. (Getty: Kelly Defina)

There were points where Garbin was sandwiched between the Silver Ferns defenders and Horjus had to step up, sharing the shooting load and scoring a total 26 goals.

Speaking with the media after the match, Horjus conceded she was nervous to start the game but grew in confidence as the minutes wore on.

"There was a lot of talk about Kelly's long arms and the defence over the shot, but after the first quarter I got a little more relaxed," Horjus said.

"Having the support from Liz and Sophie around me just to shoot it.

"I train against the best in the world every week [in Super Netball] so I think my mindset just changed a little bit and I was more confident to go to post."

Diamonds centurion and captain Liz Watson has been scrutinised in recent times, as fans call for a changing of the guard. (Getty Images: James Fearn)

Liz Watson had a much improved game at her preferred position.

Taking back the wing attack bib, the Australian captain shrugged off criticism that has followed her performances this series to finish the match with a huge tally of 50 feeds.

Jackson topped the gain stat, but newcomer Jessie Grenvold wasn't far behind. The goal keeper has been a star in her first appearances for the Diamonds at 23 years old.

Her stats sheet read: one intercept, seven deflections and one rebound.

Grenvold was the only Australian defender to consistently ruffle Kiwi powerhouse Grace Nweke's feathers throughout the Constellation Cup.

Grenvold and Amy Parmenter (three gains) helped to turn the screws in the back half of the match. They hunted ball with a sense of urgency and disrupted the flow of the Silver Ferns.

Jessie Grenvold wins the ball during the Constellation Cup. (Getty Images: Mark Metcalfe)

Head coach Taurua said her team looked tired and weary, and the Diamonds were simply too good on the night.

They may yet take out the number one ranking when World Netball does its calculations and updates its list on December 1st.

"It was a bittersweet feeling," New Zealand captain Karin Burger said.

"We still won the Cup and according to statistics we're actually equal first [in the rankings], so we'll take that for what it is and then we'll work really hard for next year."

"As I understand when we came in, we needed to win 4-0 to be number one outright, three [wins] we'd be drawn and anything less, we'd be in the same position," Taurua added.

Norma Plummer presents Grace Nweke with the Plummer-Aitken medal. (Getty: Daniel Pockett)

"We've been looking at that for six weeks which is why this series has been massive for us, to try and get that ranking."

Look back at all the action in our live blog of game three.

World.title: Live: Carey and Inglis whittle down deficit after Jansen's double-strike
World.content:
(Getty Images)

Marco Jansen has had some series.

With the bat he got scores of 26 and 35 in Durban, taking match figures of 4-113.

Then, in Gqeberha he added 85 runs and a brilliant 5-33.

His second consecutive half ton yesterday was full of quality and helped dig the South Africans out of a hole that was threatening to collapse in on themselves.

That was his fifth Test half century and, although he averages just 25.66 with the bat, he is fast becoming one of the best all rounders in world cricket - and that's not counting some of his fielding.

In fact, he is officially the number one all rounder, according to the latest ICC rankings (and slightly less objectively, by Dale Steyn).

Jansen has taken over top spot from Ravindra Jadeja, knocking the Indian star off the top for the first time in four years.

He has also climbed to the top of the Test bowling rankings, just ahead of Mitch Starc.

In the 23 Tests that he has played, Jansen's bowling average is 20.80.

He has taken 99 Test wickets.

Given the series he is having, don't count him out bringing up his century in the next few hours...

World.title: Beale called up for Wallabies Spring Tour ahead of Rugby World Cup
World.content:
Veteran playmaker Kurtley Beale has been summoned for the Wallabies' spring tour of the UK in a big development ahead of next year's Rugby World Cup in Australia.

Beale on Wednesday answered an SOS call from coach Les Kiss to join the squad for next month's three Tests against England, Scotland and Wales before the inaugural Nations Championship finals in the UK from November 21-23.

The 95-Test-capped Beale will replace midfielder Hunter Paisami, who is unavailable due to personal reasons, while James Ramm and Kalani Thomas were also named to join the touring group.

No Wallabies call yet for Nawaqanitawase The Wallabies are confident star code-crosser Mark Nawaqanitawase wants to play for Australia at next year's Rugby World Cup, but he still has a choice of three nations.

But the 37-year-old's inclusion will be the major talking point as Kiss seemingly considers biting the bullet and ending Australia's revolving door of flawed five-eighths by backing a proven number 10 to steer the wobbly ship ahead of next year's global showpiece.

Kiss's predecessors Joe Schmidt, Eddie Jones, Dave Rennie and Michael Cheika have used almost a dozen different playmakers since Bernard Foley guided the Wallabies — under Cheika — to the 2015 World Cup final in England.

But none of the likes of Noah Lolesio, Ben Donaldson, Carter Gordon, Tane Edmed or Harry McLaughlin-Phillips has been able to hold down the spot.

Fellow stalwarts James O'Connor, Quade Cooper and Matt Toomua have also had cracks without commanding the role.

Cheika has turned to Foley to rejoin the NSW Waratahs from Japan, more than a decade after the duo masterminded the club's one and only 2014 Super Rugby premiership.

Now it appears Kiss is seriously considering Beale to revive the Wallabies' fortunes after Australia slipped to number seven in the world rankings after losing the Bledisloe Cup for a 23rd straight year this month.

Kurtley Beale last played for the Wallabies against Wales in 2021. (Getty Images: Stu Forster)

Beale last appeared in a Wallabies squad in 2024 before an Achilles injury prematurely ended his season. His most recent appearance in the gold jersey was against Wales in Cardiff in 2021.

But the silky-skilled talent and former World Player of the Year nominee boasts three World Cup experiences from 2011, 2015 and 2019 since first being called up by Wallabies coach John Connolly as a schoolboy prodigy.

"With Hunter's unavailability, we're excited by what Kurtley can bring to the group," Kiss said of the super versatile talent.

"He's got 95 caps worth of Test experience, and whilst he will primarily cover inside centre, he has the versatility to play a number of positions across the back line.

"Kurtley's also been in great form for the Western Force in Super Rugby Pacific and Super Rugby AUS and is excited to contribute to the environment."

AAP

World.title: FA expecting Socceroos friendlies in Middle East to go ahead
World.content:
The Socceroos are set to forge ahead with plans to play friendlies in the Middle East next month in the face of the increasingly volatile conflict in the region.

Australia is scheduled to face Qatar in Doha on November 14 before taking on Jordan in Amman on November 17 in what will be the Socceroos' final hit-outs before coach Tony Popovic names his squad for January's Asian Cup.

But there are security concerns following violence this month, including a Houthi strike at the Riyadh airport in Saudi Arabia, which is hosting the cup.

Socceroos dates November 14: Friendly vs Qatar (Doha)

November 17: Friendly vs Jordan (Amman)

January 9: Socceroos first group match at Asian Cup finals, vs Singapore (Khobar, Saudi Arabia)

Last week nine people were gunned down by Syrian militants at an orthodox church in Jordan, one of the more stable countries in the Middle East.

The Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade advises Australians to reconsider their need to travel to Jordan. Qatar is rated as a much safer destination.

As things stand Football Australia (FA) is expecting the games with Qatar and Jordan to go ahead as scheduled.

"Football Australia is closely monitoring the situation in the Middle East ahead of the Socceroos' matches against Qatar and Jordan in November," an FA spokesperson said in a statement to AAP.

"The safety and wellbeing of our players, staff and supporters remains paramount.

"Our experienced security team is actively monitoring developments and providing regular updates, and we will be guided by the advice of our head of security.

"Risk assessment is part of our planning for every national team camp, and it will be a key focus of our preparations for November."

Popovic knocked back extension Socceroos coach Tony Popovic has revealed he turned down a four-year contract offer from Football Australia (FA) to take the team through to the 2030 World Cup.

While FA's decision to push on is encouraging, there is still no clear decision on what will happen with January's Asian Cup.

Saudi Arabia has been forced to move a friendly with South Korea to Qatar as part of the flow-on effect of the Riyadh attack, and several Asian Champions League games involving Saudi club sides have been postponed.

A decision is yet to be made as to whether the Asian Cup, which is expected to kick off with the hosts taking on Palestine in Riyadh on January 7, will still take place as scheduled.

Australia's is scheduled to take on Singapore in Khobar on January 9 for its first group game of the tournament.

There is growing concern that the Asian Cup would be delayed by 12 months, with AFC president Sheikh Salman bin Ebrahim Al Khalifa saying a decision may not be made until the end of November.

"If we need to make a decision then we will, but we could move back a year to 2028 if we need to," he said in Zurich this month.

"But at the moment we are monitoring the situation and everything is on schedule."

AAP/ABC

World.title: Fox axing from Devils VFL not due to single incident, club says
World.content:
Tasmania Devils have strongly defended their club culture after axing VFL skipper Robbie Fox following an off-field indiscretion.

The Devils also said the decision to part ways with their inaugural captain was not based on an isolated incident.

The team confirmed yesterday that Fox would not be offered a contract for the 2027 season, citing, in part, the club's "expectations regarding player behaviour and adherence to our standards".

Yesterday, the ABC revealed Fox had been involved in an incident at a Hobart pub, the Granada Tavern, where he was ejected from the venue after becoming drunk and disorderly, and acting belligerently toward some staff.

It is also understood a bottle was thrown and smashed during the incident.

Nobody is believed to have been injured, and there was no police involvement.

Kath McCann says Fox had "some areas for improvement and for growth, and he's dealing with the consequences of that". (ABC News: Ashleigh Barraclough)

The ABC can also reveal Fox had earlier played in a charity golf event at the nearby Claremont Golf Club with several Devils teammates.

Fox's foursome included vice-captain Jye Menzie and reigning best-and-fairest Hugh Dixon.

There is no suggestion those players were involved in the later incident at the Granada Tavern.

Robbie Fox (left) pictured during his tenure with the Swans. (Getty Images: AFL Photos/Michael Willson)

Chief marketing officer Kath McCann told local media today that the decision not to offer Fox a contract was, in part, the culmination of several "situations".

"I want to be really clear that there was no particular one incident that led to this decision", she said.

"There have been situations where Robbie probably had some areas for improvement and for growth, and he's dealing with the consequences of that.

"I think it's fair to say that not everybody gets everything right," she said

Fox has been contacted for comment.

McCann said the Devils's culture was strong, and that their swift decision to cut on-field ties with Fox was indicative of that.

"Our club has really high standards, and we're really proud of that," she said.

"We've said from the start that our club is focused on ensuring we work with the very best people, and the highest of standards.

" It's been a part of our success to date and will continue to be in the future. "

But McCann also confirmed that Fox would continue in his role as the club's Strategic Projects Lead, and defended the decision to keep him on as a club employee.

McCann said the club was "very comfortable" with where it had landed regarding his playing contract and that it would not divulge details around its internal processes.

"Robbie's a member of our staff, he's been an important part of our inaugural year, and he's a really great person," she said.

Fox played 13 games for the Devils in an injury-affected year, after being recruited back to his native Tasmania following his delisting by the Sydney Swans.

Under his captaincy, the Devils finished in the VFL top four and earned a finals double chance.

World.title: Former Australian Open champ Stan Wawrinka ends illustrious career
World.content:
Stan Wawrinka's illustrious tennis career finally came to an end at his home tournament in Basel.

The three-time grand slam winner was beaten by eighth-seeded Jiří Lehečka in the first round of the Swiss Indoors, losing 7-5, 7-6(2).

The 41-year-old Wawrinka's last shot as a professional tennis player was a backhand that landed wide — to the audible disappointment of the vociferous home crowd.

Wawrinka, who turned pro in 2002, had announced last December that 2026 would be his last year on tour and "Stan the Man" had received warm send-offs throughout his farewell season.

"For me, all I wanted in my career was to give everything, to have no regrets, to always fight, to always give 100 per cent in every match — out of respect for myself, for the opponent, for the tournament, for the fans, for everybody," Wawrinka told the ATP Tour website ahead of his final match.

"That was always the most important thing for more than 20 years, and that's the only way you can leave the sport: without any regrets."

Wawrinka won his three grand slam titles after defeating the then-world number 1 player in each final. He beat Rafael Nadal to win the 2014 Australian Open and downed Novak Djokovic for the French Open title in 2015 and the US Open the following year.

Wawrinka, who reached a career-high world ranking of number three in 2014, won 16 tour-level titles.

He also paired with Roger Federer to win the doubles title for Switzerland at the 2008 Beijing Olympics. The duo helped Switzerland win its first Davis Cup title in 2014.

AP

World.title: Arsenal knocked out of League Cup by fourth-tier minnow in all-time upset
World.content:
Reigning English champion Arsenal has been knocked out of the EFL League Cup by fourth-tier side Fleetwood Town in a massive boilover.

A whopping 84 positions separate the London giant from its League Two minnow opponent on the English league pyramid, but in front of home fans, Fleetwood Town completed a remarkable upset 5-3 on penalties, after the scores finished 1-1 at the end of regulation.

Fleetwood, which is sitting a lowly 18th in League Two, took the lead in the 21st minute through Aaron Loupalo-Bi, scoring with one of just two shots on goal the hosts managed for the entire match.

A 50th-minute equaliser from Arsenal striker Viktor Gyökeres brought the Premier League giants back into the contest, but the Gunners could not find another.

Arsenal teenager Max Dowman was sent off in the 86th minute before the cup tie went to penalties.

Fleetwood was perfect from all five attempts, while Bruno Guimarães's miss for Arsenal on the Gunners' fourth attempt paved the way for one of the biggest upsets in the history of the competition.

The match was halted early on after the referee noticed a drone hovering above the stadium.

Arsenal had just been awarded a free kick when the referee spotted the drone and temporarily stopped play, leading to jeers from some fans inside Fleetwood's home ground, Highbury Stadium.

The delay lasted nearly eight minutes, with the referee speaking to the stadium safety officer, both managers and then some of the players before finally restarting the game.

ABC/AP

World.title: NBA's shortest-ever player to have jersey retired
World.content:
Tyrone "Muggsy" Bogues spent his entire NBA career looking up at all other players. They'll be looking up at him now.

His name and number, anyway.

The Charlotte Hornets announced on Tuesday that the No. 1 jersey worn by Bogues — the NBA's smallest-ever player at 5-foot-3 (160 centimetres)— will be retired during a half-time ceremony when the team plays host to Milwaukee on February 11.

"How ironic is that?" Bogues said.

"After all those times that you felt like you were looking up, looking up for so many years, at people, then here comes this particular moment. And when that jersey actually goes up, it'll be like I'm the one looking down at the entire world. It's going to be a surreal moment."

Muggsy Bogues played 14 seasons in the NBA. (AP: Chris O'Meara)

Bogues will be the third player whose Hornets jersey is retired, joining Bobby Phills (13) and Dell Curry (30). He began his career with Washington, then went to Charlotte in the 1988 expansion draft and essentially has called the Carolinas home ever since.

"Charlotte embraced me with open arms," Bogues said.

"This is a place I've called home more than I've called any other place home, even growing up in the city of Baltimore. So, having this type of recognition for my family, for the organisation to look at you in this type of light, I mean, it means the world."

Bogues played in the NBA for parts of 14 seasons, spending the bulk of that time with Charlotte and having stints with Golden State, Washington and Toronto. He was the 12th selection in the 1987 draft — one spot behind Indiana taking Reggie Miller — and wound up playing more games than all but eight other members of that draft class.

He averaged 7.7 points and 7.6 assists for his career. Bogues was part of Charlotte teams that reached the 50-win mark in three consecutive seasons, plus he was part of the franchise's first post-season series victory in 1993.

"Muggsy was here from the beginning and played with a heart, toughness and competitive spirit that made him a fan favourite," Hornets co-chairmen Rick Schnall and Gabe Plotkin said in a statement on Tuesday.

"At 5-foot-3, he overcame obstacles throughout his career and proved he belonged among the best players in the world. He became a role model for generations, showing young people that their size doesn't have to limit what they can achieve."

The average NBA player during Bogues's playing career stood 6-foot-7 (200cm) and weighed 213 pounds (96kg). Bogues was 40cm shorter than that average and 35kg lighter in those years.

He has remained part of the Hornets in retirement, still often representing the team at community events and travelling the world as an NBA ambassador. And he knows he changed the game, debunking the thought that someone had to have a certain height to make the NBA.

"I was just like any kid that had a dream," Bogues said.

"I just kept believing and kept having success. And my mindset was, 'If you play against the best, and you have success against the best, you need to be included with the best.'"

AP

Tech.title: Here’s Virgin Galactic’s new Apeiron spaceship
Tech.content:
is a news writer covering all things consumer tech. Stevie started out at Laptop Mag writing news and reviews on hardware, gaming, and AI.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Virgin Galactic’s new spaceship is here, dubbed “Apeiron” by popular vote from a public poll. Apeiron is the first of the company’s new Delta-class spacecraft, but it isn’t slated to launch for nearly another year. Earlier this week, Virgin Galactic announced another delay in its launch timeline:

The lead Spaceship’s first commercial spaceflight is now expected in early Q2 2027, and the second Spaceship is expected to begin commercial spaceflight operations in late Q2/early Q3 2027. The updated timeline reflects additional time for completing avionics software integration and validation, which uses an exhaustive testing process. That testing will conclude at Spaceport America as the lead Spaceship is readied for its flight test series.

Virgin Galactic had previously delayed its next commercial spaceflight to February 2027, rather than late 2026. It’s now been over two years since Virgin Galactic’s last commercial spaceflight in June 2024, when it retired its VSS Unity spacecraft. Apeiron is leaving Virgin Galactic’s Mesa, Arizona Spaceship Factory on Wednesday onboard a captive-carry flight with its Eve launch vehicle, heading to Spaceport America in New Mexico, where Virgin Galactic says its “engineering team plans to complete avionics software validation before beginning flight tests.”

Tech.title: This is how badly X wants you to pay to promote your posts
Tech.content:
is a senior reporter who’s been covering and reviewing the latest gadgets and tech since 2006, but has loved all things electronic since he was a kid.

After Elon Musk warned that “advertisers who post ads that are ugly, shrill, strident or overstate claims about their product will be barred from advertising” on X earlier this month, the platform now appears to be using a jarring animated arm that reaches across the screen to draw attention to the “promote” button while users are composing a post.

Many X users have seen and shared images of the unsettling promotional tool, including The Verge’s Tom Warren, but it doesn’t appear for everyone on the platform. The arm seems limited to verified users, or those with a paid subscription to X Premium. Reactions, unsurprisingly, have been less than positive. “I’ve never promoted a post and HATE this screen takeover,” said Sheel Mohnot, while Jesse Middleton likened it to a Halloween prank. “I wish I could explain how jarring this hand and animation was in the @X app. It was truly shocking, almost like a Halloween gag, but I’m pretty sure it was real.”

Using the paid promote feature extends the reach of an X post to a larger audience based on their location, interests, or demographics, including those not currently following a user’s account. Posts that have been promoted look like other posts on X but are branded with a “promoted” or “ad” label.

Tech.title: TikTok is going after Yelp and Google Maps with an in-app restaurant guide
Tech.content:
is features writer with five years of experience covering the companies that shape technology and the people who use their tools.

TikTok is launching an in-app restaurant guide in a challenge to other platforms like Yelp and even Google Maps.

The company on Wednesday announced the launch of Must Eat, a new section of the TikTok app built on 40 million posts, reviews, and comments about dining on the platform. The new feature uses videos and discussions of buzzy local businesses to create restaurant recommendation guides. Users can leave reviews of restaurants, call and make reservations, and search for nearby businesses on a map.

At a launch event this week, TikTok US CEO Adam Presser called Must Eat “the compilation of all of the conversation that’s happening on the TikTok platform across creators, restaurateurs, [and] individuals” who make videos or leave comments about local restaurants. Among the featured restaurants in New York are Golden Diner (home of very viral pancakes) and hard-to-reserve spots like Semma and Via Carota.

Must Eat falls somewhere between Yelp and more curated recommendations from publications like The Infatuation. Must Eat is divided into two category tabs: “everyday eats” and “elevated dining.” Users can sort and filter by rating, distance, cuisine type, and what’s currently open, and each page for a restaurant links to videos about the business posted to TikTok. Diners can also bookmark businesses to save them for later. The feature is initially available in a few select regions — New York City, Los Angeles, and the Bay Area. The company says restaurants can’t pay to be featured in the recommendation lists.

It’s not the first time TikTok has tried to bridge the gap for users between seeing a video about a place and actually visiting in person. Earlier this year, the company added the ability to book hotels and attractions through the app. That feature, TikTok Go, allowed content creators to tag and link to locations; Must Eat is an expansion of that earlier capability.

TikTok’s deeper move into the dining space is fitting, given the app’s profound impact on restaurants. Content creators have angled to become the food critics of the short-form video era, each with their own schtick or eccentricities. The popularity of food videos has even changed what restaurants put on the menu to begin with, like extra-long cheese pulls or dramatic presentations. In its press release announcing the launch of Must Eat, TikTok says 27 million US diners went to a restaurant, cafe, or shop for the first time thanks to the platform last year.

Tech.title: Inside Amazon’s Echo hardware event
Tech.content:
is a senior reviewer with over twenty years of experience. She covers smart home, IoT, and connected tech, and has written previously for Wirecutter, Wired, Dwell, BBC, and US News.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Amazon swapped its usual big fall hardware showcase this year for a series of smaller launches throughout October. So far this month, it has announced new Fire TV devices, new Kindles, the Alexa Tablet Pro 12, Ring’s first smart lock, new hardware from AI-wearable startup Bee, and new Blink 4K cameras.

Then this week, it hosted journalists at a small event in New York City’s financial district to showcase its new Echo hardware.

Panos Panay speaking to journalists at an event in New York City this week Photo: Owen Grove / The Verge

Panay next to an “exploded” version of the new Echo Show 16 smart display. Photo: Owen Grove / The Verge

He demoed the new Alexa Photo Frame with pictures of his own family Photo: Owen Grove / The Verge

Panos Panay, senior vice president of devices, Alexa, and Leo at Amazon, kicked off proceedings by explaining the company’s approach this year. “We have so many products we’re launching that are meaningful,” he said. “However, we get to this point when we do everything at once; not all your children get enough attention.” This longer rollout allows for more focus on each launch. He also teased two more launches still to come — from Ring and some “Echo on the Go” news — before explaining that today’s focus is “the most important focus we have, which is the home.”

He demoed several new software features for the Echo Show smart displays that will start on the Show 16 and trickle down to existing Show products, including dedicated home screens, an interactive 3D map view for smart home control, and a meal planning feature.

The new Echo Studio with Home Camera can act as a video calling device for a Fire TV. Photo: Owen Grove / The Verge

Panay demoed this feature by calling his parents. Photo: Owen Grove / The Verge

Panay also revealed that they have “opened up Alexa Plus’ brain a little bit more,” unlocking a new layer of understanding in the generative-AI-powered smart assistant. He pointed out that AI in the home is still relatively new, and while it’s everywhere else, from your computer to your phone, the home has been harder to unlock.

Amazon is looking to change that with Alexa’s “new brain” — an updated version of Alexa Plus with new capabilities including the ability to do “deeper research” alongside its usual use cases, such as controlling lights, setting timers, and playing music.

To manage these deeper conversations, a new “Card” interface on Show devices collects each chat. Cards also appear in the Alexa app and on Alexa.com, so you can continue chats with the assistant wherever you are.

The Echo Time is a new smart alarm clock that Panay says could replace the need to have your phone by your bed. Photo: Jennifer Pattison Tuohy / The Verge

Photo: Jennifer Pattison Tuohy / The Verge

Alexa Cards are a new feature that allows you to go back to previous conversations with the smart assistant. Photo: Jennifer Pattison Tuohy / The Verge

Panay demos the new Alexa interface on the Show (relayed to a Fire TV) Photo: Jennifer Pattison Tuohy / The Verge

Panos Panay and Ring founder Jamie Siminoff show the new map view feature on Echo Show and Fire TVs, which cleverly integrates Ring cameras. Photo: Jennifer Pattison Tuohy / The Verge

The event continued in a selection of small rooms designed to feel like home spaces, where product engineers and designers demoed the new devices and explained their features.

Read our full coverage of all the new products in our story stream.

Tech.title: Almost all of Amazon’s new Echo gear is available now
Tech.content: While not Amazon’s first bedside alarm clock, this one’s focused on helping you sleep better, and it doesn’t have a camera. It can detect your sleep stage via ultrasound and use smart alarms to ease you into the day, but only if you want it to.

Tech.title: Everything announced at Amazon’s October 2026 hardware launch
Tech.content:
Amazon had plenty of new gadgets to share at its Echo hardware event this year, along with updates to the AI-powered Alexa Plus after it became available to everyone in the US in February. But the big news this year is screens: devices with big, beautiful ones, and those that lack them entirely.

There’s the Alexa Photo Frame, which Amazon devices chief Panos Panay describes as “the world’s smartest photo frame” and that doubles as a full Alexa speaker. There’s also the new Echo Time smart alarm clock, the screenless Echo Studio with Home Camera, a fully redesigned Echo Dot, and Amazon’s latest flagship smart display, the Echo Show 16, which comes with a whopping eight woofers and can run the full Fire TV experience by touch.

Tech.title: Amazon’s new Echo line is here: the 6 biggest updates
Tech.content:
is a news writer who covers the streaming wars, consumer tech, crypto, social media, and much more. Previously, she was a writer and editor at MUO.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Amazon has just taken the wraps off a bunch of new devices as part of a string of fall announcements. Today’s news focuses largely on new Echo speakers, with a few new smart home gadgets sprinkled in.

Here’s a roundup of all of the updates Amazon revealed on Wednesday.

Photo: Jennifer Pattison Tuohy / The Verge

Amazon’s new Echo Show 16 has a 16-inch display in an anodized aluminum frame that the company says is nearly 40 percent thinner than its predecessor. There’s a new Nanomatte display option to reduce glare, along with an audio architecture with micro woofers and two tweeters for clearer audio.

The Echo Show 16 features a wide-angle 13-megapixel camera, which Amazon says offers the “widest field of view” on an Echo Show device so far. It has 20 percent more computing power and an upgraded Omnisense fusion platform, allowing Alexa to turn up the heat when the room is too cold or turn on a light when you enter the room.

The Echo Show 16 is available for preorder today and costs $499.99, with the Nanomatte option priced at $569.99.

Photo: Jennifer Pattison Tuohy / The Verge

Amazon is launching a new digital photo frame with a semi-matte, 10-inch touchscreen. The device syncs with Amazon Photos, allowing Alexa Plus to automatically pull up pictures based on who’s in it, when it was taken, and sentiment. You can also choose people you want to feature in your frame, as well as ask the device to show you specific pictures.

The Alexa Photo Frame costs $199.99 with a black frame or $229 for the birch and walnut frames.

Photo: Jennifer Pattison Tuohy / The Verge

Amazon is rolling out an upgraded Echo Dot with a built-in smart home hub that can control devices around your home without a separate hub. Like the Echo Show 16, the Echo Dot also has the company’s Omnisense fusion platform to detect room temperature and presence. It has Amazon’s custom AZ3 chip as well, along with four microphones, a new full-range driver for 50 percent more bass than the previous generation, and a built-in Eero Wi-Fi extender. You can buy the Echo Dot today in black, white, green, and pink for $99.99.

Photo: Owen Grove / The Verge

Amazon built a camera into the Echo Studio. With this update, you can tap into a livestream of the room while you’re away from home, or ask Alexa questions about something in front of the camera. As an example, Amazon says you can hold up a board game to ask about the rules, or show it a box of cereal to order a different flavor. The Echo Studio with Home Camera will soon connect with compatible Fire TVs, too, giving you the ability to hold video calls on a larger screen.

The Echo Studio with Home Camera is available in black for $249.99, while its optional stand costs $39.99.

Photo: Jennifer Pattison Tuohy / The Verge

Amazon has revealed the Echo Time, a smart alarm clock with a circular, 3.2-inch touchscreen that you can customize with different clockfaces and layouts.

The Echo Time offers an optional smart alarm feature that can wake you up when you’re in a lighter sleep — 10 to 60 minutes before your alarm — rather than at the exact time you want to wake up. It uses Amazon’s Omnisense technology to determine when to wake you up based on temperature and presence. The display also adjusts throughout the day, gradually brightening in the morning before dimming at night.

The Echo Time is available today for $199.99 in black, white, and pink, while a Kids Echo Time starts at $209.99. There’s also an adjustable stand available for $39.99.

Photo: Jennifer Pattison Tuohy / The Verge

A new Alexa Home Map feature creates an interactive 3D map of the inside and outside of your home. It displays your Echo devices, Ring and Blink cameras, Fire TV, lights, locks, thermostats, and other smart home devices, which you can control directly through the map.

Amazon says you can create a map by entering your home address, scanning each room with a compatible iPhone, and then placing each smart home device. You can access your map in the Ring app, too, where you can view live animations of people and cars outside your home.

Alexa Home Map is rolling out in preview later this year on iOS in the Alexa Home Map, Alexa, and Ring apps. It’s also coming to larger Echo Show devices, the Ember Artline Fire TV, and new Alexa Tablets.

Tech.title: Voters in Texas agree: They hate data centers
Tech.content:
Ask Texas NAACP president Gary Bledsoe what it’s been like to see data center developers descend upon Austin and its surrounding suburbs and he can rattle off project after project facing opposition from locals.

There’s the fight in Taylor over plans to build a data center at a site that’s supposed to be a park. Temple, around 40 miles away, is another sore spot, Bledsoe says. The mayor and City Council members there face recall attempts over data center developments. And some 30 miles outside of Austin, San Marcos became the first city in all of Texas to ban data centers.

Nowhere in the world are data centers growing more explosively than in Texas. With the midterm elections looming, the data center fight “is the issue in Texas,” says Bledsoe. The state’s NAACP recently joined dozens of other groups across the political spectrum to form a coalition to stop — or at least stall — data center construction. Their grievances are just as diverse as their membership: concerns about how much water the industry consumes in a state as dry as Texas, qualms about tax subsidies, and objections to new gas plants and wind farms built to meet rising electricity demand. Together, Bledsoe estimates the coalition — named We the People Texas — represents as many as 1 million voters across the state.

If there’s one thing a broad range of voters can agree on this election season, it’s that they hate data centers and are unhappy with the status quo. A majority of Texans — 57 percent — oppose the construction of data centers, an August poll found. That included 43 percent of Republicans, 75 percent of Democrats, and 54 percent of independents.

“We have almost nothing in common in so many other ways. And yet you get us in the room with this issue, and it’s like a wall”

After initially proclaiming his state the “epicenter of AI development,” Texas Gov. Greg Abbott is now fighting for reelection against underdog Democrat Gina Hinojosa, who is seen as having a rare shot at taking a reliably red state. The state’s high-profile Senate race is no less of a nail-biter, with Republican Attorney General Ken Paxton running neck and neck against Democrat James Talarico. In each race, candidates have to win over voters who think data centers are coming for their water, land, and livelihoods. Republican and Democratic hopefuls alike are trying to distance themselves from an industry that’s taken deep root in the state — and so far, voters aren’t buying it.

“You’re talking about Democrats, libertarians, independents, Republicans, all in one fight … we have almost nothing in common in so many other ways. And yet you get us in the room with this issue, and it’s like a wall … fighting one big enemy,” says Jet Parker, who cofounded a group called Save Rural Texas that is now part of the We the People Texas coalition.

Save Rural Texas came together this year after a local county commissioners’ meeting about plans to build a new data center in the Texoma area that borders Oklahoma. Residents, including Parker, successfully delayed that project. That victory led Parker, a corporate coach and speaker, to write up a handbook for other communities trying to block data center projects, and she now spends much of her time traveling around the state to train grassroots groups.

She’s got a warning for Republicans: If they keep backing data centers, they’ll lose Texas. “You just pissed off a lot of people in rural Texas who are supposed to carry you across the [finish] line,” Parker says.

Abbott is in particularly hot water. “You brung it, so you dance with it. That’s Texas talk, you know,” Parker says. “That’s what Abbott’s done, but we’re the ones having to dance with it … we didn’t want to be in the dance at all.”

For years, however, Texas has taken among the most welcoming stances toward data centers in the country. The state passed a sales and use tax exemption for data centers in 2013 under former Gov. Rick Perry. In 2015, Abbott expanded the exemption to include hyperscale data centers, which can span millions of square feet and house tens of thousands of GPUs. As a result, qualifying data center developers don’t have to pay state taxes on equipment and electricity for up to 20 years. That essentially rolled out the red carpet for companies that need abundant electricity to power energy-hungry data centers.

Since then data centers have had a massive growth spurt in order to support new generative AI models — and that’s costing the state. The tax exemption was initially expected to cost taxpayers $14.6 million in 2014 and 2015. But in 2025, state officials estimated that the tax break would lead to $3.2 billion in lost sales tax revenue over two years.

“You brung it, so you dance with it.”

The state’s energy woes go further than that. Electricity bills have grown by 35.4 percent on average over the past five years as demand rises and utilities build expensive new infrastructure to meet that demand. Bledsoe is concerned about air pollution for communities around new gas plants. Data center electricity demand could erase decades of air quality gains in Texas, one recent study found. Parker, meanwhile, can’t stand solar and wind farms built near farmland. Neither wants to see new transmission lines snaking through their communities.

Data centers can also put pressure on already stressed water supplies, especially in a drought-prone state like Texas. While they can reuse water used on-site to cool servers, the larger part of data centers’ water footprint comes from electricity use. Data center proposals have driven a surge of gas and nuclear power projects, both of which need a lot of water for their own cooling systems.

Data center electricity demand could increase nearly tenfold by 2030, the state’s largest grid operator estimates. Meanwhile, data centers in Texas consumed about 25 billion gallons of water last year, around 0.4 percent of total water use, according to the Houston Advanced Research Center (HARC). By 2030, that figure could grow to up to 2.7 percent of the state’s total annual water use, HARC estimates. And water consumption can be much higher when zooming into certain communities. Another study by the University of Texas at Austin estimated that data center water use statewide could rise to as high as 9 percent by 2040.

Virginia has historically been the state with the most data centers, but it’s running out of space. Virginia still beats Texas 287 to 170 when it comes to the number of planned data center projects as of April, according to Pew Research. But as data centers get bigger, they’re moving out of cities and into rural areas — particularly in Texas. Data center capacity is typically measured by how much power it draws, and in this measure, Texas already takes the crown with 26GW of existing and under-construction capacity compared to 13GW in Virginia.

Facing backlash to data centers, Abbott has changed his tune. In June, he directed the state Public Utility Commission to require that data center operators cover the costs of new infrastructure built to serve them. Since then, he has also announced statewide moratoriums on permits for data center projects pending audits on their electricity and water use. He’s also said that he would support a repeal of the sales tax exemption for data centers and greater oversight of data centers’ water and electricity use.

Even so, he’s reportedly taken millions in campaign contributions from data center interests, and We the People Texas coalition members are not convinced he’s turned the page. “Is he doing enough? Absolutely not,” Parker says.

The NAACP sent a letter to Abbott’s office last month criticizing his moratoriums for not going far enough because the state is only auditing projects that connect to the power grid. However, more so than any other state, Texas has data centers building their own power supply on-site, without needing to connect to the grid. Bledsoe’s concerned that these private energy projects will be subject to less regulatory scrutiny, while also harming air quality in nearby neighborhoods. Projects that already have permits are still being built. And an October investigation by advocacy group Public Citizen and FracTracker found public records indicating that state agencies are still processing permits for data centers, although Abbott’s office denies that they have issued any approvals since he directed them to pause permitting. To Bledsoe and other coalition members, he says, the temporary moratorium looks like “an attempt to run out the clock before the election.”

Data center hyperscalers including AWS, Microsoft, Google, Meta, and others have formed their own trade group called the Data Center Coalition (DCC). For what it’s worth, DCC isn’t endorsing any candidates. But in an interview with The Verge, Jess Heck, the group’s director of Texas government affairs, says, “It’s very clear that our members share the same goals as Gov. Abbott and the legislature. We want to be true partners, good neighbors in every Texas community where we operate.” Heck didn’t confirm whether any of its members are providing any campaign support for Abbott.

“An attempt to run out the clock before the election”

Eduardo Leal, press secretary for Abbott’s campaign, said in an email to The Verge that “Under [Abbott’s] standards, data centers must pay for their own electric infrastructure, add power instead of only adding demand, reuse their own water, reduce the cost of electricity for Texans, not disrupt residential neighborhoods, and eliminate reliance on outdated taxpayer-funded incentives.”

Abbott signed a state Senate bill into law last year that directs the Public Utility Commission of Texas to reassess how it allocates transmission costs in order to keep rates from rising disproportionately for residential customers. And this June, he proposed more measures to force companies to cover the costs of infrastructure upgrades needed to serve their data centers.

Abbott’s biggest competitor, state Rep. Gina Hinojosa, has eked out a narrow lead recently in some polls after strengthening her language against data centers — calling for a moratorium on development until the state legislature passes more protections. “I think her campaign has made a ton of inroads into moderate Republican communities because of her stance on data centers,” says Anthony Elmo, public education funding defender for Good Jobs First, which recently cofounded another coalition pushing for data center reforms in Texas alongside other advocacy groups.

Hinojosa has skyrocketed from a relatively obscure local official to a serious contender for the governor’s seat, largely on a populist message that caters to residents’ frustration with Big Tech companies grabbing land for data centers. Even so, she might not be convincing enough for conservative rural voters.

Candidates from both sides of the aisle were pretty soft on data centers up until the party conventions earlier this year, says Miriam Cobb, who cofounded the Texas Coalition Against Data Centers earlier this year (which is also part of We the People Texas). Texans can see the political posturing from Hinojosa, too, she says. One of Hinojosa’s major donors has been the International Brotherhood of Electrical Workers, which recently formed an “American Infrastructure Alliance” with OpenAI and data center developers.

“[Voters] know she wasn’t against it from a place of understanding or sincerity, it’s something she knows she has to say now,” Cobb tells The Verge, adding that she’ll be writing in an independent candidate come Election Day. Even with many conservatives — some of them now claiming to be single-issue voters on data centers — skeptical of both parties’ candidates, Cobb still expects Republicans to lose seats.

Paxton, the Republican candidate for Senate, is attempting to atone for his previous support of data centers. He voted for the sales tax exemptions as a state senator in 2013, although he now says he’d support a repeal. In September, he announced an investigation into hundreds of data centers’ water use. Paxton also launched an investigation into the case in Taylor over whether it’s legal for land deeded for parkland to be developed into a data center. And he’s aligned himself with Abbott’s proposals to impose stronger light and noise restrictions on data centers, limit construction in rural areas, and push developers to cover the costs of new energy infrastructure. But he also reportedly received hundreds of thousands of dollars in campaign funding this year from data center interests.

“Trump keeps saying, you know, ‘Let them in, let them in, let them in’”

While the Senate race between Talarico and Paxton is in the national spotlight over the prospect of a Democrat flipping the seat, it’s probably less important for Texans concerned most about data centers, advocates tell The Verge. The race is too politically polarized to flip voters on the single issue, Cobb says, and neither candidate has given a very convincing position on how to rein in data centers anyway. Neither campaign responded to press inquiries from The Verge.

Working at the federal level, the best thing the senator-elect could do would be to push back against President Donald Trump’s data center agenda and ensure Texas can moderate data center development without interference, she says.

“We want assurances that you’re gonna let us deal with it instead of what’s been happening, where Trump keeps saying, you know, ‘Let them in, let them in, let them in,’” Cobb tells The Verge.

Cobb still sees construction traffic clogging two-lane rural roads leading to data center projects that have avoided Abbott’s partial moratorium. Residents are worried about the traffic jams blocking emergency vehicles, especially when fire weather kicks up. In some areas, Texans have seen property values drop, she adds. Farmers are giving up land that their families have tended to for generations. In other neighborhoods, an influx of new workers arriving for the data center “gold rush” is exacerbating housing shortages and making rent more unaffordable for locals. In either case, data center opposition coalition members say they’re worried about a loss of culture.

“It’s not for nothing,” Cobb says. “They have real community … and now they’re losing it.”

Tech.title: Amazon debuts the Alexa Photo Frame and Echo Time smart clock, plus other upgraded devices
Tech.content:
Amazon unveiled five new Alexa devices today, including two new kinds of hardware: the Alexa Photo Frame, a smart picture frame, and the Echo Time, a smart alarm clock.

The Alexa Photo Frame is Amazon’s foray into the world of digital photo displays, a product category that has transcended from a clunky, last-minute holiday gift to a sleek, attractive way to look through your camera roll.

Aura is responsible for much of the growth in this category, so it’s no coincidence that the Alexa Photo Frame has a similar aesthetic feel: The screen is much easier on the eyes than the old, bright photo frames from years past. The device is said to be specifically calibrated for sharing photos, featuring a semi-matte, anti-glare display that makes it look more like a Samsung Frame TV than a laptop screen.

Also like Aura, the Photo Frame’s 10-inch screen looks like matte photograph, helping it blend in with other artwork on your wall.

Amazon’s new device, though, adds the value of integration with users’ existing Amazon accounts. Prime members get unlimited storage on Amazon Photos, and Alexa+ is supposed to intelligently choose how and when to display photos.

“It knows to choose photos where you’re smiling and the lighting is right, and it matches the season you’re in, so you see last year’s family Halloween costumes in October instead of the middle of spring. It also knows what to skip, like screenshots and receipts,” Amazon said in a press release. You can also add voice notes to photos, and images sync automatically as you take them.

The Alexa Photo Frame is on sale now, and starts at $199.99 in Black, and $229 in Birch or Walnut wood.

Image Credits:Amazon /

Meanwhile, the Echo Time clock seems to be a response to the growing sentiment that people don’t want to rely on their phones for alarms, setting morning reminders or checking the weather.

“Millions of customers start and end their days with Alexa—checking the weather and turning on the lights from bed in the morning or winding down with white noise at night,” Amazon wrote. “But the bedroom asks for something different from a device than the kitchen or living room does—so we designed an Echo specifically for it.”

Amazon says that the Echo Time, which costs $199.99, or $209.99 for a Kids version, has opt-in sleep sensing tools. You can choose to set a smart alarm feature that wakes you up anywhere between 10 to 60 minutes of your alarm, and can wake you when it detects you’re in a lighter phase of sleep, so that it’s less jarring to begin your day.

Like the popular Hatch alarm clocks, the clock can also mimic sunrise features to ease you awake.

Image Credits:Amazon /

Amazon also showed off updates to its existing lines of devices. We now get the Echo Show 16, a new Echo Dot, and Echo Studio with Home Camera.

The biggest upgrade to the Echo Dot is that it now includes a built-in smart home hub, which also includes an eero Wi-Fi extender that adds up to 1,000 square feet of coverage, helping it connect to lights, locks, and thermostats around your home. The new Echo Dot is also powered by Amazon’s custom AZ3 silicon chip, which is said to make it better at on-device processing to speed up conversations with its AI, Alexa+.

Amazon says its most advanced speaker, however, is the Echo Studio with Home Camera. This speaker doubles as a camera so you can check on your home while you’re out, and also has visual intelligence features.

“Alexa can also see and understand what’s in front of the camera and help you in real time,” Amazon explained. “Pull out a board game box and ask Alexa+ to explain the rules or hold up a cereal box and Alexa can recognize it and help you reorder more flavors.”

The Echo Dot is available at $99.99, and the Echo Studio with Home Camera costs $249.99.

Finally, Amazon unveiled the new Echo Show 16, which includes a 16-inch display. Amazon says the device has a 10% larger viewing area than its predecessor, but with a 40% smaller frame. It has Fire TV built in, plus Smart Home tools like Family Organizer. It can also function like a digital photo frame.

The Echo Show 16 is available for pre-order for $499.99.

Tech.title: TikTok expands into restaurant guides with ‘Must Eat’ feature
Tech.content:
In Brief

TikTok has long been a go-to place for discovering new spots, with viral videos helping local restaurants attract new customers. Now, TikTok is making it easier for users to find their next favorite restaurant with a new feature called “Must Eat.”

Introduced Wednesday, the community-driven guide highlights restaurants getting attention on the platform, bringing food recommendations from across the U.S. into one place.

The move puts TikTok in more direct competition with platforms like Yelp and Google Maps. But instead of relying mainly on search results, maps, and traditional reviews, TikTok is building on what it already does well: connecting people with restaurants through recommendations shared by other users.

“Must Eat” uses more than 40 million posts and comments to pull restaurant recommendations and curated lists together in one place. Users can browse restaurants by city and filter results by cuisine, price, rating, and location, making it easier to compare options before heading out.

The recommendations are split into two categories: “Everyday Eats,” featuring casual favorites and neighborhood go-tos, and “Elevated Dining,” highlighting restaurants for celebrations, special occasions, or a night out.

Additionally, select restaurants can be booked directly through TikTok via OpenTable.

The feature is launching first in New York City, Los Angeles, and San Francisco. Users can find it through the search bar, the Local feed, restaurant pages, and location links attached to videos featuring participating restaurants.

Tech.title: Meta has a new AI pet app called Waddle World
Tech.content:
Continuing its fast-paced experiments with AI apps, Meta has now launched a new app called Waddle World, which essentially looks like a Tamagotchi clone, but with AI. The might be a test, but it could very well be a precursor to the company’s Tamagotchi-like gadget powered by Muse.

The company has launched Waddle World in the Philippines on both iOS and Android. The app, spotted by social media consultant Matt Navarra, lets you pick and grow a virtual pet, feed it, and play with it.

We have reached out to Meta for a comment on wider availability, and will update this piece if we hear back.

Basically, Tamagotchi meets ChatGPT.



Another interesting experiment from Meta as it explores AI companions.



Would you use this? 👀



📱 iOS:https://t.co/Z0mh1ggx9q



🤖 Android:https://t.co/isq6HnwoxE pic.twitter.com/4cuklTNB8v — Matt Navarra (@MattNavarra) October 27, 2026

Meta’s description of the app indicates that it doesn’t want the app to be a habit builder. The company’s page also says that the app is not a chatbot, and is flagged as suitable for users older than 18.

“Waddle World is a cozy 16-bit world where your pixel pet lives. Hatch a virtual pet, visit whenever you like, and let it get to know you. No pressure, no streaks to protect, no scores to chase — just a warm little escape in the cracks of your day,” the app’s description reads.

“Not a chatbot. Not an assistant. Not a productivity tool. It’s a pet, and a place. Stay two minutes or twenty — it’ll be happy either way.”

The app also doubles as a journal, letting users describe their day through voice or text. The pet listens to the user and writes up the note in its own voice as an entry with a doodle. The app also features mini-games that you can play over a few minutes, and can send you a weekly email based on what it learned about you.

Meta may be wanting to stay away from building companion apps, given companies like Character.AI and OpenAI have faced lawsuits that allege their products caused harm to teenagers.

Until now, the social media giant has released AI-centric apps like Pocket, which lets you vibe-code games, and Vibes, which let you quickly generate videos.

Besides virtual pets, some companies have also tried making hardware AI pets.

Tech.title: Free Fire returns to India as Garena launches localized version four years after ban
Tech.content:
More than four years after New Delhi banned Free Fire over national security concerns, Garena has brought the popular battle royale game back to India with a localized version.

On Wednesday, Garena launched the localized version, called Free Fire India, as a standalone game available on Android and iOS. The new version features India-specific content, parental controls, playtime limits, and spending caps, with user data hosted on servers in India, the firm owned by South Asian giant Sea said. The launch comes more than three years after Garena quietly postponed Free Fire India’s earlier release after announcing it in September 2023.

Free Fire was one of India’s most popular mobile games before it was banned in February 2022 alongside 53 other apps over alleged links to China. The game had become more popular after India banned its rival PUBG Mobile in September 2020. Free Fire’s ban, however, sent shares of Singapore-based Sea, Garena’s parent company, tumbling, wiping more than $16 billion off its market value in a single day. Still, Garena remained active in India. Free Fire MAX, an enhanced version of the game, was not among the banned apps and remained available to players.

PUBG Mobile’s South Korean publisher Krafton later introduced Battlegrounds Mobile India (BGMI), a version similar to PUBG Mobile but made specifically for Indian players. But BGMI has struggled to match the popularity of Garena’s Free Fire franchise. In June, the franchise had about 77.4 million monthly active users in India, compared with 20.8 million for BGMI, according to Sensor Tower data reviewed by TechCrunch.

Vaibhav Das Mundhra, Garena’s head of operations in India, told TechCrunch that Free Fire MAX would remain available alongside Free Fire India. Players will be able to use the same account across both games, play together and take part in the same events, he said.

Garena, Mundhra said, had worked with relevant Indian government authorities and incorporated their feedback while preparing Free Fire India for launch. However, he did not answer questions about why the game’s planned 2023 launch was delayed or what had changed to allow its release now.

While Free Fire India’s launch remained on hold, TechCrunch earlier reported that Garena continued developing games for the Indian market. Through its studios in Pune and Mumbai, the company worked on titles inspired by Hindu mythology, cricket, and the traditional board game Ludo, releasing some of them while the original Free Fire remained banned. One of those titles, Versus, was previously available in early access on Google Play but is no longer listed on the store.

Despite regulatory setbacks, India remains a significant market for mobile gaming companies. Mobile game downloads in the country grew 14.2% quarter-over-quarter to 2 billion in Q2, while revenue rose 3.7% to more than $106 million, per Sensor Tower.

Garena’s Free Fire MAX has also maintained a presence in India’s esports scene, with Indian teams including S8UL Esports, Apex Gaming, and Total Gaming competing at the Esports World Cup 2026.

Animesh Agarwal, co-founder and CEO of S8UL Esports, said Free Fire India’s return could open up more opportunities for players and creators. “For me, the real impact goes beyond the game itself. It’s about the players who dream of building a career in esports, the creators who have built communities around the title, and the opportunities this ecosystem can create for everyone involved,” he said.

Tech.title: Kodiak lands first commercial deal to supply driverless trucks for public highways
Tech.content:
Kodiak AI will deliver 75 self-driving trucks to freight company DTL Transport starting in 2028. It’s the company’s first binding commercial deal for driverless big rigs that will run on public highways.

The contract, announced Wednesday, comes just ahead of Kodiak’s next big milestone: pulling human safety operators out of the cab to begin operating a driverless highway service in December. The company, which went public in September 2025, plans to launch that service by carrying goods for Ikea on Interstate 45 between Dallas and Houston.

DTL Transport, a California mid-market trucking company that hauls fresh produce and goods to grocery chains, plans to use the self-driving trucks on multiple interstate highway routes, starting with Dallas to El Paso, Texas, and Interstate 20 between Dallas and Atlanta. Kodiak has already conducted testing and operations on those two routes.

“One of the things that we love about mid-market carriers (like DTL) is that they are able to move with fast execution speed, much more at the speed of a startup or a small company or a tech company like Kodiak, and that they just want to get stuff done,” Kodiak founder and CEO Don Burnette told TechCrunch in an exclusive interview. “It’s easier for them to integrate into their fleet because they’re not as large, and we think that this is a real turning point for the self-driving industry in general.”

The contract should give Kodiak a revenue boost and a positive benchmark. Its shares have fallen 87% from their opening-day price. It also puts Kodiak on a path to become an “asset-light” technology supplier, meaning it would sell its technology rather than own and run trucks itself — a goal it shares with competitor Aurora Innovation.

Today, Kodiak has a number of customers under a Trucking-as-a-Service (TaaS) model, including Charger USA, Roehl Transport, and Werner Enterprises. Under this business model, Kodiak owns and operates the self-driving trucks as a third-party carrier on behalf of other companies. It currently carries freight for these companies on a few routes in Texas. Kodiak generates revenue carrying freight daily for these companies on three active routes, but Burnette described these operations as still being in pilot stage.

Ultimately, Kodiak wants to move to a Driver-as-a-Service (DaaS) model, in which customers own and operate the trucks. Kodiak licenses its technology, charging customers by the mile for the duration of the contract. DTL is Kodiak’s first on-highway DaaS customer, a relationship that was forged during a pilot program last month in California. In that pilot, Kodiak autonomously hauled perishable goods for DTL about 225 miles along Interstate 5 and California State Route 99 between Fresno, California, and Los Angeles, with a human safety operator behind the wheel.

“You have to prove out the technology first using your own truck, show them that it works, show them that it’s safe, show them that it integrates,” Burnette said, describing the Trucking-as-a-Service model. “And then we want to be asset light. We don’t want to be in the business of running a trucking company.”

Atlas Energy Solutions has been a Driver-as-a-Service customer since 2024. Technically, Atlas was Kodiak’s first customer under a binding commercial contract, but its driverless trucks operate in off-road settings in West Texas’ remote Permian Basin. Atlas currently owns and operates 35 driverless trucks equipped with Kodiak’s self-driving system. Burnette said Kodiak is on track to have as many as 100 in service there by mid-2027.

Kodiak didn’t reveal the value of the deal with DTL Transport. However, its public 2025 investor presentation offers some clues about the contract’s potential value.

In that document, Kodiak forecast annual recurring revenue of $150,000 to $190,000 per truck. That forecast rests on several assumptions, including a per-mile licensing fee of about $0.97 (in line with current human driver costs per mile), annual mileage of about 225,000 miles a year per truck, and other factors.

Assuming those projections bear out, the deal with DTL Transport could generate at least about $11.2 million in annual recurring revenue once all 75 trucks are delivered.
