Tech.title: Jio shares surge 21% in market debut after blockbuster India IPO
Tech.content:
Jio Platforms, billionaire Mukesh Ambani’s Indian telecom and digital services unit backed by Meta and Google, surged 21% in its stock market debut on Wednesday after raising $3.2 billion in India’s largest and most subscribed IPO, which attracted more than $77 billion in investor bids.

The shares opened at ₹1,358 (about $14) apiece, up from their IPO price of ₹1,119 (around $12). That valued Jio at around ₹12.5 trillion (around $131.9 billion), making it India’s second-most valuable listed company after its parent, Reliance Industries, which is worth about ₹16 trillion (around $168.6 billion). In 2020, when Meta and Google invested, Jio was valued at up to ₹4.91 trillion (about $65 billion at the time).

The offering, which ran from October 21 to 22, drew bids for 22.19 times the shares on sale, according to exchange data. More than 13.8 million people applied. That made it India’s most subscribed stock offering on record, reflecting strong investor demand for shares in the country’s largest telecom operator.

In 2016, Jio entered what was then a crowded Indian telecom market, offering free data and low-cost services. That helped it quickly win customers from established operators including Bharti Airtel, Vodafone Idea, and state-owned BSNL. It has since become the country’s largest telecom operator. Akash Ambani (pictured above), Jio Platforms’ managing director, said at Wednesday’s listing ceremony that its platforms serve more than 540 million customers. Jio’s prices are now broadly in line with those of its rivals’, but its business has expanded into broadband, cloud services, and AI.

Akash, Mukesh Ambani’s eldest son, has taken on a larger role in Jio as his father gradually hands more responsibility to the next generation of Reliance’s leadership. At the listing ceremony, he said he wants Jio to become a global technology company. “My dream is that one day, when the world counts its great technology companies, one of them will be from India, and that company will be called Jio Platforms Limited,” he said.

Jio made ₹300.5 billion (about $3.2 billion) in profit on revenue of ₹1.47 trillion (around $15.5 billion) in the fiscal year ended March 2026, with both figures up about 15% from a year earlier. In the June quarter, Jio’s revenue grew nearly 12% and profit rose 9%.

From the IPO proceeds, Jio plans to use up to ₹275 billion (about $2.9 billion) to repay debt at its telecom subsidiary, Reliance Jio Infocomm, with the remainder going toward general corporate purposes. Jio had total borrowings of ₹613.7 billion (around $6.5 billion) as of June 30.

Jio drew billions of dollars from American investors during the COVID-19 pandemic in 2020. Meta, then known as Facebook, invested $5.7 billion, while Google put in $4.5 billion. General Atlantic, Silver Lake, and Vista Equity Partners were among the other investors that backed the company. None sold shares in the IPO, which consisted entirely of newly issued shares.

Tech.title: VCs will make billions on Anthropic’s IPO, but Amazon is set to make much (much) more
Tech.content:
Many investors stand to win big when Anthropic goes public. Stakes held by firms including Menlo Ventures, Sequoia, Sound Ventures, and Spark Capital are expected to return billions.

Yet according to Anthropic’s S-1, none of those VC firms owns 5%, the threshold for being included in the principal stockholders’ table. That’s highly unusual. In a typical tech IPO, lead venture investors hold double-digit-percentage stakes in the startups they backed. The reason is Anthropic’s size. At its $965 billion private valuation, a 1% stake is worth nearly $10 billion, so, for example, Menlo’s roughly $14 billion position is only about 1.5% of the company, according to recently reported Bloomberg figures.

While the venture firms may lack sizable percentage stakes, Anthropic sold large stakes to strategic partners, companies that are also its business partners. Indeed, Amazon is likely the single largest financial beneficiary of the IPO.

Amazon first backed Anthropic in 2023 with a commitment to invest up to $4 billion in the AI company. Since then, Amazon has poured billions more into Anthropic. Instead of taking stock upfront, Amazon structured much of its investment as convertible notes, a type of debt that converts into shares upon an IPO or sale.

According to the S-1, Amazon holds convertible notes with $6.2 billion in principal outstanding as of June 30. That is Anthropic’s entire debt load. But as Anthropic’s valuation soared across successive funding rounds, the shares those notes will convert into became far more valuable. Amazon’s own filings valued its note holdings at $97.9 billion as of June 30.

As the value of Amazon’s convertible notes surged, Anthropic had to record the growing value of what it owes on its books. It reported the adjustments on its income statement under “change in fair value of convertible notes, derivative liabilities, and SAFEs,” a line that totaled $72.4 billion for the first half of 2026. The charge is non-cash, meaning no money left the company.

Amazon’s notes could convert into as many as 1.84 billion shares, according to the S-1. But a cap limits Amazon to 12% of Anthropic’s “partially diluted” share count, a figure that counts some shares not yet issued, such as stock options. Amazon can waive the cap. Notes that can’t convert will stay outstanding and convert in later quarters, subject to the same limit.

But the notes are only part of Amazon’s holdings. It further invested $10 billion in nonvoting preferred stock (a type of equity), in the second quarter, according to Amazon’s quarterly report for the period ended June 30. Amazon did this by investing $5 billion in each of Anthropic’s last two funding rounds. Combined with the $8 billion it invested in the notes from 2023 through 2025, that brings Amazon’s total investment to about $18 billion.

Beyond its stock gains, Amazon will also continue to earn significant revenue from Anthropic, which has committed to spend at least $110 billion on AWS over the next 10 years.

Google, too, is set for a major windfall from both the listing and its cloud computing deals with Anthropic. The search giant held about 14% of Anthropic as of early last year, according to court filings that were reported by The New York Times, and has invested more since, including $10 billion in April. (Google was likely diluted in subsequent and massive funding rounds, with PitchBook analyst Harrison Rolfes telling TechCrunch he estimates its current stake at closer to 5.6%.) It has also secured at least $114 billion in cloud commitments from the Anthropic through 2033.

While VCs set for massive paydays have little reason to complain, the S-1 makes it clear that the biggest winners of Anthropic’s IPO may well be tech giants like Amazon, which backed a would-be rival early on and now sell it much of the computing power it runs on.

The S-1 itself warns that some of those cloud providers also build rival AI models and that they may not always want the same things that Anthropic does.

Tech.title: What’s the Best Kindle of 2026 (So Far)?
Tech.content:
Comparing Our Favorite Kindles

What Are the Newest Kindles?

Amazon recently announced a whole new generation of Kindles is coming, with every model getting a new version. I'll update this guide with thoughts as I review each new model. Here are the current details:

Kindle is also releasing a handful of new accessories, including the Kindle Click ($35) Bluetooth remote that will work with Kindle models as early as 2024, a Page Turn Cover ($80) that will only work with the Paperwhite and Colorsoft Signature Editions, a Charging Dock ($60) designed to work with the pogo pins on the Signature Editions, and new Kindle covers in a variety of colors and textures. I’m most excited about the remote; I will update this guide and our Best Kindle Accessories guide with my notes as I test.

Why Are Kindles More Expensive Now?

Amazon raised its prices across its product categories, including Kindle devices. The price increases hit several current Kindle models, leaving only Kindle Scribe models with their original price tags. Amazon declined to comment to WIRED, but a spokesperson told CNET the price hikes were due to rising costs in memory and storage components. Interestingly, none of the more powerful Scribe models needed a price update, but it’s also a relief since all three of those models are significantly more expensive than a regular Kindle.

Here are all the increases, including for the Signature versions:

If you have your eyes on one of these Kindles, I’d wait until Black Friday to shop, as they'll likely be on sale.

What About the New Kindle Scribes?

Kindle has three new Kindle Scribes that launched between late 2025 and June 2026. There are now the Kindle Scribe ($500), Kindle Scribe Colorsoft ($630), and the Kindle Scribe Without Front Light ($430). All three have a similar design and software experience, though the Scribe Colorsoft has a color screen and a shorter battery life—only eight weeks of reading time, compared to 12 weeks on the $500 Scribe and an impressive 16 weeks on the Scribe Without Front Light.

All three models have a new, taller design with an 11-inch screen, a slightly slimmer form factor, and an updated stylus. They both also have a quad-core chip, a new homepage, and will support a variety of AI features, including AI search (along with some AI tools for summarizing books you’re reading without giving spoilers, though those won’t arrive until next year). Users can connect to Google Drive and Microsoft OneDrive to mark up documents, which the older model can’t do.

Overall, I’d say they’re good devices, but as long as the cheaper second-generation Kindle Scribe is available, I think it’s the better buy. It has some AI capabilities but no AI search, and has a different homepage design that matches a classic Kindle rather than the notebook-forward design seen on the new ones. Amazon said it’ll get the same homepage this year, but I haven’t seen it so far. I’m disappointed these new devices are so much more expensive; at that price, you might as well shop reMarkable’s line of digital notebooks and get better features and accessories.

Accessories for Easier Reading

Ever had an e-reading session so long that you get hand cramps? These accessories might help. You can check out more options in our Best Kindle Accessories guide.

There are two receptacles built into it, one of which is big enough for my larger mugs. I usually drop a snack or my phone into the other one. Photograph: Nena Farrell Save to wishlist Save to wishlist Lamicall Gooseneck iPad Holder $23 $20 (13% off) Amazon $32 Shop This gooseneck tablet holder does a great job of holding up your Kindle by clamping onto something nearby, like your bed frame or a table. It’s 3 feet tall and has plenty of length to work in various spots.

Cases and Covers

Amazon Kindles are, thankfully, not as fragile as a pricey smartphone, but you may still want to add a cover to protect the screen if you’re frequently toting it around in a bag. These aren’t padded for serious drops, but they are some of the best Kindle cases I’ve found for daily protection from scratches and scuffs. Also, don’t forget that the Kids’ editions come with cases, so if you’re buying one of those, you won’t need to buy a case.

Photograph: Nena Farrell Chevron Chevron Save to wishlist Save to wishlist Moko Blue Twill Kindle Case $26 Amazon If you’re looking for a full cover and a strap, this option has it all. This case only comes in blue, but it fully covers the front of your Kindle. When you open it, that cover has a built-in hand strap. It also has a little stand built into it, too, so it can stand up on its own for you to read. Photograph: Nena Farrell Save to wishlist Save to wishlist PopSockets PopCase Kindle and PopGrip $40 PopSockets (Kindle Case) $30 PopSockets (PopGrip) PopSockets came out with its own line of Kindle cases that have a built-in MagSafe adapter, so you can more easily add your PopSocket grip of choice. There are matching sets of cases and grips you can shop for, or you can mix and match as you please.

About Those Older Kindles

Amazon usually takes a few years between new Kindle models. Whenever a new one arrives, its predecessor’s stock starts to dwindle. It’s not that I don’t recommend these older models per se, but I only suggest them if you they're on sale for the right price. And don’t buy too old a model, since Amazon has started pulling support for older Kindles.

Before making your purchase, cross-check the price against the latest model to make sure you’re paying a fair amount less for the older device.

Kindle (2022, 11th Generation): This is the smallest of the lot at 6.2 inches tall and 4.3 inches wide, with a 6-inch screen. If you find tablets too cumbersome to hold with one hand, consider this one, with 16 GB of storage and a 300 pixels per inch (PPI) resolution. It’s tough to find, and I usually don’t see it for less than $75 these days.

Kindle Paperwhite (2021, 11th Generation): This is the next step up from the basic model. It has a bright 6.8-inch screen with adjustable warm lighting, a fast page-turn rate, a USB-C port, and 16 gigs of storage. It’s waterproof, too. I like the Signature Edition, which also includes auto-adjust brightness and 32 GBs of storage. I don’t recommend spending more than $100 on this one.

Kindle Scribe (1st Generation): The original Scribe is a great option for note-takers. It has a giant 10.2-inch screen for taking notes, marking up PDFs, or drawing, and numerous paper formats you can choose, like college-ruled or dotted. It also comes with the Basic Pen, which feels natural to write with and attaches to the side of the Scribe magnetically. It’s only worth it for $230 or less, and I often see it for below $200 on eBay.

Kindle Kids (2022): This is an older kid-friendly model. It comes with a cover, a year’s subscription to Amazon Kids+, parental controls, and a two-year warranty, but the fact that it’s only available secondhand means you’ll likely miss out on the subscription window and may or may not still have a cover. Ideally, you won't spend more than $70 on this one.

Kindle Paperwhite Kids (2021): This older Paperwhite version is a step up from the previous basic Kids models. It has a high-resolution 300-ppi display with an adjustable warm screen and is also waterproof. You shouldn’t spend more than $110 on this one if you can find it at all. (I couldn't find any resellers for this older model at the time of writing.)

If you’re trying to figure out which model you're dealing with, this Amazon page includes photos, specs, and release years for the entire lineup. Once you know which one you have, you may be able to trade it in for credit toward a newer model. Most old Kindles probably still work, just with fewer bells and whistles. It’s best to avoid Kindles with keyboards or any other physical buttons other than page-turn buttons. Some older models lost the ability to browse, purchase, or borrow new books directly from the device. However, you may still be able to do this via Amazon on your computer or phone and have it sent to your Kindle, which is a better experience anyway. How Do You Get Free Ebooks on a Kindle? AccordionItemContainerButton LargeChevron If you buy every single book you want to read on a Kindle, it can add up! But there are ways to save some money while reading as much as your heart desires. You may want to subscribe to Kindle Unlimited for $12 a month. You can only choose from the Unlimited catalog, but it features millions of titles, including audiobooks and magazines. Start out with the 30-day free trial. If you already pay for a Prime account, you’re eligible for some free ebooks through Prime Reading. It doesn't include as many options as Kindle Unlimited, and in a lot of cases, you’ll see both Unlimited and Prime options lumped together; you’ll have to look closely to find the free ebooks. It’s still something, though, and there are even a few magazines. If you don’t want another monthly subscription and don’t want to continue giving your money to Amazon, take advantage of the ebooks available with your library card. Browsing a digital catalog is not as magical as spending an afternoon looking over every shelf in a library, but such is the ebook life (no one says you can’t read both!). We have a detailed how-to on this that you should check out, but here are some of the takeaways: Get a library card for your local branch.

Check your branch’s website for its ebook offerings. Many libraries use a service called OverDrive.

Download directly to your Kindle library. The titles in question will automatically be removed when they’re due back. If you know someone else with a Kindle, you can lend books between your libraries, just as you would with a physical copy. Follow these instructions from Amazon if you want to share an ebook, but keep in mind that not all books are loanable. What Else Can a Kindle Do? AccordionItemContainerButton LargeChevron Kindles have other helpful features you may want to use. Long-press a word or phrase to see its definition, highlight it, or take notes. You can also search the entire book for that particular word or phrase or translate it to or from other languages. Word Wise shows short definitions in small text within the lines. Unfortunately, it’s not available for all books, but when it is, you can turn it on or off and choose more and fewer hints. Clicking the short definition opens a longer one from Word Wise and the New Oxford American Dictionary or Oxford Dictionary of English (you can switch between the two), plus translations and a Wikipedia page, if applicable. While reading, tap the top of the screen and click “Aa” to change font size or type. There’s a font called OpenDyslexic that helps make reading easier for people with dyslexia. You can control margin sizes and line spacing from that menu, too. When a Kindle connects to a Bluetooth speaker or headphones, VoiceView Screen Reader (accessed through Settings > Accessibility) allows you to use gestures to navigate your device and reads aloud what you’ve pressed. It can also read a book aloud, though it doesn’t sound nearly as nice as an audiobook. Amazon owns Goodreads, so it syncs seamlessly to Kindles (press the three-dot menu > Goodreads). If you have a Goodreads account, you can review the Kindle books you’ve read or browse your bookshelf and recommendations. Long-pressing a word or phrase, in addition to what is mentioned above, opens up an option to share quotes directly to Goodreads. There’s also a web browser if you’re connected to the internet (three-dot menu > Web Browser). It’s not the best, so I’d reserve it for emergency searches. What Do I Do If My Kindle Colorsoft Has a Yellow Bar? AccordionItemContainerButton LargeChevron Following customer complaints in 2024 of a yellow bar at the bottom of the Colorsoft Signature’s screen and discoloration along the edges, an Amazon spokesperson confirmed to WIRED that "customers who notice this can reach out to our customer service team for a replacement or refund.” The company also said it’s “making the appropriate adjustments to ensure that new devices will not experience this issue moving forward.” However, there are still customer complaints about this issue, even with the new model out. We have not run into this issue while testing the Colorsoft, Colorsoft Signature, or Scribe Colorsoft. Is Now a Good Time to Buy a Kindle? AccordionItemContainerButton LargeChevron The best time to buy a Kindle is during a major sale event like Amazon Prime Day, Prime Big Deals Days, Black Friday, or Cyber Monday, when Amazon often offers steep discounts on its products. Are Kindles Good for Students? AccordionItemContainerButton LargeChevron Kindles are great for students, though the model that's best for each student depends on how they'll use it. If they want to pair it with a stylus for highlighting and be able to take notes, they should consider a Kindle Scribe model. These have long battery life, making them great for students to use for weeks on end without worrying about charging. Some textbooks are also available on Kindles. For students who love to read but don’t want to take a ton of notes, a regular Kindle or Kindle Paperwhite will work well.

Tech.content:
It's worth noting that while the price of these new models is the same as the 2024 editions, it's because Kindle raised the prices of its 2024 versions back in August. At first, it seemed like this was intended to make Amazon sales look better than they actually were heading into Prime Day and Black Friday, but now it's clear it was probably a way to make these new models feel worth buying, since you won't find a cheaper model as easily. And it's a valid move: These models will be my new picks, because if you're spending the same amount, why wouldn't you want the latest model?

But that doesn't necessarily help you decide if it's worth upgrading. It might be worth it if you're desperate for page-turner buttons, which is easily my favorite part of this new line of Kindles. If you don't have a Kindle already and are on a mission to select your first one, this latest version of the Paperwhite remains a good choice unless you're determined to splurge on a color screen. The warm light is a big benefit for anyone who reads in the evening, and you'll have to choose one of these two models from Kindle's lineup to get it anyway.

The Base Lineup

The 2026 Kindle Paperwhite (left) and 2026 Kindle Colorsoft (right). Photograph: Nena Farrell

The Kindle Paperwhite and Kindle Colorsoft are, to some degree, the same device. You'll see a similar laundry list of features: a 7-inch screen, a front light with adjustable brightness and warmth, and 16 GB of storage in the base models. Both have the same new look of a flush-front screen and ever-so-slightly-smaller body when compared to the 2024 Paperwhite and 2025 Colorsoft (the first Colorsoft in 2024 was later renamed the Signature Edition, and a cheaper base model came out in 2025).

Tech.title: Amazon Adds an Alexa Photo Frame and a Bedside Clock to Its Echo Family
Tech.content:
Panos Panay, Amazon's senior vice president of Devices and Alexa, says a couple hundred million people now use Alexa+, the revamped version of the decade-old voice assistant, on its Echo devices. He says people talk to Alexa+ two to three times more than before its AI glow-up, cook with it five times more, listen to music three times more, and create routines twice as much.

To keep that momentum going, Amazon has new Echo products to deliver a richer Alexa+ experience, including minor refreshes on existing hardware and entirely new categories. Announced Wednesday and available for purchase now, they include the Echo Dot ($100), Echo Studio With Home Camera ($250), Echo Show 16 ($500), Echo Time ($200), and the first Alexa Photo Frame ($200).

“I don't think anyone's really doing AI at all in the home, and if they are, they aren't doing it well,” Panay says at an intimate media-only event in New York City. As people have “deeper” conversations with Alexa+, Panay says devices need to be in premium shape—a strategy Amazon has been focusing on after announcing more premium Kindles and Alexa Tablets in early October.

You can see that premiumization in the hardware pricing: The Echo Dot—once the affordable, entry-level $50 smart speaker—now starts at $100. That's higher than the marked-up prices on existing Amazon devices from this summer, which Amazon blamed on the memory shortage.

Echo Dot

The new Echo Dot costs $100 and comes in four colors. Photograph: Julian Chokkattu

Panay says Amazon has sold more than 100 million Echo Dots, and in 2026 alone, people spent more than a trillion minutes listening to music on the diminutive orb. So, the main goal for the new Dot? Boost the sound. The full-range driver reportedly delivers 50 percent stronger bass performance and crisper vocals.

With four beamforming microphones (up from three) and Amazon's AZ3 chip, Alexa can isolate your voice in a noisy environment and track your commands more effectively. It also has Omnisense like last year's Echo Dot Max, which can sense the environment to, say, detect when you walk into the home and turn on the lights.

The Dot now supports the Matter standard and works as a Thread border router, turning it into a hub for setting up and controlling smart home devices. If you have an Eero router, it can also turn into a Wi-Fi extender.

Tech.title: Sauerkraut at Every Meal? These Fermentation Fanatics Tried That Long Before MAHA
Tech.content:
Waking early, I put a small jar of my sauerkraut into my messenger bag, hop on my bicycle, ride to Seattle's King Street Station, and board a train heading to the Portland Fermentation Festival, the yearly gathering affectionately nicknamed “Stinkfest.”

Usually the sheer existence of a festival like this is enough to get people revved up to come together and talk about their favorite ferments, but in an interesting twist, fermented foods are enjoying a popularity boost from a different crowd. The MAHA movement, and particularly the Donald Trump cabinet, are big into fermented food, eating meat, usually steak, with fermented sides like kimchi or sauerkraut at every meal.

I've come to Portland, Oregon, wondering if there was going to be any overlap in the Venn diagram between festival attendees and the MAHA steak-and-ferment crowd. I mentioned this to my cousin-in-law Erick, who's been part of the Portland food scene for years, and he laughed out loud.

“It'll be more like a Venn dumbbell,” he said, making a pair of thumb-and-forefinger circles and tracing a line in the air between them. “No overlap, but food will be the bridge.”

Still, I was curious. I’d check.

Tech.title: Pornhub Stars Want to Teach You How to Make Dinner
Tech.content:
Porn star Sweetie Fox is known for all kinds of gamer cosplay. She’s performed as a sex-hungry vault dweller from Fallout, as Lara Croft “The Dick Rider.” On Pornhub, one of the platforms where she uploads content, her character videos do massive numbers. (One of her more popular vids netted 12 million views).

But Fox is also a miner—the term for someone who plays Minecraft—and in September, she posted a video of herself playing the game fully clothed. In less than a month, it has surpassed 1 million views on the site.

It’s the kind of content Pornhub is betting its future on. Starting this month, the adult entertainment site is inviting performers to earn new viewers from gaming, cooking, podcasting—or basically anything that doesn’t involve sex.

Ever wanted to learn what “physics-informed neural networks” are from Zara Dar, or what Jenna Starr likes to cook for dinner? (Steak and potatoes, by the way.) According to insights from the company, interest in safe-for-work content is blowing up on the platform. Podcast and gaming categories rose triple digits in 2025—podcasts alone spiked 327 percent—as did searches for “SFW,” which were up 114 percent.

Alex Kekesi, vice president of brand and community at Pornhub, believes these categories are gaining traction because viewers want to get to know performers beyond their adult roles. Nonexplicit content—which Kekesi says isn’t intended to replace X-rated videos on the site but rather complement creators’ existing content libraries—will be featured across video pages, search results, recommendations, and Pornhub’s various categories, in addition to Shorties, its scrollable vertical video feed.

Tech.title: Apple AirPods Max 2 Are $100 Off Ahead of Black Friday
Tech.content:
Apple makes some of the best headphones on the market. I almost never want to pay full price for them, though. Here at WIRED, we spend a lot of time testing Apple gear and tracking prices, so we know when it’s a smart time to buy and when it’s best to wait.

Right now, Apple AirPods Max 2 are $100 off on Amazon. If you prefer wireless earbuds, the Apple AirPods Pro 3 are also $49 off. We’ve seen both products go for a bit less, and they are likely to drop further for Black Friday. But if you've been eyeing Apple's headphones for a while and need them sooner than late November, now is a good time to buy.

For more of our Apple recommendations, check out our guides to the Best Apple Watches, iPhones, and iPads.

Apple AirPods Max 2 for $449 ($100 Off)

The AirPods Max 2 are the best-sounding headphones for Apple loyalists. I have been testing them for about three months now, and they have become my favorite headphones for travel. They unfortunately can’t prevent airplane ear, but their plush over-ear cuffs feel way more comfortable than cramming buds into my ear canals for hours on end. The headphones deliver up to 1.5 times more automated noise-canceling (ANC) performance than the previous version, support lossless audio, and can be plugged in via USB-C for ultralow latency audio.

This sale applies to all five colorways (midnight, blue, orange, purple, and starlight). I’ve seen the AirPods Max 2 go for cheaper, but $449 is still a good deal. If you already own the OGs, I wouldn’t upgrade, but if you need a new pair, think these over.

Apple AirPods Pro 3 for $200 ($49 Off)

This isn’t the best deal I’ve seen on the flagship AirPods Pro 3, so if you can hold out until Black Friday, I’d wait. But if you need a new pair of earbuds now and own an iPhone, these are my favorite, and $49 off is still better than full price.

When I'm out and about, working out, or want the convenience of removing an earbud to hear something—though transparency mode often makes that unnecessary—I reach for my AirPods Pro 3. They are my go-to for runs because their silicone ear tips stay in place even when I start to sweat. They may not be as new as AirPods 5, but they are better, with three times more ANC and built-in heart rate sensing for workouts. That's in addition to Apple's adaptive EQ and hearing aid features. Battery life is around eight hours with ANC enabled and up to 24 hours with the charging case. You get five sizes of ear tips to tailor the fit.

Tech.title: Macmillan Staff Say the Publisher Threw a Party for a Workplace AI Assistant That Was Later Killed
Tech.content:
As staff at the Lower Manhattan headquarters of Macmillan Publishers headed into work one morning in January 2024, they filed past something strange on the walls—flyers welcoming a new member of the team named “NOA.” The cafeteria was festooned with purple balloons and banners, according to several workers present, and with NOA’s name in light-up marquee letters. A plate full of doughnuts spelled out “NOA IS HERE.”

NOA was an acronym for No Ordinary Assistant, which many of Macmillan’s human assistants found “offensive,” multiple employees tell WIRED. In an email to staff, NOA was introduced as an AI chatbot developed by the German software company Chaptr, which is “backed” by Holtzbrinck, Macmillan’s parent company.

The email also assured employees NOA was “a safe environment where you can input proprietary information without the risk of sharing that data with any third party.” Ostensibly, this means NOA was a closed-loop enterprise tool that did not retain or share data for model training.

Macmillan staffers say they were warned during training sessions that NOA could hallucinate and would always need to be fact-checked by humans. Still, employees say, they were encouraged to use NOA for composing emails, drafting copy, doing marketing research, and generating ideas. Multiple staffers say they were told to “only” paste a “percentage” of authors’ manuscripts into NOA. Employees could also adjust NOA’s speaking tone, with options including “lighthearted,” “spartan,” pessimistic,” “sarcastic,” and “regretful.”

One Macmillan employee remembers a Chaptr representative reassuring workers during an early in-person training session that Chaptr understood publishers were dealing with something very important—content. “And here I thought we were publishing literature,” the employee says.

Tech.title: Please Let the Internet Die
Tech.content:
Generative AI, briefly considered an amusing novelty, is now a turbocharged slop engine for the web, filling feeds and comment sections with useless, grotesque content. As humans scroll past headlines about AI taking their jobs, confusing fantasy for reality, and contributing to cognitive decline, any consumer appeal the technology might have is turning to anguish. The data centers that power it have become increasingly unpopular, and politically radioactive.

To be online, many now admit, is to be endlessly manipulated and exploited. In December, Oxford University Press declared rage bait to be the word of the year, noting that use of the term had tripled over the previous 12 months. The lexical spike represented a heightened awareness that monetized social accounts churn out bad-faith takes and extremist content, automating this abusive behavior with generative AI, simply to profit off hostile engagement. Billionaire oligarchs have opened the floodgates to such inauthentic activity, conspiracy-mongering, and hate speech by rolling back moderation.

WIRED Ghost Stories Five hauntings from the other side of technology. Have a ghost story of your own? Share it in the comments below.

In short, when you hang around online in 2026, you see little worth saving. Perhaps a decade ago, you felt that the glimmers of community and joy, of artistic and intellectual exchange, were enough to balance out the toxic junk. No longer.

It’s not necessarily that people have gotten worse. “Dead Internet Theory”—the proposition that a vast majority of the interactions on the web are fake, bots talking to other bots—has accrued more supporting evidence recently. One cybersecurity firm concluded this spring that agents already outnumber human users, their traffic surging by 8,000 percent through 2025. No wonder seemingly everyone has at some point caught themselves scrolling through a wasteland of brainrot and asked, “What the hell am I even looking at?” Underlying that question is another: “Is it always going to be like this?”

Tech.title: Fox One Will Track 2026 Midterm Election Results With New App Experience
Tech.content:
The 2026 midterm elections are less than a week away, and Fox has unveiled a new interactive experience for Fox One app subscribers on Election Day, Tuesday, Nov. 3, to keep up with the news and results as they come in across the country.

With hundreds of House, Senate, gubernatorial and local races happening all at once, it can be tough to follow along with every update. According to a statement, Fox One has launched an interface to keep track of everything, “where a race in one state reframes the math in another and where what matters most to viewers may be a ballot measure in their own county.”

The Fox One election experience will add context to Fox’s broadcast coverage. Fox One

The features that’ll appear as part of this rollout include a command center on the Fox One home screen, with widgets that update in real time on things like voter polls, contest results and Fox News “Election Insights” on key races; a curated election hub that’ll include all of Fox’s election coverage; and a new Elections Mode version of Ask Fox, the app’s AI-powered chatbot, where viewers can ask election-based questions and receive answers in real time.

More from CNET

“The results don’t arrive in order, and no two viewers are following the same set of races,” said Amit Dudakia, senior vice president and head of product at Fox Direct to Consumer. “With Fox One, we’re keeping coverage from Fox News and Fox Stations at the center and building the context around it, so viewers aren’t toggling between a stream and a second screen to understand what just happened.”

Fox One’s complete channel portfolio includes Fox News Channel, Fox Nation, Fox Sports, B1G, FS1, FS2, the Fox Network and local Fox stations. It is available at no additional cost for cable and satellite TV customers and is priced at $20 a month for a stand-alone subscription to the app. The new in-app election experience will launch on Election Day.

Tech.title: Amazon’s $500 Echo Show 16 Wants to Be the Center of Your Home
Tech.content:
Amazon is betting there’s room for another screen in your home, and that you’ll pay $500 for it.

The company announced the Echo Show 16 on Wednesday, a new 16-inch smart display that combines Alexa Plus, Fire TV and a customizable home dashboard into a single device. It starts at $500, with a $570 version featuring an anti-glare screen.

The Echo Show 16 is now available for preorder, with a $100 discount for early buyers. Amazon says the device will ship later this year, but hasn’t announced an exact date.

More from CNET

As CNET’s smart home expert Tyler Lacoma notes, Amazon is going in a very different direction than Apple this year. Amazon

The new smart display is designed to do a little bit of everything, whether that’s controlling lights, managing your family’s calendar, making video calls or streaming Netflix while you’re cooking dinner.

A bigger screen and an optional anti-glare upgrade

The Echo Show 16 has a full HD display that Amazon says offers 10% more viewing area than the Echo Show 15. It also has a redesigned aluminum frame that’s nearly 40% thinner than its predecessor, which could make it less obtrusive when mounted on a wall. A new 10-speaker system is designed to deliver fuller sound for music, TV shows and video calls.

One of the biggest additions is an optional Nanomatte display, which Amazon says reduces glare by more than 90%. That could make a difference if you’re using the Echo Show in a kitchen with bright overhead lighting or near a window.



The Echo Show 16 also includes a 13-megapixel wide-angle camera for video calls, with automatic framing to keep people in the shot. Amazon says it more than doubles the range of Visual ID, which can recognize household members and personalize what’s on the screen, from 8 feet to 17 feet.

The Echo Show 16 is also the first in the lineup to offer night vision, letting you see what’s happening at home even in the dark.

Amazon says a dedicated button can disable the microphones and camera. That’s worth noting given previous concerns about changes to Alexa’s privacy settings.

A smart home dashboard that doubles as a TV

The Echo Show 16 is somewhere between a TV and a smart display. Amazon

Amazon is introducing three new screen styles that change how the Echo Show 16 home screen looks and functions. Smart Home turns the display into an always-on control center for connected devices, including lights, thermostats and speakers. Family Organizer brings together shared calendars, to-do lists, meal plans and recipes. Photos turns the screen into a digital photo frame.

There’s also a customizable favorites bar for quick access to frequently used features.

The Echo Show 16 comes with Fire TV built in, letting you stream content from services including Netflix, Disney Plus, YouTube and Prime Video. The box includes a remote, so you won’t have to rely entirely on voice commands or the touchscreen.

Fire TV is already available on the Echo Show 15 and 21, but the new customizable dashboards give the Echo Show 16 more ways to serve as a central home hub.

Alexa Plus gets a more visual experience

An upgraded display on the Echo Show 16 costs even more. Amazon

The Echo Show 16 also runs Amazon’s Alexa Plus AI assistant, which can handle more conversational requests and multi-step tasks. Alexa Plus isn’t exclusive to the new display, though. Amazon previously introduced Echo Show 8 and Echo Show 11 models designed for the upgraded assistant.

Instead of simply displaying a transcript of a conversation, the new interface can generate interactive content, including comparison charts, videos and recommendations, as you speak to Alexa.

Amazon is also introducing Cards, which organize previous Alexa conversations into topics you can revisit. For example, a conversation about planning a weekend trip could produce a Card containing relevant links, reservations and other details.

Certain features require Alexa Plus, which is included with a Prime membership. Without Prime, the full Alexa Plus experience costs $20 a month.

The Echo Show 16 costs $500 with the standard display or $570 with Nanomatte. Both versions are eligible for a $100 preorder discount. It doesn’t include a stand, so you’ll need to mount it on a wall or buy one separately. Amazon offers a $70 basic stand or a $125 swivel-and-tilt version.

For comparison, Amazon’s larger 21-inch Echo Show 21 launched in 2024 at $400. Add the Nanomatte display and swivel-and-tilt stand, and the Echo Show 16 comes to nearly $700 before taxes and the preorder discount. That’s a steep price for a smart display, even one that wants to double as a TV, family organizer and smart home hub.

Tech.title: The Latest Echo Smart Speakers Double as Nanny Cams and Wi-Fi Extenders
Tech.content:
Amazon dropped a flurry of new and updated smart home devices today, including its first-ever smart frame and an alarm clock that apparently knows when you’re in a deep sleep and automatically snoozes the alarm until your slumber lightens.

At the heart of the Echo smart speaker lineup are the Echo Dot, which brings simple smart home convenience, and the Echo Studio, Amazon’s premium listening speaker with a richer sound. Both received big upgrades: The Dot now includes a built-in smart home hub and Wi-Fi extender, while a new Studio adds a camera for live in-home monitoring.

We got a sneak peek at the new smart home speakers at Amazon’s launch event. David Carnoy/CNET

The Studio is the first Echo smart speaker with a camera

Cameras are making their way into products they have no logical business being in, like dishwashers, but a camera in the $250 Echo Studio with Home Camera turns the humble smart speaker into a useful nanny cam, letting you keep tabs on family and pets via its live view. If you’re deciding between a pet cam and a smart speaker, the Echo device should offer a reliable version of both.

More from CNET

You can still buy the Echo Studio without a camera for $220.

The cam does more than let you watch the dog chew slippers

The Studio Home Camera serves as a nanny cam and uses adaptive vision to help with small tasks. David Carnoy/CNET

Through the Home Camera, Alexa “gains visual intelligence to make everyday experiences more personal and helpful,” according to Amazon. Alexa can “see and understand what’s in front of the camera and help. Pull out a board game box and ask Alexa to explain the rules or hold up a cereal box and Alexa can recognize it and help you reorder more flavors.”

Adaptive sound and volume for tailored listening

Camera shamera, the Echo Studio also has fancy new audio features. David Carnoy/CNET

Expect the same souped-up sound quality that Studio built its name on, including a high-excursion woofer for deep, immersive bass, three optimally placed full-range drivers, and Dolby Atmos to fill the room with immersive spatial audio.

The Best Smart Speakers We Tested See at CNET

A new feature called Advanced Room Adaptation adjusts the sound to your space’s unique acoustics, while Adaptive Volume adjusts the volume based on how close or far you are from the device. The latter sounds particularly useful for those of us who doddle about the house cooking and cleaning while trying to follow a podcast or audiobook.

Echo Dot is now a smart home hub and Wi-Fi extender

The smaller Echo Dot gets its own updates, including a smart home hub feature and a built-in Wi-Fi extender.

For the first time, Amazon has integrated a smart home hub to connect and control compatible devices like your smart thermostat, lights and locks without the need for a standalone hub. The latest iteration adds a built-in Eero Wi-Fi extender that extends internet coverage by up to 1,000 square feet to an existing Eero network.

For the first time, the Echo Dot features a built-in smart home hub and Wi-Fi extender. David Carnoy/CNET

Echo Dot is now powered by AZ3, Amazon’s custom-designed silicon, enabling advanced on-device

processing for faster, more natural conversations with Alexa Plus. Speaking of Alexa, there’s now a fourth speaker (all the better to hear you with, my dear).

Echo Dot and Studio pricing

Tech.title: Amazon’s New Alarm Clock ‘Knows’ if You’re in a Deep Sleep and Lets You Sleep Longer
Tech.content:
Amazon is revamping its smart home devices, and it’s adding a new smart alarm clock to the lineup for the first time. Called the Amazon Echo Time, this alarm clock with unique AI sleep features is designed specifically for bedrooms — and bucking Big Tech’s “pervert tech” trend, it includes no cameras. It’s available now for $200 and starts shipping in December.

Amazon’s first clock is smart and customizable

The Echo Time looks like a regular Alexa speaker with one key difference: a 3.2-inch screen. You can customize the display to show an analog or digital clock, including themed variants from popular franchises, like Harry Potter, the DC Universe and Scooby-Doo. It’s one of many devices that Amazon dropped on Wednesday, including a revamped Echo Show, Echo Studio and a first-ever smart picture frame.

Customize the display to show an analog or digital clock and use popular themes including Harry Potter, the DC Universe and Scooby-Doo. David Carnoy/CNET

Inside, the device uses tech that adapts to your daily routines. For example, it can gradually get brighter in the morning to support your wake-up routine and reduce blue light at night to help you fall asleep. Those features are similar to other smart clocks, like the popular Hatch Sleep Clock. The clock also comes in two versions built specifically for kids, with controls parents can use, including Amazon’s Sleep Studio for bedtime-routine management.

More from CNET

A wild (opt-in) AI feature pushes the alarm back if you’re in a deep sleep

Like nearly every piece of tech these days, the Echo Time has optional AI features. If you don’t need to jump out of bed at a certain time, you can let the Echo Time handle your alarm. The clock then uses sensors that monitor room temperature and movement, including ultrasonic detectors for your breathing, to decide when to wake you. It works within a 60-minute window around your wake-up time, letting you get a deep sleep or waking you early if it detects your sleep is no longer “restful.”

If that sounds creepy or like something that will make you run late in the morning, don’t worry: It’s optional, and it requires an Alexa Plus subscription.

The new Echo Time clocks come in graphite, glacier white and coral pink for adults, with galactic grape and cosmic lime options for kids. David Carnoy/CNET

While this feature could be dangerous during workdays or before a flight, it sounds perfect for sleepy weekends when you’re trying to catch up on rest.

There have never been more smart home tech options. Earlier this month, Apple revamped its options and introduced a brand-new device called the Home View. Apple’s new devices impressed CNET reviewers, particularly with their easy-to-use setup. But families that already use Amazon devices will likely want to stay within the same ecosystem.

Tech.title: Amazon’s 5 New Smart Home Devices: Everything You Need to Know
Tech.content:
About two weeks after Apple unveiled its HomeView smart display and HomePod Mini 2 smart speaker, Amazon countered on Wednesday with not one, not two, but five new smart devices and a new smart home feature. Some of the new devices put a spotlight on sleep and memories, while others offer greater control over every corner of your home.

Here’s a rundown of all six new product announcements from Amazon.

Echo Time

Echo Time is a camera-free smart alarm clock powered by Alexa Plus, Amazon’s generative AI assistant. The device has hundreds of selectable clock faces and built-in sleep tracking sensors designed to monitor your rest and optimize wake-up times.

More from CNET

Here’s how it works: With the optional smart alarms feature, Alexa will detect when you’re in light sleep and wake you within 10 to 60 minutes of your scheduled alarm. It uses sensor technology called Omnisense to monitor room temperature, your presence, proximity and breathing.

Echo Time received the National Sleep Foundation’s SleepMark, which is awarded to products that meet evidence-based sleep standards.

Echo Time is now available for $200 in graphite, glacier white and coral pink, with an adjustable stand sold separately for $40. Certain features will require Alexa Plus, which comes with a Prime membership ($15 a month or $139 a year).

Customizable clock faces allow you to choose between analog designs, nature backdrops, seasonal themes or your favorite sports teams and characters. David Carnoy/CNET

Amazon Kids Echo Time

There’s also a version for kids, called Amazon Kids Echo Time, that lets them set alarms, ask questions, swap out clock faces and check the weather. A Sleep Studio feature offers curated bedtime content.

Parents can use the Amazon Parent Dashboard to control sleep schedules and more, as the Amazon Kids Echo Time is powered by Kids Plus, a subscription with parental controls and for content selected with kids in mind.

Available in galactic grape and cosmic lime, the Amazon Kids Echo Time starts at $210, and a one-year Kids Plus subscription is included. After that, plans start at $8 a month.

Echo Show 16

Echo Show is Amazon’s smart speaker and display. The new Echo Show 16 has a 16-inch high-definition screen, built-in Fire TV and screen styles that let you turn the Show 16 into a digital photo frame, a smart home dashboard to control all your Alexa devices or a family organizer to manage tasks, color-coded schedules and meal plans.

When compared to the Echo Show 15, the latest model has 10% more viewing area, a frame that’s about 40% thinner, 20% more computing power, upgraded audio and a new wide-angle 13-megapixel camera with the widest field of view ever offered on an Echo Show. Now, there’s also night vision.

Echo Show 16 comes with Alexa Plus, which is required for certain features and included in a Prime membership.

With the Echo Show 16 Fire TV, you can stream content from Netflix, Disney Plus, YouTube, Prime Video, HBO Max and more. David Carnoy/CNET

It will ship later this year, but the Echo Show 16 is now available for preorder with $100 off. The standard display costs $500, while the anti-glare Nanomatte version is $570. A standard stand costs $70, while a flexible swivel-and-tilt stand costs $125. Both are sold separately.

Alexa Photo Frame

The Alexa Photo Frame works with Amazon Photos to automatically sync and display your photos on its 10-inch, anti-glare, high-definition touchscreen.

It’s the first and only photo frame with Alexa built in, so you can ask Alexa to show your favorite photos based on when they were taken, their mood or who’s in them. You can also add voice notes to any photo.

The Alexa Photo Frame is available in black, birch and walnut frames. David Carnoy/CNET

The Alexa Photo Frame starts at $200. It comes with 90 days of Alexa Plus. For Prime members, Amazon Photos offers unlimited photo storage.

Echo Studio with Home Camera

The new Echo Studio speaker uses Advanced Room Adaptation to automatically adapt sound to your space, while Adaptive Volume adjusts what’s playing based on where you are in the room.

It uses the built-in Home Camera to do so, giving Alexa visual intelligence and letting you operate Live View to see your home when you’re away. In the future, you’ll be able to pair the Echo Studio with Home Camera and a Fire TV device, allowing you to take video calls on a larger screen. No specific date for this integration has been announced.

All Echo devices have a dedicated button to turn off the microphones and cameras, and visual indicators let you know when an Echo device’s camera is streaming images or video to the cloud. For those who don’t want a camera, the standard Echo Studio is still available.

The Echo Studio with Home Camera is only available in graphite, a dark gray. David Carnoy/CNET

Echo Studio with Home Camera is now available for $250. An optional stand is $40. The standard version is still available for $220.

Echo Dot

The new sixth-generation Echo Dot speaker delivers crisper vocals and 50% more bass than the previous model. Upgraded on-device processing and a fourth microphone allow for faster, better conversations with Alexa Plus.

For the first time, the Echo Dot also has a built-in smart home hub, so you can control compatible smart devices without a separate device.

Amazon Kids Echo Dot offers the same features as the Echo Dot, plus a year of the Kids Plus subscription included.

You can get the Echo Dot in graphite, glacier white, agave green and coral pink. David Carnoy/CNET

Echo Dot is now available for $100. Amazon Kids Echo Dot starts at $110.

Alexa Home Map

On compatible apps, Echo and Alexa devices and Fire TVs, Alexa Home Map will roll out as an interactive 3D map feature that shows both the inside and outside of your home. With a compatible Ring camera, you can see animations showing where people and cars are located. Through Ring’s Familiar Faces tool, an AI facial-recognition feature that has drawn privacy criticism, the display can identify specific recognized visitors by name.

Alexa Home Map also displays the locations of all other smart home devices, including Echo devices, Ring and Blink cameras, Fire TV, lights, locks and thermostats.

From the interactive map, you can check security cameras, turn off lights and monitor device activity at a glance. Visual status cues appear directly on the layout, where smart lights reflect their current brightness and color, and active smart speakers display animated musical notes.

To get started, add your address to Alexa Home Map, and it will automatically generate your home’s exterior. Using a compatible iPhone, walk through your house to map the interior. Then, manually add your devices’ locations on the map.

The Alexa Home Map updates in real time to show you the weather, cars and people. Amazon

Later this year, Alexa Home Map will roll out in preview on its own iOS app, the Alexa and Ring apps, the Ember Artline Fire TV, new Alexa Tablets and larger Echo Show devices, including the Echo Show 16.

Certain features will require Alexa Plus, a Ring Pro subscription ($20 a month or $200 a year) or a Virtual Security Guard subscription ($99 a month) with compatible Ring cameras.

Tech.title: Amazon’s New Digital Picture Frame Is Clever and Classy
Tech.content:
Amazon just dropped its first-ever digital picture frame, right in time for the holiday gifting rush, along with a whole batch of new Echo-based gadgets. We got a peek at the Alexa Photo Frame at a launch event in New York, and it has a few neat tricks and design touches you won’t find on most frames.

The big standout is that the frame syncs automatically with Amazon Photos and picks out the “best” shots for you, so you’re not stuck watching all 300 photos from your upstate leaf-peeping trip on repeat. We love the idea, but we haven’t tested it yet, so we can’t say how well it curates.

Smart Home Gift Buying Guide 2026: Upgrades Everyone Will Love See at CNET

The first smart frame with Alexa built in

Alexa prompts fetch the exact photos or photo types you want to see.

Amazon’s frame, which comes with unlimited storage for Prime members, is the first with Alexa built in, so you can ask to see photos of certain people, places or events.

More from CNET

“Alexa, nobody believes me that I met Dolly Parton at Costco; please bring up the selfie,” is one example for locating photos.

You can also use AI-style prompts to create a specific slideshow, such as “show pictures of the kids” or “absolutely no pictures of the kids, please.”

We’ve tested generative AI frames before, and most left us wanting more. SwitchBot recently came out with a second-gen AI frame model, but we haven’t seen anything like this Alexa hybrid approach before, which makes us really want to try it out.

High-definition picture that adjusts to changing light

Brightness automatically adjusts as ambient light changes. Amazon

The 10-inch high-definition, semi-matte, anti-glare finish was impressive, making photos look more like a physical photo than a screen, and they show clearly from almost any angle. A clever light sensor automatically adjusts the screen brightness from day to night.

The wood frame may be the best part

The frame comes in birch or walnut wood.

What first caught our eye was the textured, soft-white matting and the real wood frames, available in walnut, lighter birch or black. If you’ve browsed digital frames online, you’ve likely noticed a trend: drab black plastic designs with little warmth or visual appeal. Amazon’s wood options are a welcome departure from the norm, even if they cost more.

You can add voice notes to photos for some reason

Perhaps the strangest feature is the ability to add voice notes to accompany images as they pass across the screen to “capture the story behind the moment.” I suppose this might enhance the picture-frame experience in some cases, but I can’t think of many.

Pricing and availability

The frame comes in three finishes, including two wood options, and begins shipping Dec. 16. Amazon

The Alexa Photo Frame costs $200 in black plastic and $229 in one of two wood finishes, walnut or birch. Frames start shipping Dec. 16, just in time for Christmas gifting.

Tech.title: Samsung Galaxy Buds On Are the Premium Clip-On Earbuds You Didn’t Know You Were Waiting For
Tech.content:
Clip-on open earbuds are all the rage, and Samsung is the latest major brand to add clip-ons to its line of Galaxy earbuds with its new Galaxy Buds On. The style has grown so rapidly that it’s hard to believe Samsung didn’t already have a pair, but here we are. Available in black at launch, the Buds On list for $229 and ship in early November.

The Galaxy Buds On look like a lot of other clip-on buds already on the market. But at $230, they’re definitely one of the more premium-priced offerings. Though I haven’t tried them yet, I suspect they’ll offer strong performance for the category and be comparable to Bose’s new Sport Open Earbuds ($200), Sony’s LinkBuds Clip ($230) and Shokz’s Open Dots 2 ($200).

They have 11.3-millimeter drivers with dual woofers (TwinBoost Speaker, Samsung calls the drivers) to increase bass performance, which can often be suboptimal with open earbuds. Additionally, they’re equipped with three microphones along with a Voice Pickup Unit and AI algorithms (Intelligent Clear Call) that help eliminate background noise while homing in on your voice during calls.

More from CNET

This type of earbuds tends to fit quite comfortably and securely, and they’re an appealing choice for runners and bikers who want to hear the outside world for safety reasons. They have an IP54 rating, which means they’re splashproof and dust-resistant, and according to Samsung, “Computational modeling helped optimize speaker and battery geometry to create a low-pressure fit around the ear, while refining the stiffness and shape of the band for a secure, comfortable fit.”

Weighing 6.7 grams per earbud, the Galaxy Buds On have tap controls and support for head gestures. Samsung lists their battery life rating at up to 9.5 hours of music playback on a single charge — and up to 38 hours in total with the charging case, which features wireless charging.

The charging case appears to be very similar to other Galaxy earbuds charging cases. Samsung

With open earbuds like these that have drivers that sit over your ear canals without covering them, sound leakage can be an issue when you play your music loudly in quiet environments. These buds don’t have active noise canceling, but they are equipped with Samsung’s Audio Leakage Reduction technology that “reduces escaping sound before it travels outward by projecting reversed sound waves from the rear of the speaker, keeping audio more private to the listener.”

It’s also worth noting that the Galaxy Buds On are powered by Qualcomm’s Snapdragon S7 Gen 1 Sound Platform, which Samsung says facilitates extended playback periods at elevated volume levels with the help of a high-efficiency class-D amplifier “intricately designed to optimize power consumption.”

Samsung

If you have a Google Gemini account, you get always-on access to Gemini just by saying, “Hey Google, let’s talk live. Also, there’s a Quick Voice Memo feature that you can access by long-pressing on the earbuds and simply speaking (and thanks to Bixby, Samsung says, users can search recordings hands-free).

While the earbuds can be used with iPhones and other Apple devices, as their name implies, the Galaxy Buds On work best with Samsung Galaxy devices, with easy pairing and access to controls and EQ settings through a shortcut in Samsung’s Quick Panel. There’s also automatic audio switching between any Galaxy devices you own, though multipoint Bluetooth support is missing for owners of non-Samsung Galaxy devices. Android users can install Samsung’s Wearable app for customization options and firmware updates, but there’s no app support for Apple users (Samsung’s Galaxy Buds app for iOS only supports a few older legacy Samsung buds).

I’ll have a full review of the Galaxy Buds On in the coming days and will compare them to the aforementioned buds along with Bose’s Ultra Open Earbuds (2nd Gen), which earned a CNET Editors’ Choice award for having the best sound in the category, though they’re $300 price makes them even more expensive than the Galaxy Buds On. The Anker AeroClip 2 currently have the best voice-calling performance for clip-on earbuds, so we’ll see how these Samsung clip-ons stack up against those Anker buds for calls.

Tech.title: Amazon’s New Echo Lineup Goes in the Opposite Direction of Apple HomeView
Tech.content:
Apple made a big splash early this October with its massive smart home announcement, including new Siri AI features, the company’s first smart display called HomeView and the long-awaited smart speaker, the HomePod Mini 2.

Now Amazon’s here with its new Echo lineup, and we’re all comparing these smart speakers and smart displays with what Apple is offering. What’s interesting is that Amazon is taking a completely different path with its new home devices — especially the latest Echo Show, which is currently available for preorder. Here’s what that means and why it matters for potential buyers this holiday season.

Amazon’s Echo Show 16 is everything the HomeView is not

The Echo Show 16 is different from the HomeView in nearly every way. Amazon

Apple’s first smart display relies heavily on Siri AI and audio features as a selling point, with a design a bit like the Echo Show 11. During Apple’s announcement, I noted this created dissonance since the 7-inch screen is too small to easily watch the latest Apple TV shows, or much else, even if the audio is excellent. That’s one reason companies like Amazon have been making Echo Show devices bigger and bigger.

More from CNET



Now with the Echo Show 16, Amazon is embracing the idea of a second TV device for the kitchen or hallway more fully than ever. This new Show ditches the big speaker for a series of small woofers and tweeters (and a stand design perhaps pointedly reminiscent of Mac computers).

I’ll have to listen to the result in person, but it looks like Amazon is backing away from the 360-degree, room-filling sound for something that acts more like a traditional TV, while still including the touchscreen, camera and mic of past smart displays. It supports wall mounting if you’d rather not use a stand.

The Echo Show 16 backs up its new size and design with a built-in Fire TV platform, something previously limited to only larger, wall-mount-only Echo Shows. Fire TV not only makes it easier to access Amazon Prime content, but also handles third-party apps and more complex controls better.

You can spring for an upgraded display on the Echo Show 16, but it will cost even more. Amazon

Those deeply invested in catching up on shows or sports can upgrade to an enhanced Nanomatte display designed to cut glare and improve color accuracy. While Apple is a bit coy about which third-party apps will be supported alongside Apple TV, Amazon says the Echo Show will support Netflix, Disney Plus, YouTube, HBO Max/Peacock, Tubi and Pluto, which should reassure streaming fans.

The drawback to all this new tech is the price, something Apple HomeView fans will know well. While the small-screened HomeView starts at $299, Amazon’s Echo Show 16 starts at $499.99, and the Nanomatte display bumps the price up to $569.99. Plus, you’ll want a compatible stand, which starts at $69.99 but can go up to $150, so you can see how prices quickly rise.

That high price is a tough sell for anyone who already has a smart display or is leaning toward the HomeView, but people looking for a second Fire TV screen may find it more palatable. I want to test them both out before I make an ultimate recommendation.

Amazon adds an Echo camera to compete with the HomePod Mini 2

Amazon’s added a camera to its studio speaker, although I’m not sure it’s a good idea. Amazon

The Echo Show 16 wasn’t the only Amazon device aimed at Apple’s latest releases. The company also announced a new Echo Studio model, starting at $249.99 and comparable to Apple’s HomePod Mini 2 — with one big difference. This latest Studio comes with a built-in, nearly invisible home camera.

Amazon says the camera is meant to gather visual intelligence for Alexa, which rings privacy warning bells to me, but the camera could let the voice assistant answer questions about what’s happening in the room when users are away or offer live views, sort of like a mini security camera.

I’m not convinced this camera add-on is worth it, but it does help Amazon differentiate the Studio from the $149 HomePod Mini 2, which might otherwise seem similar to the casual buyer.

Amazon also announced a noncamera Echo Dot, more affordable at $99.99, upgraded with an AZ3 custom-designed silicon chip for faster Alexa responses, and a kid’s version of the same model.

And while Apple may have showed how the iPhone Duo could be used as an impromptu alarm clock, Amazon showed up with its own dedicated smart clock, the aptly named Echo Time, a round, dial-like smart display meant to serve as a nightstand clock with the addition of Alexa Plus. It includes unique smart alarm features to help manage waking up in a slower fashion. But again, Amazon is setting prices very high at $199.99 for the clock.

Alexa Plus is ready to duel with Siri AI

Alexa Plus has new tricks to go along with the new display. Amazon

I’d be remiss not to talk about Alexa Plus and how the AI voice assistant is now going head-to-head with Apple’s Siri AI. Both add new capabilities to the new smart displays. Siri AI gets home control functions and an easier way to display information pulled from emails, text messages and other iPhone sources.

Alexa Plus, meanwhile, will have a new interface on the Echo Show 16, which ditches the old transcription visual (which I kind of liked) and replaces it with an interactive display that can pull up visuals, videos, events and more as you talk with Alexa. Each conversation gets its own Card icon, so you can revisit and pick up past conversations as needed. Alexa also has a new Home Map mode which acts like a living layout of all your smart devices, letting you control what‘’’s on or off, room by room.

I already like Alexa Plus a bit more than Siri AI, even if the voice assistant gets a little too talkative, and now I’ll have new experiences to test out. Of course, cost is yet again a factor here: Apple notes that more advanced Siri AI features do require iCloud Plus subscriptions, although it’s still light on details. Alexa Plus, meanwhile, is free with an Amazon Prime subscription, but otherwise, it costs a steep $20 per month for most features.

Final thoughts

Ultimately, Apple is treading carefully with its first-ever smart display, but that tiny screen is a tough sell for me. Amazon, meanwhile, is betting big that people want a second TV experience in their display and are willing to pay for it. Both AI voice assistants are showing up with new tricks I can’t wait to try.

Meanwhile, Amazon is trying out new avenues in the smart home, like giving its flagship smart speaker a built-in camera — which I’m dubious about — and releasing targeted screens for alarms, picture frames and more. It’s all very expensive, which gives Apple a surprise advantage for the holidays, but Amazon’s vision is strikingly different, so I’m not sure they’re after the same audience.
